Diagnosis is by paired serology or early polymerase chain reaction testing
Doxycycline is most effective when started within the first week of illness
Skin testing and serology are mandatory before Q fever vaccination
explanation.pearls: Persisting fever with a new murmur months after Q fever suggests chronic infection with endocarditis, which requires prolonged doxycycline combined with hydroxychloroquine rather than a repeat short course.

options.rationale: Leptospirosis is the near alternative in this occupational group but typically follows freshwater or rodent urine exposure and causes conjunctival suffusion and renal impairment, which are absent here (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

Vaccinating a person with existing immunity or current infection can cause a severe local or systemic reaction, which is why skin and serological screening always precedes the vaccine (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

Q fever is a culture negative zoonosis of abattoir workers diagnosed on paired serology, and doxycycline is started empirically because treatment within the first week of illness shortens it substantially (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Australian Immunisation Handbook).

Marrow examination is for suspected haematological malignancy or an unexplained pancytopenia, and a mild isolated thrombocytopenia with transaminitis in an acute zoonotic illness does not require it (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Q Fever).

Delaying treatment misses the window in which antibiotics shorten the illness and risks progression to hepatitis, endocarditis or a chronic fatigue syndrome (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Compression is the single most effective treatment for a venous leg ulcer and roughly doubles the healing rate, but it is dangerous if significant arterial disease coexists, so the ankle brachial pressure index is measured before any compression is applied. An index between 0.8 and 1.3 permits full strength compression, 0.5 to 0.8 allows only reduced compression with specialist input, and below 0.5 compression is contraindicated and the patient needs vascular assessment. Diabetes and chronic kidney disease cause medial arterial calcification that makes the vessels incompressible, so an index above 1.3 is falsely reassuring and should prompt a toe brachial index or arterial duplex instead. The venous phenotype of a shallow ulcer near the medial malleolus with haemosiderin staining, lipodermatosclerosis and relief on elevation contrasts with the arterial phenotype of a punched out painful ulcer over pressure points or toes with a cool foot and night pain relieved by hanging the leg down.
key_points: Never apply compression before measuring the ankle brachial pressure index
An index of 0.8 to 1.3 permits full strength compression
Diabetes and renal disease can falsely elevate the index through calcified vessels
Mixed flora on a swab is colonisation and does not warrant antibiotics
Biopsy an ulcer that fails to heal after three months of adequate treatment
explanation.pearls: An ankle brachial pressure index above 1.3 in a long standing diabetic is a warning of incompressible calcified vessels rather than good perfusion, and the toe brachial index is the test that gives a truthful answer.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Ulcer and Wound Management

options.rationale: Compression is the correct treatment for venous ulceration but applying it over undiagnosed arterial disease can precipitate tissue necrosis and limb loss (Source: Australian Wound Management Association; Therapeutic Guidelines: Ulcer and Wound Management).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Ulcer and Wound Management

options.rationale: All chronic ulcers are colonised and mixed flora on a swab does not indicate infection, so antibiotics are reserved for spreading cellulitis or systemic features (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

The index determines whether compression is safe and at what strength, and the pulses cannot be assessed clinically through this degree of oedema (Source: Australian Wound Management Association; Therapeutic Guidelines: Ulcer and Wound Management).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Ulcer and Wound Management

options.rationale: Biopsy is indicated for an ulcer with rolled or everted edges or one that fails to heal after three months of appropriate treatment, and no adequate treatment has yet been given (Source: Australian Wound Management Association).

Urgent revascularisation is for critical limb ischaemia with rest pain, tissue loss and absent perfusion, and her foot is warm with adequate capillary refill and no rest pain (Source: Australian Wound Management Association).

explanation.summary: Metformin reduces ileal absorption of the vitamin B12 and intrinsic factor complex in a dose and duration dependent way, so deficiency is common after several years of therapy and is easily attributed to diabetic neuropathy instead. The clinical clue that the neuropathy is not simply diabetic is involvement of the posterior columns and corticospinal tracts, giving impaired vibration and joint position sense, a positive Romberg test, and the combination of absent ankle jerks with extensor plantar responses. Haematological and neurological manifestations do not track together, so a normal haemoglobin never excludes cord involvement and treatment must not wait for anaemia. Neurological disease is treated with parenteral hydroxocobalamin loading rather than oral replacement, the underlying cause is still investigated with intrinsic factor antibodies since pernicious anaemia can coexist, and recovery is best when treatment begins within the first months of symptoms.
key_points: Metformin causes dose and duration dependent malabsorption of vitamin B12
Absent ankle jerks with extensor plantars indicate combined cord and nerve involvement
Neurological disease can occur with a completely normal haemoglobin
Parenteral loading is used when there are neurological features
Check intrinsic factor antibodies because pernicious anaemia can coexist
explanation.pearls: Never give folate to a patient with an unexplained macrocytosis before the vitamin B12 result is back, since folate corrects the anaemia while allowing subacute combined degeneration of the cord to progress unchecked.

options.rationale: Stopping metformin removes the cause of ongoing malabsorption but does nothing for the existing deficit, and three months of untreated cord involvement risks permanent disability (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

High dose oral replacement is effective for uncomplicated deficiency, but neurological involvement is treated parenterally to guarantee repletion and to reverse the deficit fast (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

Diabetic peripheral neuropathy is the expected diagnosis in this man, but it does not cause impaired proprioception with extensor plantar responses, which indicate posterior column and corticospinal involvement (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

Posterior column and pyramidal signs with a low vitamin B12 indicate cord involvement requiring parenteral loading, and the cause must still be established since metformin and pernicious anaemia can coexist (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook; Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

Cord imaging may show the characteristic posterior column signal change but is not needed to justify treatment, and waiting for it delays replacement in a time-critical deficit (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

explanation.summary: The first discriminator in dysphagia is whether it affects solids alone or solids and liquids equally, because a mechanical obstruction such as a stricture, ring or tumour causes progressive solid dysphagia while a motility disorder affects both from the outset. Achalasia arises from loss of inhibitory ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus, producing failure of lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation with absent peristalsis, and it typically presents with years of symptoms, regurgitation of undigested food, nocturnal cough or soiling of the pillow, weight loss and a poor response to acid suppression. Endoscopy is performed first, primarily to exclude pseudoachalasia from a tumour at the gastro oesophageal junction, but it is normal or shows only retained food, so high resolution manometry is the test that makes the diagnosis and assigns the subtype. That subtype matters directly, since type II responds well to pneumatic dilatation or myotomy, type III spastic disease favours a tailored longer myotomy, and treatment choice cannot be made without it.
key_points: Dysphagia to solids and liquids equally from the outset suggests a motility disorder
Regurgitation of undigested food and nocturnal soiling of the pillow are characteristic
Endoscopy is done first mainly to exclude a tumour mimicking achalasia
High resolution manometry is the diagnostic standard and assigns the subtype
Subtype determines whether dilatation or myotomy is the better treatment
explanation.pearls: Suspect pseudoachalasia from an infiltrating gastro oesophageal junction tumour when symptoms have lasted under six months, weight loss is disproportionate, or the patient is over 55, since manometry cannot distinguish it from primary achalasia.

options.rationale: A second endoscopy is warranted for suspected pseudoachalasia from an infiltrating tumour, which is suggested by a junction that resists passage of the scope rather than one traversed easily (Source: GESA: Dysphagia).

Ambulatory pH testing quantifies acid exposure in refractory reflux, and dysphagia equally to solids and liquids with regurgitation of old food is a motility rather than an acid problem (Source: GESA: Dysphagia).

Cross sectional imaging is used to look for an extrinsic or infiltrating malignancy once that is suspected, and it cannot demonstrate the sphincter physiology that this presentation turns on (Source: GESA: Dysphagia).
A barium study is a useful adjunct but is less sensitive than manometry, and treating without subtype classification risks choosing the wrong intervention (Source: GESA: Dysphagia).

Dysphagia equally to solids and liquids with regurgitation of undigested food, weight loss and a normal endoscopy points to a motility disorder, and manometry is the diagnostic standard that also determines the subtype guiding treatment (Source: GESA: Dysphagia).

explanation.summary: Hereditary haemochromatosis in Australia is overwhelmingly due to homozygosity for the C282Y variant in the HFE gene, which is common in people of northern European ancestry, although penetrance is incomplete so many homozygotes never accumulate clinically important iron. Transferrin saturation is the earliest abnormality and ferritin reflects the accumulated burden, and treatment is indicated once ferritin exceeds the reference range even in the absence of symptoms, because the organ damage of cirrhosis, diabetes, arthropathy, hypogonadism and cardiomyopathy is largely irreversible once established. Induction venesection removes roughly 500 mL weekly, taking about 250 mg of iron each time, until ferritin falls to around 50 mcg/L, after which maintenance venesection a few times a year keeps it in the low normal range. A ferritin above 1000 mcg/L with abnormal liver enzymes identifies the group at real risk of cirrhosis who need fibrosis assessment and ongoing hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance.
key_points: C282Y homozygosity is the usual genotype and penetrance is incomplete
Raised transferrin saturation appears before ferritin rises
Treat once ferritin exceeds the reference range even without symptoms
Induction venesection targets a ferritin around 50 mcg/L before maintenance
Ferritin above 1000 mcg/L with abnormal liver enzymes prompts fibrosis assessment
explanation.pearls: First degree relatives of a C282Y homozygote should be offered genetic testing and iron studies, since identifying and venesecting an affected sibling before ferritin passes 1000 mcg/L essentially removes their cirrhosis risk.

options.rationale: Dietary iron restriction has a negligible effect on total body iron burden and cannot substitute for removing iron from the circulation (Source: HSANZ: Haemochromatosis).

Biopsy is reserved for a ferritin above 1000 mcg/L with raised transaminases or clinical features of liver disease, because the risk of significant fibrosis below that threshold is very low (Source: HSANZ: Haemochromatosis).
Chelation is used when venesection is not possible, such as in transfusional overload with anaemia, and it is more toxic and far more expensive than removing blood (Source: HSANZ: Haemochromatosis).
Iron accumulation is silent until organ damage is established, and treating before symptoms appear is what prevents cirrhosis, diabetes and cardiomyopathy (Source: HSANZ: Haemochromatosis).

A ferritin above the reference range with a raised transferrin saturation in a C282Y homozygote indicates iron loading, and induction venesection to a low target followed by maintenance prevents end-organ damage (Source: HSANZ: Haemochromatosis; GESA: Haemochromatosis).

explanation.summary: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura is caused by severely deficient ADAMTS13 activity, usually from an acquired autoantibody, which leaves ultra large von Willebrand factor multimers in the circulation to trap platelets and shear red cells in the microvasculature. The clinical result is microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia with fragments on the film, profound thrombocytopenia, and organ ischaemia that most often manifests as fluctuating neurological signs, with fever and renal impairment variably present. The finding that separates it from disseminated intravascular coagulation is a normal international normalised ratio, activated partial thromboplastin time and fibrinogen, since this is a platelet consumptive process rather than a coagulation factor consumptive one. Untreated mortality approaches 90 per cent and falls to around 10 per cent with plasma exchange, so exchange is arranged on clinical suspicion while the ADAMTS13 sample is still in the laboratory, and platelet transfusion is avoided unless there is life threatening bleeding.
key_points: Fragments with severe thrombocytopenia and normal coagulation define the syndrome
Normal fibrinogen and clotting times exclude disseminated intravascular coagulation
Plasma exchange is started on suspicion and not delayed for the ADAMTS13 result
Platelet transfusion can worsen microvascular thrombosis and is generally avoided
Corticosteroid and rituximab are used alongside exchange in acquired disease
explanation.pearls: Send the ADAMTS13 sample before the first plasma exchange, because exchange replaces the enzyme and a post exchange sample can produce a falsely normal activity level that obscures the diagnosis retrospectively.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura

options.rationale: Platelet transfusion in this microangiopathy fuels further platelet consumption in the microcirculation and is associated with worsening ischaemic events (Source: HSANZ: Thrombotic Microangiopathy).

Immune thrombocytopenia gives isolated thrombocytopenia with a normal haemoglobin and no fragments, and neither anaemia with fragmentation nor a raised lactate dehydrogenase belongs to it (Source: HSANZ: Thrombotic Microangiopathy).

Fragmentation haemolysis with severe thrombocytopenia, neurological change and normal coagulation identifies a thrombotic microangiopathy in which plasma exchange is life saving and must not wait for the enzyme assay (Source: HSANZ: Thrombotic Microangiopathy).
Disseminated intravascular coagulation is the near differential but it prolongs the clotting times and consumes fibrinogen, and both are normal here (Source: HSANZ: Thrombotic Microangiopathy).

Imaging is appropriate for focal deficits or suspected intracranial haemorrhage, and a fluctuating global conscious state without focal signs should not delay exchange (Source: HSANZ: Thrombotic Microangiopathy).

explanation.summary: Melioidosis is caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, an environmental organism of soil and surface water in northern Australia and South East Asia, and cases cluster sharply in the wet season when heavy rain aerosolises and mobilises the bacterium. The dominant risk factors are diabetes, hazardous alcohol use, chronic kidney and lung disease, and it presents most often as severe pneumonia with a striking tendency to upper lobe consolidation and cavitation, frequently with bacteraemia and metastatic abscesses in the prostate, liver, spleen or bone. Its critical property for the emergency clinician is intrinsic resistance to the agents used in standard severe pneumonia regimens, including ceftriaxone, penicillin and gentamicin, so an unrecognised case receives ineffective therapy during the hours when mortality is decided. Treatment is an intensive phase of at least two weeks of intravenous ceftazidime or meropenem, with meropenem preferred for neurological or critically severe disease, followed by three to six months of oral eradication therapy with trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole.
key_points: Wet season presentation in tropical northern Australia is the key epidemiological clue
Diabetes and hazardous alcohol use are the dominant host risk factors
Upper lobe cavitating pneumonia with septic shock is the typical severe presentation
The organism is intrinsically resistant to ceftriaxone, penicillin and gentamicin
Intensive intravenous therapy is followed by months of oral eradication treatment
explanation.pearls: Omitting the three to six month oral eradication phase after successful intravenous treatment leads to relapse in a substantial minority, which is why trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole is continued long after the patient feels entirely well.

options.rationale: That regimen covers typical and atypical community-acquired pneumonia but neither agent is reliably active against the tropical pathogen that this exposure history and cavitating pattern indicate (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

Third generation cephalosporin cover is the standard severe pneumonia regimen in temperate Australia but is inadequate for this organism, which is intrinsically resistant to ceftriaxone and to aminoglycosides (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

This targets resistant staphylococcal and hospital acquired organisms plus influenza, but he has no healthcare exposure and piperacillin tazobactam is not the recommended agent for this pathogen (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

A carbapenem does cover this organism, but meropenem is reserved for neurological or very severe disease and rifampicin has no established role in the intensive phase (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

Wet season presentation in the tropical north with diabetes, alcohol use, soil and water exposure and cavitating upper lobe pneumonia indicates melioidosis, for which ceftazidime is the recommended intensive phase agent (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Royal Darwin Hospital Melioidosis Guideline).

explanation.summary: Amiodarone is highly lipophilic with a half life of many weeks and accumulates in lung, liver, thyroid, skin, cornea and nerve, producing a distinctive spread of adverse effects that includes both hyperthyroidism and hypothyroidism, hepatotoxicity, photosensitivity with slate grey pigmentation, corneal microdeposits and peripheral neuropathy. Pulmonary toxicity is the most feared, affecting a few per cent of patients on long term therapy, and it usually appears as subacute interstitial pneumonitis with progressive breathlessness, dry cough, weight loss and sometimes low grade fever over weeks to months. The diagnosis is one of exclusion supported by a new interstitial pattern on imaging, a fall in transfer factor from baseline, and the absence of heart failure or infection, which is why a normal natriuretic peptide with preserved systolic function is such a useful discriminator in a patient who also has cardiac disease. Management is prompt cessation of the drug in consultation with cardiology, corticosteroid for moderate or severe disease, and awareness that improvement is slow because the drug persists in tissue for months after the last dose.
key_points: Amiodarone accumulates in lung, liver, thyroid, cornea, skin and nerve
Pulmonary toxicity presents subacutely over weeks to months, not acutely
A normal natriuretic peptide with preserved systolic function argues against heart failure
A fall in transfer factor from baseline is the most useful physiological marker
Recovery is slow because the drug has a tissue half life of many weeks
explanation.pearls: Obtain baseline lung function including transfer factor before starting long term amiodarone, since a fall from that baseline is the earliest objective sign of pulmonary toxicity and is far more useful than a single later measurement.

options.rationale: Decompensated heart failure is the expected explanation in this patient, but preserved systolic function, a normal natriuretic peptide and no congestive signs argue firmly against it (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

Infection is plausible given the intermittent fevers, but four months of progressive dyspnoea with a reduced transfer factor and new reticular change is not an infective time course (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory).

Thyroid and hepatic monitoring is part of routine surveillance on this drug and his thyroid function is already normal, so continuing the drug allows the pulmonary process to progress (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

Invasive haemodynamic testing is for suspected pulmonary vascular disease, and diffuse reticular change with a reduced transfer factor points to the lung parenchyma instead (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory).

Progressive dyspnoea with a new reticular pattern and a reduced transfer factor on long term amiodarone indicates pulmonary toxicity, and stopping the drug alongside definitive imaging is the step that changes the outcome (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook; Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory).

explanation.summary: Diabetic gastroparesis is a manifestation of autonomic neuropathy and typically appears after many years of diabetes in people who already have retinopathy, nephropathy and peripheral neuropathy, so its presence in isolation should raise doubt about the diagnosis. The characteristic story is early satiety, postprandial fullness, nausea and vomiting of recognisable food eaten many hours earlier, and a particularly useful clue is glycaemic instability with hypoglycaemia soon after a meal because the insulin acts before the food is absorbed. Diagnosis requires three elements in order, namely compatible symptoms, exclusion of mechanical obstruction by endoscopy, and objective demonstration of delayed emptying by scintigraphy over four hours, and skipping the endoscopy risks missing a pyloric or antral malignancy or stricture. Treatment combines glycaemic optimisation, small low fat low fibre meals, and a prokinetic, with metoclopramide limited by tardive dyskinesia risk and domperidone requiring attention to the QT interval.
key_points: Gastroparesis usually accompanies other established microvascular complications
Postprandial hypoglycaemia followed by later hyperglycaemia is a characteristic pattern
Endoscopy to exclude mechanical obstruction precedes any emptying study
Scintigraphic emptying is measured over four hours rather than two
Review opioids, anticholinergics and glucagon like peptide 1 agonists as contributors
explanation.pearls: Australian and international advice restricts continuous metoclopramide to about five days because of tardive dyskinesia risk, so longer term prokinetic treatment usually means domperidone with an electrocardiogram to check the QT interval first.

options.rationale: A prokinetic is a mainstay of treatment but starting it before mechanical obstruction is excluded risks treating a stricture or tumour as a motility problem (Source: GESA: Gastroparesis).
Post pyloric feeding is reserved for refractory disease with recurrent admissions or an inability to maintain nutrition, and she has not yet had any specific treatment (Source: GESA: Gastroparesis).

The erratic profile reflects a mismatch between insulin action and unpredictable gastric emptying, so raising basal insulin without addressing the emptying will worsen the early hypoglycaemia (Source: GESA: Gastroparesis).
Cross sectional imaging can identify an extrinsic cause but is less sensitive than endoscopy for mucosal and pyloric lesions and does not allow biopsy (Source: GESA: Gastroparesis).

Retained food and a succussion splash require exclusion of mechanical obstruction by endoscopy before delayed emptying can be confirmed scintigraphically and treated as a motility disorder (Source: GESA: Gastroparesis).

explanation.summary: Inflammatory back pain is defined by onset before 45, duration beyond three months, insidious onset, morning stiffness over 30 minutes, improvement with exercise but not with rest, night pain waking the patient, and a good response to anti inflammatory drugs. Recognising the pattern is what separates this from the far commoner mechanical back pain, and the extra articular clues here, a painful red eye suggesting anterior uveitis and a family history of inflammatory bowel disease, add substantially to the probability. Plain radiographs are normal for years in the non radiographic form of axial spondyloarthritis, which affects women as often as men and carries the same symptom burden. Magnetic resonance imaging of the sacroiliac joints is therefore the investigation of choice, and it matters because effective treatment exists and delay costs spinal mobility that does not return.
key_points: Night pain that improves with movement is the defining symptom pattern
Anterior uveitis, psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease are associated features
Plain radiographs remain normal for years in early disease
Magnetic resonance imaging shows sacroiliac bone marrow oedema early
Human leucocyte antigen B27 supports but does not establish the diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about a previous painful red eye, because anterior uveitis occurs in a substantial minority of people with axial spondyloarthritis and is often the only extra articular clue in an otherwise ordinary back pain history.

options.rationale: The antigen is carried by around 8 per cent of the Australian population and by many people who never develop disease, so it shifts probability but cannot establish or exclude the diagnosis alone (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association).

Radiographic sacroiliitis takes years to appear and waiting for it is precisely what produced the historical diagnostic delay of nearly a decade in this disease (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association).

Magnetic resonance imaging detects bone marrow oedema in the sacroiliac joints years before radiographic change and is what allows the non radiographic form of axial disease to be diagnosed and treated (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association).

Computed tomography shows established bony change well but is insensitive to active inflammation and delivers substantial gonadal radiation to a young man (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association).

Exercise therapy is a mainstay of treatment and will be needed, but starting it without a diagnosis withholds the biologic therapy that changes the disease course in those who fail anti inflammatory treatment (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association).

explanation.summary: Ferritin is an acute phase reactant, so it rises with inflammation, alcohol, malignancy and metabolic liver disease far more often than it rises from iron overload, and the transferrin saturation is what separates these. A saturation above about 45 per cent with a high ferritin points to genuine loading and triggers HFE genotyping, with C282Y homozygosity accounting for the great majority of cases in people of northern European ancestry. The arthropathy of the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints is a characteristic early clue that is frequently dismissed as osteoarthritis. A ferritin above 1000 mcg/L predicts advanced fibrosis and cirrhosis, which changes surveillance because established cirrhosis carries an ongoing risk of hepatocellular carcinoma even after iron is removed. First degree relatives are offered testing once the genotype is known, since treatment before organ damage develops gives a normal life expectancy.
key_points: Transferrin saturation separates iron overload from a reactive ferritin rise
HFE genotyping is the diagnostic test in the right ancestry group
Ferritin above 1000 mcg/L predicts significant hepatic fibrosis
Second and third metacarpophalangeal arthropathy is a characteristic clue
Offer testing to first degree relatives once the genotype is confirmed
explanation.pearls: Cirrhosis established before venesection begins does not regress, and the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma persists after iron depletion, so those patients need six monthly ultrasound surveillance for life.

options.rationale: Fatty liver and inflammation raise ferritin as an acute phase protein but leave the transferrin saturation normal or low, and a saturation of 68 per cent indicates genuine iron loading (Source: HSANZ Iron Overload).

Venesection is likely to be the treatment, but establishing the genetic diagnosis first determines family testing and the assessment of liver fibrosis that must accompany it (Source: HSANZ Iron Overload).

Biopsy has been displaced by genetic testing and magnetic resonance quantification for diagnosis, and it is now reserved for staging fibrosis when non-invasive assessment is inconclusive (Source: GESA Haemochromatosis).
Reducing alcohol is worthwhile, but four standard drinks a week does not explain a transferrin saturation of 68 per cent and the delay wastes three months (Source: GESA Haemochromatosis).

A raised transferrin saturation with a high ferritin in this ancestry group is the indication for HFE genotyping, and a ferritin above 1000 mcg/L is the threshold at which significant fibrosis becomes likely and must be assessed (Source: GESA Haemochromatosis; HSANZ Iron Overload).

explanation.summary: Intracranial aneurysms occur in a minority of people with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, and they cluster strongly in families, which is why screening is targeted rather than universal. The accepted indications are a family history of subarachnoid haemorrhage or intracranial aneurysm, a previous aneurysm, a high risk occupation such as a pilot, or planned major surgery or anticoagulation. Non contrast magnetic resonance angiography is preferred because it avoids radiation and iodinated contrast in a population with reduced kidney function. A negative scan is repeated at intervals of several years in those who remain at high risk, and a positive result goes to a neurosurgical or neurointerventional service, where the decision to treat weighs aneurysm size, site and morphology against the risk of the procedure. Blood pressure control and smoking cessation reduce rupture risk regardless of the imaging result.
key_points: Aneurysms cluster in families with polycystic kidney disease
Family history of haemorrhage or aneurysm is the main screening indication
Magnetic resonance angiography avoids contrast and radiation
Universal screening of all patients is not recommended
Blood pressure control and not smoking reduce rupture risk
explanation.pearls: Rescreening after a negative magnetic resonance angiogram is generally offered at intervals of about five years while the person remains high risk, rather than annually, because de novo aneurysm formation is slow.

options.rationale: Aneurysms are asymptomatic until they bleed, so the absence of symptoms is exactly the situation in which targeted screening is worthwhile (Source: KHA-CARI Polycystic Kidney Disease).

A family history of subarachnoid haemorrhage or intracranial aneurysm raises the prevalence several fold and is the accepted indication for screening in this disease, with non contrast magnetic resonance angiography as the modality of choice (Source: KHA-CARI Polycystic Kidney Disease).

Computed tomography angiography needs iodinated contrast and repeated radiation, and annual imaging is far more frequent than the intervals used after a negative screen (Source: KHA-CARI Polycystic Kidney Disease).

Universal screening has not been shown to be worthwhile because the prevalence without a family history is too low to justify the anxiety and the risks of treating incidental small aneurysms (Source: KHA-CARI Polycystic Kidney Disease).
Blood pressure control reduces rupture risk and is essential, but it does not eliminate the risk conferred by the familial clustering of aneurysms (Source: KHA-CARI Polycystic Kidney Disease).

explanation.summary: Growth hormone excess develops so gradually that patients and their families rarely notice, and the average delay from onset to diagnosis is measured in years, with the diagnosis often prompted by a dentist noticing widening interdental spaces or by old photographs. The systemic burden is what makes early diagnosis worthwhile: hypertension, impaired glucose tolerance, obstructive sleep apnoea, cardiomyopathy, arthropathy, carpal tunnel syndrome and an increased incidence of colonic polyps. The biochemical sequence runs from insulin like growth factor 1 as the screening test, to failure of growth hormone suppression during an oral glucose tolerance test as confirmation, and only then to pituitary imaging, since incidental pituitary lesions are common. Transsphenoidal surgery is the first line treatment, with somatostatin analogues, a growth hormone receptor antagonist and radiotherapy for residual disease, and successful treatment reverses much of the metabolic burden.
key_points: Insulin like growth factor 1 is the screening test and needs age matched ranges
Random growth hormone levels are uninterpretable because secretion is pulsatile
Failure of suppression during an oral glucose tolerance test confirms the diagnosis
Image the pituitary only after biochemical confirmation
Screen for sleep apnoea, cardiomyopathy, glucose intolerance and colonic polyps
explanation.pearls: Ask the patient to bring photographs from 10 and 20 years ago, because the slow change in facial soft tissue is invisible to the family who see it daily and is often the single most persuasive piece of evidence at the first consultation.

options.rationale: This is the screening test because it reflects integrated growth hormone secretion over days rather than a moment, and it must be interpreted against age matched ranges since the normal level falls with age (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia; Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).
Growth hormone is secreted in pulses with undetectable troughs in healthy people, so a single random value can be normal in disease and high in health (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia).

Imaging follows biochemical confirmation, because incidental pituitary lesions are found in around one in ten adults and would otherwise generate a false diagnosis (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia).

Failure of growth hormone to suppress after glucose is the confirmatory test, used when the screening result is raised or equivocal rather than as the opening investigation (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia).

Sleep apnoea affects most patients with growth hormone excess and will need treating, but investigating it first leaves the underlying cause of the whole picture undiagnosed (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia).

explanation.summary: Bleeding from oesophageal varices still carries a mortality of the order of 15 to 20 per cent at six weeks, and the interventions that alter that figure are given before the endoscope arrives. A vasoactive agent such as terlipressin or octreotide lowers portal inflow and is started as soon as variceal bleeding is suspected. Antibiotic prophylaxis is the intervention most often forgotten, yet it reduces infection, rebleeding and death independently, because bacterial translocation both provokes and follows the bleed. Transfusion is deliberately restrictive, aiming at around 70 g/L, because filling the circulation raises portal pressure and precipitates rebleeding. Endoscopic band ligation within 12 hours is the definitive treatment, with a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt for failure or for high risk patients, and secondary prophylaxis afterwards combines a non selective beta blocker with a banding program.
key_points: Start a vasoactive drug as soon as variceal bleeding is suspected
Antibiotic prophylaxis reduces rebleeding and mortality independently
Transfuse restrictively to about 70 g/L rather than normalising the haemoglobin
The international normalised ratio in cirrhosis does not measure bleeding risk
Band ligation within 12 hours is the definitive endoscopic treatment
explanation.pearls: Antibiotic prophylaxis, usually intravenous ceftriaxone, is given to every cirrhotic patient with upper gastrointestinal bleeding whatever the source, and it is the omitted step most closely tied to avoidable death in this presentation.

options.rationale: Liberal transfusion raises portal pressure and worsens rebleeding and mortality in this population, and a restrictive target of about 70 g/L gives better outcomes (Source: GESA Portal Hypertension).

The prolonged ratio in cirrhosis reflects reduced synthesis of both procoagulant and anticoagulant factors rather than a bleeding tendency, and plasma expands volume and raises portal pressure (Source: GESA Portal Hypertension).

Tamponade is a rescue measure for uncontrollable bleeding, usually in an intubated patient, when endoscopy has failed or is unavailable, and endoscopy is available within the hour (Source: GESA Portal Hypertension).

A vasoactive drug reduces portal inflow and improves haemostasis, while antibiotic prophylaxis independently reduces bacterial infection, rebleeding and mortality in cirrhotic patients bleeding from any upper gastrointestinal source (Source: GESA Portal Hypertension; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

Acid suppression is reasonable while the source is unknown and is continued if an ulcer is found, but it does nothing for portal pressure and is not the treatment for variceal bleeding (Source: GESA Portal Hypertension).

explanation.summary: The first branch point in haematuria is glomerular versus non glomerular, and it is settled by urine microscopy rather than by imaging: dysmorphic red cells, red cell casts and proteinuria indicate the glomerulus. Visible haematuria arising within a day or two of a mucosal infection is the hallmark of immunoglobulin A nephropathy, and it is distinguished from post streptococcal glomerulonephritis by the latency, which is one to three weeks there, and by the normal complement here. Prognosis is determined by proteinuria, blood pressure and renal function at presentation rather than by the number of visible bleeding episodes, and biopsy provides the histological scoring that predicts progression. Long term management centres on blood pressure control, blockade of the renin angiotensin system and reduction of proteinuria, with immunosuppression reserved for defined higher risk groups.
key_points: Dysmorphic red cells and casts localise bleeding to the glomerulus
Haematuria within a day or two of a sore throat suggests immunoglobulin A nephropathy
Post streptococcal disease has a one to three week latency and a low C3
Proteinuria, blood pressure and creatinine at presentation drive prognosis
Urological imaging is for non glomerular bleeding
explanation.pearls: Proteinuria sustained above 1 g per day despite maximal blockade of the renin angiotensin system is the threshold at which immunosuppression is considered in immunoglobulin A nephropathy, which is why quantifying protein at diagnosis matters more than counting bleeding episodes.

options.rationale: Antibiotic treatment of the pharyngitis does not alter the glomerular process, and the near simultaneous onset with the sore throat is itself the clue that this is not a post infectious illness (Source: KHA-CARI Glomerulonephritis).

Dysmorphic red cells with casts identify a glomerular source, and the combination of proteinuria above 50 mg/mmol with hypertension is the accepted trigger for biopsy to establish the diagnosis and guide immunosuppression (Source: KHA-CARI Glomerulonephritis).

Urological imaging pursues a non glomerular source and is indicated for painless visible haematuria in an older patient with isotropic red cells, not when casts and proteinuria point to the glomerulus (Source: KHA-CARI Glomerulonephritis).

Post streptococcal disease follows the infection by one to three weeks and is accompanied by a low C3 and a rising antistreptolysin O titre, and neither pattern is present here (Source: KHA-CARI Glomerulonephritis).

Blockade of the renin angiotensin system will be part of his long term treatment, but starting it as the whole plan leaves the underlying glomerular disease undiagnosed and unstaged (Source: KHA-CARI Glomerulonephritis).

explanation.summary: Management of acute diverticulitis has shifted substantially, and the modern first question is whether the episode is uncomplicated on imaging and whether the patient has any feature that puts them outside the trial populations. Immunosuppression, significant comorbidity, systemic sepsis, inability to tolerate oral intake and lack of access to review all push towards antibiotics and admission. In everyone else, analgesia with clear instructions on what should prompt return performs as well as antibiotics without the harms of unnecessary treatment. Colonoscopy is arranged six to eight weeks after resolution when the segment has not been examined recently, because a small proportion of apparent diverticulitis is a perforated carcinoma. Elective resection is a shared decision rather than a fixed rule after a given number of attacks.
key_points: Antibiotics are not required for uncomplicated diverticulitis in a well immunocompetent patient
Immunosuppression or systemic features move the patient into antibiotic treatment
Explicit return advice replaces the antibiotic prescription as the safety net
Interval colonoscopy at six to eight weeks excludes an underlying malignancy
Elective resection is individualised, not triggered by episode count
explanation.pearls: Arrange interval colonoscopy six to eight weeks after an episode of acute diverticulitis unless the colon has been examined within the past year, because a small but real proportion of these presentations turn out to be a perforated colonic carcinoma.

options.rationale: Randomised evidence shows no benefit from antibiotics in immunocompetent patients with computed tomography confirmed uncomplicated disease and no systemic sepsis, so supportive care with defined review is the recommended course (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; GESA Diverticular Disease).

Oral antibiotics are reserved for patients with systemic features, immunosuppression or significant comorbidity, and routine use has not been shown to speed recovery or prevent complications (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

Intravenous therapy and admission are for complicated disease with abscess or perforation, or for patients who cannot maintain oral intake, and she is well and eating (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

Endoscopy during acute inflammation carries a higher perforation risk, and the interval examination to exclude an underlying tumour is scheduled six to eight weeks after resolution (Source: GESA Diverticular Disease).

Elective resection is an individualised decision based on symptom burden, complications and fitness rather than an automatic consequence of a set number of episodes (Source: GESA Diverticular Disease).

explanation.summary: Antiviral therapy for shingles is most effective when started within 72 hours of rash onset, and the indication is strongest in people over 50, those with moderate to severe pain or rash, those with facial or ocular involvement, and the immunocompromised. Beyond 72 hours it is still given where new vesicles are appearing or there is ophthalmic or disseminated disease, since active viral replication continues. Pain control matters in its own right, because poorly controlled acute pain predicts postherpetic neuralgia, which is treated with amitriptyline, gabapentinoids or lidocaine patches. Any involvement of the tip or side of the nose warns of nasociliary branch involvement and requires same day ophthalmology review. Recombinant zoster vaccine is offered after the episode has resolved, and it is funded in Australia for older adults and for defined immunocompromised groups.
key_points: Start antivirals within 72 hours of rash onset wherever possible
Age over 50 is itself an indication for antiviral treatment
Effective early analgesia reduces the risk of postherpetic neuralgia
Lesions on the tip or side of the nose demand urgent eye review
Offer recombinant zoster vaccine after the episode resolves
explanation.pearls: Vesicles on the tip or side of the nose, the Hutchinson sign, indicate nasociliary nerve involvement and predict ocular disease, so that finding converts a routine antiviral prescription into a same day ophthalmology referral.

options.rationale: Topical antiviral does not achieve therapeutic tissue levels in the affected ganglion and dermatome and has no role in the treatment of shingles (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

Antibacterial cover is added only if there is genuine secondary infection with spreading erythema and purulence, and the vesicles here are typical uninfected zoster lesions (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
Corticosteroid alone provides modest acute pain relief without reducing postherpetic neuralgia, and it worsens glycaemic control in a man with diabetes (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

Antiviral therapy started within 72 hours of rash onset shortens the acute illness and reduces the duration of pain, and adequate early analgesia is itself associated with less postherpetic neuralgia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; AMH).
Antiviral therapy is recommended for all patients over 50 regardless of immune status, because age is the dominant risk factor for postherpetic neuralgia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Irritable bowel syndrome is diagnosed positively on symptom criteria rather than by exhaustive exclusion, and open ended investigation reinforces illness anxiety while rarely changing the outcome. The limited workup in a young patient with no alarm features is a full blood count, inflammatory markers, coeliac serology and, where diarrhoea predominates, faecal calprotectin to separate inflammatory bowel disease. Coeliac serology must be taken while gluten is still in the diet, which is why the growing habit of self imposed elimination diets before presenting matters clinically. Explaining the gut brain mechanism and giving the diagnosis a name is itself therapeutic, and treatment then follows the predominant symptom with dietary modification, antispasmodics, laxatives or low dose neuromodulators.
key_points: Diagnose positively on symptom criteria in the absence of alarm features
Take coeliac serology while the patient is still eating gluten
Faecal calprotectin helps where diarrhoea predominates
Alarm features are bleeding, weight loss, anaemia, nocturnal symptoms and onset after 50
Naming the diagnosis and explaining the mechanism is part of the treatment
explanation.pearls: A patient who has already removed gluten before serology needs at least six weeks of a normal gluten containing diet before the test is valid, so ask about elimination diets before ordering it rather than after a negative result.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia Bowel Cancer Screening

options.rationale: Endoscopy is driven by alarm features such as bleeding, weight loss, anaemia, nocturnal symptoms, onset after 50 or a relevant family history, and none are present (Source: GESA Irritable Bowel Syndrome).

Antibiotic treatment for suspected overgrowth is not first line in Australian practice, is not funded for this indication, and the diagnosis is poorly defined by available breath testing (Source: GESA Irritable Bowel Syndrome).
Acid suppression targets reflux and dyspepsia and has no effect on pain that is relieved by defecation and linked to a change in stool form (Source: GESA Irritable Bowel Syndrome).

Faecal occult blood testing is a population screening tool for asymptomatic people aged 45 and over and is not a diagnostic test in a symptomatic 27-year-old (Source: Cancer Council Australia Bowel Cancer Screening).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia Bowel Cancer Screening

options.rationale: Symptom based criteria with no alarm features allow a positive diagnosis after limited testing, and coeliac serology is the one test that must be done while she is still eating gluten because coeliac disease mimics this picture (Source: GESA Irritable Bowel Syndrome; GESA Coeliac Disease).

explanation.summary: Constipation affects the great majority of patients taking regular opioids and, unlike nausea and sedation, tolerance to it does not develop, so it must be treated for as long as the opioid continues. Every opioid prescription should be accompanied by a regular laxative from the outset, and the omission here is the reason for the presentation. The combination of a stimulant with an osmotic agent addresses both the reduced peristalsis and the increased water absorption. Reversible contributors deserve a moment's thought at each review, particularly hypercalcaemia in malignancy, hypokalaemia, hypothyroidism, dehydration and other anticholinergic drugs. Rectal examination distinguishes the loaded rectum needing a suppository or enema from the empty rectum of higher loading or obstruction, which changes the treatment entirely.
key_points: Tolerance does not develop to opioid induced constipation
Prescribe a regular laxative whenever a regular opioid is started
Combine a stimulant with an osmotic agent and titrate to effect
Exclude hypercalcaemia and other reversible contributors
Peripheral opioid antagonists follow failure of optimised laxatives
explanation.pearls: Check the corrected calcium in any patient with bone metastases and new constipation, because hypercalcaemia presents exactly this way and treating it changes the bowels, the appetite and the confusion together.

options.rationale: Bulking agents need substantial fluid intake and normal propulsion, and in an inactive patient on opioids they add mass to a slow colon and worsen distension (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care).

Docusate as a single agent has repeatedly failed to outperform placebo in palliative populations and does not address the reduced propulsion that opioids cause (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care).

Opioids reduce propulsion and increase water absorption, so a stimulant to restore peristalsis combined with an osmotic agent to soften is the standard regimen and it is prescribed regularly rather than as required (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care).

A peripherally acting opioid antagonist is the option once optimised conventional laxatives have failed, and it must not be given if bowel obstruction is suspected (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care).

Trading pain control for bowel function is unnecessary when the constipation is treatable, and undertreated bone pain has its own effect on function and mood (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care).

explanation.summary: Acute gout has three effective treatments and the choice is made almost entirely by comorbidity. Non-steroidal anti inflammatory drugs are excluded by renal impairment, heart failure, anticoagulation and peptic ulcer disease, colchicine requires dose reduction in renal impairment and interacts with clarithromycin, verapamil and ciclosporin, and corticosteroids are the fallback that suits most patients with multiple comorbidities. A serum urate within the reference range during an attack does not exclude gout, because levels fall acutely, so the diagnosis rests on the clinical picture with joint aspiration where doubt remains. Urate lowering therapy is a separate conversation, started at a low dose with anti inflammatory cover for the first months and titrated to a target below 0.36 mmol/L, or below 0.30 mmol/L where tophi are present.
key_points: Comorbidity rather than efficacy dictates the choice of anti inflammatory
Serum urate can be normal during an acute attack
Colchicine needs dose reduction in renal impairment
Corticosteroid is the practical choice with renal disease, heart failure and warfarin
Start urate lowering therapy low, with prophylaxis, and titrate to target
explanation.pearls: Aim for a serum urate below 0.36 mmol/L, and below 0.30 mmol/L when tophi are present, because tophi only dissolve when the level is held under saturation for months.

options.rationale: A non-steroidal anti inflammatory drug is contraindicated by the combination of an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 35, heart failure with a loop diuretic, and warfarin (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology; AMH).

A short course of oral corticosteroid is as effective as a non-steroidal anti inflammatory drug for an acute attack and is the option that respects renal impairment, heart failure and anticoagulation together (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology).
Colchicine can be used in reduced dose, but this regimen exceeds the recommended maximum for the first day and is not adjusted for his renal impairment, which is how toxicity occurs (Source: AMH).

Urate lowering therapy is started at a low dose with prophylactic cover and titrated slowly, and 300 mg is an inappropriate starting dose at this level of renal function (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology).

Cellulitis and septic arthritis are the key mimics, but they present with fever, a portal of entry or ascending erythema, and none of those features is present alongside a tophus on the ear (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Bullous pemphigoid is the commonest autoimmune blistering disease of older adults, produced by antibodies against hemidesmosomal antigens at the dermoepidermal junction, which gives a subepidermal split and therefore tense blisters with a negative Nikolsky sign. Pemphigus vulgaris, by contrast, splits within the epidermis, so the blisters are flaccid, rupture early, spread with lateral pressure and almost always involve mucosa. The urticarial prodrome of pemphigoid can precede blisters by weeks and is frequently mistaken for eczema or urticaria. Two specimens are needed, and the site of the immunofluorescence specimen is the detail that most often decides whether the diagnosis is made. Treatment is with potent topical corticosteroid for localised disease, which performs at least as well as oral corticosteroid with fewer adverse effects, and systemic therapy with steroid sparing agents for extensive disease.
key_points: Tense blisters with a negative Nikolsky sign indicate a subepidermal split
Mucosal involvement points towards pemphigus rather than pemphigoid
Take immunofluorescence from perilesional normal appearing skin
Blood eosinophilia is common in bullous pemphigoid
Potent topical corticosteroid is effective and often preferred for localised disease
explanation.pearls: Direct immunofluorescence taken from within a blister is falsely negative in a large proportion of cases, so the specimen must come from normal looking skin within about 1 cm of a lesion.

options.rationale: Histology needs the edge of an intact lesion to show the split and its inflammatory pattern, while direct immunofluorescence must be taken from normal appearing skin beside the blister because immune deposits are destroyed within the blister itself (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists; Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

Bullous impetigo produces flaccid superficial blisters with honey coloured crust in a localised area, and it does not present as widespread tense bullae on urticarial plaques (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

Sampling within the blister is the classic technical error, because inflammation degrades the immunoglobulin and complement deposits and the result comes back falsely negative (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists).

Corticosteroid before sampling alters both the histology and the immunofluorescence, and the diagnosis determines a treatment course likely to run for a year or more (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

Patch testing investigates delayed contact hypersensitivity, which produces vesicles confined to the site of contact rather than widespread tense bullae with blood eosinophilia (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists).

explanation.summary: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms is separated from ordinary drug exanthems by three features: a long latency of two to eight weeks after the drug is started, systemic involvement with fever, lymphadenopathy and facial oedema, and laboratory findings of eosinophilia, atypical lymphocytes and organ dysfunction. Allopurinol, aromatic anticonvulsants, sulfonamides and vancomycin are the usual culprits, and the risk with allopurinol is strongly associated with a particular human leucocyte antigen allele that is more prevalent in some ancestries. The liver is the organ most often involved, but myocarditis, nephritis and pneumonitis all occur, and thyroiditis can appear months after apparent recovery, so follow up thyroid function is part of the plan. The reaction can flare weeks after the drug is stopped, and reintroduction of the culprit is dangerous, so documenting the drug allergy properly is as important as the acute treatment.
key_points: Latency of two to eight weeks distinguishes this from a simple drug exanthem
Fever, facial oedema and lymphadenopathy accompany the rash
Eosinophilia with atypical lymphocytes and transaminitis is the laboratory signature
Stopping the culprit drug is the most important intervention
Check thyroid function months later because thyroiditis can appear late
explanation.pearls: Repeat thyroid function testing about three months after recovery, because autoimmune thyroiditis develops in a recognised minority of survivors long after the rash and liver enzymes have returned to normal.

sources.label: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy

options.rationale: Continuing the culprit drug in a reaction with fever, eosinophilia and hepatitis allows organ injury to progress, and antihistamines do nothing for this mechanism (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy).
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy

options.rationale: Burns unit transfer is for toxic epidermal necrolysis, which is defined by mucosal involvement, a positive Nikolsky sign and sheets of detaching epidermis, none of which are present (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists).

Empirical antibiotics add another potential sensitiser during an active severe reaction, and the eosinophilia with atypical lymphocytes and transaminitis is not a bacterial pattern (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy).
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy

options.rationale: Withdrawal of the culprit drug is the single most important step, and admission with systemic corticosteroid and serial monitoring of liver, renal, cardiac and thyroid function is the accepted management of this reaction (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy; Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy

options.rationale: Immunoglobulin has been studied in severe epidermal necrolysis and has no established first line role in this eosinophilic drug reaction (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

explanation.summary: Hypocalcaemia after parathyroidectomy has two mechanisms that need different treatment, and the phosphate tells them apart. When parathyroid tissue is lost, phosphate rises because renal phosphate excretion falls. When a chronically stimulated skeleton suddenly loses its parathyroid drive, the bone takes up calcium and phosphate together and both fall while alkaline phosphatase stays high. Patients with a preoperative alkaline phosphatase above about 400 U/L and long standing renal bone disease are at highest risk and often need calcium infusions plus calcitriol for weeks. Undertreating risks laryngospasm, seizures and QT prolongation with arrhythmia.
key_points: Check phosphate before deciding why calcium has fallen after parathyroidectomy
Low phosphate with high alkaline phosphatase points to skeletal remineralisation
High phosphate with low calcium points to loss of parathyroid hormone
Calcitriol rather than colecalciferol is required when renal hydroxylation is lost
Correct magnesium before labelling hypocalcaemia refractory
explanation.pearls: A preoperative alkaline phosphatase above 400 U/L predicts hungry bone syndrome, and these patients can need more than 10 mmol per hour of elemental calcium with calcitriol 2 to 4 micrograms daily for several weeks after surgery.

options.rationale: Colecalciferol needs renal 1 alpha hydroxylation to become active, and this man is anephric on dialysis, so it cannot raise calcium quickly enough for symptomatic hypocalcaemia (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).
Cinacalcet lowers parathyroid hormone and calcium further, which is the opposite of what is needed after the glands have been removed (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

Hypomagnesaemia does cause refractory hypocalcaemia by impairing parathyroid hormone release and action, but the magnesium here is 0.86 mmol/L, so magnesium is not the limiting factor (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

A low phosphate with a markedly raised alkaline phosphatase after parathyroidectomy indicates avid skeletal uptake of calcium and phosphate, which needs an intravenous calcium infusion plus large doses of active vitamin D as calcitriol and oral calcium (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology; KHA-CARI Guidelines).

Postoperative hypoparathyroidism raises phosphate because there is no parathyroid hormone to drive phosphaturia, whereas this man has a low phosphate, and withholding calcium from a symptomatic patient is unsafe in either case (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

explanation.summary: Ross River virus is the most commonly notified mosquito borne infection in Australia and typically causes a symmetrical polyarthritis of wrists, ankles and small hand joints with a transient maculopapular rash and marked fatigue. It is easily mistaken for early seropositive inflammatory arthritis because morning stiffness and raised inflammatory markers are shared features, so the negative rheumatoid factor and negative anti cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody carry weight. Serological interpretation is the crux: an isolated IgM is unreliable because it can persist for a year or arise non specifically, whereas IgM with IgG in a patient several weeks into the illness confirms recent infection. Most patients improve substantially within three to six months, and a minority have arthralgia and fatigue for longer, which is managed with graded activity rather than immunosuppression.
key_points: Symmetrical polyarthritis plus a transient rash and profound fatigue suggests alphaviral infection
An isolated positive IgM alone does not confirm recent Ross River virus infection
Negative rheumatoid factor and anti cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody argue against early rheumatoid arthritis
Treatment is analgesia and graded activity, not a disease modifying drug
Ross River virus infection is notifiable to the state health department
explanation.pearls: In Ross River virus infection the joint symptoms usually settle by three to six months, and the single most useful serological rule is that an isolated IgM without IgG needs a repeat sample two weeks later to demonstrate IgG seroconversion before the diagnosis is accepted.

sources.label: CDNA Ross River Virus Infection SoNG

options.rationale: Hydroxychloroquine treats inflammatory arthritis expected to persist and does nothing for a self-limiting alphaviral arthropathy, and committing to it here mislabels her as having a chronic rheumatic disease (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association).

Positive IgM together with positive IgG on a single sample in a patient three weeks into a compatible illness confirms recent Ross River virus infection, for which treatment is symptomatic with non-steroidal anti inflammatory drugs or paracetamol and a graded return to activity (Source: CDNA Ross River Virus Infection SoNG; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
source_refs: CDNA Ross River Virus Infection SoNG

options.rationale: Methotrexate is for persistent inflammatory arthritis, and starting it in the first weeks of a viral polyarthritis exposes her to marrow and liver toxicity for a condition that resolves without it (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association).

Doxycycline would treat rickettsial or Lyme like illness, neither of which produces a symmetrical small joint polyarthritis with a resolving truncal rash and positive alphavirus serology (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

Paired serology is needed only when IgM is positive but IgG is negative, because a rising IgG is then required to separate true infection from a false positive IgM, and here both are already positive (Source: CDNA Ross River Virus Infection SoNG).
source_refs: CDNA Ross River Virus Infection SoNG

explanation.summary: Chronic digoxin toxicity in older people is usually precipitated by a fall in renal clearance, most often after a diuretic, an angiotensin blocking drug or an intercurrent illness. The classic picture is gastrointestinal upset, confusion and disturbed colour vision with bradyarrhythmias, and the serum concentration correlates poorly with severity so clinical features and potassium drive treatment. Hyperkalaemia arises because the sodium potassium adenosine triphosphatase pump is poisoned, so potassium leaks out of cells, and it is a marker of the poisoning rather than a separate problem to be shifted. Digoxin specific antibody fragments correct the rhythm and the potassium together, and standard hyperkalaemia measures can be harmful or unnecessary when given first.
key_points: Serum digoxin concentration correlates poorly with toxicity in chronic poisoning
Potassium above 5.5 mmol/L in acute poisoning is an indication for antibody fragments
Calcium is relatively contraindicated in cardiac glycoside associated hyperkalaemia
Dialysis does not remove digoxin because the volume of distribution is very large
Look for the precipitant, most often a new diuretic or an acute kidney injury
explanation.pearls: In chronic digoxin poisoning give two vials of digoxin specific antibody fragments and repeat after 30 minutes if the rhythm has not improved, rather than calculating the full neutralising dose used in acute overdose.

options.rationale: A potassium above 5.5 mmol/L in acute on chronic digoxin poisoning predicts death and is an indication for digoxin specific antibody fragments, which bind digoxin and reverse both the bradyarrhythmia and the hyperkalaemia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology; Australian Medicines Handbook).

Calcium is the reflex response to hyperkalaemia with a broad or bradycardic rhythm, but in cardiac glycoside poisoning it is relatively contraindicated because intracellular calcium is already high and further loading risks refractory arrest (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

Shifting potassium intracellularly treats the number rather than the poisoning, and once antibody fragments are given the potassium falls rapidly, so pre emptive shifting risks a sudden fall to hypokalaemia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

Transvenous pacing in glycoside poisoning frequently provokes ventricular arrhythmia through the irritable myocardium and is reserved for bradycardia that persists after antibody fragments have been given (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

Digoxin has a very large volume of distribution and is not appreciably removed by dialysis, which distinguishes it from lithium and salicylate where dialysis is effective (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

explanation.summary: Overwhelming post splenectomy infection carries a mortality of around 50 per cent and can progress from first rigor to death within 24 hours, so the whole management strategy is speed rather than precision. Encapsulated bacteria dominate, but a dog bite adds Capnocytophaga canimorsus, which is carried in canine saliva and produces exactly this picture of fever, hypotension, purpura and disseminated intravascular coagulation in the asplenic host. Australian practice through Spleen Australia is to give asplenic patients a supply of antibiotics to take at the first sign of fever and to seek care immediately, alongside pneumococcal, meningococcal and Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccination. This man had neither prophylaxis nor a low threshold for presenting, which is the common failure point years after the operation.
key_points: Fever in an asplenic patient is a medical emergency until proven otherwise
Capnocytophaga canimorsus from dog saliva causes fulminant sepsis with purpura in asplenia
Give the first intravenous antibiotic dose before waiting for any result
Small wounds with minimal cellulitis can still seed overwhelming bacteraemia
Register asplenic patients for vaccination and standby antibiotic supply
explanation.pearls: Spleen Australia advises asplenic adults to carry standby amoxicillin 2 g to take at the onset of fever and to present the same day, and to receive lifelong pneumococcal, meningococcal ACWY and B, Haemophilus influenzae type b and annual influenza vaccination.

options.rationale: Waiting for microbiology in a patient without a spleen who is already hypotensive with purpura wastes the only window that changes outcome, since death can follow within hours of the first rigor (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

Oral amoxicillin with clavulanate is the right drug class for an uncomplicated dog bite, but the anti pattern here is treating a septic asplenic patient on the bite pathway rather than the sepsis pathway (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

This is overwhelming post splenectomy infection, and piperacillin with tazobactam covers both the encapsulated organisms and the Capnocytophaga species carried in dog saliva that cause fulminant sepsis with purpura in asplenic hosts (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Spleen Australia).

Flucloxacillin covers staphylococci and streptococci but has no activity against Capnocytophaga or Gram negative organisms, and a wound with 5 mm of erythema and no collection does not need debridement (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

Vancomycin with gentamicin misses the fastidious Gram negative rods from dog saliva and adds nephrotoxicity in a patient whose creatinine is already rising (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Familial hypercholesterolaemia affects about one in 250 Australians and fewer than one in ten of them have been identified, so opportunistic recognition in general practice matters. The Dutch Lipid Clinic Network score combines untreated low density lipoprotein cholesterol, tendon xanthomata, corneal arcus before 45 years of age, personal and family history of premature coronary disease, and a causative variant if known. Secondary causes such as hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, cholestasis and poorly controlled diabetes must be excluded before the diagnosis is accepted, which is why the normal thyroid function and urine albumin to creatinine ratio matter here. Treatment aims for at least a 50 per cent reduction in low density lipoprotein cholesterol, and each identified index case leads on average to one further affected relative for every one to two people tested.
key_points: Tendon xanthomata are close to specific for familial hypercholesterolaemia in this age group
Exclude hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome and cholestasis before making the diagnosis
Aim for at least a 50 per cent reduction in low density lipoprotein cholesterol
Cascade testing of first degree relatives is part of treating the index case
A zero coronary calcium score does not exclude high lifetime risk in a young patient
explanation.pearls: An untreated low density lipoprotein cholesterol above 6.5 mmol/L scores 8 points on the Dutch Lipid Clinic Network criteria on its own, and adding tendon xanthomata at 6 points makes the diagnosis definite before any genetic test is ordered.

options.rationale: Genetic testing supports the diagnosis and helps relatives but a negative result does not exclude the condition, and delaying treatment adds years of exposure to a very high low density lipoprotein cholesterol (Source: FH Australasia Network Guidance).

Ezetimibe lowers low density lipoprotein cholesterol by only about 18 per cent as monotherapy and is added to a statin rather than used instead of one in familial hypercholesterolaemia (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

A low statin dose will not approach the target reduction of at least 50 per cent, and calcium scoring is often zero in young patients with this condition so a reassuring score would be misleading (Source: FH Australasia Network Guidance).

Diet reduces low density lipoprotein cholesterol by around 10 per cent at best and cannot correct a receptor defect, and this man is already lean, active and a non smoker (Source: FH Australasia Network Guidance).

Low density lipoprotein cholesterol above 6.5 mmol/L with tendon xanthomata and premature coronary disease in a first degree relative gives a definite Dutch Lipid Clinic Network diagnosis, which calls for a high intensity statin and cascade testing of first degree relatives (Source: FH Australasia Network Guidance; Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Amiodarone contains about 37 per cent iodine by weight and disturbs thyroid function in up to a fifth of people taking it. Thyrotoxicosis comes in two forms that look identical biochemically but need opposite drugs: the iodine loaded form arises in an abnormal gland with nodules or autoimmunity and increases hormone synthesis, while the destructive form damages normal follicular cells and spills preformed hormone. Colour Doppler flow is the practical discriminator in Australian practice, being increased or normal in the first form and absent in the second, with a negative receptor antibody and a structurally normal gland supporting the destructive type. Mixed pictures occur and are treated with both a glucocorticoid and an antithyroid drug, with the response over one to two weeks clarifying the mechanism.
key_points: Colour Doppler flow separates the two forms of amiodarone associated thyrotoxicosis
Absent vascularity with a normal gland indicates a destructive thyroiditis
Glucocorticoid treats the destructive form and antithyroid drugs treat the iodine loaded form
Radioiodine uptake is blocked for months after amiodarone exposure
Continuing amiodarone is acceptable when it is controlling a life threatening arrhythmia
explanation.pearls: Prednisolone 40 mg daily usually produces a fall in free thyroxine within one to two weeks in destructive amiodarone associated thyrotoxicosis, and failure to respond by two weeks should prompt addition of carbimazole for a mixed picture.

options.rationale: Carbimazole blocks new hormone synthesis, which helps when excess iodine drives an overactive gland, but it cannot stop the release of preformed hormone from a gland that is being destroyed (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

Absent colour Doppler flow in a normal sized gland with negative receptor antibody indicates a destructive thyroiditis driven by amiodarone, which responds to glucocorticoid rather than to antithyroid drugs (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology; Australian Medicines Handbook).

Perchlorate blocks thyroid iodine uptake and is added to carbimazole for the iodine loaded form, where the gland is nodular or hypervascular, a pattern the ultrasound here excludes (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).
Radioiodine is ineffective for months to a year after amiodarone because the iodine load saturates the gland and blocks tracer uptake (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

Amiodarone has a half life of around 50 days, so stopping it alone leaves the patient thyrotoxic for months, and the decision to stop is separate from the decision to treat (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Thiazide associated hyponatraemia typically appears in the first few weeks of therapy and is commonest in older, smaller women. The biochemistry mimics inappropriate antidiuresis with a low serum osmolality, an inappropriately concentrated urine and a urine sodium above 30 mmol per litre, which is why thyroid and adrenal function are checked before the label is applied. The accompanying hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis are useful clues that a thiazide rather than an intrinsic antidiuretic hormone excess is responsible. Correction should not exceed 8 mmol per litre in 24 hours because these patients are at particular risk of osmotic demyelination once the drug is withdrawn and free water excretion resumes abruptly.
key_points: Thiazide hyponatraemia usually presents within weeks of starting the drug
Hypokalaemia alongside hyponatraemia points to a thiazide rather than antidiuretic hormone excess
Exclude hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency before accepting inappropriate antidiuresis
Isotonic saline can worsen hyponatraemia when the urine is highly concentrated
Hypertonic saline is reserved for seizures or a depressed conscious state
explanation.pearls: After a thiazide is withdrawn the sodium can rise abruptly as free water excretion resumes, so recheck within 6 to 12 hours and be prepared to give desmopressin with 5 per cent glucose if the rise exceeds 8 mmol per litre in 24 hours.

options.rationale: Thiazides impair urinary dilution and cause hyponatraemia most often within the first weeks of therapy, so with mild symptoms and no seizure the treatment is to remove the drug and monitor the sodium as it corrects (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology; Australian Medicines Handbook).

Fluid restriction is the mainstay when the cause of a syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis cannot be removed, and leaving the offending drug in place means the sodium will not reliably recover (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

Tolvaptan is reserved for persistent inappropriate antidiuresis that has failed simpler measures and carries a risk of overly rapid correction, which is unjustified when a reversible cause is sitting on the medication chart (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).
