Hypertonic saline boluses are for severe symptoms such as seizures, obtundation or respiratory arrest, and giving one for lethargy alone risks correcting faster than 8 mmol per litre in 24 hours (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

Isotonic saline given when urine osmolality exceeds 400 mmol per kilogram can be excreted as concentrated urine and leave behind free water, which paradoxically lowers the sodium further (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

explanation.summary: Sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors cause ketoacidosis at glucose concentrations that look reassuringly normal, which is why the diagnosis is often missed after surgery. Glycosuria depletes carbohydrate stores, insulin secretion falls and glucagon rises, so fasting and the catabolic stress of an operation tip the patient into ketogenesis without hyperglycaemia. Australian Diabetes Society advice is therefore to withhold the drug for three days around elective surgery and to check blood ketones rather than glucose in anyone who becomes unwell postoperatively. Metformin can generally be continued until the day of surgery when renal function is normal, and the sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor is restarted once the patient is eating, drinking and no longer at risk of dehydration.
key_points: Ketoacidosis with these drugs occurs at near normal blood glucose concentrations
Withhold for three days in total around elective surgery
Measure blood ketones rather than glucose in the unwell postoperative patient
Restart only once the patient is eating and drinking normally
Emergency surgery without a withholding period requires ketone monitoring throughout
explanation.pearls: A blood ketone level above 1.0 mmol/L in a postoperative patient taking a sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor warrants a venous blood gas, and treatment with insulin and dextrose is started even when the blood glucose is below 11 mmol/L.

options.rationale: Omitting a single dose does not clear the drug effect, because sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibition on the renal tubule and the resulting ketogenic state persist for several days after the last tablet (Source: Australian Diabetes Society Perioperative Alert).

A normal preoperative ketone level does not protect against ketoacidosis that develops during the fasting and surgical stress that follow, so monitoring is not a substitute for withholding (Source: Australian Diabetes Society Perioperative Alert).

A seven day gap gives no additional protection and worsens glycaemic control unnecessarily, and the drug can be restarted once the patient is eating and drinking normally (Source: Australian Diabetes Society Perioperative Alert).

Australian Diabetes Society advice is to withhold a sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor for at least three days in total, meaning the two days before the procedure and the day of the procedure, to prevent euglycaemic ketoacidosis (Source: Australian Diabetes Society Perioperative Alert; Australian Medicines Handbook).

Substituting a sulfonylurea introduces a hypoglycaemia risk during fasting and is unnecessary for a patient whose glycated haemoglobin is 7.2 per cent on two agents (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Metformin reduces calcium dependent ileal absorption of the vitamin B12 and intrinsic factor complex, and around one in ten long term users become deficient, with risk rising with dose and duration. These patients already carry a diagnosis that explains peripheral numbness, so the neuropathy is attributed to diabetes and the deficiency is never sought. Dorsal column involvement is the discriminator, producing loss of vibration and proprioception, a positive Romberg sign and gait unsteadiness that is worse in the dark, none of which belong to typical diabetic polyneuropathy. Haematological changes can be absent in up to a quarter of patients with neurological disease, so a normal full blood count does not exclude the diagnosis, and methylmalonic acid is measured when the vitamin B12 sits in the indeterminate range.
key_points: Long term metformin causes vitamin B12 malabsorption in around 10 per cent of users
Worse balance in the dark and a positive Romberg sign indicate dorsal column disease
Neurological disease can occur without anaemia or macrocytosis
Replace the vitamin before or with folate, never folate alone
Recovery is less complete when treatment is delayed beyond several months
explanation.pearls: Australian practice is hydroxocobalamin 1 mg intramuscularly on alternate days until no further improvement in neurological disease, then 1 mg every two to three months, rather than the standard three monthly schedule used for uncomplicated deficiency.

options.rationale: Diabetic polyneuropathy is length dependent and small fibre predominant and does not produce a positive Romberg sign with a macrocytosis, and a glycated haemoglobin of 6.9 per cent makes it an unlikely explanation for this degree of deficit (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

Folate also treats macrocytic anaemia, but giving folate first can correct the blood picture while the neurological damage progresses, and his red cell folate is normal anyway (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

A low vitamin B12 with macrocytosis and dorsal column signs indicates subacute combined degeneration and needs parenteral replacement without delay, with the long term metformin identified as the likely cause of malabsorption (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook; Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

Removing the cause without replacing the vitamin leaves a symptomatic deficiency untreated for months, and neurological recovery becomes less complete the longer treatment is delayed (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

Nerve conduction studies assess large fibre function but add nothing when the deficiency is already demonstrated biochemically, and the delay costs recoverable spinal cord function (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

explanation.summary: Denosumab is a reversible inhibitor of receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa B ligand, so its effect on osteoclasts disappears entirely when dosing stops. Osteoclast precursors that accumulated during treatment are then released, producing a rebound in bone turnover that exceeds baseline and causes rapid loss of the bone mineral density gained, with a characteristic pattern of multiple vertebral fractures. This risk applies to any interruption, which is why a delayed injection beyond seven months is treated as urgent rather than routine. Australian practice is to plan the exit before the first injection is given and to consolidate with a bisphosphonate, usually zoledronic acid, timed for when the next denosumab dose would have been due.
key_points: Denosumab effect is fully reversible and stopping causes rebound bone resorption
Multiple vertebral fractures are the characteristic rebound pattern
Any delay beyond seven months from the last dose carries the same risk
Consolidate with a bisphosphonate rather than simply stopping
Plan the exit strategy at the time denosumab is first started
explanation.pearls: Give zoledronic acid 5 mg intravenously about six months after the final denosumab injection, at the point the next dose would have been due, and recheck a bone turnover marker or bone density at 12 months because a second infusion is sometimes required.

options.rationale: Stopping without follow on therapy produces a rebound rise in bone turnover with rapid loss of the gains and a documented excess of multiple vertebral fractures, often within the first year (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook; Healthy Bones Australia).
Raloxifene is a weak antiresorptive that does not adequately suppress the rebound in bone turnover after denosumab, and it adds venous thromboembolic risk (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

Teriparatide is an anabolic agent given after denosumab is associated with transient further bone loss at the hip, so it is not the agent used to prevent rebound, and it also requires daily injections she wishes to avoid (Source: Healthy Bones Australia).
Calcium and vitamin D are supportive measures that do not suppress osteoclast activity and cannot prevent the surge in resorption that follows the last injection (Source: Healthy Bones Australia).

A potent bisphosphonate given as the next dose falls due binds to bone and blunts the rebound in resorption, and a single annual zoledronic acid infusion also suits a patient who is moving away from regular monitoring (Source: Healthy Bones Australia; Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Herpes zoster reactivates when varicella specific cell mediated immunity wanes, so the people most likely to need protection are often the people in whom a live vaccine is unsafe. The recombinant subunit vaccine solved this problem because it contains glycoprotein E with an adjuvant and no replicating virus, giving efficacy above 90 per cent that is preserved in immunocompromised adults. In Australia it is funded on the National Immunisation Program for adults from 65 years of age, for First Nations adults from 50 years of age, and for immunocompromised people from 18 years of age under defined conditions. Reactogenicity is high, with fever and marked injection site pain common for a day or two, and patients should be warned so they return for the second dose.
key_points: Live attenuated zoster vaccine is contraindicated in significant immunosuppression
The recombinant subunit vaccine contains no live virus and is safe in this group
Two doses are required, with a shortened minimum interval in immunocompromised adults
Efficacy remains above 90 per cent in older and immunocompromised adults
Warn patients about marked reactogenicity so they complete the second dose
explanation.pearls: In immunocompromised adults the second dose of recombinant zoster vaccine may be brought forward to one to two months after the first rather than the usual two to six months, so that protection is complete before further immunosuppression is escalated.

options.rationale: Live attenuated zoster vaccine is contraindicated in significant immunosuppression because the attenuated virus can disseminate, and methotrexate at this dose with daily prednisolone meets that threshold (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

The recombinant subunit vaccine contains no live virus, is the preferred product in immunocompromised adults, and is given as two doses with a minimum interval of one to two months in this group (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

Interrupting effective disease modifying therapy risks a flare, and a four week washout is insufficient because immune reconstitution after methotrexate and corticosteroid is not assured in that period (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook; Australian Rheumatology Association).

This confuses the contraindication that applies only to the live product with a blanket rule, and it withholds protection from precisely the group at highest risk of severe zoster and postherpetic neuralgia (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

Continuous antiviral prophylaxis is used around haematopoietic stem cell transplantation rather than for routine rheumatological immunosuppression, and it does not generate the durable cellular immunity a vaccine provides (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Newly detected atrial fibrillation during an acute illness still warrants stroke risk assessment, because most of these patients have paroxysmal atrial fibrillation that persists after the illness resolves. Australian practice uses the CHA2DS2-VA score, which drops the sex category, and recommends anticoagulation at a score of two or more. The commonest prescribing error in this population is failing to apply dose reduction criteria in small older patients, which more than doubles bleeding risk, and the second commonest is choosing an agent whose renal clearance makes it unsafe. Renal function should be rechecked at least six monthly, and more often during intercurrent illness, because a falling clearance can move a patient across a dosing threshold.
key_points: CHA2DS2-VA of two or more warrants anticoagulation in Australian practice
Apixaban is reduced when two of age, weight and creatinine criteria are met
Dabigatran is contraindicated below a creatinine clearance of 30 mL per minute
Rivaroxaban is reduced to 15 mg daily below a clearance of 50 mL per minute
Aspirin is not an acceptable substitute for anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation
explanation.pearls: The apixaban reduction criteria are age 80 years or more, weight 60 kg or less and serum creatinine 133 micromol per litre or more, and any two of the three trigger 2.5 mg twice daily regardless of the calculated creatinine clearance.

options.rationale: She meets two of the three reduction criteria of age 80 years or more, weight 60 kg or less and creatinine 133 micromol/L or more, so the reduced dose applies, and apixaban is the only direct oral anticoagulant with an Australian dose for a creatinine clearance in the high twenties (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).
The full dose applies only when fewer than two reduction criteria are met, and she satisfies both the age and the weight criterion (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

Rivaroxaban is reduced to 15 mg daily once creatinine clearance falls below 50 mL per minute, so the 20 mg dose would be an overdose at a clearance of 28 mL per minute (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

Dabigatran is the most renally cleared of the direct oral anticoagulants at around 80 per cent and is contraindicated below a creatinine clearance of 30 mL per minute (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

Aspirin gives negligible stroke protection in atrial fibrillation while retaining much of the bleeding risk, and it is no longer recommended as an alternative to anticoagulation (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).

explanation.summary: Australian guidance treats out of office measurement as the reference standard for diagnosing hypertension because clinic readings misclassify a substantial minority of patients in both directions. The diagnostic thresholds are lower out of office, with a daytime ambulatory or home average of 135/85 mmHg corresponding to a clinic reading of 140/90 mmHg, and a 24 hour average threshold of 130/80 mmHg. The white coat pattern carries a cardiovascular risk intermediate between normotension and sustained hypertension, so it is followed rather than ignored. The mirror image, masked hypertension, has normal clinic readings with a raised out of office average and carries risk equivalent to sustained hypertension, which is why ambulatory monitoring is also indicated when target organ damage appears despite normal clinic readings.
key_points: Out of office measurement is the reference standard for diagnosing hypertension
Daytime ambulatory threshold is 135/85 mmHg, not the clinic threshold of 140/90 mmHg
The white coat pattern needs surveillance rather than drug treatment
Assess target organ damage before deciding, using renal, cardiac and retinal findings
Masked hypertension carries risk equivalent to sustained hypertension
explanation.pearls: A nocturnal fall in blood pressure of less than 10 per cent identifies a non dipping pattern that independently predicts cardiovascular events, so read the night time average on every ambulatory report rather than only the daytime figure.

sources.label: National Heart Foundation of Australia Hypertension Guideline

options.rationale: Treating on clinic readings alone in this situation exposes a normotensive man to drug adverse effects and to symptomatic hypotension outside the consulting room (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia Hypertension Guideline).
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia Hypertension Guideline

options.rationale: Changing the drug class does not change the underlying problem, which is that the out of office average is below the diagnostic threshold and there is no target organ damage (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia Hypertension Guideline).
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia Hypertension Guideline

options.rationale: Secondary hypertension is pursued when hypertension is confirmed and is resistant, of early onset, or accompanied by suggestive features such as hypokalaemia, none of which apply here (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia Hypertension Guideline).
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia Hypertension Guideline

options.rationale: A daytime ambulatory average below 135/85 mmHg with normal renal, cardiac and retinal assessment defines the white coat pattern, which is managed with lifestyle measures and periodic repeat monitoring because a proportion progress to sustained hypertension (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia Hypertension Guideline).
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia Hypertension Guideline

options.rationale: Escalating on clinic readings compounds the original error and is the mechanism by which patients with this pattern accumulate three or more unnecessary antihypertensive drugs (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia Hypertension Guideline).
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia Hypertension Guideline

explanation.summary: Augmentation is the paradoxical worsening of restless legs syndrome caused by long term dopaminergic therapy and affects a substantial proportion of patients treated with dopamine agonists for several years. It is recognised by symptoms starting earlier in the day, spreading to previously unaffected body parts, becoming more intense, and by a shorter latency at rest, with each dose increase producing only temporary relief. It is frequently misread as progression of the underlying disorder, and the resulting dose escalation accelerates the process. Withdrawal is uncomfortable and should be gradual, with an alpha 2 delta ligand introduced before the taper begins, and iron studies repeated because low brain iron lowers the threshold for augmentation even when the ferritin is not frankly low.
key_points: Augmentation means earlier onset, greater intensity and spread to new body regions
Each dose increase gives only temporary relief and worsens the underlying process
Alpha 2 delta ligands such as gabapentin or pregabalin do not cause augmentation
Withdraw the dopamine agonist gradually because rebound symptoms are severe
Check ferritin and transferrin saturation before attributing symptoms to augmentation
explanation.pearls: In restless legs syndrome the iron treatment threshold is a ferritin below 75 micrograms per litre or a transferrin saturation below 20 per cent, which is far higher than the threshold used to diagnose iron deficiency anaemia.

options.rationale: Escalating the dopamine agonist makes this worse, because each increase drives further augmentation and produces earlier and more widespread symptoms within months (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

Iron replacement is first line when ferritin is below 75 micrograms per litre or transferrin saturation below 20 per cent, and neither threshold is crossed here so iron will not help (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

Earlier onset of symptoms in the day, spread to the arms and loss of response to each dose increase define augmentation, which is managed by withdrawing the dopamine agonist slowly and substituting an alpha 2 delta ligand such as gabapentin (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology; Australian Medicines Handbook).

Rotigotine is another dopamine agonist and although its continuous delivery causes augmentation less often, switching within the same class while continuing the oral drug perpetuates the problem (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).
A benzodiazepine may improve sleep continuity but does nothing for the daytime urge to move, and adding it in an older man risks falls and daytime sedation (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is diagnosed on cell count, not on culture, and any patient with new ascites, fever, abdominal pain, encephalopathy or unexplained renal decline earns a diagnostic tap before antibiotics are given. A low ascitic protein below 15 g/L marks the patients at highest risk because opsonic activity in the fluid is poor. Once treated, survivors need long term oral quinolone prophylaxis and assessment for liver transplantation, since one year mortality after a first episode approaches a third. The commonest reason for a missed diagnosis is anchoring on encephalopathy as a primary event rather than as the presenting sign of an infective precipitant.
key_points: Ascitic polymorphonuclear count 250 x10^6/L or above is diagnostic even with a negative Gram stain and negative culture.
Third generation cephalosporin plus albumin is the treatment pair when creatinine is above 88 micromol/L or bilirubin is above 68 micromol/L.
Ascitic protein above 10 g/L with a low ascitic glucose and multiple organisms points to a surgical secondary peritonitis instead.
Encephalopathy or unexplained renal decline in cirrhosis is an indication for a diagnostic tap, not for empirical lactulose alone.
After a first episode, secondary prophylaxis and transplant assessment both become due.
explanation.pearls: Albumin is given as 1.5 g/kg within six hours of diagnosis and 1 g/kg on day three; this pairing, not the antibiotic alone, is what cuts hepatorenal syndrome and in hospital mortality.

sources.label: EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines: Decompensated Cirrhosis

options.rationale: Large volume paracentesis relieves tense ascites but does nothing for infection, and withholding the antibiotic in a man whose creatinine is already 118 micromol/L invites hepatorenal syndrome (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).

An ascitic polymorphonuclear count at or above 250 x10^6/L establishes the diagnosis irrespective of the Gram stain, and adding albumin on the first and third days reduces progression to renal failure and death in patients with a raised creatinine or bilirubin (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).

Norfloxacin has a role in primary and secondary prophylaxis rather than in treating an established episode, and an oral agent alone is inadequate in a man who is already hypotensive and encephalopathic (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).

Ascitic culture is sterile in a large proportion of genuine episodes because organism density is low, so treatment is committed on the cell count alone and delay increases mortality (Source: EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines: Decompensated Cirrhosis).
source_refs: EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines: Decompensated Cirrhosis

options.rationale: Secondary bacterial peritonitis from a perforated viscus is suggested by multiple organisms on Gram stain, ascitic protein above 10 g/L, ascitic glucose below 2.8 mmol/L and a raised ascitic lactate dehydrogenase, none of which is present here (Source: EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines: Decompensated Cirrhosis).
source_refs: EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines: Decompensated Cirrhosis

explanation.summary: Heparin induced thrombocytopenia is a clinical diagnosis made on the 4Ts score, because immunoassays are sensitive but poorly specific and functional assays take days to return. The counterintuitive feature is that the thrombocytopenia is a marker of platelet consumption in thrombus rather than a bleeding risk, so the correct response is more anticoagulation, not less. Thrombosis occurs in roughly half of cases and may be venous or arterial, including at unusual sites such as adrenal vein or skin necrosis at injection sites. Failing to document the reaction risks lethal re exposure at a later admission.
key_points: The 4Ts score weighs magnitude of platelet fall, timing at day five to ten, thrombosis or sequelae, and absence of other causes.
All heparin including flushes and heparin bonded lines must stop the moment the diagnosis is suspected.
A therapeutic non heparin anticoagulant is started immediately, not after antibody confirmation.
Warfarin is withheld until the platelet count exceeds 150 x10^9/L because of venous limb gangrene risk.
Platelet transfusion is reserved for active bleeding, not for the count itself.
explanation.pearls: Timing is the single most discriminating element of the 4Ts: a fall beginning between day five and day ten of first heparin exposure, or within 24 hours if heparin was given in the previous 30 days, is what separates this from postoperative dilutional thrombocytopenia.

sources.label: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: High dose immunoglobulin is reserved for refractory or autoimmune forms after heparin has already been stopped, and continuing the drug that drives the antibody makes any adjunct futile (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: The antibody is directed at platelet factor 4 bound to heparin of any kind, so unfractionated heparin cross reacts fully and would sustain the thrombotic process (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

A platelet fall of more than 50 per cent between days five and ten with new thrombosis and no other cause gives a high 4Ts score, and management is immediate withdrawal of all heparin plus a therapeutic non heparin anticoagulant such as danaparoid while confirmatory antibody testing is sent (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Warfarin started while the platelet count is still falling depletes protein C faster than the vitamin K dependent procoagulants and precipitates venous limb gangrene, so it is deferred until platelets recover above 150 x10^9/L (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand).
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: This is a prothrombotic rather than a bleeding disorder, and prophylactic platelet transfusion adds substrate to the activation process without treating the thrombus (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Acute variceal bleeding is managed on three simultaneous fronts before the endoscope arrives: restrictive resuscitation, a splanchnic vasoconstrictor, and antibiotic prophylaxis. Restrictive transfusion matters because rapid volume expansion restores portal pressure and provokes rebleeding, so a haemoglobin trigger of 70 g/L with a target of 70 to 90 g/L is used unless there is ongoing massive loss or ischaemic heart disease. Antibiotic prophylaxis is the intervention with the clearest mortality benefit, because translocation driven sepsis is what kills many of these patients in the week after the bleed. Band ligation within 12 hours, then non selective beta blockade plus a repeat banding program, complete the pathway.
key_points: Antibiotic prophylaxis in cirrhosis with any gastrointestinal bleed reduces infection, rebleeding and death.
A vasoactive agent is started on suspicion and continued for two to five days after endoscopy.
Transfusion is restrictive with a trigger of 70 g/L; liberal transfusion raises portal pressure.
Correcting the international normalised ratio with plasma does not correct the rebalanced haemostasis of cirrhosis.
Non selective beta blockade belongs to secondary prophylaxis, not the acute episode.
explanation.pearls: Terlipressin causes hyponatraemia that can fall by more than 10 mmol/L in 72 hours, most sharply in patients whose baseline sodium is normal and whose liver disease is well compensated, so the sodium is checked daily while it runs.

sources.label: EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines: Decompensated Cirrhosis

options.rationale: Non selective beta blockade is secondary prophylaxis begun after the acute episode has settled; introducing it during hypotension blunts the compensatory tachycardia and drops perfusion further (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).

Tranexamic acid did not reduce death in gastrointestinal bleeding and increased venous thromboembolism, and plasma given for a raised international normalised ratio in cirrhosis expands volume and raises portal pressure without restoring haemostasis (Source: EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines: Decompensated Cirrhosis).
source_refs: EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines: Decompensated Cirrhosis

options.rationale: A proton pump inhibitor is reasonable while the bleeding source is unknown but does not address varices, and a liberal transfusion target above 70 to 80 g/L raises portal pressure and increases rebleeding (Source: EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines: Decompensated Cirrhosis).
source_refs: EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines: Decompensated Cirrhosis

options.rationale: A splanchnic vasoconstrictor started before endoscopy improves haemostasis, and antibiotic prophylaxis in a bleeding cirrhotic reduces rebleeding, bacterial infection and mortality, so both are given at presentation rather than after the scope (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).

Vitamin K will not correct a coagulopathy driven by synthetic liver failure within the timeframe of an active bleed, and it leaves the portal pressure untreated (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: A monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance carries a risk of progression of roughly one per cent per year, but that average conceals a wide spread that three factors predict: paraprotein concentration, isotype other than IgG, and an abnormal free light chain ratio. Patients with none of these can be followed with serial bloods alone, while those with one or more warrant marrow and imaging assessment at baseline. The distinction from smouldering myeloma is entirely quantitative, resting on marrow plasma cell percentage and paraprotein concentration, and the distinction from active myeloma rests on end-organ damage or the three myeloma defining biomarkers. Getting the baseline assessment right sets the surveillance interval for the next decade.
key_points: Risk factors for progression are paraprotein at or above 15 g/L, non IgG isotype, and an abnormal free light chain ratio.
Low risk disease with none of these can be followed with serum electrophoresis alone.
Any risk factor prompts baseline marrow examination and whole body low dose computed tomography.
Plain radiograph skeletal survey is no longer the standard because of poor sensitivity for early lytic disease.
End-organ damage or a myeloma defining biomarker is required before treatment is started.
explanation.pearls: A serum free light chain ratio of 100 or more with an involved chain of at least 100 mg/L is itself a myeloma defining event, converting an otherwise asymptomatic patient into one who needs treatment without waiting for hypercalcaemia or bone lesions.

sources.label: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand
International Myeloma Working Group Consensus Criteria

options.rationale: The plain film survey misses lesions until roughly 30 per cent of trabecular bone is lost, so it has been replaced by whole body low dose computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand).
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Treatment requires either end-organ damage or a biomarker of malignancy such as 60 per cent marrow plasma cells, a light chain ratio of 100 or more, or a focal marrow lesion on magnetic resonance imaging, none of which has been established (Source: International Myeloma Working Group Consensus Criteria).
source_refs: International Myeloma Working Group Consensus Criteria

options.rationale: Six monthly surveillance alone is appropriate for low risk disease, defined by an IgG paraprotein below 15 g/L with a normal light chain ratio, and this man meets neither condition (Source: International Myeloma Working Group Consensus Criteria).
source_refs: International Myeloma Working Group Consensus Criteria

options.rationale: A paraprotein at or above 15 g/L combined with an abnormal free light chain ratio places him beyond the low risk group, and marrow examination with whole body low dose computed tomography is needed to separate smouldering myeloma from a benign gammopathy before any surveillance interval is set (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand).
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Bone protection is indicated once lytic disease or myeloma related osteoporosis is proven, and starting it now would treat a complication that has not been demonstrated (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Malignant spinal cord compression complicates around five per cent of solid cancers, most often breast, prostate, lung and myeloma, and back pain precedes neurological signs by a median of several weeks. Ambulatory status at the time treatment starts is the strongest predictor of ambulatory status afterwards, which is why the steroid is given before imaging rather than after it. Imaging must cover the whole spine because synchronous lesions at other levels change the radiation field or the surgical plan. Definitive management is decompressive surgery followed by radiotherapy in fit patients with a single level and reasonable prognosis, and radiotherapy alone otherwise.
key_points: New back pain that is worse lying flat or at night in a patient with cancer is a red flag for epidural disease.
Corticosteroid is given on clinical suspicion, before imaging returns.
Magnetic resonance imaging must cover the whole spine because multilevel disease is common.
Ambulatory status at treatment start predicts long term ambulatory status.
Surgery followed by radiotherapy outperforms radiotherapy alone in selected single level disease.
explanation.pearls: Once sphincter function is lost the chance of regaining independent walking falls below one in ten, so the window that matters is the interval between leg heaviness and retention, usually only a day or two.

options.rationale: Plain films cannot exclude epidural disease and a delay of a day in a patient who is still walking risks the irreversible loss of ambulation that defines outcome in this condition (Source: Cancer Council Australia).

A bone scan shows osteoblastic activity in the vertebral body but does not image the epidural space or the cord itself, so it cannot define the level or extent that surgical and radiation oncology decisions depend on (Source: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online).

Leptomeningeal disease does present with back pain, but it typically gives patchy multilevel and cranial nerve signs rather than a single sensory level, and lumbar puncture below a compressive lesion can precipitate deterioration (Source: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online).
Mechanical back pain does not produce a sensory level or clonus, and the nocturnal and recumbent pattern of this pain is itself a red flag for an epidural process (Source: Cancer Council Australia).

Progressive leg weakness with a sensory level and upper motor neurone signs in a woman with prior breast cancer is compression until proven otherwise, and high dose corticosteroid is given at once while urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the entire spine is arranged because a third of patients have disease at more than one level (Source: Cancer Council Australia).

explanation.summary: Acute kidney injury in cirrhosis has four common causes: prerenal from diuretics or bleeding, acute tubular necrosis, hepatorenal syndrome and post renal obstruction. The diagnosis of hepatorenal syndrome is one of exclusion and requires no improvement after two days off diuretics with albumin expansion, absence of shock, no recent nephrotoxin, and no parenchymal disease on urinalysis and ultrasound. This sequence matters because vasoconstrictor therapy is costly and carries ischaemic risk, while a patient who is simply over diuresed recovers with volume alone. Any patient reaching a confirmed diagnosis should be assessed for liver transplantation at the same time as vasoconstrictor therapy is started.
key_points: Urinary sodium below 20 mmol/L cannot distinguish prerenal azotaemia from hepatorenal syndrome; both avidly retain sodium.
Diuretic withdrawal plus albumin 1 g/kg daily for two days is the diagnostic challenge.
Bland urinary sediment argues against acute tubular necrosis and against glomerular disease.
Terlipressin with albumin is the treatment only after the challenge has failed.
Transplant assessment runs in parallel with medical treatment.
explanation.pearls: Albumin for the diagnostic challenge is capped at 100 g per day, because volumes beyond that give no additional expansion and precipitate pulmonary oedema in a patient whose oncotic gradient is already deranged.

sources.label: EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines: Decompensated Cirrhosis

options.rationale: A low urinary sodium and bland sediment are shared by both prerenal azotaemia and hepatorenal syndrome, so neither can be diagnosed on those findings; the defining step is failure of the creatinine to improve after diuretic withdrawal plus albumin volume expansion at 1 g/kg daily for two days (Source: EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines: Decompensated Cirrhosis).
source_refs: EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines: Decompensated Cirrhosis

options.rationale: Vasoconstrictor therapy is reserved for hepatorenal syndrome that persists after the albumin challenge, and committing to it now would treat a diagnosis that has not yet been earned (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).

Crystalloid does not hold in the intravascular space when the albumin is low and portal pressure is high, so it worsens ascites and peripheral oedema while doing less than albumin to restore effective arterial volume (Source: EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines: Decompensated Cirrhosis).
source_refs: EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines: Decompensated Cirrhosis

options.rationale: Renal dose dopamine has repeatedly failed to prevent or reverse acute kidney injury in randomised trials and adds arrhythmia risk without altering the course (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

Biopsy has a place when there is proteinuria, haematuria or casts pointing to an intrinsic glomerular lesion, but the sediment here is bland and the coagulopathy makes biopsy hazardous (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).

explanation.summary: Dysphagia that involves liquids as early as solids points to a motility disorder, whereas dysphagia that begins with solids and progresses to liquids points to a structural narrowing. Endoscopy still comes first in every case, both to exclude mucosal disease and to take biopsies, but a normal endoscopy does not end the workup. High resolution manometry defines the three treatment relevant subtypes, and the response to pneumatic dilatation and myotomy differs sharply between them. Untreated disease leads to progressive oesophageal dilatation, aspiration pneumonia and a small long term risk of squamous carcinoma.
key_points: Simultaneous solid and liquid dysphagia suggests a motility disorder rather than a stricture.
Regurgitation of undigested, non acidic food and nocturnal cough are characteristic.
Endoscopy is done first but a normal result does not exclude the diagnosis.
High resolution manometry confirms the diagnosis and assigns the subtype that guides therapy.
Malignancy at the junction can mimic the picture and is suspected with older age, short history and marked weight loss.
explanation.pearls: The endoscopic finding of retained food or saliva in an oesophagus with normal mucosa has a very high positive predictive value for a motility disorder, and its absence is why endoscopy alone misses roughly a third of cases.

options.rationale: An empirical acid suppression trial delays diagnosis in a man who has already lost 6 kg, and the biopsies have already excluded the eosinophilic oesophagitis that such a trial would be testing for (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).

Dysphagia to both solids and liquids from the outset with regurgitation of undigested food and a normal mucosa is a motility problem, and manometry is the test that both confirms failed lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation and assigns the subtype that determines whether dilatation, myotomy or peroral endoscopic myotomy is offered (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia).

A timed barium study is a useful adjunct for measuring emptying before and after treatment, but it cannot assign the motility subtype and a normal study does not exclude the diagnosis (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia).

Reflux monitoring answers a different question, and the regurgitated material here tastes of the meal rather than being acidic, which points away from acid reflux as the mechanism (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia).

Cross sectional imaging is reserved for suspected malignancy at the junction, suggested by onset after 55 years, a history of under six months and rapid weight loss, a pattern this man does not fit (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Achalasia).

explanation.summary: An inflammatory myopathy with characteristic skin disease is one of the few rheumatological diagnoses that mandates a malignancy hunt at presentation, since the association is strongest in adults over 45 and in the first three years after diagnosis. Ovarian, lung, breast, colorectal, pancreatic and gastric cancers are over represented, and in some populations nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Antibody testing helps stratify this risk further, with certain myositis specific antibodies conferring high malignancy risk and others associating instead with interstitial lung disease. Screening for interstitial lung disease with high resolution imaging and lung function, and swallow assessment for pharyngeal weakness, run alongside the malignancy search.
key_points: Adult onset inflammatory myopathy with characteristic skin disease carries a several fold malignancy risk.
Risk concentrates in the three years around diagnosis and rises with age above 45.
Cross sectional imaging plus age and sex appropriate screening is done at presentation.
Myositis specific antibodies stratify risk of malignancy versus interstitial lung disease.
Interstitial lung disease and pharyngeal weakness are the other two assessments due at diagnosis.
explanation.pearls: Anti transcription intermediary factor 1 gamma antibody in an adult carries a malignancy risk approaching one in two, while anti melanoma differentiation associated gene 5 antibody instead flags rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease with a near normal creatine kinase.

options.rationale: Imaging guided biopsy confirms the inflammatory nature of the myopathy and is often done, but it does not address the malignancy association that changes this woman's prognosis and management most (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association).

Electrophysiology separates myopathic from neurogenic weakness, but the raised creatine kinase with preserved reflexes and normal distal power has already made that distinction (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Dermatomyositis).

Hypothyroid and osteomalacic myopathy are reasonable considerations in proximal weakness, but the thyroid function is already normal and neither produces a creatine kinase in the thousands with a photodistributed rash (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Dermatomyositis).

Cutaneous lupus shares an interface dermatitis on histology, but lupus rash spares the knuckles and involves the skin between them, so a biopsy would not change management (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists).

The combination of proximal myopathy with the periorbital and knuckle skin changes carries a several fold increase in occult malignancy, concentrated in the three years around diagnosis, so cross sectional imaging with age and sex appropriate screening is performed at presentation rather than deferred (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association).

explanation.summary: Superior vena caval obstruction was once treated as an emergency requiring immediate radiotherapy, but the modern approach separates the small group with true airway or neurological compromise from the majority who are stable with collateral flow. In the stable group, tissue diagnosis comes first because the histology dictates whether systemic therapy or radiotherapy is the primary modality. Around three quarters of cases are due to lung cancer, most commonly small cell, with lymphoma and germ cell tumours making up much of the remainder, and all three of those are chemosensitive. Intravascular thrombus around an indwelling device is the important non malignant cause and is managed with anticoagulation rather than irradiation.
key_points: Stridor, laryngeal oedema, reduced consciousness or haemodynamic compromise mark the group needing immediate intervention.
In stable patients, histology precedes treatment because it determines modality.
Corticosteroid before biopsy risks a non diagnostic specimen in lymphoma.
Endovascular stenting gives the fastest relief when symptoms are severe.
Catheter associated thrombus is the main non malignant cause and is treated with anticoagulation.
explanation.pearls: The chest wall collateral veins that make this diagnosis obvious take several weeks to develop, so their presence is itself reassurance that the obstruction has been gradual and that there is time to biopsy before treating.

options.rationale: Without airway compromise or cerebral oedema there is time to obtain histology, and histology determines everything that follows because small cell carcinoma and lymphoma respond to systemic therapy while non small cell disease is treated with radiotherapy or a stent (Source: Cancer Council Australia).

Corticosteroid given before biopsy can lyse lymphoma cells and render the specimen non diagnostic, which is why it is held back unless there is airway or cerebral compromise (Source: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online).

Stenting gives the fastest symptom relief and is the right move for severe or life threatening obstruction, but this man is stable with established collaterals, and stenting first commits him to anticoagulation and can complicate subsequent biopsy access (Source: Cancer Council Australia).

Empirical irradiation of the mediastinum destroys the diagnostic yield of subsequent biopsy and may deliver the wrong modality entirely if the tumour turns out to be chemosensitive (Source: eviQ Cancer Treatments Online).
Anticoagulation is indicated when the obstruction is caused by catheter associated thrombus rather than extrinsic compression, which the imaging here does not show (Source: Cancer Council Australia).

explanation.summary: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia divides on the thermal amplitude of the antibody, and the direct antiglobulin pattern is what makes the split: immunoglobulin G with or without complement indicates a warm antibody, while complement alone indicates a cold one. That distinction changes treatment completely, because warm disease responds to corticosteroid and splenectomy while cold disease does not. Primary cold agglutinin disease is now recognised as a low grade clonal bone marrow lymphoproliferative disorder, which is why B cell directed therapy with rituximab, with or without a plasma cell or complement directed agent, has become the treatment of choice when transfusion dependence or symptoms demand it. Secondary cold agglutinins follow mycoplasma pneumonia or Epstein Barr virus infection and are usually self-limiting.
key_points: Complement only positivity on the direct antiglobulin test indicates a cold reactive antibody.
Red cell clumping at room temperature causes a spuriously high mean cell volume and a spuriously low red cell count.
Corticosteroid and splenectomy are effective in warm disease but not in cold disease.
Cold avoidance and a blood warmer for transfusion are the immediate measures.
Primary disease reflects a marrow B cell clone and responds to rituximab based therapy.
explanation.pearls: Warming the sample to 37 degrees Celsius before running it corrects the clumping artefact, so a mean cell volume above 120 fL that normalises on a warmed repeat is a laboratory clue to the diagnosis before any antiglobulin test is back.

sources.label: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Corticosteroid is first line in warm autoimmune haemolysis, where the antiglobulin test is positive for immunoglobulin G and destruction is splenic; in the cold reactive form clearance is complement mediated and hepatic, and steroids are largely ineffective (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand).
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Splenectomy helps when antibody coated cells are removed by splenic macrophages, but complement coated cells are cleared by Kupffer cells in the liver, so the operation removes the wrong organ (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand).
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Immunoglobulin blocks Fc receptor mediated clearance and has little effect where complement drives destruction, and the response even in warm disease is brief and unreliable (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

Exchange removes circulating antibody transiently and is reserved for fulminant haemolysis as a bridge, not as the management of a stable outpatient with a haemoglobin of 82 g/L (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand).
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: A direct antiglobulin test positive for complement alone, with cold triggered acrocyanosis and in vitro red cell clumping, identifies a cold reactive antibody, and the first line measures are avoidance of cold exposure and use of a blood warmer if transfusion is needed, with specialist assessment for an underlying lymphoproliferative clone (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand).
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand

explanation.summary: Chronic pancreatitis destroys acinar tissue long before it destroys islets, so steatorrhoea usually precedes diabetes, and more than 90 per cent of exocrine function must be lost before fat malabsorption becomes clinically apparent. Faecal elastase is the practical test because it is stable in stool and unaffected by concurrent enzyme replacement, unlike faecal fat collections. Enzyme replacement is dosed by lipase units taken with every meal and snack, titrated to symptoms and weight rather than to a repeat test. These patients also need bone density assessment, since osteoporosis is present in around a quarter, and surveillance for the increased long term risk of pancreatic carcinoma.
key_points: Faecal elastase below 100 mcg/g indicates severe exocrine insufficiency and is unaffected by concurrent enzyme therapy.
Enzymes are taken with every meal and snack, not on a fixed daily schedule.
A prolonged international normalised ratio in this setting reflects vitamin K malabsorption.
Fat restriction worsens malnutrition and is not the treatment.
Bone density assessment and vitamin D replacement are part of long term care.
explanation.pearls: Adding a proton pump inhibitor rescues around a third of patients whose steatorrhoea persists on adequate lipase doses, because pancreatic bicarbonate output is lost alongside the enzymes and the unbuffered duodenal acid denatures the replacement lipase.

options.rationale: Acid suppression is a useful adjunct when enzyme replacement alone fails because acid inactivates lipase in the duodenum, but it does nothing on its own, and coeliac serology has already returned negative with an adequate immunoglobulin A (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).

Tissue sampling is indicated when imaging shows a focal mass or when weight loss is unexplained, but the scan here shows diffuse calcification without a mass and the elastase already explains the weight loss (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia).

A faecal elastase below 100 mcg/g with pancreatic calcification confirms exocrine insufficiency, and lipase replacement taken with every meal and snack is the treatment, with vitamins A, D, E and K measured because the prolonged international normalised ratio here reflects vitamin K malabsorption rather than liver disease (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia).

Fat restriction reduces the visible steatorrhoea but worsens the energy deficit and the fat soluble vitamin deficiency in a man who has already lost 8 kg, and elastase does not recover with dietary change (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia).

An antimotility agent is aimed at the wrong mechanism, since the problem is undigested fat rather than accelerated transit, and he describes no urgency or increased frequency (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).

explanation.summary: Median nerve compression at the wrist is graded clinically by whether symptoms are intermittent, constant, or accompanied by motor loss, and that grading drives the management branch rather than the duration of symptoms alone. Sparing of sensation over the thenar eminence is the anatomical clue that the lesion sits under the flexor retinaculum, because the palmar cutaneous branch leaves the median nerve proximal to the tunnel. Secondary causes worth excluding before surgery include hypothyroidism, diabetes, pregnancy, acromegaly and inflammatory arthritis. Nerve conduction studies grade severity and are usually requested by the operating surgeon, but a clear clinical picture with wasting does not need them to justify referral. Delay matters because thenar recovery after release is far less complete once wasting is visible.
key_points: Constant numbness plus abductor pollicis brevis weakness or wasting marks severe disease and warrants surgical referral.
Preserved sensation over the thenar eminence localises the lesion to within the tunnel rather than proximally.
Night splinting and corticosteroid injection are for intermittent symptoms without motor signs.
Full pain free neck movement with symmetrical reflexes argues against a C6 radiculopathy.
Check thyroid function and glucose, since correctable causes change the conservative options.
explanation.pearls: Thenar wasting means the axons are already dying: functional recovery of abductor pollicis brevis after release falls sharply once wasting is visible, which is why severe disease is referred rather than splinted for six weeks.

sources.label: RACGP: Carpal tunnel syndrome in general practice
BMJ Best Practice: Carpal tunnel syndrome

options.rationale: A C6 radiculopathy would give neck pain on movement, an altered biceps reflex and sensory change extending onto the forearm, none of which is present (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Carpal tunnel syndrome).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Carpal tunnel syndrome

options.rationale: Night splinting is the first line only for intermittent symptoms without motor signs, and offering it here delays release while the thenar muscle continues to denervate (Source: RACGP: Carpal tunnel syndrome in general practice).
source_refs: RACGP: Carpal tunnel syndrome in general practice

options.rationale: Injection gives useful but usually temporary relief in mild to moderate disease and is a reasonable bridge in pregnancy, whereas established wasting is an indication to proceed to definitive release (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Carpal tunnel syndrome).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Carpal tunnel syndrome

options.rationale: Persistent sensory loss with wasting and weakness of abductor pollicis brevis defines severe disease, and once axonal motor loss is established conservative measures rarely reverse it, so surgical release is the intervention that preserves function (Source: RACGP: Carpal tunnel syndrome in general practice).
source_refs: RACGP: Carpal tunnel syndrome in general practice

options.rationale: Oral corticosteroid produces only short lived benefit measured in weeks and carries systemic risk without altering the compressive mechanism (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology).

explanation.summary: Inflammatory back pain is defined by onset before age 45, insidious onset, improvement with exercise but not rest, night pain with waking, and duration beyond three months. Recognising it matters because the mechanical pattern is vastly more common and gets managed with reassurance and activity, whereas the inflammatory pattern needs a rheumatologist, a scheduled non-steroidal anti inflammatory trial and consideration of biologic therapy. Acute anterior uveitis, psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease are the extra articular partners that raise pre test probability substantially. The radiographic and non radiographic forms sit on one disease spectrum and respond similarly to treatment, so the absence of erosions is not a reason to withhold referral. Untreated axial inflammation over years produces syndesmophytes and irreversible loss of spinal mobility.
key_points: Normal sacroiliac radiographs do not exclude axial spondyloarthritis; structural change lags inflammation by years.
Fluid sensitive magnetic resonance sequences show subchondral marrow oedema, the finding that defines non radiographic disease.
Improvement with exercise and not with rest, plus night waking, is the inflammatory pattern.
Acute anterior uveitis is the commonest extra articular feature and should prompt the question in a young person with back pain.
Human leucocyte antigen B27 weights probability but is neither necessary nor sufficient for diagnosis.
explanation.pearls: Scheduled rather than as needed non-steroidal anti inflammatory therapy for at least two to four weeks at maximum tolerated dose is the recognised first line, and failure of two such agents is the usual gateway to a tumour necrosis factor inhibitor.

sources.label: ASAS classification criteria for axial spondyloarthritis

options.rationale: Computed tomography shows established erosion and ankylosis better than plain film but cannot show marrow oedema, so it misses the early inflammatory phase while delivering pelvic radiation to a young man (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial spondyloarthritis).

Structural change on plain film lags the onset of inflammation by years, so a normal radiograph does not exclude the diagnosis and marrow oedema in the subchondral bone on a fluid sensitive sequence is what establishes non radiographic disease (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial spondyloarthritis).

The allele is carried by roughly 8 per cent of the Australian population so a positive result raises but does not confirm probability, and it is used to weight the classification criteria rather than to replace imaging (Source: ASAS classification criteria for axial spondyloarthritis).
source_refs: ASAS classification criteria for axial spondyloarthritis

options.rationale: Waiting a year to see whether erosions appear concedes an untreated inflammatory year, which is the specific anti pattern that the non radiographic category was created to prevent (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial spondyloarthritis).

Lumbar imaging targets disc and nerve root disease, which the negative straight leg raise and normal reflexes already argue against, and gadolinium adds nothing when fluid sensitive sequences answer the question (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology).

explanation.summary: Falls in residential care are almost always multifactorial, and a structured review separates the modifiable contributors into medicines, vision, footwear, environment, continence and gait. Among medicines, the sedative hypnotics, antipsychotics and anticholinergics carry the strongest and most reversible association, and long-acting agents matter more than short-acting ones because the drug is still present at the pre dawn toilet trip. Deprescribing is done one agent at a time so that the effect of each withdrawal is interpretable, starting with the drug that has the weakest indication and the strongest harm signal. Abrupt cessation of a benzodiazepine taken for years risks rebound insomnia, agitation and seizures, so the withdrawal is staged over weeks with the resident and family informed. A timed up and go above 12 seconds already flags a person who needs a physiotherapy strength and balance program alongside the medication change.
key_points: Long-acting benzodiazepines are the highest yield first deprescribing target after falls in aged care.
Paired lying and standing pressures with a small drop remove postural hypotension from the differential.
Withdraw one agent at a time so the effect of each change can be judged.
Taper rather than stop, because seizures and rebound insomnia follow abrupt withdrawal after chronic use.
Pair the medication change with a strength and balance program and a vitamin D review.
explanation.pearls: Nitrazepam has an elimination half life of about 24 to 30 hours and is longer still in an older person with reduced clearance, which is why the 10 pm dose is still acting at the 5 am toilet trip that produced the fall.

sources.label: NPS MedicineWise: Deprescribing in older people

options.rationale: Antihypertensives are a legitimate falls target but the paired lying and standing readings show a drop of only 4 mmHg, which removes postural hypotension as the mechanism here (Source: NPS MedicineWise: Deprescribing in older people).
source_refs: NPS MedicineWise: Deprescribing in older people

options.rationale: Statin withdrawal is a reasonable later conversation about benefit horizon but statins do not cause unsteadiness or morning sedation, so it does not address the fall mechanism (Source: NPS MedicineWise: Deprescribing in older people).
source_refs: NPS MedicineWise: Deprescribing in older people

options.rationale: A long-acting benzodiazepine accumulates in an older person with reduced renal clearance and produces exactly this pattern of pre dawn unsteadiness with morning cognitive slowing, and gradual withdrawal reduces fall rates without precipitating a withdrawal syndrome (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Serotonergic antidepressants do raise fall and hyponatraemia risk, but her sodium is normal and abrupt withdrawal risks relapse of depression, so it ranks behind the sedative with the longer half life (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

Long term proton pump inhibitor use is worth reviewing for fracture and infection risk, but it does not cause gait instability and stopping it will not change tonight's fall risk (Source: NPS MedicineWise: Deprescribing in older people).
source_refs: NPS MedicineWise: Deprescribing in older people

explanation.summary: Delayed multiorgan drug hypersensitivity is distinguished from a simple exanthem by its long latency, its systemic features and the fact that it keeps evolving after the drug is withdrawn. Allopurinol, the aromatic anticonvulsants, sulfonamides, vancomycin and minocycline account for most Australian cases. Liver involvement is the commonest visceral manifestation and the usual cause of death, while thyroiditis and type 1 diabetes can appear months into recovery, so follow up thyroid function and glucose are scheduled rather than optional. Reactivation of human herpesvirus 6 is characteristic and partly explains the relapsing course during steroid taper. The culprit drug and its cross reactors must be recorded as an adverse drug reaction, since rechallenge produces a faster and more severe episode.
key_points: Latency of two to eight weeks distinguishes this reaction from an immediate hypersensitivity or a simple exanthem.
Eosinophilia, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy and transaminitis together make the diagnosis.
Negative Nikolsky sign with intact mucosae argues against epidermal necrolysis.
Systemic corticosteroid with a taper over six to eight weeks is indicated once visceral organs are involved.
Schedule thyroid function and glucose testing for months after recovery.
explanation.pearls: Taper prednisolone over at least six to eight weeks rather than two, because rapid withdrawal reliably produces a rebound flare of rash and hepatitis driven by herpesvirus reactivation.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms

options.rationale: Continuing the culprit drug in a reaction with hepatic and renal involvement allows the syndrome to escalate, and antihistamines relieve itch without touching the underlying T cell driven organ injury (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

Withdrawal alone suffices for a simple morbilliform exanthem but not once transaminases and creatinine are rising, because the reaction characteristically continues to worsen for weeks after the drug is stopped (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

Fever with facial oedema, eosinophilia above 1.5 x10^9/L, lymphadenopathy and hepatitis appearing three to eight weeks after drug exposure is the recognised pattern, and systemic corticosteroid with a slow taper over six to eight weeks is the accepted treatment for visceral involvement (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

Immunoglobulin is used in epidermal necrolysis where keratinocyte apoptosis and skin detachment dominate, and the negative Nikolsky sign with intact mucosae places this on a different axis from that diagnosis (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms

options.rationale: A febrile rash with lymphadenopathy invites an infective label, but eosinophilia with transaminitis points away from staphylococcal infection and a new beta lactam risks adding a second sensitising drug (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Prolactin concentration scales with lactotroph tumour volume, so the size of the mass and the height of the hormone should match, and a mismatch is itself the diagnostic finding. A large mass with only a modest elevation has two explanations: a non secreting lesion raising prolactin by compressing the stalk and interrupting dopamine delivery, or a genuine macroprolactinoma whose result is artefactually low because the immunoassay is saturated. Stalk effect rarely pushes prolactin above about 2000 to 3000 mIU/L, so the ceiling is the clue. The distinction is decisive because a true macroprolactinoma is treated medically with a dopamine agonist that usually shrinks the tumour and restores vision, whereas a non secreting adenoma compressing the chiasm goes to surgery. Any drug history of antipsychotics, metoclopramide, domperidone or high dose oestrogen, plus pregnancy, hypothyroidism and renal failure, must be excluded before the tumour is blamed.
key_points: Prolactin should be proportional to lactotroph tumour size; a mismatch demands explanation before treatment.
Assay saturation causes a falsely low result with very large tumours and is unmasked by serial dilution.
Macroprolactin causes the opposite artefact, a falsely high result in an asymptomatic person.
Stalk compression alone rarely raises prolactin beyond about 2000 to 3000 mIU/L.
A confirmed macroprolactinoma is treated with a dopamine agonist first, not with surgery, even with chiasmal compression.
explanation.pearls: Ask the laboratory specifically for a 1 in 100 dilution when a pituitary mass larger than 3 cm returns a prolactin under about 4000 mIU/L; the undiluted assay can under report a true value of more than 100000 mIU/L.

sources.label: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Hyperprolactinaemia

options.rationale: Surgery is the right answer for a chiasmal compressing mass that is not prolactin secreting, but committing to theatre before the prolactin is correctly measured risks operating on a tumour that would shrink on a tablet (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

Starting a dopamine agonist on an uncorrected result gambles that the mass is lactotroph derived, and a non secreting adenoma treated this way loses months of vision while the chiasm stays compressed (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

Macroprolactin is the mirror image problem, an inert immunoglobulin bound complex that makes prolactin look falsely high in an asymptomatic person, so it explains an unexpectedly raised result rather than an unexpectedly low one (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Hyperprolactinaemia).
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Hyperprolactinaemia

options.rationale: Screening for co secretion of growth hormone or cortisol is reasonable in a large adenoma but neither acromegalic features nor cushingoid features are present, and it does not resolve the discrepancy driving the treatment decision (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

A 3.4 cm lactotroph tumour should generate a prolactin in the tens of thousands, and when antibody binding sites are saturated the assay reports a falsely low value, so dilution unmasks the true concentration and decides between a tablet and an operation (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Hyperprolactinaemia).
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Hyperprolactinaemia

explanation.summary: Prostate specific antigen testing in Australia is an informed decision rather than a population screening program, offered every two years from age 50 to 69 to men who choose to test after a discussion of benefits and harms. Age related thresholds are used because the reference range rises with prostatic volume, and a result above the threshold triggers confirmation rather than immediate referral. Ejaculation, vigorous cycling, digital rectal examination, urinary infection and instrumentation all raise the value transiently, while five alpha reductase inhibitors halve it and require the result to be doubled for interpretation. Men with a first degree relative diagnosed young, or with a known pathogenic BRCA2 variant, start testing earlier and test more often. The harm the pathway is designed to avoid is overdiagnosis of indolent disease, which is why active surveillance features heavily once low risk cancer is found.
key_points: Confirm an initial raised result with a repeat sample in one to three months before referring.
Testing is offered two yearly from 50 to 69 years after an informed decision, not as universal screening.
Ejaculation, cycling, infection and instrumentation transiently raise the value.
Five alpha reductase inhibitors halve the measured value, so double it before comparing with the threshold.
Digital rectal examination is not used alone as a screening test in primary care.
explanation.pearls: A man taking finasteride or dutasteride for six months or more has a measured value about half his true value, so a reading of 2.5 mcg/L on treatment should be read as 5 mcg/L and acted on accordingly.

sources.label: Prostate Cancer Foundation of Australia and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines
RACGP: Guidelines for preventive activities in general practice

options.rationale: Australian practice is to confirm an initial elevation with a second sample within one to three months before any referral, because biological variation, unrecognised prostatitis and recent instrumentation mean a substantial share of raised results settle on repeat (Source: Prostate Cancer Foundation of Australia and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines).
source_refs: Prostate Cancer Foundation of Australia and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines

options.rationale: Referral for tissue sampling follows a confirmed elevation, and proceeding on one unconfirmed result exposes a man to sepsis and haematuria for a value that may normalise (Source: Prostate Cancer Foundation of Australia and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines).
source_refs: Prostate Cancer Foundation of Australia and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines

options.rationale: Multiparametric imaging is the right next test once the elevation is confirmed and the man has accepted a diagnostic pathway, but it sits after confirmation rather than replacing it (Source: Prostate Cancer Foundation of Australia and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines).
source_refs: Prostate Cancer Foundation of Australia and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines

options.rationale: A two yearly interval applies to men whose result sits below the age related threshold, and applying it to a value of 5.2 mcg/L defers a genuinely abnormal result (Source: RACGP: Guidelines for preventive activities in general practice).
source_refs: RACGP: Guidelines for preventive activities in general practice

options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics to lower the value are a recognised anti pattern that delays diagnosis, and the sterile urine without pyuria gives no support for treating prostatitis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Warfarin reversal is graded by whether bleeding is present and how severe it is, not by the numerical value alone. With no bleeding and a value under 10, omitting doses with or without low dose oral vitamin K is enough; with no bleeding and a value of 10 or above, oral vitamin K is added; with clinically significant bleeding, factor replacement is given regardless of the number. Trimethoprim, metronidazole, amiodarone, fluconazole and the macrolides are common Australian precipitants of a sudden rise because they inhibit warfarin metabolism or displace it. The dose of intravenous vitamin K used in bleeding is deliberately high because the aim is durable correction rather than preserving future warfarin sensitivity. Restarting anticoagulation after the bleeding source is controlled is a separate decision that weighs stroke risk against rebleeding, and in atrial fibrillation it is usually resumed within days.
key_points: Clinically significant bleeding on warfarin means factor concentrate plus intravenous vitamin K, whatever the number.
Vitamin K alone takes six to twenty four hours because it requires new factor synthesis.
Fresh frozen plasma is the fallback only when concentrate is unavailable.
Trimethoprim and other enzyme inhibitors are frequent precipitants of a sudden rise.
A raised value without bleeding is managed by omission with or without oral vitamin K.
explanation.pearls: Prothrombinex-VF is dosed at 25 to 50 units per kilogram by indication and corrects the international normalised ratio within about fifteen minutes, but its factor half life is shorter than warfarin's, so omitting the concurrent vitamin K produces rebound coagulopathy overnight.

sources.label: Australasian Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis: Warfarin reversal consensus guidelines
National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines

options.rationale: Simple omission is the strategy for a raised value without bleeding, and it leaves this woman anticoagulated for another day while she continues to bleed (Source: Australasian Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis: Warfarin reversal consensus guidelines).
source_refs: Australasian Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis: Warfarin reversal consensus guidelines

options.rationale: Clinically significant bleeding on warfarin calls for immediate factor replacement, which restores the vitamin K dependent factors within minutes, together with intravenous vitamin K to sustain the correction once the concentrate is cleared (Source: Australasian Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis: Warfarin reversal consensus guidelines).
source_refs: Australasian Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis: Warfarin reversal consensus guidelines

options.rationale: Vitamin K takes six to eight hours to begin correcting and up to a day for full effect because new factor synthesis is required, so it cannot be the sole agent when bleeding is active (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

Plasma remains the fallback where concentrate is unavailable, but it corrects incompletely and delivers a large volume load to an older woman, so it is second choice (Source: National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines).
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines

options.rationale: Red cells and antifibrinolytics address the consequences of blood loss rather than the coagulopathy driving it, and neither lowers the international normalised ratio (Source: National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines).
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines

explanation.summary: Psoriatic arthritis is under recognised because up to a sixth of patients present with joints before skin, and the skin that is present hides in the scalp, natal cleft, umbilicus and nails. Its five recognised patterns are asymmetric oligoarthritis, distal interphalangeal predominant disease, symmetric polyarthritis resembling rheumatoid disease, spondylitis, and arthritis mutilans. Dactylitis reflects inflammation of the flexor tendon sheath as well as the joint, which is why the whole digit swells rather than the joint line alone. Diagnosis is clinical and supported by the classification criteria, since no serological test confirms it and inflammatory markers are normal in a third of patients. Early treatment matters because erosive damage accrues within the first two years, and methotrexate or a targeted biologic is started rather than waiting for radiographic change.
key_points: Examine the scalp, umbilicus, natal cleft and nails when an inflammatory arthritis has no obvious skin disease.
Dactylitis is whole digit swelling from tenosynovitis plus synovitis and is highly suggestive.
Distal interphalangeal involvement separates this from rheumatoid arthritis, which spares those joints.
Normal inflammatory markers occur in about a third of patients and do not exclude the diagnosis.
Reactive arthritis needs a mucocutaneous clue such as conjunctivitis, urethritis or keratoderma.
explanation.pearls: Nail pitting of more than twenty pits across the fingernails carries a strong association with distal interphalangeal joint disease, because the nail matrix and the extensor enthesis of that joint share a continuous connective tissue attachment.

options.rationale: The enteric illness fits the timing, but reactive arthritis does not produce nail pitting or scaly plaques, and it usually brings conjunctivitis or urethritis, both absent here (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology).

Rheumatoid disease is symmetrical, spares the distal interphalangeal joints and does not cause whole digit swelling, so the distribution here argues against it despite the negative serology (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Psoriatic arthritis).

Whole digit swelling from combined tenosynovitis and synovitis, distal interphalangeal involvement, nail pitting and hidden scalp and umbilical plaques together make this the diagnosis even when the patient has never reported a skin condition (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Psoriatic arthritis).

Gout can involve the toe and knee together, but a serum urate of 0.34 mmol/L between attacks and the absence of tophi make crystal disease an unlikely explanation for eight weeks of swelling (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology).
