Plaques do not undergo malignant transformation and do not warrant scheduled surveillance CT
A new unilateral pleural effusion after exposure is mesothelioma until proven otherwise
Documenting exposure supports access to state dust diseases compensation schemes
explanation.pearls: Mesothelioma latency typically exceeds 30 years from first exposure, so a new unilateral pleural effusion in a patient with plaques warrants pleural fluid cytology and early thoracoscopic biopsy rather than a period of observation.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Asbestos-related Disease
BMJ Best Practice: Asbestos-related Pleural Disease

options.rationale: Asbestosis is interstitial fibrosis of the lung parenchyma producing a restrictive pattern and basal reticulation, and his parenchyma and spirometry are normal, so the two entities are being conflated. Antifibrotic agents are used in progressive pulmonary fibrosis, not in pleural disease. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Asbestos-related Disease)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Asbestos-related Disease

options.rationale: Discrete plaques do not restrict lung expansion and are not amenable to or improved by surgery. Decortication is considered for a trapped lung from diffuse pleural thickening causing symptomatic restriction. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Asbestos-related Disease)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Asbestos-related Disease

options.rationale: Plaques themselves do not undergo malignant change and no screening program has shown benefit, so interval CT delivers radiation and incidental findings without proven gain. Repeat imaging is driven by new symptoms rather than by a fixed schedule. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Asbestos-related Disease)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Asbestos-related Disease

options.rationale: Calcification reflects the age of the plaque rather than any protective effect, and the underlying exposure still carries a lifetime risk of mesothelioma and lung cancer. Reassurance must therefore be paired with advice about reporting new symptoms. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Asbestos-related Pleural Disease)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Asbestos-related Pleural Disease

options.rationale: Discrete pleural plaques are the commonest manifestation of asbestos exposure, are not premalignant in themselves and do not cause symptoms or functional impairment, so the appropriate advice is reassurance with clear safety netting. Their presence does confirm exposure and supports registration for compensation entitlements. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Asbestos-related Disease)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Asbestos-related Disease
BMJ Best Practice: Asbestos-related Pleural Disease

explanation.summary: Prosthetic joint infection divides into early, delayed and late presentations, and the delayed form caused by low virulence organisms such as coagulase negative staphylococci and Cutibacterium is the one most often missed. Its hallmark is persistent pain from the time of the operation that never resolves, often with normal or only mildly raised inflammatory markers and no fever, in contrast to the dramatic presentation of acute haematogenous infection. Peri-prosthetic lucency on radiography indicates loosening, which may be aseptic or septic, and these cannot be distinguished radiologically. Synovial fluid analysis is central, combining cell count with differential, crystal examination and prolonged culture, and multiple intraoperative tissue samples are taken if surgery follows. Because a patient can have both crystal disease and infection, finding crystals never excludes sepsis, and treatment usually requires surgical management alongside prolonged targeted antimicrobial therapy.
key_points: Pain that never settles after joint replacement suggests chronic low grade infection rather than wear
Low virulence organisms produce minimal fever and only modest inflammatory marker rises
Radiographic lucency shows loosening but cannot separate septic from aseptic causes
The presence of crystals in synovial fluid does not exclude coexisting infection
Hold antibiotics until adequate samples are taken unless the patient is septic
explanation.pearls: A serum uric acid level is useless for diagnosing an acute crystal flare, since it is often normal during an attack, so in any prosthetic joint the aspirate must go for cell count, polarised microscopy and prolonged culture together.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Prosthetic Joint Infection

options.rationale: Treating for crystal disease without sampling risks suppressing the inflammatory signs of an infected prosthesis while the biofilm progresses, and a raised serum uric acid does not confirm a flare because levels are often normal or high independent of acute crystal inflammation. Steroids become reasonable once infection has been formally excluded. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Oral antibiotics started before sampling reduce the culture yield that determines the entire surgical and antimicrobial plan, and outpatient management understates the seriousness of a loosening prosthesis. Empirical therapy is reserved for the septic or rapidly deteriorating patient. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Nuclear imaging cannot reliably separate infection from aseptic loosening, which is the actual question, and it delays the test that answers it. Its role is largely limited to cases where the diagnosis remains unclear after aspiration. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Prosthetic Joint Infection)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Prosthetic Joint Infection

options.rationale: Arthroscopic washout does not adequately debride a prosthesis and is not the recognised surgical approach for an infected implant, where debridement with liner exchange or staged revision is required. Proceeding to surgery without an organism also removes the chance of targeted therapy. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Prosthetic Joint Infection)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Prosthetic Joint Infection

options.rationale: Pain present from the time of surgery that never settles, with peri-prosthetic lucency and a raised C-reactive protein, raises chronic low grade prosthetic infection, and aspiration is the single test that separates it from a crystal flare or aseptic loosening. Withholding antibiotics until the sample is taken preserves the culture yield needed to plan revision surgery. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Prosthetic Joint Infection

explanation.summary: Intermittent claudication is reproducible muscular pain brought on by a predictable walking distance and relieved within minutes by rest, which distinguishes it from neurogenic claudication where relief requires sitting or spinal flexion rather than simply stopping. The ankle brachial index is the key bedside investigation, with values from 0.91 to 1.40 considered normal, 0.90 or below diagnostic of peripheral arterial disease, and values above 1.40 indicating incompressible calcified vessels that require toe pressures instead. The presence of peripheral arterial disease marks a cardiovascular risk equivalent to established coronary disease, so the priority is aggressive secondary prevention with lipid lowering, antiplatelet therapy, blood pressure and glycaemic control, and smoking cessation. Supervised exercise therapy improves maximal walking distance substantially and is recommended before considering revascularisation. Rest pain, ulceration or gangrene define chronic limb threatening ischaemia and demand urgent vascular referral.
key_points: Claudication is relieved by stopping alone; neurogenic pain needs sitting or forward flexion
An ankle brachial index of 0.90 or below is diagnostic of peripheral arterial disease
An index above 1.40 indicates calcified incompressible vessels and requires toe pressure measurement
Cardiovascular death, not limb loss, is the dominant risk in stable claudication
Supervised exercise therapy precedes revascularisation for stable symptoms
explanation.pearls: Diabetes and chronic kidney disease calcify the tibial vessels and can push the ankle brachial index above 1.40 despite severe disease, so a falsely reassuring index in these patients should be replaced by a toe brachial index.

sources.label: National Heart Foundation of Australia: Peripheral Arterial Disease
BMJ Best Practice: Peripheral Arterial Disease

options.rationale: Urgent referral is driven by rest pain, tissue loss or an acutely threatened limb, none of which is present in stable claudication with warm perfused feet. Revascularisation is considered when symptoms remain disabling despite an adequate trial of medical therapy and exercise. (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia: Peripheral Arterial Disease)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia: Peripheral Arterial Disease

options.rationale: Neurogenic claudication is relieved by spinal flexion and provoked by standing, and both features are specifically absent, while the reduced ankle brachial index gives a vascular explanation. Imaging the spine would be appropriate if the pulses and index were normal. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Peripheral Arterial Disease)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Peripheral Arterial Disease

options.rationale: Pentoxifylline has minimal effect on walking distance and does not modify cardiovascular risk, so it addresses neither the symptom nor the underlying danger. Symptom directed pharmacotherapy is a later consideration after risk factor treatment and exercise. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Peripheral Arterial Disease)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Peripheral Arterial Disease

options.rationale: A reduced ankle brachial index identifies established atherosclerosis in which cardiovascular death, not limb loss, is the dominant risk, so intensive secondary prevention plus supervised exercise is the first line intervention. Structured exercise reliably improves claudication distance and complements rather than competes with risk factor treatment. (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia: Peripheral Arterial Disease)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia: Peripheral Arterial Disease
BMJ Best Practice: Peripheral Arterial Disease

options.rationale: Avoiding exercise removes the intervention with the best evidence for improving walking distance and allows deconditioning, so it worsens the condition it aims to protect. Monitoring alone also leaves a very high cardiovascular risk untreated. (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia: Peripheral Arterial Disease)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia: Peripheral Arterial Disease

explanation.summary: Engineered stone contains a far higher crystalline silica content than natural granite or marble, and dry cutting generates respirable particles that have produced an epidemic of accelerated silicosis in young Australian benchtop workers, prompting a national prohibition on the manufacture, supply and installation of the product. Accelerated disease develops within three to ten years of intense exposure, in contrast to the classical form that appears after decades, and it can progress even after exposure ends. Imaging typically shows upper zone small rounded opacities with hilar lymphadenopathy that may calcify peripherally, and high resolution CT is required for staging because plain radiography understates the extent of disease. No treatment reverses the fibrosis, so management rests on exposure cessation, statutory notification with workplace assessment, screening of coworkers, vaccination, and surveillance for the recognised complications of tuberculosis, autoimmune disease, lung cancer and progressive massive fibrosis. Lung transplantation is the only option in advanced disease.
key_points: Engineered stone dry cutting causes accelerated silicosis within three to ten years of exposure
Upper zone nodularity with hilar lymphadenopathy is the characteristic imaging pattern
High resolution CT is required because plain radiography understates disease extent
The disease is notifiable, which triggers workplace assessment and coworker screening
There is no treatment that reverses the fibrosis; exposure cessation is the key intervention
explanation.pearls: Silicosis raises tuberculosis risk roughly three-fold and the risk persists after exposure ends, so patients need testing for latent infection at diagnosis and treatment of a positive result even when they are entirely asymptomatic.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Silicosis

options.rationale: Corticosteroids do not alter the course of silica induced fibrosis and would expose him to harm while the causative exposure continues. They are the mainstay in sarcoidosis, which the normal angiotensin converting enzyme and clear occupational history make far less likely. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Silicosis)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Silicosis

options.rationale: A negative interferon gamma release assay with no fever, sweats or weight loss makes active tuberculosis unlikely as the primary diagnosis. Tuberculosis remains an important complication of silicosis, so it must be excluded, but empirical treatment is not justified on this evidence. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Silicosis)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Silicosis

options.rationale: The diagnosis rests on the combination of a clear exposure history and characteristic imaging, so biopsy is usually unnecessary and carries risk. It is reserved for cases where imaging and exposure history are discordant. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Silicosis)

Progression is driven by continuing exposure and there is no treatment that reverses established fibrosis, so ending exposure is the intervention that most changes his trajectory, alongside statutory notification that triggers workplace assessment and screening of coworkers. High resolution CT is far more sensitive than radiography for staging and for detecting progressive massive fibrosis. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Silicosis)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Silicosis

options.rationale: His spirometry shows a restrictive pattern with a preserved ratio rather than airflow obstruction, so inhaled therapy targets a physiology he does not have. These agents would be appropriate if the ratio were reduced with reversible obstruction. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Silicosis)

explanation.summary: Syncope without warning, particularly while standing or exerting, should be presumed cardiac until proven otherwise, and the absence of a postictal phase helps separate it from seizure. Second degree atrioventricular block is divided by whether the PR interval lengthens progressively before the dropped beat, which indicates block within the node and is often benign, or whether P waves fail to conduct with a constant PR interval, which indicates disease in the His-Purkinje system below the node. The infranodal form is dangerous because the escape rhythm is slow and unreliable, progression to complete heart block is unpredictable, and an accompanying bundle branch block confirms diffuse conduction system disease. Reversible contributors such as rate limiting drugs, hyperkalaemia, hypothyroidism and ischaemia must be excluded, but where none is found and syncope has occurred, permanent pacing is indicated. Australian driving standards require a period off driving after syncope and after device implantation.
key_points: Abrupt syncope without prodrome and with rapid full recovery suggests an arrhythmic cause
Dropped beats without progressive PR lengthening indicate infranodal block
Coexisting bundle branch block signals diffuse conduction system disease
Exclude rate limiting drugs, electrolyte disturbance, hypothyroidism and ischaemia first
Syncope with high grade block is an indication for permanent pacing, not for further monitoring
explanation.pearls: The PR interval before the dropped beat is the discriminator: constant PR with a sudden non-conducted P wave localises block below the node and mandates pacing, whereas progressive PR lengthening usually needs only observation.

sources.label: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Cardiac Pacing and Implantable Devices
BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of Syncope

options.rationale: The diagnostic finding is already present on the resting ECG, so ambulatory monitoring adds nothing while leaving him unmonitored and at risk of asystole in the interim. Holter monitoring is for symptoms without a captured rhythm abnormality. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Cardiac Pacing and Implantable Devices)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Cardiac Pacing and Implantable Devices

options.rationale: These measures treat orthostatic intolerance, which is excluded by normal postural blood pressures, and abrupt collapse without warning is not the pattern of vasovagal or orthostatic syncope. They would suit a patient with a documented postural drop and prodromal symptoms. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of Syncope)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of Syncope

options.rationale: A loop recorder is for unexplained recurrent syncope after the initial workup is negative, whereas the mechanism here has already been identified on the ECG. Inserting one would delay definitive therapy in a patient with a high risk conduction abnormality. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Cardiac Pacing and Implantable Devices)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Cardiac Pacing and Implantable Devices

options.rationale: Non-conducted P waves without progressive PR lengthening indicate block below the atrioventricular node, which is unpredictable and can progress abruptly to complete block or asystole, and syncope makes this a class one pacing indication. Monitored admission covers the interval until the device is implanted. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Cardiac Pacing and Implantable Devices)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Cardiac Pacing and Implantable Devices
BMJ Best Practice: Assessment of Syncope

options.rationale: Pharmacological attempts to enhance conduction are unreliable and have no place in managing infranodal block with syncope. Chronotropic agents are used as a temporising measure in symptomatic bradycardia while pacing is arranged, not as definitive therapy. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Cardiac Pacing and Implantable Devices)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Cardiac Pacing and Implantable Devices

explanation.summary: Rational antiemetic prescribing works backwards from the likely emetic pathway rather than reaching for a familiar drug, because each pathway is dominated by different receptors. Chemical causes such as opioids, hypercalcaemia and uraemia act on the chemoreceptor trigger zone, which is rich in dopamine receptors and is best treated with haloperidol. Gastric stasis and partial outlet obstruction produce large volume vomits with early satiety and respond to a prokinetic such as metoclopramide. Vestibular causes respond to antihistamines or anticholinergics, chemotherapy and radiotherapy act largely through serotonin release, and raised intracranial pressure or bowel obstruction responds to corticosteroids. Opioid induced nausea usually settles within five to seven days as tolerance develops, so the antiemetic can often be withdrawn rather than continued indefinitely.
key_points: Identify the emetic pathway first, then select the antiemetic that blocks its dominant receptor
Opioids, hypercalcaemia and uraemia act chemically and respond to dopamine blockade
Large volume vomits with early satiety indicate gastric stasis and call for a prokinetic
Serotonin antagonists are most useful for chemotherapy and radiotherapy induced nausea
Consider hypercalcaemia in any patient with malignancy and new nausea
explanation.pearls: Opioid induced nausea is usually self-limiting through tolerance within five to seven days, so review the antiemetic at one week and stop it rather than continuing a drug that adds anticholinergic or extrapyramidal burden.

options.rationale: This antispasmodic is used for colic and secretions in bowel obstruction, and the soft abdomen with normal bowel sounds and no distension excludes that mechanism. It would be appropriate for the vomiting of malignant obstruction with colicky pain. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

Nausea beginning after an opioid dose increase, worse with movement and without features of obstruction or gastric stasis, is driven by stimulation of the chemoreceptor trigger zone, where dopamine blockade is the mechanistically matched treatment. Low dose haloperidol is the preferred agent for opioid induced nausea. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

Prokinetic therapy suits gastric stasis with early satiety, large volume vomits and a succussion splash, none of which she has. Unlike haloperidol, metoclopramide is chosen for its prokinetic action, and there is no stasis here to treat. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

Serotonin antagonists are most effective for chemotherapy and radiotherapy induced nausea, and her last chemotherapy was six weeks ago, so the driving mechanism is different. They also worsen the constipation that opioids already cause. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Corticosteroids address nausea from raised intracranial pressure or bowel obstruction, and she has no headache, visual change or obstructive features to justify this. Dexamethasone is often added as an adjuvant when a single agent fails rather than chosen first. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Palliative Care)

explanation.summary: Autoimmune exocrinopathy causes lymphocytic infiltration and destruction of the lacrimal and salivary glands, producing dry eyes and dry mouth together with fatigue and arthralgia, and it is far more common in women in their fifth and sixth decades. Because subjective dryness is extremely common and often drug induced, diagnosis requires objective evidence of reduced tear or saliva production alongside serology, with labial gland biopsy reserved for seronegative cases. Anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies are the characteristic specificities, and a polyclonal rise in immunoglobulin G with a raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate but normal C-reactive protein is a typical pattern. Beyond the glandular disease, patients face accelerated dental caries, corneal damage, interstitial lung and renal involvement, and a markedly increased lifetime risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Anti-Ro antibodies also carry obstetric significance because of the risk of congenital heart block in a future pregnancy.
key_points: Objective testing of tear or saliva production is required because subjective dryness is non-specific
Anti-Ro and anti-La are the characteristic antibodies; biopsy is for seronegative cases
A polyclonal immunoglobulin G rise with a raised sedimentation rate and normal C-reactive protein is typical
Rheumatoid factor is often positive without rheumatoid arthritis being present
Persistent asymmetrical parotid enlargement raises concern for lymphoma
explanation.pearls: Anti-Ro antibodies cross the placenta and carry roughly a two per cent risk of congenital complete heart block, so a woman of reproductive age with these antibodies needs serial fetal cardiac monitoring from around 16 weeks in any future pregnancy.

options.rationale: This combination assesses systemic lupus erythematosus, which characteristically presents with rash, serositis, cytopenias or nephritis rather than isolated glandular dryness. It would be pursued if she had photosensitivity, proteinuria or unexplained cytopenias. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Sjogren Syndrome)

A positive rheumatoid factor here is a common accompaniment of glandular autoimmunity rather than evidence of rheumatoid arthritis, and she has arthralgia without synovitis. This testing is indicated when persistent joint swelling is present on examination. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Sjogren Syndrome)

Sarcoidosis can cause parotid enlargement and a dry mouth, but it usually produces respiratory symptoms and hilar lymphadenopathy, and the enzyme level lacks both sensitivity and specificity. It becomes a consideration when there is cough, breathlessness or erythema nodosum. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Sjogren Syndrome)

The combination of sicca symptoms, parotid enlargement, a raised polyclonal immunoglobulin G and a speckled antinuclear antibody points to autoimmune exocrinopathy, in which these specific antibodies together with an objective dryness measure form the diagnostic criteria. Objective testing is essential because subjective dryness alone is far too common to be diagnostic. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Sjogren Syndrome)

Aspiration is used to investigate a discrete or asymmetrical parotid mass raising concern for lymphoma, whereas bilateral diffuse enlargement in this context does not require it initially. It becomes important if one gland enlarges persistently or asymmetrically. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Sjogren Syndrome)

explanation.summary: Pulmonary hypertension is characteristically diagnosed late because the early symptom is isolated exertional breathlessness with a normal chest radiograph and normal spirometry, and patients are frequently treated for asthma or deconditioning for months to years first. The physiological fingerprint is a disproportionate reduction in diffusing capacity with preserved lung volumes and no airflow obstruction, and the physical signs of right ventricular pressure overload appear as the disease advances. Exertional syncope is an ominous feature indicating that cardiac output cannot rise with demand. Echocardiography is the screening investigation of choice, and it also excludes the left heart disease that accounts for the majority of cases, while right heart catheterisation remains the diagnostic reference standard performed in a specialist centre. Ventilation perfusion scanning is mandatory in the work up because chronic thromboembolic disease is the one form that is potentially curable by surgical endarterectomy.
key_points: A reduced diffusing capacity with normal volumes and no obstruction suggests pulmonary vascular disease
Failure to respond to adequate inhaled therapy should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis
Loud pulmonary second sound, parasternal heave and raised jugular venous pressure are late signs
Exertional syncope indicates a fixed cardiac output and carries a poor prognosis
Echocardiography screens; right heart catheterisation confirms at a specialist centre
explanation.pearls: A ventilation perfusion scan is mandatory in every pulmonary hypertension work up because chronic thromboembolic disease is the only potentially curable form, and CT pulmonary angiography can miss the chronic organised thrombus that the scan detects.

sources.label: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pulmonary Hypertension
Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pulmonary Hypertension

options.rationale: Breathlessness with a loud pulmonary second sound, parasternal heave, raised jugular venous pressure and an isolated fall in diffusing capacity with clear lungs points to pulmonary vascular disease, and echocardiography is the recommended screening test. It also identifies the left heart and valvular causes that are far commoner than primary pulmonary vascular disease. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pulmonary Hypertension)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pulmonary Hypertension
Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pulmonary Hypertension

options.rationale: Interstitial disease reduces the diffusing capacity but almost always restricts the forced vital capacity and produces crackles, and her volumes and examination are normal. This imaging becomes the priority when restriction accompanies the reduced diffusing capacity. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pulmonary Hypertension)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pulmonary Hypertension

options.rationale: Exercise testing quantifies functional limitation but does not identify the anatomical cause, and it is used to refine assessment once the structural diagnosis is known. It is most valuable when the resting workup is normal and the cause of breathlessness remains unexplained. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pulmonary Hypertension)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pulmonary Hypertension

options.rationale: Catheterisation is the diagnostic reference standard but is invasive and is performed at a specialist centre after non-invasive screening has raised the probability. Ordering it first would invert the recognised diagnostic sequence. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pulmonary Hypertension)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pulmonary Hypertension

options.rationale: Asthma does not reduce the diffusing capacity or raise the jugular venous pressure, and two adequate inhaled treatment trials have already failed. Provocation testing is reserved for suspected asthma with normal spirometry and no cardiovascular signs. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pulmonary Hypertension)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pulmonary Hypertension

explanation.summary: Antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures was progressively restricted after evidence showed that cumulative bacteraemia from chewing and toothbrushing vastly exceeds that from a single dental visit, and that prophylaxis prevents very few cases. Current Australian recommendations confine prophylaxis to patients at highest risk of a poor outcome should endocarditis occur: those with a prosthetic valve or prosthetic material used in valve repair, previous infective endocarditis, specified congenital heart disease, cardiac transplant recipients with valvulopathy, and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander patients with rheumatic heart disease. The procedures that warrant cover are those involving manipulation of gingival tissue, the periapical region of a tooth, or perforation of the oral mucosa. A single oral dose given shortly before the procedure is the standard regimen, with clindamycin used for immediate penicillin hypersensitivity. Meticulous oral hygiene and regular dental review reduce endocarditis risk far more than episodic prophylaxis.
key_points: Prosthetic material in a valve repair, including an annuloplasty ring, confers highest risk status
Risk category depends on the cardiac condition, not on current lesion severity
Only procedures involving gingival or periapical manipulation or mucosal perforation require cover
A single pre-procedural oral dose is the regimen; no post-procedural course is given
Mitral valve prolapse and bicuspid aortic valve no longer warrant prophylaxis
explanation.pearls: Give the single oral amoxicillin dose in the 60 minutes before the procedure, and substitute clindamycin only for immediate hypersensitivity, since a delayed rash to penicillin does not preclude amoxicillin use.

sources.label: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Infective Endocarditis Prophylaxis

options.rationale: Prosthetic material used in a valve repair, including an annuloplasty ring, places a patient in the highest risk category regardless of whether the native leaflets were preserved. The distinction between a repaired and a replaced valve does not determine prophylaxis when foreign material is present. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Prosthetic material used in valve repair places him in the group at highest risk of adverse outcomes from endocarditis, and a dental extraction involves manipulation of the gingival tissue, so a single dose shortly before the procedure is indicated. Amoxicillin is the recommended agent in the absence of penicillin allergy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Infective Endocarditis Prophylaxis

options.rationale: Risk categorisation depends on the underlying cardiac condition rather than the current severity of the lesion, so a good haemodynamic result does not remove the indication. Severity would matter for surveillance and surgical planning, not for prophylaxis. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Infective Endocarditis Prophylaxis)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Infective Endocarditis Prophylaxis

options.rationale: Prophylaxis is a single dose given before the procedure to cover the transient bacteraemia, and a post-procedural course adds toxicity and resistance without benefit. Extended therapy is treatment for established infection, not prevention. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

This reasoning underpins the narrowing of prophylaxis to high risk patients only, but it does not apply to someone in the highest risk category undergoing a gingival procedure. It correctly explains why patients with mitral valve prolapse or bicuspid valves no longer receive prophylaxis. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Infective Endocarditis Prophylaxis)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Infective Endocarditis Prophylaxis

explanation.summary: Raynaud phenomenon is common and usually primary, but a set of clinical features reliably separates the benign form from vasospasm secondary to connective tissue disease. Primary disease typically begins in the teens or twenties, is symmetrical, spares the thumbs in a variable pattern, and shows normal nailfold capillaries with negative serology and no tissue damage. Features that mandate investigation include onset after the age of 30, asymmetry, digital ulcers or pitting scars, abnormal capillaroscopy, and a positive antinuclear antibody, especially with a nucleolar or centromere pattern. In systemic sclerosis, vasospasm commonly precedes other manifestations by years, so it represents an opportunity for early diagnosis before organ damage occurs. Baseline assessment of lung function with diffusing capacity, echocardiography and blood pressure monitoring is essential, because interstitial lung disease and pulmonary hypertension are now the leading causes of death, and renal crisis remains a treatable emergency.
key_points: Onset after age 30 with digital pitting and skin tightening indicates secondary disease
Abnormal nailfold capillaroscopy is one of the strongest predictors of connective tissue disease
A nucleolar antinuclear antibody pattern is characteristic of systemic sclerosis
Vasospasm often precedes other features by years, offering a window for early diagnosis
Interstitial lung disease and pulmonary hypertension are the leading causes of death
explanation.pearls: Scleroderma renal crisis presents with accelerated hypertension and a rapid creatinine rise, and is treated with an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor even as renal function deteriorates, which is the reverse of usual practice in acute kidney injury.

options.rationale: Primary vasospasm requires normal capillaroscopy, negative serology, no digital ulceration and no skin change, and each of those conditions is violated here. Reassurance alone would miss an evolving connective tissue disease with organ risk. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Systemic Sclerosis)

Nifedipine is appropriate symptomatic therapy but treating the vasospasm alone leaves the underlying systemic disease unassessed and unmonitored. It should accompany, not replace, evaluation for internal organ involvement. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Systemic Sclerosis)

Large vessel disease produces asymmetrical symptoms, absent pulses or a subclavian bruit, and does not explain skin thickening or abnormal capillaroscopy. Duplex imaging is indicated for unilateral digital ischaemia or a suspected thoracic outlet lesion. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Raynaud Phenomenon)

Late onset vasospasm with skin tightening, a digital pit, reflux and abnormal capillaroscopy on a strongly positive nucleolar antinuclear antibody indicates secondary disease, where specific antibody subtypes stratify risk and baseline screening detects the interstitial lung disease and pulmonary hypertension that drive mortality. Identifying organ involvement early is what alters outcome. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Systemic Sclerosis)

Acid suppression treats one manifestation but a six month delay allows undetected lung or renal involvement to progress unmonitored. Symptomatic treatment of reflux is part of management rather than a substitute for systemic assessment. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Systemic Sclerosis)

explanation.summary: Microscopic colitis is a common and underdiagnosed cause of chronic watery diarrhoea, particularly in women over 50, and it accounts for a substantial minority of patients investigated for non-bloody diarrhoea with a normal endoscopic appearance. It comprises two histological subtypes, collagenous colitis with a thickened subepithelial collagen band and lymphocytic colitis with increased intraepithelial lymphocytes, which behave similarly and are managed identically. Because the mucosa looks normal, the diagnosis is missed entirely unless random biopsies are taken from both the right and left colon during the procedure. Several drugs are implicated, most consistently proton pump inhibitors, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and ranitidine, and withdrawal of the offending agent alone can produce remission. Where symptoms persist, budesonide is the treatment with the strongest evidence for inducing and maintaining remission, and there is an association with coeliac disease and other autoimmune conditions.
key_points: Suspect it in chronic watery non-bloody diarrhoea with a normal colonoscopy in an older woman
Nocturnal diarrhoea and weight loss are alarm features that exclude a functional diagnosis
Diagnosis requires random biopsies from right and left colon, since the mucosa appears normal
Proton pump inhibitors, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and serotonergic agents are recognised triggers
Budesonide has the strongest evidence for inducing remission when drug withdrawal fails
explanation.pearls: Screen every patient for coeliac disease, because it coexists in a substantial minority and its presence changes management entirely; then stop the implicated drug before committing to budesonide, since withdrawal alone can resolve symptoms.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic Diarrhoea

options.rationale: Nocturnal diarrhoea and weight loss are alarm features that place this outside a functional diagnosis, which requires the absence of such features. Serotonergic drugs can loosen stools but would not produce eight months of nocturnal symptoms with weight loss. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic Diarrhoea)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic Diarrhoea

options.rationale: Chronic watery non-bloody diarrhoea including at night in an older woman with a macroscopically normal colonoscopy is the defining presentation, and the diagnosis rests entirely on the random biopsies that were taken. Proton pump inhibitors and serotonergic agents are both recognised precipitants. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic Diarrhoea)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic Diarrhoea

options.rationale: Bile acid malabsorption typically follows ileal resection, ileal Crohn disease or cholecystectomy, and her terminal ileum was visualised and normal with no surgical history. It remains a differential that is tested by a trial of a bile acid sequestrant if histology is normal. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic Diarrhoea)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic Diarrhoea

options.rationale: Crohn disease produces macroscopically visible aphthous ulceration or strictures and usually a substantially higher calprotectin with raised inflammatory markers. Both raise calprotectin, but only microscopic colitis leaves the mucosa looking entirely normal. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Microscopic Colitis)

Bacterial overgrowth characteristically causes bloating, flatulence and steatorrhoea rather than large volume watery nocturnal stools, and it does not raise faecal calprotectin. It would be tested by breath testing if the histology returned normal. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic Diarrhoea)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Chronic Diarrhoea

explanation.summary: Melioidosis is caused by an environmental Gram negative bacillus found in soil and surface water across northern Australia, and cases cluster in the wet season after exposure to mud and heavy rain. The major risk factors are diabetes, hazardous alcohol use, chronic lung or kidney disease, and immunosuppression, and presentations range from pneumonia, often cavitating, to abscesses and septic shock. The organism is intrinsically resistant to penicillins, ceftriaxone and aminoglycosides, so patients characteristically deteriorate on standard community-acquired pneumonia therapy while the culture is incubating. Treatment has two phases: intensive intravenous therapy with meropenem for severe disease or ceftazidime for less severe disease, for at least two weeks, followed by three months of oral eradication therapy, usually trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole, because relapse is otherwise common.
key_points: Wet season soil exposure with diabetes or heavy alcohol use is the classic risk profile in northern Australia
The organism is intrinsically resistant to ceftriaxone, penicillins and aminoglycosides
Severe disease or septic shock is treated with meropenem rather than ceftazidime
Oral eradication therapy for about three months is required to prevent relapse
explanation.pearls: A patient in the tropical north who is deteriorating on ceftriaxone for pneumonia after wet season soil exposure has melioidosis until the cultures say otherwise: switch to meropenem for severe disease and plan three months of oral eradication therapy, because stopping at the intravenous phase is what produces relapse.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Community acquired pneumonia

options.rationale: Staphylococcal pneumonia does cavitate and is worth considering in this setting, but the organism in the blood is a Gram negative bacillus, which excludes it. Adding glycopeptide cover would leave the actual pathogen inadequately treated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Melioidosis)

Bipolar safety pin staining of a Gram negative bacillus in a diabetic man exposed to wet soil in the tropical north during the wet season indicates melioidosis, which is intrinsically resistant to ceftriaxone and gentamicin. Intensive therapy uses meropenem in severe disease or in those with septic shock, followed by months of oral eradication therapy to prevent relapse. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Melioidosis)

Ceftriaxone does not reliably treat this organism, which is one of the classic reasons that patients in the tropical north deteriorate on standard community-acquired pneumonia therapy. Antiviral therapy addresses a different pathogen entirely and does not explain a Gram negative bacteraemia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Melioidosis)

This combination covers leptospirosis and rickettsial infection, which are reasonable wet season considerations in northern Australia, but neither produces a Gram negative bacillus with this staining pattern. Narrowing to penicillin in septic shock from this organism would be dangerous. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Melioidosis)

Anaerobic cover is appropriate for aspiration associated cavitation, which fits his alcohol use, but an aspiration process would not produce this blood culture result. Adding metronidazole leaves the identified organism untreated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Melioidosis)

explanation.summary: Australian elapid envenoming is diagnosed on laboratory and clinical criteria rather than on the appearance of the bite, which is frequently trivial or invisible, and brown snakes in particular often cause severe coagulopathy with almost no local signs. Venom induced consumption coagulopathy, shown here by an unrecordable international normalised ratio with undetectable fibrinogen, is systemic envenoming and is the indication for antivenom. Australian data support a single vial as the initial dose, since larger doses do not improve outcome, given with adrenaline immediately available because anaphylaxis to antivenom is the main hazard. The pressure immobilisation bandage stays on until antivenom is running, factor replacement is reserved for bleeding or urgent procedures after antivenom, and coagulation studies are then repeated serially since recovery of fibrinogen typically takes many hours.
key_points: A trivial or absent bite site does not exclude severe systemic envenoming
Venom induced consumption coagulopathy is itself the indication for antivenom
One vial is the initial dose, with adrenaline prepared for anaphylaxis
Keep the pressure immobilisation bandage on until antivenom is running
explanation.pearls: Treat the coagulation profile, not the puncture marks: an unrecordable international normalised ratio with undetectable fibrinogen after a suspected snake bite is systemic envenoming, and one vial of the appropriate antivenom goes in before the pressure bandage comes off, with adrenaline drawn up at the bedside.

sources.label: Australian Snakebite Project: Snakebite management guidelines
Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology, Snakebite

options.rationale: The coagulation results already establish systemic envenoming, so there is nothing further to observe for before treating, and removing the bandage before antivenom is drawn up allows a further bolus of venom to enter the circulation. Serial testing is used to follow recovery after antivenom, not to decide whether to give it. (Source: Australian Snakebite Project: Snakebite management guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Snakebite Project: Snakebite management guidelines

options.rationale: Factor replacement without antivenom is consumed by circulating venom and does not correct the coagulopathy, so it is given only after antivenom and generally only when there is significant bleeding or a need for an urgent procedure. Treating the laboratory result rather than the envenoming wastes time and product. (Source: Australian Snakebite Project: Snakebite management guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Snakebite Project: Snakebite management guidelines

options.rationale: The detection kit guides antivenom selection where the snake group is uncertain and multiple monovalent products are stocked, but it never determines whether to treat and its result should not delay antivenom in a patient with established coagulopathy. In much of Australia geography predicts the likely group well enough to proceed. (Source: Australian Snakebite Project: Snakebite management guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Snakebite Project: Snakebite management guidelines

options.rationale: Undetectable fibrinogen with an unrecordable international normalised ratio is venom induced consumption coagulopathy, which is systemic envenoming and mandates antivenom regardless of how unimpressive the bite site looks or how well the patient feels. Australian evidence supports a single vial as the initial dose, given with adrenaline drawn up for anaphylaxis, and the pressure bandage stays in place until the infusion is running. (Source: Australian Snakebite Project: Snakebite management guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Snakebite Project: Snakebite management guidelines

options.rationale: Antivenom is stocked in this department and delaying it for a two hour transfer allows further venom mediated consumption and the risk of collapse or intracranial haemorrhage in transit. Retrieval is arranged in parallel with treatment, not instead of it. (Source: Australian Snakebite Project: Snakebite management guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Snakebite Project: Snakebite management guidelines

explanation.summary: Mammalian meat allergy is a tick induced sensitisation to a carbohydrate present in beef, lamb, pork and other mammalian meats but absent from fish, poultry and primates. It is well recognised along the eastern seaboard of Australia, particularly the New South Wales north coast and Sydney northern beaches, where the paralysis tick is endemic. The hallmark is delayed anaphylaxis, typically two to six hours after a meal, which frequently wakes the patient at night and is often misclassified as idiopathic because the timing breaks the expected immediate pattern and standard skin prick panels do not include the allergen. Diagnosis is by serum specific immunoglobulin E to the carbohydrate, and management combines avoidance of mammalian meat and related products, an adrenaline autoinjector with an action plan, and instruction in correct tick removal, since further bites sustain the sensitisation.
key_points: The delay of two to six hours after the meal is the feature that identifies this syndrome
Sensitisation follows tick bites and involves a carbohydrate absent from fish and poultry
Standard skin prick food panels do not contain the allergen, so negative testing is expected
Management includes avoidance, an adrenaline autoinjector, and correct tick removal advice
explanation.pearls: Anaphylaxis that wakes someone in the early hours is a dietary history question about the evening meal, not an idiopathic label: beef, lamb or pork four to six hours earlier in a tick exposed patient on the eastern seaboard calls for specific immunoglobulin E to galactose-alpha-1,3-galactose, which the standard skin prick panel will never show.

sources.label: ASCIA Guidelines: Acute management of anaphylaxis

options.rationale: Tryptase confirms that mast cell degranulation occurred and a persistently raised baseline would point toward a clonal mast cell disorder, but it identifies no trigger. It is a useful adjunct rather than the test that explains this pattern. (Source: ASCIA: Mammalian meat allergy)

Challenge is hazardous when the reactions have been anaphylactic and the delayed timing makes the observation period impractical, running to six hours or more after ingestion. It is not the first line test when a specific serological marker exists. (Source: ASCIA: Mammalian meat allergy)

Urinary mediator metabolites are used in the assessment of suspected mast cell disorders, particularly where flushing and diarrhoea dominate. They neither identify an allergen nor distinguish an allergic from a non-allergic mast cell process. (Source: ASCIA: Mammalian meat allergy)

Patch testing detects delayed cell mediated contact hypersensitivity of the skin, a different mechanism from the immediate antibody mediated reaction underlying urticaria, angioedema and wheeze. The delay in this syndrome comes from digestion and absorption, not from a cell mediated response. (Source: ASCIA: Mammalian meat allergy)

Delayed anaphylaxis several hours after beef, lamb or pork in someone with heavy tick exposure is mammalian meat allergy, in which sensitisation to a mammalian carbohydrate occurs through tick bites and the delay reflects the time taken for the allergen to be processed and absorbed in lipid particles. Serum specific immunoglobulin E to that carbohydrate is the confirmatory test, since standard skin prick panels do not contain it. (Source: ASCIA: Mammalian meat allergy)

explanation.summary: Engineered stone contains a far higher proportion of crystalline silica than natural stone, and dry cutting in poorly ventilated workshops produced an epidemic of accelerated silicosis in young Australian benchtop workers, leading to a national prohibition on the fabrication of engineered stone from mid 2024. The clinical picture is progressive breathlessness in a young never-smoker with upper zone predominant nodules, conglomerate masses and hilar nodes that may calcify peripherally. There is no disease modifying drug treatment, so the priorities are complete removal from exposure, notification so that the workplace is inspected and coworkers screened, and referral for compensation. Long term surveillance covers tuberculosis, autoimmune connective tissue disease, chronic kidney disease and lung cancer, with transplantation considered for end stage disease.
key_points: Engineered stone dry cutting causes accelerated disease after only a few years of exposure
Upper zone nodularity with conglomerate masses in a young never-smoker is the characteristic pattern
Exposure removal and notification are the interventions that change outcomes
Screen long term for tuberculosis, autoimmune disease, renal impairment and lung cancer
explanation.pearls: Ask what a young breathless never-smoker does for work before ordering anything: nine years of dry cutting engineered stone benchtops makes silicosis the diagnosis on imaging alone, and the treatment is permanent removal from dust plus notification to the work health authority so that the whole workshop is screened.

sources.label: Safe Work Australia: National guidance on silicosis and crystalline silica
Lung Foundation Australia: Occupational lung disease resources

options.rationale: The only intervention that alters the course of this disease is stopping exposure, and because it is a notifiable occupational condition in Australian jurisdictions the notification also triggers workplace inspection and screening of his coworkers. Ongoing surveillance is needed for the recognised complications, which include tuberculosis, autoimmune disease, chronic kidney disease and lung cancer, and he should be referred for compensation assessment. (Source: Safe Work Australia: National guidance on silicosis and crystalline silica)
source_refs: Safe Work Australia: National guidance on silicosis and crystalline silica

options.rationale: Corticosteroids have no established role in this disease and expose him to metabolic and infective complications, including reactivation of latent mycobacterial infection to which he is already predisposed. They are used for hypersensitivity pneumonitis or sarcoidosis, neither of which fits this exposure and imaging pattern. (Source: Safe Work Australia: National guidance on silicosis and crystalline silica)
source_refs: Safe Work Australia: National guidance on silicosis and crystalline silica

options.rationale: Antifibrotics are approved for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and for progressive pulmonary fibrosis of other causes, a decision made after exposure control and multidisciplinary assessment rather than at first presentation. An upper zone nodular pattern in a young never-smoker is not the basal reticulation that drives that decision. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Occupational lung disease resources)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia: Occupational lung disease resources

options.rationale: This condition substantially increases the risk of tuberculosis and screening is part of follow up, but the interferon gamma release assay is negative and there are no constitutional symptoms or cavitation. Empirical quadruple therapy would expose him to significant toxicity without evidence of infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Tuberculosis)

The exposure history and characteristic imaging make the diagnosis without tissue, and biopsy carries real morbidity in a man with a reduced transfer factor. It is reserved for cases where the pattern or the exposure history genuinely does not fit. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: Occupational lung disease resources)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia: Occupational lung disease resources

explanation.summary: Obstruction of the superior vena cava presents with facial and upper limb swelling, distended non-pulsatile neck veins and visible chest wall collaterals, characteristically worse on bending forward or lying flat. Malignancy causes the majority of cases, most often lung cancer or lymphoma, although catheter associated thrombosis is an increasingly common benign cause. It is only a true emergency when there is stridor or airway compromise, or cerebral oedema with altered conscious state, and in the stable patient the priority is a contrast computed tomography followed by urgent tissue diagnosis. Treating with radiotherapy before biopsy risks rendering histology uninterpretable and may deny the patient the correct systemic therapy, while endovascular stenting is reserved for severe or refractory symptoms.
key_points: Facial swelling worse on bending, with non-pulsatile distended neck veins and chest wall collaterals
Stridor or altered conscious state converts this into a true emergency needing immediate intervention
Obtain tissue before radiotherapy so that chemosensitive tumours can be identified
Anticoagulation treats catheter associated thrombosis, not extrinsic compression by tumour
explanation.pearls: Stable superior vena cava obstruction buys you the days needed for a diagnosis: get contrast computed tomography and tissue first, because radiotherapy given before biopsy can render the histology uninterpretable and cost the patient the chemotherapy that a lymphoma or small cell carcinoma would have responded to.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer clinical practice guidelines

options.rationale: Radiotherapy given before tissue is obtained can make subsequent histology uninterpretable and may preclude the diagnosis of a chemosensitive tumour such as lymphoma or small cell carcinoma, which would be treated quite differently. Immediate radiotherapy without tissue is reserved for genuine airway compromise or neurological deterioration. (Source: eviQ: Superior vena cava obstruction)

Anticoagulation is indicated when obstruction is caused by catheter associated thrombosis, which is not the case in a woman with no line and an obvious mediastinal mass. Extrinsic compression by tumour does not respond to anticoagulation. (Source: eviQ: Superior vena cava obstruction)

Although she is currently stable, obstruction with established collateral circulation and a new mass warrants inpatient workup because deterioration can be rapid and the diagnostic pathway needs to run in days. A two week outpatient wait is too slow for a syndrome with this trajectory. (Source: eviQ: Superior vena cava obstruction)

Stenting gives rapid relief and is the right choice for severe or refractory symptoms, particularly airway compromise or cerebral oedema, but it is not required first in a patient who is stable with a normal conscious state. Proceeding to stent before tissue diagnosis also commits her to antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy that can complicate an urgent biopsy. (Source: eviQ: Superior vena cava obstruction)

Contrast imaging defines the level and cause of the obstruction, shows the collateral circulation and identifies the safest target for sampling, while histology determines whether the tumour is one that responds rapidly to systemic therapy. Since she is stable with no airway or neurological compromise, there is time to obtain the diagnosis that dictates every subsequent treatment decision. (Source: eviQ: Superior vena cava obstruction)

explanation.summary: Immune checkpoint inhibitor colitis typically appears within the first few months of treatment and is graded by stool frequency above baseline together with features such as nocturnal stools, blood, pain and dehydration. Infection must be excluded, since the treatment is immunosuppression, but once stool studies are negative and imaging shows diffuse colitis the diagnosis is made clinically. Severe disease is managed by withholding the checkpoint inhibitor and starting high dose intravenous corticosteroid immediately, with flexible sigmoidoscopy to confirm and grade the mucosal injury. Failure to improve within about three days defines steroid refractory disease and prompts infliximab, or vedolizumab where a tumour necrosis factor inhibitor is undesirable, and steroids are then tapered slowly over four to six weeks because rapid tapering causes relapse.
key_points: Exclude infection first, then treat severe colitis as an immune mediated injury without further delay
Withhold the checkpoint inhibitor and give high dose intravenous corticosteroid
Lack of response within about three days defines steroid refractory disease and prompts infliximab
Taper corticosteroids over four to six weeks, since rapid reduction causes relapse
explanation.pearls: Nocturnal stools and blood are the features that move checkpoint inhibitor diarrhoea out of the loperamide category: once stool studies are negative, withhold the drug and start high dose intravenous methylprednisolone the same day, and if there is no improvement by day three, escalate to infliximab rather than waiting out the steroid.

sources.label: eviQ: Immune related adverse events, gastrointestinal toxicity
Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Clostridioides difficile infection

options.rationale: Antimotility agents are appropriate for low grade diarrhoea without alarm features, but with ten stools daily, nocturnal symptoms and blood they risk masking progression toward toxic dilatation and perforation. Continuing the drug during active grade three toxicity compounds the injury. (Source: eviQ: Immune related adverse events, gastrointestinal toxicity)
source_refs: eviQ: Immune related adverse events, gastrointestinal toxicity

options.rationale: Colitis of this severity from checkpoint inhibition is treated as an immune mediated injury with the drug withheld and high dose corticosteroid started without waiting, since delay increases the risk of perforation and of steroid refractory disease. Gastroenterology involvement allows early flexible sigmoidoscopy to confirm the diagnosis and grade the mucosal injury, and identifies those who will need infliximab or vedolizumab if there is no response within three days. (Source: eviQ: Immune related adverse events, gastrointestinal toxicity)
source_refs: eviQ: Immune related adverse events, gastrointestinal toxicity

options.rationale: Repeat or empirical treatment is reasonable when pretest probability is high, such as after recent antibiotics or hospitalisation, and neither applies here with a negative toxin test. Treating an infection he does not have delays the immunosuppression that this colitis requires. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Clostridioides difficile infection)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Clostridioides difficile infection

options.rationale: Infliximab is the standard second line agent for colitis that does not respond to corticosteroids within about three days, and skipping the steroid trial exposes most patients to a biologic they would not have needed. It is also contraindicated until perforation and infection have been excluded, which requires the assessment described in the correct option. (Source: eviQ: Immune related adverse events, gastrointestinal toxicity)
source_refs: eviQ: Immune related adverse events, gastrointestinal toxicity

options.rationale: Stopping the drug is necessary but insufficient, because the inflammatory process continues for weeks after the last dose given the long duration of receptor occupancy. Supportive care alone leaves a patient at real risk of perforation. (Source: eviQ: Immune related adverse events, gastrointestinal toxicity)
source_refs: eviQ: Immune related adverse events, gastrointestinal toxicity

explanation.summary: Active Charcot neuroarthropathy presents as a warm, swollen, erythematous foot in a person with dense peripheral neuropathy and good arterial supply, often with minimal pain and no systemic illness. A temperature difference of more than two degrees Celsius between the feet, in the presence of intact skin and normal inflammatory markers, is the key discriminator from infection. Plain radiographs are normal in the early stage, which is exactly when offloading changes the outcome, so a normal film must never be used to exclude the diagnosis, and magnetic resonance imaging showing bone marrow oedema is the confirmatory test. Treatment is immediate immobilisation in a total contact cast with avoidance of weight bearing, continued for months and guided by resolution of the temperature difference, because continued walking on the affected foot causes midfoot collapse, deformity and eventual ulceration.
key_points: A skin temperature difference above two degrees Celsius with intact skin suggests Charcot rather than infection
Normal radiographs are expected early and do not exclude the diagnosis
Immediate total contact casting and offloading prevents irreversible midfoot collapse
Magnetic resonance imaging showing bone marrow oedema confirms active disease
explanation.pearls: Measure both feet with an infrared thermometer whenever a neuropathic foot is swollen: more than two degrees Celsius of difference with unbroken skin and a normal C-reactive protein means active Charcot neuroarthropathy, and the cast goes on that day rather than after the magnetic resonance scan is reported.

sources.label: Australian Diabetes Society: Australian evidence-based guideline for diabetes-related foot disease

options.rationale: Cellulitis requires a portal of entry and is usually accompanied by systemic features or raised inflammatory markers, and here the skin is intact with a C-reactive protein of 4 mg/L. Antibiotics would allow continued weight bearing through an unstable foot for another fortnight. (Source: Australian Diabetes Society: Australian evidence-based guideline for diabetes-related foot disease)
source_refs: Australian Diabetes Society: Australian evidence-based guideline for diabetes-related foot disease

options.rationale: Acute gout is intensely painful even in the presence of neuropathy and characteristically affects the first metatarsophalangeal joint rather than producing diffuse midfoot warmth and swelling over three weeks. The painless, indolent course does not fit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology, Gout)

Dependent oedema is bilateral, painless, cool and resolves substantially with elevation, whereas this foot is unilateral, several degrees warmer than the other side and only partly improved by elevation. Compression over an unrecognised unstable foot risks skin breakdown. (Source: Australian Diabetes Society: Australian evidence-based guideline for diabetes-related foot disease)
source_refs: Australian Diabetes Society: Australian evidence-based guideline for diabetes-related foot disease

options.rationale: Critical limb ischaemia presents with rest pain, pallor on elevation, absent pulses and tissue loss, and his pulses and toe pressures are normal. Pursuing revascularisation would delay the offloading that protects the foot architecture. (Source: Australian Diabetes Society: Australian evidence-based guideline for diabetes-related foot disease)
source_refs: Australian Diabetes Society: Australian evidence-based guideline for diabetes-related foot disease

options.rationale: A hot swollen foot in a person with dense neuropathy and intact skin is active Charcot neuroarthropathy until proven otherwise, and plain radiographs are normal in the earliest stage when intervention matters most. Immediate offloading in a total contact cast prevents the collapse that produces a rocker bottom deformity and subsequent ulceration, and magnetic resonance imaging detects the bone marrow oedema that confirms the diagnosis. (Source: Australian Diabetes Society: Australian evidence-based guideline for diabetes-related foot disease)
source_refs: Australian Diabetes Society: Australian evidence-based guideline for diabetes-related foot disease

explanation.summary: Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis is a shift hypokalaemia in which thyroid hormone excess amplifies sodium potassium pump activity, so that insulin release after a carbohydrate load, rest after exercise, or a high salt meal precipitates sudden proximal weakness. It occurs predominantly in young men, is most common in patients of Asian background, and may be the first manifestation of thyrotoxicosis. Because total body potassium is normal, aggressive replacement leads to rebound hyperkalaemia once the shift reverses, and deaths have resulted, so replacement is given in small cautious doses with frequent monitoring. A non-selective beta blocker such as propranolol counteracts the adrenergic drive and often reverses the attack, while definitive prevention depends on treating the underlying thyrotoxicosis.
key_points: Sudden proximal weakness with normal sensation and profound hypokalaemia suggests a shift rather than a loss
Carbohydrate loads, rest after exercise and high salt meals are typical precipitants
Aggressive potassium replacement causes rebound hyperkalaemia because total body stores are normal
A non-selective beta blocker often aborts the attack, and definitive treatment is of the thyrotoxicosis
explanation.pearls: Check a thyroid stimulating hormone in any young man with sudden painless proximal weakness and a potassium under 2.5 mmol/L: the potassium has shifted rather than been lost, so replace it in small cautious increments alongside propranolol, and expect rebound hyperkalaemia if you infuse it as you would for a diuretic induced deficit.

options.rationale: The potassium here has shifted into cells rather than being lost from the body, so aggressive replacement is followed by rebound hyperkalaemia as the shift reverses, which has caused fatal arrhythmias in this syndrome. Replacement is given cautiously in small increments with frequent measurement. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology, Thyrotoxicosis)

Guillain-Barre syndrome produces ascending weakness with areflexia over days, usually with sensory symptoms and often autonomic involvement, and does not cause a potassium of 2.1 mmol/L. The abrupt overnight onset with profound hypokalaemia points elsewhere. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology, Neuromuscular disorders)

Cord compression produces a sensory level, sphincter disturbance and upper motor neurone signs below the lesion, none of which are present, and it does not explain a symmetrical proximal pattern with normal sensation. Imaging would delay treatment of a rapidly correctable metabolic cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology, Neuromuscular disorders)

This is the treatment for hyperkalaemia, and insulin would drive even more potassium into cells and deepen the paralysis in a man whose potassium is already 2.1 mmol/L. The electrocardiographic changes described are those of hypokalaemia with U waves rather than of hyperkalaemia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology, Thyrotoxicosis)

The weakness comes from potassium shifting into muscle cells under the combined drive of thyroid hormone excess, insulin release after a carbohydrate load and exercise, so small cautious potassium doses restore power while avoiding the rebound hyperkalaemia that follows overcorrection. A non-selective beta blocker blocks the beta adrenergic drive of that shift and often reverses the paralysis, and definitive prevention requires rendering him euthyroid. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology, Thyrotoxicosis)

explanation.summary: Alcohol related hepatitis presents with rapid onset jaundice, tender hepatomegaly and a neutrophil leucocytosis on a background of sustained heavy drinking, with aspartate aminotransferase characteristically higher than alanine aminotransferase and rarely exceeding about 300 U/L. Severity is quantified by the discriminant function derived from the prothrombin time and bilirubin, with a value above 32 marking severe disease and high short term mortality. Corticosteroid therapy improves short term survival in that group, provided active infection, gastrointestinal bleeding and significant renal failure have been addressed, and response is reassessed at day seven using a composite score so that non-responders are not continued on futile immunosuppression. Abstinence, thiamine, withdrawal management and nutritional support are given to every patient regardless of severity and are the interventions that determine long term outcome.
key_points: Aspartate aminotransferase exceeds alanine aminotransferase and is rarely above 300 U/L
A discriminant function above 32 defines severe disease with high short term mortality
Exclude and treat infection before starting corticosteroid, since it is the main contraindication
Reassess response at day seven and stop steroid in non-responders
explanation.pearls: Calculate the discriminant function before deciding anything in alcohol related hepatitis: a value above 32 identifies the patients for whom corticosteroid improves short term survival, and the same calculation tells you to reassess at day seven and stop rather than continue immunosuppressing a non-responder.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal, Alcohol related liver disease
Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology, Paracetamol poisoning
Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Liver disease resources

options.rationale: A discriminant function above 32, calculated from the prothrombin time prolongation and the bilirubin, defines severe disease with a high short term mortality, and corticosteroid is the only therapy shown to improve survival in that group. Infection must be excluded or treated first because it is the main contraindication, and the day seven response score determines whether to continue the course or stop it as futile. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal, Alcohol related liver disease)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal, Alcohol related liver disease

options.rationale: Paracetamol toxicity produces transaminases in the thousands with a comparatively low bilirubin early on, and he takes none. N-acetylcysteine has been studied as an adjunct in this condition but is not the primary treatment decision here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology, Paracetamol poisoning)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology, Paracetamol poisoning

options.rationale: A raised white cell count is expected in this condition and is not by itself evidence of infection in an afebrile man with a negative screen. Empirical antibiotics without a source delay a time-critical treatment decision. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal, Alcohol related liver disease)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal, Alcohol related liver disease

options.rationale: Biopsy confirms the diagnosis and is used where the history or biochemistry is ambiguous, but here the drinking history, the ratio of aminotransferases and the exclusion of other causes make it unnecessary. Waiting for a procedure would delay treatment in a condition with high short term mortality. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal, Alcohol related liver disease)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal, Alcohol related liver disease

options.rationale: Abstinence, thiamine, withdrawal management and aggressive nutritional support are essential in every case and improve outcomes, but on their own they do not address the mortality risk that defines severe disease. They accompany corticosteroid rather than replacing it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal, Alcohol related liver disease)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal, Alcohol related liver disease

explanation.summary: Adult onset Still disease is a systemic autoinflammatory disorder whose defining pattern is a daily fever spike returning to baseline, a salmon coloured rash that appears with the fever and fades as it settles, arthralgia or arthritis, and sore throat with an unremarkable pharynx. Laboratory findings include a neutrophil predominant leucocytosis, high inflammatory markers, transaminitis and a strikingly elevated ferritin, often more than five times the upper limit, with a low glycosylated fraction. Because it has no confirmatory test, the diagnosis requires exclusion of infection, malignancy and other connective tissue disease, which is why repeated cultures, echocardiography, cross sectional imaging and autoantibodies all feature in the workup. The major complication to watch for is macrophage activation syndrome, signalled by falling cell counts, falling fibrinogen, rising triglycerides and a further ferritin rise, and treatment begins with corticosteroids before moving to interleukin 1 or interleukin 6 blockade.
key_points: The rash appears only with the fever spike, so it is missed on routine daytime ward rounds
Ferritin is typically in the thousands with a neutrophil predominant leucocytosis
Negative antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor support rather than refute the diagnosis
Watch for macrophage activation syndrome with falling counts and fibrinogen and rising triglycerides
explanation.pearls: Ask nursing staff to look at the skin at the moment of the temperature spike rather than on the morning round: the salmon rash of adult onset Still disease is present only during the fever, and pairing that with a ferritin in the thousands and a neutrophil leucocytosis is what turns a prolonged fever workup into a diagnosis.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology, Adult onset Still disease
Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology, Systemic lupus erythematosus
RHD Australia: Australian guideline for acute rheumatic fever

options.rationale: Endocarditis would be supported by a new murmur, embolic phenomena or vegetations, and the echocardiogram is clear after two admissions and a week of ceftriaxone without response. It also does not produce a rash that appears only with the fever spike. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology, Adult onset Still disease)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology, Adult onset Still disease

options.rationale: Lupus is effectively excluded by a negative antinuclear antibody, and it characteristically causes leucopenia rather than a neutrophil count of 21.6 x10^9/L. Its rash is fixed and photosensitive rather than evanescent with fever. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology, Systemic lupus erythematosus)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology, Systemic lupus erythematosus

options.rationale: Lymphoma remains an important consideration in prolonged fever with splenomegaly and is the reason tissue sampling is often pursued, but the once daily fever pattern with a fever linked evanescent rash and a ferritin near 10000 micrograms/L is not its usual behaviour. Nodes here are small and reactive rather than bulky. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology, Adult onset Still disease)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology, Adult onset Still disease
