options.rationale: Acute rheumatic fever requires evidence of preceding streptococcal infection and produces a migratory large joint arthritis with carditis, chorea or erythema marginatum, which is a ring shaped rather than salmon coloured eruption. Neither the serology nor the echocardiogram supports it. (Source: RHD Australia: Australian guideline for acute rheumatic fever)
source_refs: RHD Australia: Australian guideline for acute rheumatic fever

options.rationale: The combination of once daily fever spikes, an evanescent salmon rash appearing only with the fever, arthralgia, sore throat with a normal pharynx, neutrophil leucocytosis, transaminitis and a ferritin in the thousands is the recognised pattern of this disorder. Negative cultures, serology and imaging complete the diagnosis, which is made by exclusion and is treated with corticosteroids and then interleukin 1 or interleukin 6 directed therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology, Adult onset Still disease)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology, Adult onset Still disease

explanation.summary: Nitrous oxide inactivates cobalamin by oxidising its cobalt centre, producing a functional deficiency that damages the dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts as well as peripheral nerves. The characteristic examination finding is a mixture of upper and lower motor neurone signs, with brisk knee reflexes and extensor plantars alongside absent ankle jerks, together with sensory ataxia that worsens without visual input. Serum vitamin B12 is often normal or borderline because the molecule is present but non-functional, so elevated homocysteine and methylmalonic acid are the tests that reveal the deficiency, and macrocytosis may or may not be present. Management is immediate cessation of exposure with parenteral hydroxocobalamin, since recovery depends heavily on how long the deficiency has persisted, and a magnetic resonance scan of the cord may show the inverted V sign of dorsal column signal change.
key_points: Brisk knee reflexes with absent ankle jerks signals combined cord and peripheral nerve involvement
Serum vitamin B12 may be normal because the molecule is inactivated rather than depleted
Homocysteine and methylmalonic acid are the tests that establish functional deficiency
Cessation plus prompt parenteral replacement determines whether the deficits reverse
explanation.pearls: A normal serum vitamin B12 does not exclude functional deficiency in nitrous oxide users: send homocysteine and methylmalonic acid, and start parenteral hydroxocobalamin the same day, because dorsal column and corticospinal damage becomes permanent the longer the exposure continues.

options.rationale: Thiamine deficiency causes a painful predominantly sensory neuropathy or Wernicke encephalopathy, and he does not drink alcohol or have ocular or cognitive signs. It also would not explain the dorsal column and corticospinal involvement. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology, Peripheral neuropathy)

Electrophysiology will describe the axonal and demyelinating components but changes nothing about the immediate treatment, and the combination of upper and lower motor neurone signs already localises the lesion to cord and nerve. Delaying replacement risks irreversible cord damage. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology, Peripheral neuropathy)

Symptomatic neuropathic agents may help the paraesthesiae but do nothing about the ongoing functional deficiency that is damaging the cord. Six weeks of continued exposure without replacement risks permanent disability. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology, Peripheral neuropathy)

A demyelinating event would produce a sensory level and would not be accompanied by macrocytosis with a raised homocysteine and methylmalonic acid. Corticosteroids would leave the metabolic cause untreated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology, Multiple sclerosis)

Nitrous oxide irreversibly oxidises the cobalt core of cobalamin, so the vitamin is present in serum but functionally inactive, which is why the level looks near normal while homocysteine and methylmalonic acid are elevated. Treatment is to stop the exposure and give parenteral replacement promptly, since the combined degeneration of dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts becomes irreversible if it persists. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology, Peripheral neuropathy)

explanation.summary: Cervical artery dissection is a leading cause of stroke in adults under 50 and characteristically produces local pain days before the ischaemic event, giving a window in which the diagnosis can be made. In internal carotid dissection the mural haematoma compresses the sympathetic fibres travelling on the vessel wall, producing a partial Horner syndrome with ptosis and miosis but preserved facial sweating, because the sudomotor fibres travel with the external carotid. Trivial mechanical precipitants such as heavy lifting, sporting neck movement or coughing are common, and there is often no conventional vascular risk factor. Diagnosis rests on computed tomography or magnetic resonance angiography of the neck vessels, and antithrombotic treatment with either an antiplatelet agent or anticoagulation is given for three to six months with repeat imaging.
key_points: Pain typically precedes the ischaemic event by days, which is the window for diagnosis
Ptosis and miosis with preserved facial sweating localises the lesion to the internal carotid wall
Minor mechanical precipitants are common and conventional vascular risk factors are often absent
Vessel imaging of the neck rather than cardiac workup is the immediate priority
explanation.pearls: In any stroke or transient ischaemic attack under 50, ask about neck or facial pain in the preceding fortnight and look specifically for a small pupil with a droopy lid on the painful side. Ptosis and miosis with normal facial sweating means carotid dissection, and the next test is angiography of the neck vessels rather than an echocardiogram.

sources.label: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management
Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology, Giant cell arteritis

options.rationale: Paradoxical embolism through a patent foramen ovale is a genuine consideration in young stroke and echocardiography belongs in the workup, but it does not explain unilateral neck pain with an ipsilateral partial Horner syndrome. It would also not change acute management today. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management

options.rationale: Xanthochromia testing follows a suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage with sudden maximal headache and a normal early scan, whereas her headache has been present for five days alongside focal deficit and a Horner syndrome. The pattern points to a vessel wall problem rather than to blood in the subarachnoid space. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management

options.rationale: Neck pain with an ipsilateral partial Horner syndrome and subsequent cerebral ischaemia in a young person without vascular risk factors is arterial dissection, where a torn intimal layer produces a mural haematoma that stretches the sympathetic fibres running along the vessel and generates embolus. Angiography of the neck vessels is the test that demonstrates it and determines whether antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy is chosen. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management

options.rationale: Giant cell arteritis causes headache with scalp tenderness, jaw claudication and visual loss, and it occurs in people over 50 rather than in a 38-year-old. It does not produce a Horner syndrome or follow a mechanical precipitant. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology, Giant cell arteritis)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology, Giant cell arteritis

options.rationale: Extended rhythm monitoring is standard for cryptogenic stroke once structural and arterial causes have been excluded, and it is appropriate later in this workup. Starting with it would miss an arterial lesion that is actively embolising and needs a treatment decision today. (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management

explanation.summary: Q fever is an occupational infection of abattoir workers, farmers, shearers and veterinarians, acquired by inhaling aerosols from birth products, particularly placental material, where the organism is shed in vast quantities. The acute illness is a prolonged febrile syndrome with severe headache, sweats and myalgia, frequently accompanied by a hepatitis and mild thrombocytopenia, and routine blood cultures are always negative because the organism does not grow in standard media. Diagnosis is serological, with paired samples two to three weeks apart demonstrating a fourfold rise, and treatment is doxycycline for two weeks started on clinical suspicion. Australia has a licensed vaccine that requires pre-vaccination skin testing and serology to exclude prior exposure, and it is recommended for at risk occupational groups, while a small proportion of untreated patients develop chronic infection presenting as endocarditis or vascular infection months to years later.
key_points: Exposure to birth products from livestock is the classic route, not necessarily contact with sick animals
Routine blood cultures are negative because the organism does not grow in standard media
Paired serology two to three weeks apart is the diagnostic test, with doxycycline started on suspicion
Vaccination requires prior skin testing and serology, and is recommended for at risk occupations
explanation.pearls: Ask a febrile abattoir or farm worker whether they were present at any births or handled placental material: Q fever is acquired from birth product aerosols, cannot be cultured from blood, and needs paired serology plus doxycycline started on suspicion rather than another set of blood cultures.

options.rationale: Malaria requires travel to an endemic area, and Australia has been free of local transmission for decades, so films would be negative in a man who has not left the country. Fever with sweats alone is not enough to justify this pathway without exposure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Q fever)

Marrow examination is a reasonable late step in prolonged fever of unknown origin, particularly with cytopenias, but it is invasive and the exposure history here points to a specific treatable infection with a simple serological test. The mild thrombocytopenia and transaminitis fit that infection well. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Q fever)

Functional imaging has a role in prolonged fever after first line investigations have failed, and it may identify vascular or bone infection. Using it before serology for an occupationally acquired pathogen that is easy to diagnose and treat inverts the order of investigation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Q fever)

Endocarditis would be suggested by a murmur, embolic phenomena or a predisposing valve lesion, none of which are present in this man. It is worth revisiting if the illness becomes chronic, since the pathogen suggested by his exposure can itself cause endocarditis months later. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Q fever)

Abattoir work and assisting with calving are the classic Australian exposures for Q fever, whose organism is shed in enormous numbers in birth products and inhaled as an aerosol, and which does not grow in routine blood culture bottles. A fourfold rise between paired samples confirms acute infection, and doxycycline is started on clinical suspicion rather than waiting for the second sample. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic, Q fever)

explanation.summary: Pyelonephritis complicates approximately 1-2% of pregnancies and carries important obstetric consequences: septic shock, preterm labour and adult respiratory distress syndrome. Admission for IV antibiotics, adequate hydration and fetal monitoring is standard. Empirical therapy per eTG Complete is IV cefazolin 2 g eight-hourly OR IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily, with step-down to an oral cephalosporin per culture and sensitivity; total course is 10-14 days. Gentamicin is reserved for severe sepsis or for cephalosporin failure. Trimethoprim (folate antagonism, first trimester) and nitrofurantoin (neonatal haemolysis at term, poor tissue penetration) are cystitis-only agents. Follow-up urine culture is standard to confirm eradication.
key_points: IV cefazolin or ceftriaxone is first-line empirical pyelonephritis therapy in pregnancy.
Step down to oral cephalosporin per susceptibility for a total 10-14 day course.
Nitrofurantoin does NOT treat pyelonephritis (renal tissue penetration inadequate).
Trimethoprim contraindicated first trimester; nitrofurantoin avoided at term.
Follow-up culture confirms eradication; consider suppressive antibiotic if recurrence.
explanation.pearls: For pyelonephritis at 24 weeks, admit for IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily and step down to oral cefalexin per susceptibility for a total ten to fourteen day course - nitrofurantoin never treats pyelonephritis.

sources.label: eTG Complete Antibiotic: pyelonephritis in pregnancy

options.rationale: Oral antibiotics are inappropriate for a woman with pyelonephritis in pregnancy who is systemically unwell with vomiting; poor absorption from vomiting undermines efficacy and misses septic complications. Admission for IV therapy is the standard. (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic: pyelonephritis in pregnancy)
source_refs: eTG Complete Antibiotic: pyelonephritis in pregnancy

options.rationale: Trimethoprim is contraindicated in the first trimester and cautioned throughout pregnancy because of folate antagonism. It is not adequate monotherapy for pyelonephritis and is not the correct empirical agent. (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic: pyelonephritis in pregnancy)
source_refs: eTG Complete Antibiotic: pyelonephritis in pregnancy

options.rationale: Gentamicin is reserved for severe sepsis or when a resistant organism is documented in pregnancy given the fetal ototoxicity concerns. It is not the routine first-line agent for straightforward pyelonephritis in pregnancy when a cephalosporin is appropriate. (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic: pyelonephritis in pregnancy)
source_refs: eTG Complete Antibiotic: pyelonephritis in pregnancy

options.rationale: First-line empirical therapy for pyelonephritis in pregnancy per eTG Complete is IV cefazolin OR IV ceftriaxone with step-down to an oral cephalosporin per susceptibility. Ceftriaxone once daily is a convenient equivalent, well studied in pregnancy, and covers the usual E coli spectrum. Total duration ten to fourteen days. (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic: pyelonephritis in pregnancy)
source_refs: eTG Complete Antibiotic: pyelonephritis in pregnancy

options.rationale: Nitrofurantoin achieves urinary but not renal tissue concentrations sufficient to treat pyelonephritis; it is a cystitis-only agent. It also should be avoided at term because of haemolysis risk in the neonate. (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic: pyelonephritis in pregnancy)
source_refs: eTG Complete Antibiotic: pyelonephritis in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Migraine prevention is offered when attacks are frequent (three or more per month), disabling, or acute treatments are inadequate or overused. Australian first-line agents are propranolol, amitriptyline, topiramate, candesartan, and pizotifen; CGRP-targeted monoclonal antibodies are reserved for treatment-refractory disease with public subsidy criteria. Selection is driven by comorbidity: hypertension favours propranolol or candesartan; depression favours amitriptyline; epilepsy or obesity favours topiramate; contraception planning favours candesartan or propranolol. Combined hormonal contraception is contraindicated in migraine with aura because of stroke risk. Triptans are contraindicated in ischaemic vascular disease and uncontrolled hypertension; this woman's triptan use should be reviewed with a neurologist.
key_points: Preventive threshold: three or more disabling attacks per month, or inadequate acute treatment.
First-line Australian agents: propranolol, amitriptyline, topiramate, candesartan, pizotifen.
Combined hormonal contraception contraindicated in migraine with aura (stroke risk).
Triptans contraindicated in ischaemic vascular disease, uncontrolled hypertension.
CGRP monoclonal antibodies are treatment refractory second/third line under PBS criteria.
explanation.pearls: In migraine with aura and a prior ischaemic stroke, first line prevention is propranolol 40-160 mg per day and combined hormonal contraception is contraindicated - review the triptan too, because triptans should be avoided after ischaemic stroke.

sources.label: eTG Complete Sexual health: contraception in migraine

options.rationale: Combined hormonal contraceptives are contraindicated in migraine with aura because of the additional stroke risk. This patient already has a documented ischaemic stroke and a PFO; starting oestrogen-containing agents is unsafe. Progestogen-only regimens are not established migraine prophylaxis. (Source: eTG Complete Sexual health: contraception in migraine)
source_refs: eTG Complete Sexual health: contraception in migraine

options.rationale: Amitriptyline is a legitimate second-line preventive but its anticholinergic burden, orthostatic hypotension risk and weight gain make it less desirable when a beta blocker is well tolerated. Riboflavin and magnesium have modest evidence and should not replace evidence-based first-line agents. (Source: eTG Complete Neurology: migraine prevention)

Topiramate is an alternative first-line preventive but has cognitive slowing, paraesthesiae, renal stones and teratogenicity concerns that make propranolol a better default when there is no contraindication. Not clearly superior in this patient. (Source: eTG Complete Neurology: migraine prevention)

Verapamil is first line for cluster headache, not migraine prevention. Australian guidance places it much lower in the migraine preventive hierarchy and there is no reason to preference it here. (Source: eTG Complete Neurology: migraine prevention)

Propranolol is a first-line migraine preventive with the best evidence base in Australia and is well tolerated at 40-160 mg per day. It is not contraindicated by a prior ischaemic stroke in the absence of significant conduction disease. Its neutral cardiovascular profile suits secondary stroke prevention. (Source: eTG Complete Neurology: migraine prevention)

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency anaemia affects up to a third of patients with inflammatory bowel disease and is multifactorial: chronic blood loss, chronic inflammation reducing absorption via elevated hepcidin, and oral iron intolerance. The Gastroenterological Society of Australia endorses IV iron as first line in IBD when oral iron is not tolerated, ineffective, or during active disease. Ferric carboxymaltose (1000 mg per infusion, maximum single dose 15 mg/kg or 1000 mg) and iron polymaltose (slower infusion) are the available preparations. Total dose is calculated by the Ganzoni formula or the simplified fixed-dose approach; a 1000 mg dose typically replenishes stores in a 60-90 kg adult with moderate anaemia. Response is assessed at eight weeks with FBC and ferritin. Transfusion is reserved for symptomatic severe anaemia.
key_points: IV iron is first-line for iron deficiency in IBD if oral not tolerated, ineffective, or active disease.
Ferric carboxymaltose maximum single dose 15 mg/kg or 1000 mg per infusion.
IM iron is no longer recommended (staining, poor absorption).
Reassess FBC and ferritin at eight weeks after infusion.
Watch for post-infusion hypophosphataemia (ferric carboxymaltose specific).
explanation.pearls: For iron deficiency in IBD with oral iron intolerance, use IV ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg over 15 minutes and reassess FBC and ferritin at eight weeks - watch for hypophosphataemia specific to ferric carboxymaltose.

sources.label: GESA Iron deficiency in IBD position statement

options.rationale: Alternate-day oral iron reduces gastrointestinal side effects and improves absorption in some patients, but a substantial GI intolerance history in active or previously active IBD is a recognised indication for switching to IV iron rather than a further oral trial. (Source: GESA Iron deficiency in IBD position statement)
source_refs: GESA Iron deficiency in IBD position statement

options.rationale: Packed red cell transfusion is reserved for symptomatic anaemia, haemodynamic instability, or very low haemoglobin (typically below 70 g/L outside cardiovascular disease). This patient is haemodynamically stable at 102 g/L and IV iron alone will address the deficit safely. (Source: NBA Patient Blood Management Guidelines)

Intramuscular iron produces persistent painful skin staining, unreliable absorption and inferior haematological response compared with IV iron. It is no longer recommended and is not offered in current Australian practice. (Source: AMH: iron preparations)

There is no evidence of active disease (calprotectin 92, SCCAI 1, no visible bleeding). Colectomy is not indicated by iron deficiency alone in an otherwise remitting patient. Iron deficiency in IBD often reflects reduced absorption and chronic inflammation rather than ongoing loss. (Source: GESA Iron deficiency in IBD position statement)
source_refs: GESA Iron deficiency in IBD position statement

options.rationale: GESA endorses IV iron as first line in iron deficiency anaemia complicating IBD when oral iron is not tolerated, ineffective, or during active disease. Ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg as a single infusion is standard for a 72 kg patient with haemoglobin 102 g/L; repeat FBC and ferritin at eight weeks assesses response and stores. (Source: GESA Iron deficiency in IBD position statement)
source_refs: GESA Iron deficiency in IBD position statement

explanation.summary: Denosumab is a RANKL inhibitor whose bone effect reverses rapidly on cessation because it does not embed in bone. Discontinuation without a bisphosphonate hand-over causes a rebound in bone remodelling with reported multiple vertebral fractures 8-18 months after the last dose. Australian endocrine consensus is to continue denosumab dosing on schedule and give a single dose of intravenous zoledronic acid 5 mg six months after the last denosumab dose, at the time the next injection would have been due. Repeat DXA and consider a second zoledronic acid dose at 12-24 months based on bone turnover markers and DXA. Oral bisphosphonates (alendronate 70 mg weekly) are an alternative if IV administration is impractical, though evidence is stronger for the IV route. Calcium, vitamin D sufficiency and fall prevention support any regimen.
key_points: Denosumab effect reverses rapidly on cessation because it does not embed in bone.
Multiple vertebral fractures 8-18 months after last dose are reported without hand-over.
Standard hand-over: zoledronic acid 5 mg IV at the time the next denosumab dose was due.
Alendronate 70 mg weekly is an alternative when IV is impractical.
Teriparatide after denosumab is associated with accelerated hip bone loss in the first year.
explanation.pearls: When stopping denosumab, give a single dose of IV zoledronic acid 5 mg six months after the last denosumab dose, at the time the next injection was due - waiting for DXA decline before intervening misses the rebound vertebral fracture window.

sources.label: RACGP Osteoporosis: prevention, diagnosis and management
Endocrine Society of Australia denosumab discontinuation statement

options.rationale: Discontinuation is legitimate provided the transition is managed. Indefinite denosumab in a patient in the osteopenic range (hip T-score -2.2, spine -1.6 on treatment) after four years without fracture is not mandated; the risk lies in stopping without a bone-antiresorptive hand-over. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis: prevention, diagnosis and management)
source_refs: RACGP Osteoporosis: prevention, diagnosis and management

options.rationale: Simply stopping denosumab without bisphosphonate cover produces rebound multiple vertebral fractures typically 8-18 months later, with reports of six or more concurrent vertebral fractures at re-presentation. Observation and supplements do not mitigate this. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia denosumab discontinuation statement)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia denosumab discontinuation statement

options.rationale: Discontinuation of denosumab is followed within 6-9 months by a rebound in bone remodelling with documented multiple vertebral fractures. Endocrine Society of Australia and Osteoporosis Australia endorse a bisphosphonate hand-over: continue on-time denosumab dosing until the transition, then give zoledronic acid IV at the time the next denosumab dose would have been due. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia denosumab discontinuation statement)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia denosumab discontinuation statement
RACGP Osteoporosis: prevention, diagnosis and management

options.rationale: Teriparatide after denosumab is associated with accelerated bone loss at the hip in the first year and does not prevent the rebound resorption of denosumab discontinuation. It is not the correct sequence; teriparatide is best used before denosumab or bisphosphonate. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia denosumab discontinuation statement)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia denosumab discontinuation statement

options.rationale: DXA decline lags the rebound resorption by many months and the fractures often occur before a detectable T-score drop. Waiting for imaging change misses the therapeutic window; hand-over antiresorptive is planned at the time of the missed dose. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia denosumab discontinuation statement)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia denosumab discontinuation statement

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis in known primary adrenal insufficiency is precipitated by infection (most commonly gastroenteritis), surgery, trauma or physical stress; mortality is 6% per crisis and higher when steroid delivery is delayed. Diagnosis is clinical: hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, hypercalcaemia, prerenal acute kidney injury, non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. Treatment is immediate IV or IM hydrocortisone 100 mg followed by 200 mg per 24 hours as continuous infusion or 50 mg every six hours, plus rapid isotonic fluid resuscitation. Fludrocortisone is not needed while hydrocortisone dose is above 40-50 mg per day because mineralocorticoid receptors are saturated. Patient education on sick-day rules (double or triple oral dose for fever, IM hydrocortisone for vomiting) prevents recurrence.
key_points: Adrenal crisis = hypotension + hyponatraemia + hyperkalaemia + hypoglycaemia + prerenal AKI in known Addison.
First step: hydrocortisone 100 mg IV or IM (not oral, not delayed), then 200 mg per 24 hours.
Isotonic saline resuscitation restores volume and corrects hyponatraemia safely.
Fludrocortisone not needed while hydrocortisone above 40-50 mg per day.
Sick-day rules: double or triple oral dose for fever; IM hydrocortisone if vomiting.
explanation.pearls: In known Addison disease with vomiting, give IM or IV hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately then 200 mg per 24 hours - waiting to see if she can keep oral tablets down is where adrenal crisis mortality happens.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia adrenal crisis guideline

options.rationale: Oral hydrocortisone cannot be relied on in an actively vomiting patient in adrenal crisis. Delay in giving IV or IM hydrocortisone is directly associated with mortality. Fluid resuscitation is correct but must be paired with immediate parenteral glucocorticoid. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia adrenal crisis guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia adrenal crisis guideline

options.rationale: Potassium of 5.8 mmol/L without significant ECG change (no wide QRS, no peaked T waves) is not the immediate life threat; the hypovolaemic shock and cortisol deficiency are. IV hydrocortisone and saline correct both the hyperkalaemia (via mineralocorticoid effect and volume) and the shock. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia adrenal crisis guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia adrenal crisis guideline

options.rationale: Dexamethasone is second choice when the diagnosis of adrenal insufficiency is not yet made and short synacthen testing is planned. In known Addison disease with adrenal crisis, hydrocortisone is preferred because of its mineralocorticoid activity at high dose and long clinical experience. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia adrenal crisis guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia adrenal crisis guideline

options.rationale: Adrenal crisis in a woman with a gastroenteritis trigger who cannot absorb oral therapy needs immediate IV hydrocortisone 100 mg followed by 200 mg per 24 hours (as a continuous infusion or 50 mg every 6 hours) plus aggressive isotonic fluid resuscitation. Fludrocortisone is unnecessary at these hydrocortisone doses because they saturate mineralocorticoid receptors. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia adrenal crisis guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia adrenal crisis guideline

options.rationale: The hyponatraemia is hypovolaemic and cortisol-deficiency related and resolves with isotonic saline and hydrocortisone. Rapid correction with hypertonic saline in this setting increases the risk of osmotic demyelination. Delaying hydrocortisone is dangerous. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia adrenal crisis guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia adrenal crisis guideline

explanation.summary: The 2017 revision of the McDonald criteria allows a diagnosis of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis after a first clinical attack (a clinically isolated syndrome) when MRI shows dissemination in space (T2 lesions in at least two of four typical locations: periventricular, juxtacortical or cortical, infratentorial, spinal cord) and dissemination in time (the simultaneous presence of enhancing and non-enhancing lesions on the same scan, OR a new T2 or gadolinium-enhancing lesion on a follow-up scan). CSF-specific oligoclonal bands substitute for dissemination in time when dissemination in space is fulfilled. Early disease-modifying therapy reduces long-term relapse rate and disability accrual. Australian first-line DMTs include glatiramer acetate, interferon beta and dimethyl fumarate; higher-efficacy options include fingolimod, ocrelizumab, ofatumumab and natalizumab, chosen with the neurology team.
key_points: McDonald 2017: dissemination in space in 2 of 4 typical locations plus DIT.
DIT is met by simultaneous enhancing and non-enhancing lesions, new lesion on follow-up MRI, or CSF-specific oligoclonal bands.
Aquaporin-4 IgG for NMOSD; MOG-IgG for MOG-antibody disease - both differentials to exclude.
IV methylprednisolone shortens relapse duration but does not alter MS natural history.
Early DMT reduces long-term relapse rate and disability accrual.
explanation.pearls: A first optic neuritis with periventricular plus juxtacortical lesions and CSF-specific oligoclonal bands meets 2017 McDonald criteria today - bands substitute for dissemination in time and start the clock on disease-modifying therapy.

options.rationale: Under McDonald 2017 criteria, dissemination in space AND time can both be met on a single scan when both enhancing and non-enhancing lesions coexist. CSF-specific oligoclonal bands substitute for dissemination in time in the setting of dissemination in space. This patient meets MS criteria now. (Source: 2017 McDonald criteria for MS diagnosis)

IV methylprednisolone shortens the optic neuritis relapse duration but does not alter the natural history of MS. Recognising she meets MS criteria and referring for disease-modifying therapy is what changes long-term outcomes. Corticosteroid alone is insufficient. (Source: MS Society Australia clinical guideline)

Aquaporin-4 IgG is negative and MOG-IgG is negative; the imaging pattern is not typical of NMOSD (NMOSD usually shows longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis and area postrema lesions). Empirical rituximab commits to a costly and immunosuppressive regimen for the wrong disease. (Source: 2017 McDonald criteria for MS diagnosis)

Optic neuritis plus periventricular and juxtacortical lesions provides dissemination in space; the coexistence of enhancing and non-enhancing lesions provides dissemination in time. CSF-specific oligoclonal bands provide an additional route to dissemination in time in the 2017 revision. Early DMT reduces long-term disability. (Source: 2017 McDonald criteria for MS diagnosis)

MOG-IgG and JCV are relevant to differential diagnosis and monitoring, but MOG-IgG has already returned negative and JCV serology is used to stratify natalizumab progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy risk, not to make an MS diagnosis. Delaying diagnosis for these is not indicated. (Source: 2017 McDonald criteria for MS diagnosis)

explanation.summary: Acute HIV seroconversion causes a mononucleosis-like illness two to six weeks after exposure in most newly infected people. Fourth-generation HIV combination assays detect both p24 antigen and antibodies and are usually reactive by day 15-20; the confirmatory antibody blot may be indeterminate in the earliest phase. Plasma HIV RNA is diagnostic in the acute window (typical viral loads above 100 000 copies/mL). ASHM endorses immediate antiretroviral therapy regardless of CD4 for individual benefit (reservoir seeding, faster CD4 recovery, lower comorbidity) and public health (Undetectable = Untransmissible). Partner notification, sexually transmitted infection screening, hepatitis B and C screening and vaccination review complete the initial workup.
key_points: Acute retroviral syndrome: fever, pharyngitis, adenopathy, mucocutaneous ulcers, rash 2-6 weeks post-exposure.
Fourth-generation combination test reactive with indeterminate blot suggests acute seroconversion; confirm with HIV RNA.
Immediate antiretroviral therapy is standard regardless of CD4 count.
PEP is a 72-hour preventive window; not applicable once seroconversion has occurred.
Concurrent screening for other STIs, hepatitis B and C is standard at diagnosis.
explanation.pearls: Reactive fourth-generation HIV combination assay with indeterminate blot 28 days after exposure is acute seroconversion until an HIV RNA proves otherwise - ASHM endorses immediate antiretroviral therapy regardless of CD4.

sources.label: ASHM Australian HIV testing and management guidelines
Australasian Society for HIV Medicine antiretroviral treatment guideline

options.rationale: In acute HIV seroconversion the antibody response is incomplete, giving a reactive combination test but indeterminate confirmatory blot. An HIV plasma RNA above about 100000 copies/mL confirms acute infection during the window. ASHM recommends specialist referral for immediate antiretroviral therapy, which reduces reservoir seeding, viral setpoint and onward transmission. (Source: ASHM Australian HIV testing and management guidelines)
source_refs: ASHM Australian HIV testing and management guidelines
Australasian Society for HIV Medicine antiretroviral treatment guideline

options.rationale: A reactive fourth-generation combination assay with a compatible acute retroviral syndrome and a high-risk exposure four weeks ago should trigger urgent same-day HIV plasma RNA quantification and specialist referral. Delaying diagnosis and therapy exposes further sexual contacts and misses the option of early antiretroviral therapy. (Source: ASHM Australian HIV testing and management guidelines)
source_refs: ASHM Australian HIV testing and management guidelines

options.rationale: PEP is a 72-hour post-exposure preventive regimen for HIV-negative individuals. This patient is already reactive on the combination assay and presenting at 28 days after exposure with an acute retroviral syndrome; he needs treatment not prophylaxis. Using PEP mislabels the situation and delays specialist care. (Source: ASHM Australian HIV testing and management guidelines)
source_refs: ASHM Australian HIV testing and management guidelines

options.rationale: Monospot and EBV IgM are negative, making glandular fever unlikely. A reactive fourth-generation combination test with compatible symptoms and exposure requires urgent RNA testing on the current presentation, not deferred repeat serology. (Source: ASHM Australian HIV testing and management guidelines)
source_refs: ASHM Australian HIV testing and management guidelines

options.rationale: Corticosteroids have no role in acute HIV; they immunosuppress at a critical moment. Australian and international guidelines recommend immediate antiretroviral therapy in all confirmed HIV infection regardless of CD4 count, both for individual benefit and to end transmission. (Source: ASHM Australian HIV testing and management guidelines)
source_refs: ASHM Australian HIV testing and management guidelines

explanation.summary: Direct oral anticoagulant related intracranial haemorrhage carries very high mortality and needs rapid, agent-specific reversal. Idarucizumab (5 g IV as two 2.5 g boluses) reverses dabigatran specifically. Andexanet alfa reverses apixaban and rivaroxaban; the ANNEXA-4 dosing regimen is by drug, dose and time since last dose (low-dose 400 mg bolus plus 4 mg/min infusion for up to 120 minutes; high-dose 800 mg bolus plus 8 mg/min for recent large doses within 8 hours). Four-factor PCC 25-50 IU/kg is the alternative when andexanet is unavailable, though evidence is observational. Concurrent care includes rapid systolic blood pressure lowering to under 140 mmHg (INTERACT-2 and INTERACT-3), IV tranexamic acid 1 g, seizure prophylaxis if clinically indicated, and urgent neurosurgical review for haematoma evacuation or external ventricular drainage as appropriate.
key_points: Dabigatran: idarucizumab 5 g IV as two 2.5 g boluses.
Apixaban/rivaroxaban: andexanet alfa (low or high dose per ANNEXA-4 algorithm); PCC 25-50 IU/kg if andexanet unavailable.
Vitamin K, protamine, fresh frozen plasma do NOT reverse DOAC effect.
Target systolic BP under 140 mmHg per INTERACT-2 in acute ICH.
Empirical reversal in life-threatening bleeding; do not wait for anti-Xa level.
explanation.pearls: For life-threatening ICH on apixaban within about 18 hours of the last dose, give andexanet alfa empirically (low dose 400 mg bolus then 4 mg/min for up to 120 minutes) - waiting for the anti-Xa level costs a couple of hours of haematoma expansion.

options.rationale: In a life-threatening intracranial haemorrhage on a factor Xa inhibitor within about 18 hours of the last dose, reversal is empirical. Waiting 90 minutes for the anti-Xa level costs meaningful haematoma expansion and does not change the reversal decision. (Source: HSANZ DOAC reversal consensus)

Four-factor PCC 50 IU/kg is reasonable when andexanet is unavailable but is second-line to andexanet in life-threatening bleeding on a factor Xa inhibitor. Vitamin K has no role in DOAC reversal. Permissive BP above 160 systolic on active bleeding is contrary to INTERACT-2 and worsens haematoma expansion. (Source: HSANZ DOAC reversal consensus)

Idarucizumab is a specific reversal agent for dabigatran, not for factor Xa inhibitors such as apixaban. Fresh frozen plasma does not reverse DOAC effect and delays definitive management. (Source: HSANZ DOAC reversal consensus)

For a life-threatening bleed on a factor Xa inhibitor within about 18 hours of the last dose, andexanet alfa is the specific reversal agent supported by ANNEXA-4. Dose is determined by apixaban dose and time since last dose (this scenario meets low-dose criteria). Parallel BP control (INTERACT protocol target under 140 systolic), tranexamic acid and early neurosurgical review round out the bundle. (Source: HSANZ DOAC reversal consensus)

Protamine reverses unfractionated heparin and partially reverses low molecular weight heparin, not apixaban. Empirical red cell transfusion in the absence of anaemia does not treat DOAC-associated ICH. Targeting a systolic of 180 mmHg promotes expansion. (Source: HSANZ DOAC reversal consensus)

explanation.summary: Acute Stanford type A aortic dissection (involving the ascending aorta) is a surgical emergency: untreated mortality is about 1-2% per hour in the first 48 hours, and about half of untreated patients die within 24 hours. Presentation classically includes tearing interscapular chest pain, inter-arm blood pressure difference greater than 20 mmHg, and malperfusion syndromes (limb, cerebral, coronary, renal, mesenteric, spinal). Immediate management is impulse control - heart rate reduction with a beta blocker (esmolol infusion titrated to a rate of 60) to reduce dP/dt, THEN systolic reduction to 100-120 mmHg with vasodilator (glyceryl trinitrate or sodium nitroprusside). Anticoagulation, thrombolysis and pericardiocentesis are dangerous unless there is haemodynamic collapse from tamponade. Definitive treatment is emergency cardiothoracic surgical repair, often with concurrent endovascular fenestration for malperfusion.
key_points: Stanford A (ascending aorta involved) is a surgical emergency; medical alone has ~50% 24-hour mortality.
Impulse control: heart rate first (beta blocker), then systolic 100-120 with vasodilator.
Never give vasodilator before adequate beta blockade (reflex tachycardia worsens dissection).
Anticoagulation and thrombolysis are contraindicated in acute aortic dissection.
Malperfusion syndromes are managed intraoperatively or with endovascular fenestration.
explanation.pearls: In acute Stanford type A dissection with malperfusion, start esmolol first (heart rate 60), THEN vasodilator to systolic 100-120 mmHg, and activate cardiothoracic surgery immediately - each hour without repair is roughly 1-2% additional mortality.

options.rationale: Stanford type A dissection is a surgical emergency; medical management alone has around 50% 24-hour mortality. Initial temporising is impulse control (heart rate first with beta blocker to reduce dP/dt) then systolic target 100-120; add vasodilator only after adequate beta blockade to prevent reflex tachycardia and shear stress. Malperfusion syndromes are addressed intraoperatively or by simultaneous endovascular fenestration. (Source: eTG Complete Cardiovascular: aortic dissection)

Nitroprusside without prior beta blockade causes reflex tachycardia and increases aortic wall shear stress, worsening propagation. Medical management alone is inappropriate for type A dissection because it is a surgical emergency. (Source: eTG Complete Cardiovascular: aortic dissection)

Anticoagulation in acute aortic dissection risks catastrophic aortic rupture or worsening pericardial haemorrhage into tamponade. Malperfusion is treated by restoring true lumen flow surgically or endovascularly, not by anticoagulation. (Source: eTG Complete Cardiovascular: aortic dissection)

Thrombolysis in acute aortic dissection is contraindicated and precipitates catastrophic bleeding into the false lumen and pericardium. The neurological deficit here reflects malperfusion from arch vessel involvement, not thrombotic stroke, and is treated by emergency surgical repair. (Source: eTG Complete Cardiovascular: aortic dissection)

Pericardiocentesis in dissection-related haemopericardium can precipitate rapid rebleeding and circulatory collapse and is generally deferred until the aorta is repaired unless there is immediate cardiovascular collapse from tamponade. Small pericardial effusion without tamponade physiology is not an indication. (Source: STS/AATS Aortic Dissection Guideline)

explanation.summary: Uncomplicated cystitis in non-pregnant women without immune compromise, renal tract abnormality, or recent healthcare exposure is treated empirically without waiting for culture.
key_points: First-line uncomplicated cystitis: trimethoprim 3 days OR nitrofurantoin 5 days.
Amoxicillin has too much E coli resistance to be empirical.
Cefalexin is kept for when trimethoprim and nitrofurantoin cannot be used; fluoroquinolones are reserved for resistance or complicated infection.
explanation.pearls: Australian empirical uncomplicated cystitis therapy is trimethoprim 300 mg nightly for 3 days, or nitrofurantoin 100 mg 6-hourly for 5 days; culture is sent but treatment does not wait for the result.

sources.label: PSA: Treatment guideline for pharmacists - Cystitis

options.rationale: Fluoroquinolones are reserved for complicated infections, resistance, or intolerance in the Australian empirical UTI pathway. (Source: eTG: Antibiotic; TGA fluoroquinolone advisory)
Amoxicillin has high resistance in Australian E coli isolates (about 40-50%) and is not an empirical first-line for cystitis. (Source: eTG: Antibiotic)

Australian eTG first-line for uncomplicated cystitis in non-pregnant women without risk factors is trimethoprim 300 mg nightly for 3 days, or nitrofurantoin 100 mg 6-hourly for 5 days. (Source: eTG: Antibiotic)

Cefalexin 500 mg 12-hourly for 5 days is one of the Australian regimens for acute cystitis, but it is broader in spectrum and is reserved for when trimethoprim and nitrofurantoin cannot be used, such as allergy or documented resistance. Documented resistance to both first-line agents on a culture is the situation in which cefalexin becomes the empirical pick. (Source: eTG: Antibiotic; PSA: Treatment guideline for pharmacists - Cystitis)
source_refs: PSA: Treatment guideline for pharmacists - Cystitis

options.rationale: Fosfomycin is available in Australia via the Special Access Scheme for multidrug-resistant uncomplicated cystitis; it is not an empirical first-line agent. (Source: eTG: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Emergency therapy for hyperkalaemia shifts potassium rather than removing it, so the level rebounds within hours. Patients treated for hyperkalaemia with electrocardiogram changes are admitted for continuous monitoring and serial potassium measurement.
key_points: Insulin and salbutamol shift potassium; only binders, diuresis or dialysis remove it.
Recheck potassium within two to four hours and again as the shifting effect ends.
Continue cardiac monitoring until the potassium is stable and the cause is controlled.
explanation.context: Total body potassium is around 3500 mmol in an adult, and only about 2% of it sits in the extracellular space. That is why shifting a small quantity inside cells produces a dramatic fall in the measured value and why the improvement is borrowed rather than earned. Unless the kidney, a binder or the dialyser has actually excreted potassium, the level climbs back as insulin and beta agonist effects decay. Treating the number and discharging on it is a recognised way to return the same patient in extremis a few hours later.

sources.label: Kidney Health Australia CARI - Hyperkalaemia management

options.rationale: Insulin and salbutamol move potassium into cells for a few hours; they do not remove it, so the potassium rebounds as the effect wears off. A patient who needed emergency treatment stays on a monitor with serial levels until the cause is controlled. (Source: Kidney Health Australia CARI - Hyperkalaemia management)
source_refs: Kidney Health Australia CARI - Hyperkalaemia management

options.rationale: Discharge with outpatient testing suits mild hyperkalaemia found incidentally in a well outpatient with a normal electrocardiogram and a reversible cause already removed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Renal Dysfunction)
source_refs: Kidney Health Australia CARI - Hyperkalaemia management

options.rationale: Dietary advice belongs in the longer-term plan, particularly where a salt substitute or a high potassium diet contributed. Diet does not address the coming rebound. (Source: Kidney Health Australia CARI - Hyperkalaemia management)
source_refs: Kidney Health Australia CARI - Hyperkalaemia management

options.rationale: Neither timeframe fits: binders act over hours to days and one further hour does not span the period when shifted potassium returns. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Kidney Health Australia CARI - Hyperkalaemia management

options.rationale: Cardiology follow up fits where the electrocardiogram abnormality is primarily cardiac rather than metabolic. Here the rhythm changes were driven by potassium and the problem is renal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Renal Dysfunction)

explanation.summary: Suspected PE is worked up in steps: estimate the pre-test probability, use a D-dimer only when PE is unlikely, and image when PE is likely or the D-dimer is positive. The two-level Wells score calls PE unlikely at 4 points or less and likely above 4. D-dimer rises with age, so a fixed 0.5 mg/L FEU cut-off sends many older patients to CTPA unnecessarily; NICE advises considering an age-adjusted threshold (age x 0.01 mg/L FEU) over 50. Once PE is excluded, her pleuritic pain still needs a diagnosis.
key_points: Two-level Wells: 4 or less is PE unlikely; more than 4 is PE likely and goes straight to CTPA.
In the PE-unlikely group, a negative D-dimer excludes PE without imaging.
Age-adjusted D-dimer threshold over 50 years: age x 0.01 mg/L FEU (0.82 mg/L at 82).
PERC applies only to patients under 50 with a pre-test probability below 15%.
explanation.pearls: NICE NG158 advises using a fully quantitative test when a point-of-care D-dimer is used.

options.rationale: CTPA is the next test when the two-level Wells score is more than 4 or the D-dimer is positive. NICE advises considering an age-adjusted D-dimer threshold for people over 50, which at 82 is 0.82 mg/L FEU, so her 0.64 mg/L is a negative result. (Source: NICE NG158: Venous thromboembolic diseases)

THANZ prefers CTPA for suspected PE and V/Q scanning in pregnancy, and NICE turns to V/Q when there is contrast allergy, a creatinine clearance below 30 mL/min or a high radiation risk. Age alone is not one of these, and she needs no imaging. (Source: THANZ VTE guideline (MJA 2019); NICE NG158: Venous thromboembolic diseases)

Her two-level Wells score is 3 (PE the most likely diagnosis, no other items), which is PE unlikely. THANZ states that a non-high pre-test probability with a negative D-dimer safely excludes VTE without imaging, and 0.64 mg/L is below her age-adjusted threshold of 0.82 mg/L. (Source: THANZ VTE guideline (MJA 2019); NICE NG158: Venous thromboembolic diseases)

Interim therapeutic anticoagulation covers patients whose D-dimer or imaging result cannot be obtained within 4 hours while PE is still being investigated. Here the D-dimer has already excluded PE, so anticoagulation would add bleeding risk for no benefit. (Source: NICE NG158: Venous thromboembolic diseases)

THANZ limits PERC to patients younger than 50 with an estimated PE probability below 15%, so at 82 PERC cannot rule PE out for her. In the PE-unlikely group over 50, the age-adjusted D-dimer is the rule-out test. (Source: THANZ VTE guideline (MJA 2019))

explanation.summary: Prosthetic valve endocarditis differs from native-valve infection in that biofilm on the prosthesis harbours organisms that are less accessible to standard antibiotics, so empirical therapy for staphylococci adds rifampicin to vancomycin and gentamicin.
key_points: Prosthetic valve staphylococcal empirical therapy: vancomycin PLUS rifampicin PLUS gentamicin.
Rifampicin is specifically added for biofilm penetration.
Native-valve MSSA endocarditis is treated with flucloxacillin.
explanation.pearls: Rifampicin 600 mg 12-hourly is the specific added agent in prosthetic-valve staphylococcal endocarditis because it penetrates biofilm; gentamicin is added for the first 2 weeks.

options.rationale: Staphylococcal prosthetic valve endocarditis with methicillin susceptibility unknown needs vancomycin to cover methicillin-resistant strains, rifampicin for biofilm on the prosthesis, and gentamicin. (Source: eTG: Antibiotic)
Flucloxacillin monotherapy is native-valve MSSA coverage; prosthetic-valve infection requires vancomycin plus rifampicin. (Source: eTG: Antibiotic)

Benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin is empirical for streptococcal or enterococcal native-valve endocarditis, not staphylococcal prosthetic valve infection. (Source: eTG: Antibiotic; Australian endocarditis guidelines)
This is a HACEK regimen adaptation and not correct empirical prosthetic-valve staphylococcal endocarditis therapy; it does not cover methicillin-resistant staphylococci. (Source: eTG: Antibiotic)
Meropenem is not the empirical choice for staphylococcal endocarditis; it does not cover methicillin-resistant staphylococci. (Source: eTG: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is precipitated by inability to increase steroid replacement in intercurrent illness (infection, surgery, trauma) or by missed doses in an established primary or secondary adrenal insufficiency.
key_points: Adrenal crisis: hypotension, vomiting, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia in known adrenal insufficiency.
IV hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately then 200 mg per 24 hours; do not wait for cortisol result.
0.9% sodium chloride resuscitation and glucose replacement.
explanation.pearls: Give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV immediately in any suspected adrenal crisis; testing cortisol should not delay treatment in an established Addison patient.

options.rationale: Cortisol result is not needed to treat a known Addison patient in crisis; treatment is empirical based on the clinical picture. (Source: eTG: Endocrinology)

Adrenal crisis in an established Addison patient with intercurrent sepsis, vomiting, hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia needs intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately with 0.9% sodium chloride resuscitation. (Source: eTG: Endocrinology; Endocrine Society adrenal insufficiency)
Dexamethasone can be used when a diagnostic short synacthen test is still to be done in a previously unaffected patient. (Source: eTG: Endocrinology)
Oral therapy is not reliable in a vomiting hypotensive patient; parenteral hydrocortisone is essential. (Source: eTG: Endocrinology)
Fludrocortisone is oral and slow-acting; it is not first-line in acute crisis when high-dose hydrocortisone covers mineralocorticoid needs. (Source: eTG: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Diabetic foot osteomyelitis is diagnosed clinically (probe-to-bone, chronic ulcer over bony prominence, elevated inflammatory markers) and confirmed radiologically (MRI is the most sensitive imaging), with bone biopsy to identify the organism.
key_points: Probe-to-bone with ESR over 70 is highly predictive of osteomyelitis.
MRI is most sensitive imaging; plain film lags 2 weeks.
Deep bone biopsy for culture; superficial swabs are unreliable.
explanation.pearls: In suspected diabetic foot osteomyelitis, get an MRI and a bone biopsy before starting empirical antibiotics; targeted therapy is then given for 6 weeks.

options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics without confirming diagnosis and organism in chronic osteomyelitis lead to under-treatment or partial treatment. (Source: eTG: Antibiotic; IWGDF diabetic foot)
Superficial swabs grow surface contaminants and do not represent the deep tissue and bone microbiology in diabetic foot osteomyelitis. (Source: IWGDF diabetic foot)

Probe-to-bone in a chronic ulcer with a raised ESR (over 70) has a high positive predictive value for osteomyelitis, and MRI with bone biopsy defines the extent and the organism so that targeted antibiotics can be given for at least 6 weeks. (Source: IWGDF diabetic foot; eTG: Antibiotic)
Amputation is a last-line intervention when antibiotics with limited surgical debridement fail, or when there is critical limb ischaemia. (Source: IWGDF diabetic foot)
MRI is more specific than bone scan in the diabetic foot, and empirical narrow-spectrum oral therapy without cultures risks inadequate treatment. (Source: IWGDF diabetic foot)

explanation.summary: Massive haemoptysis (typically >100 mL/hour or >600 mL/24 hours) is life-threatening because a small amount of blood floods alveoli and causes asphyxia.
key_points: Massive haemoptysis kills by asphyxia not exsanguination; protect the unaffected lung first.
Bleeding-side-down positioning or selective mainstem intubation.
Bronchial artery embolisation is definitive first-line (90% of bleeding is BA source).
explanation.pearls: In right-sided massive haemoptysis lie the patient right-side down to protect the left lung, then expedite bronchial artery embolisation; do NOT sit them upright.

options.rationale: CT is often part of the workup but positioning and haemostasis come first; imaging in a critically bleeding, unstable patient waits until the airway is protected. (Source: TSANZ)
Supine positioning risks flooding the good lung with blood. Bleeding-side down protects the unaffected lung. (Source: TSANZ)
NIV in massive haemoptysis risks aspiration; the priority is protection of the unaffected lung with positioning and, if needed, intubation. (Source: TSANZ)
In massive haemoptysis the priority is to prevent aspiration to the unaffected lung: lie the patient bleeding-side down. (Source: eTG: Respiratory; TSANZ)
Bronchial artery embolisation is first-line for non-traumatic massive haemoptysis and is less morbid than emergency lobectomy. (Source: TSANZ)

explanation.summary: Modern ischaemic stroke reperfusion has two strands: intravenous thrombolysis (tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg or alteplase) within 4.5 hours from onset or within an extended wake-up window selected by imaging, and endovascular thrombectomy for large-vessel occlusion.
key_points: Large-vessel occlusion with favourable imaging is a thrombectomy indication regardless of thrombolysis eligibility.
Thrombolysis is contraindicated with major surgery within 14 days.
Direct-to-thrombectomy is Australian standard when thrombolysis carries additional risk.
explanation.pearls: Recent major surgery within 14 days makes IV thrombolysis unsafe, but does NOT contraindicate endovascular thrombectomy; go direct to clot retrieval.

options.rationale: Major surgery within 14 days is a relative contraindication to IV thrombolysis because of bleeding risk at the surgical site. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia guidelines)

MRI DWI-FLAIR mismatch is used in wake-up strokes when CT perfusion is not available; here CT perfusion already shows a favourable core-penumbra mismatch. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia guidelines)
Aspirin alone in a large-vessel occlusion with substantial penumbra fails to restore flow and misses the reperfusion window. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia guidelines)

Reduced-dose alteplase is not a standard Australian practice; recent surgery makes thrombolysis unsafe and delaying thrombectomy for 24 hours forfeits salvageable penumbra. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia guidelines)

Ischaemic stroke with large vessel occlusion and favourable core-penumbra mismatch is a thrombectomy indication regardless of thrombolysis eligibility. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia guidelines; DIRECT-MT)

explanation.summary: Provoked VTE with a resolvable trigger is treated for 3 months. Unprovoked proximal DVT or PE has a recurrence rate of about 10% at 1 year and about 30% at 5 years off anticoagulation and is treated with indefinite anticoagulation unless bleeding risk is high. AMPLIFY-EXT showed apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily beyond the initial 6 months of full dose was as effective as 5 mg with lower bleeding. Cancer associated VTE is treated with LMWH or edoxaban or apixaban for a minimum 6 months and often ongoing while cancer active. Antiphospholipid syndrome VTE is treated with warfarin, not a DOAC.
key_points: Provoked VTE: 3 months anticoagulation
Unprovoked proximal VTE or PE: indefinite anticoagulation unless bleeding risk high
Apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily is the extended phase dose (AMPLIFY-EXT)
Antiphospholipid syndrome VTE: warfarin, not DOAC
explanation.pearls: Distal isolated calf DVT and subsegmental PE without symptoms have different rules and may be managed with surveillance in selected patients - a proximal or symptomatic segmental PE is not one of them.

options.rationale: There is no advantage of warfarin over apixaban in unprovoked PE without antiphospholipid syndrome; nine months of warfarin then cessation still stops at a point where recurrence risk remains high. (Source: eTG: Venous thromboembolism)

Six months of anticoagulation is only sufficient for provoked venous thromboembolism where the transient trigger has resolved; unprovoked PE has too high a recurrence rate to safely stop. (Source: eTG: Venous thromboembolism)

Unprovoked PE has an annual recurrence risk of about 10% in the first year off anticoagulation; indefinite anticoagulation is recommended unless bleeding risk is high, and the AMPLIFY-EXT trial supports apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily beyond 6 months with a low bleeding rate. (Source: eTG: Venous thromboembolism; AMPLIFY-EXT NEJM 2013)

Aspirin reduces VTE recurrence by only about 30% compared with anticoagulation and is inferior to low dose apixaban continuation; ASPIRE and WARFASA trials do not support aspirin instead of a DOAC. (Source: eTG: Venous thromboembolism)

IVC filters are reserved for patients with acute VTE and an absolute contraindication to anticoagulation; they do not treat existing thrombus and carry their own long term complications. (Source: eTG: Venous thromboembolism)

explanation.summary: Acute pyelonephritis in an adult requiring admission is treated empirically with IV gentamicin plus amoxicillin (or ampicillin) per eTG, covering E coli and Enterococcus. Ceftriaxone 1 g daily IV is an alternative when aminoglycosides are contraindicated. Duration is 10-14 days total with switch to oral therapy guided by susceptibilities once systemically well. Ciprofloxacin is reserved for beta lactam allergy or susceptibility results. Nitrofurantoin and trimethoprim have no role in pyelonephritis. Mild pyelonephritis with tolerable oral therapy may be treated as an outpatient with amoxicillin clavulanate or cefalexin per susceptibilities.
key_points: First line IV pyelonephritis: gentamicin plus amoxicillin
Ceftriaxone alternative when aminoglycosides contraindicated
Total duration 10-14 days with early oral switch when possible
Nitrofurantoin does not treat pyelonephritis (poor tissue penetration)
explanation.pearls: Gentamicin dosing in acute settings is 5 mg/kg once daily; check gentamicin trough level at 24 h if continued beyond 48 h and reassess renal function daily.

options.rationale: Trimethoprim is not first line for pyelonephritis due to rising resistance, and this woman cannot tolerate oral therapy due to vomiting; oral trimethoprim is used for simple cystitis, not pyelonephritis. (Source: eTG: Acute pyelonephritis)

eTG empirical therapy for acute pyelonephritis in an adult tolerating IV is gentamicin plus amoxicillin (or ampicillin), covering E coli and Enterococcus with excellent renal tissue penetration; oral therapy is used only for mild pyelonephritis and she is vomiting and unable to tolerate oral. (Source: eTG: Acute pyelonephritis)

Ciprofloxacin is reserved for beta lactam allergy or documented resistance in AU guidance due to fluoroquinolone associated side effects and resistance concerns; she can be given the first line IV regimen. (Source: eTG: Acute pyelonephritis)

Vancomycin adds no useful cover for the uropathogens (E coli, Klebsiella, Enterococcus) in a woman with no MRSA risk factors and no penicillin allergy; gentamicin plus amoxicillin is the AU first line. (Source: eTG: Acute pyelonephritis)
Nitrofurantoin does not achieve adequate tissue concentrations in the kidney and is contraindicated in pyelonephritis; she also cannot tolerate oral therapy. (Source: eTG: Acute pyelonephritis)

explanation.summary: Adult DKA management follows a sequence of fluid, then potassium consideration, then fixed rate insulin infusion, plus glucose monitoring and dextrose addition when glucose falls under 14 mmol/L. First hour is 0.9% saline 1 L. Potassium is added at 40 mmol/L when serum potassium is under 5.5, held when 5.5 or higher. Fixed rate insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour after fluid started. Ketosis clearance is the endpoint, not glucose normalisation - target beta hydroxybutyrate fall of 0.5 mmol/L/hour and bicarbonate rise of 3 mmol/L/hour. Bicarbonate is reserved for pH under 6.9.
key_points: First hour: 0.9% saline 1 L
Add 40 mmol/L potassium when K+ under 5.5
Fixed rate insulin infusion 0.1 units/kg/hour
Add 10% dextrose when glucose falls under 14 mmol/L to allow continued insulin
explanation.pearls: Ketosis, not hyperglycaemia, is the target of DKA treatment - keep insulin running until beta hydroxybutyrate is under 0.6 mmol/L even if that requires simultaneous dextrose to prevent hypoglycaemia.

options.rationale: Bicarbonate in DKA is reserved for pH under 6.9 or life threatening hyperkalaemia; giving it at pH 7.14 does not improve outcomes and can worsen intracellular acidosis and cerebral oedema. (Source: eTG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

His glucose is 26.4 mmol/L and dextrose is not indicated as initial fluid; dextrose is added later when glucose falls to under 14 mmol/L to allow continued insulin without hypoglycaemia. (Source: eTG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

0.45% saline is a hypotonic maintenance fluid not indicated for initial resuscitation of DKA; rapid infusion of hypotonic fluid raises cerebral oedema risk especially in younger patients. (Source: eTG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

AU consensus DKA pathway (RACGP, endocrine consensus) starts with 0.9% saline 1 L in the first hour to restore intravascular volume; potassium is added when serum potassium is under 5.5 and fixed rate insulin infusion started at 0.1 units/kg/hour after initial fluid. His potassium is at 5.6 so no potassium is added yet. (Source: eTG: Diabetic ketoacidosis; ADS/ADEA position statement 2020)

Potassium is added only when serum potassium is under 5.5 mmol/L; giving 40 mmol potassium with his admission potassium of 5.6 mmol/L risks worsening hyperkalaemia and precipitating a cardiac arrest. (Source: eTG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is a clinical diagnosis when a known Addison patient presents with vomiting, hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia during physiological stress. Immediate management is IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus, followed by 200 mg/24 h by continuous infusion or 50 mg every 6 hours IV or IM, plus rapid IV saline (1-2 L in the first hour, guided by response), correction of hypoglycaemia with IV dextrose, and treatment of the precipitant. Cortisol and ACTH samples should be taken pre steroid where possible but treatment must not be delayed for the result. Patients receive a sick day management plan with parenteral hydrocortisone at home.
key_points: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus, then 200 mg/24 h infusion or 50 mg IV/IM q6h
IV saline 1-2 L first hour then guided by response
Correct hypoglycaemia with IV dextrose
Sick day rules: double dose oral if unwell, parenteral IM hydrocortisone if vomiting
explanation.pearls: Every patient with Addison's disease should carry a medic alert bracelet and a home IM hydrocortisone Act-O-Vial that they and family can use before ambulance arrival - the difference between minor illness and cardiac arrest can be one missed cover dose.

options.rationale: He is vomiting and cannot keep oral medication down; the sick day rule for oral doubling has failed and parenteral therapy is required. Oral now delays effective treatment. (Source: eTG: Adrenal insufficiency)

Adrenal crisis is a clinical diagnosis in a known Addison patient with vomiting, hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia; immediate management is 100 mg hydrocortisone IV bolus with rapid saline resuscitation and correction of glucose. Do not wait for cortisol result. (Source: Endocrine Society adrenal insufficiency guideline 2016; eTG: Adrenal insufficiency)

Hydrocortisone is preferred in acute adrenal crisis because it provides both glucocorticoid and some mineralocorticoid activity; awaiting synacthen results before treatment risks death. Dexamethasone can be used only if cortisol assay is pending and hydrocortisone is unavailable. (Source: Endocrine Society adrenal insufficiency guideline 2016)

Fludrocortisone is a pure mineralocorticoid and does not provide the glucocorticoid activity urgently needed in adrenal crisis; hydrocortisone at stress doses covers both. (Source: eTG: Adrenal insufficiency)

The hyponatraemia is driven by cortisol and aldosterone deficiency; hypertonic saline is not indicated as first line correction here and correcting sodium too rapidly risks osmotic demyelination without addressing the crisis. (Source: eTG: Adrenal insufficiency)

explanation.summary: SJS and TEN are severe cutaneous adverse reactions on a spectrum defined by percentage of body surface area with detachment (SJS under 10%, SJS-TEN overlap 10-30%, TEN over 30%). Culprit drugs in AU include allopurinol, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, sulfonamides and NSAIDs. Immediate management is cessation of the culprit drug, transfer to a burns or HDU for meticulous supportive care (fluid balance, temperature, wound care, ophthalmology and urology involvement), and SCORTEN prognosis calculation. Systemic corticosteroids, IVIG and ciclosporin are used in some centres but evidence is inconsistent. HLA B*58:01 screening before allopurinol is now recommended for South East Asian, Han Chinese, Korean and Thai ancestry patients due to strong association.
key_points: SJS/TEN classification: SJS under 10% BSA, overlap 10-30%, TEN over 30%
First step: cease culprit drug immediately, transfer to burns unit
Allopurinol is the highest risk AU culprit for SCAR
HLA B*58:01 screening for allopurinol in Southeast Asian and Han Chinese ancestry
explanation.pearls: SCORTEN uses 7 parameters (age, malignancy, tachycardia, BSA detached, serum urea, bicarbonate, glucose) at 24 h to estimate mortality; each point roughly doubles risk.

sources.label: ADRAC alert on allopurinol HLA B*58:01

options.rationale: Continuing the culprit drug is contraindicated in SJS/TEN; systemic corticosteroids have inconsistent evidence and are not recommended as first line without specialist input, and a general ward cannot provide the burns level care required. (Source: eTG: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions)

SJS/TEN suspected by mucosal involvement at two or more sites plus epidermal detachment mandates immediate cessation of the culprit drug (allopurinol is the highest risk in AU) and transfer to a burns or high dependency unit; SCORTEN estimates mortality and drives resource allocation. Supportive care mirrors burns management. (Source: eTG: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions; ADRAC alert on allopurinol HLA B*58:01)
source_refs: ADRAC alert on allopurinol HLA B*58:01

options.rationale: This is not cellulitis and empirical antibiotics can worsen the reaction by introducing further culprit drugs; biopsy can be done but must not delay drug cessation and transfer to specialist care. (Source: eTG: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions)

SJS/TEN mortality with TEN over 30% BSA reaches 30-50% and requires intensive supportive care; outpatient management is inconsistent with the diagnosis and puts the patient at risk of sepsis and death. (Source: eTG: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions)

Rechallenge with the culprit drug in SJS/TEN is contraindicated; a lower dose is not safer, the reaction is idiosyncratic and immune mediated. Rechallenge has caused fatal recurrence. (Source: eTG: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions)

explanation.summary: Myasthenic crisis is defined by neuromuscular respiratory failure requiring ventilator support or imminent respiratory failure. Precipitants include infection and specific medications (macrolides, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, beta blockers, magnesium). Bedside markers of imminent decompensation are vital capacity under 15 mL/kg (or 1 L) and NIF worse than -20 cmH2O; hypercapnia is a late finding. First line rescue therapies are plasma exchange or IVIG (equal efficacy), with concurrent high dose steroids introduced cautiously due to early worsening. Non-invasive ventilation may buy time in selected patients; early elective intubation avoids decompensation.
key_points: Crisis markers: VC under 15 mL/kg, NIF worse than -20 cmH2O, hypercapnia is late
First line rescue: plasma exchange OR IVIG (equal efficacy)
Macrolides, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, beta blockers all worsen MG
Cholinergic crisis mimics MG crisis but has muscarinic features (sweating, salivation, miosis)
explanation.pearls: Early transfer to ICU for airway management prevents catastrophic respiratory arrest - a patient who cannot count to 20 in one breath should not stay on the ward.

options.rationale: Myasthenic crisis with vital capacity under 15 mL/kg and NIF worse than -20 cmH2O predicts imminent respiratory failure; ICU monitoring for elective intubation before decompensation is essential. Plasma exchange and IVIG are equally effective first line rescue therapies. Azithromycin and other macrolides worsen weakness in myasthenia gravis and must be ceased. (Source: RANZCP neurology practice; ANZAN myasthenia guidance; eTG: Myasthenia gravis)

Pyridostigmine escalation risks cholinergic crisis with similar weakness and increased secretions; higher doses do not treat the underlying immune process and delay definitive rescue therapy. (Source: eTG: Myasthenia gravis)

High dose steroids can transiently worsen myasthenic weakness in the first 5-10 days and must be given with rescue cover in place; ward observation without ICU monitoring risks unrecognised respiratory failure. (Source: eTG: Myasthenia gravis)
The dysphagia is neuromuscular from the crisis and not structural; oesophagoscopy is not indicated and would delay life saving treatment. (Source: eTG: Myasthenia gravis)

Edrophonium (Tensilon) was historically used diagnostically but is no longer available in AU and does not change management in a known seropositive MG patient in crisis; treatment should not be delayed. (Source: ANZAN myasthenia guidance)

explanation.summary: Warfarin associated intracerebral haemorrhage requires immediate reversal with prothrombin complex concentrate 25-50 units/kg (dose by INR and weight) plus IV vitamin K 10 mg. PCC restores clotting factors within minutes; vitamin K keeps INR reversed as PCC effect wanes. FFP is slower, larger volume and inferior. Intensive systolic blood pressure lowering to 130-140 mmHg within one hour (INTERACT2, ATACH-2) reduces haematoma expansion and improves functional outcome compared with a 180 mmHg target. Neurosurgical consultation is indicated for supratentorial haematomas with mass effect and cerebellar haemorrhage over 3 cm; DOAC reversal uses agent specific antidotes (idarucizumab for dabigatran, andexanet alfa or 4-factor PCC for factor Xa inhibitors).
key_points: Warfarin ICH: PCC 25-50 units/kg plus vitamin K 10 mg IV
Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran; andexanet or 4F-PCC for factor Xa DOACs
Target systolic BP 130-140 mmHg within one hour (INTERACT2, ATACH-2)
Alteplase is contraindicated in haemorrhagic stroke
explanation.pearls: PCC dose depends on both INR and weight - a common AU shortcut for high INR is 50 units/kg capped at 3000 units for adults, but the local haematology pathway should always be followed.

options.rationale: Warfarin associated ICH needs immediate reversal with prothrombin complex concentrate (dose by INR and weight, typically 25-50 units/kg) plus vitamin K 10 mg IV for sustained reversal; PCC works within minutes while vitamin K sustains it. INTERACT2 and ATACH-2 support rapid intensive systolic BP lowering to 130-140 mmHg within one hour, better than 180 mmHg or higher targets. (Source: eTG: Anticoagulant reversal; INTERACT2 NEJM 2013; NHFA/CSANZ acute stroke guideline)

FFP takes hours to fully reverse warfarin and requires large volumes with fluid overload risk; PCC gives faster reversal with less volume. Permissive hypertension in ICH is inconsistent with INTERACT2 evidence for lowering to 130-140 mmHg. (Source: eTG: Anticoagulant reversal; INTERACT2 NEJM 2013)

Alteplase is absolutely contraindicated in intracerebral haemorrhage and would extend the haematoma with lethal effect; the CT already demonstrates haemorrhagic stroke. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ acute stroke guideline)

Vitamin K alone takes 6-24 hours to reverse warfarin, which is too slow in the setting of an expanding intracerebral haematoma; PCC is required for immediate reversal with vitamin K as adjunct for sustained effect. (Source: eTG: Anticoagulant reversal)

Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran, not warfarin; using it here provides no reversal and delays PCC administration. Systolic BP target of 180 is above INTERACT2 evidence for intensive lowering. (Source: eTG: Anticoagulant reversal)

explanation.summary: Australian HIV opportunistic infection prophylaxis is anchored by CD4 threshold. At CD4 below 200, start trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia; at CD4 below 100 with positive toxoplasma serology, the same trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole regimen covers toxoplasmosis. At CD4 below 50, azithromycin 1200 mg weekly for Mycobacterium avium complex is the traditional prophylaxis (modern guidance in some regions defers if antiretroviral therapy is imminent and reliably tolerated). Primary cryptococcal, cytomegalovirus and antituberculous prophylaxis are guided by antigen, quantitative polymerase chain reaction and tuberculosis screening respectively. Prophylaxis can be discontinued after immune reconstitution.
key_points: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia prophylaxis threshold CD4 <200; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
Toxoplasma prophylaxis threshold CD4 <100 with positive toxoplasma IgG; same trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole covers both.
Mycobacterium avium complex prophylaxis threshold CD4 <50; azithromycin 1200 mg weekly.
explanation.pearls: CD4 42 cells/microL with toxoplasma IgG positive: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole double strength daily covers Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and toxoplasmosis; add azithromycin 1200 mg weekly for Mycobacterium avium complex.

sources.label: US DHHS Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Opportunistic Infections in Adults and Adolescents with HIV

options.rationale: At CD4 below 100 with positive toxoplasma serology, the trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole regimen also covers toxoplasmosis and no additional agent is required for toxoplasmosis, but Mycobacterium avium complex prophylaxis is separately considered. (Source: ASHM HIV Management in Australasia)

Primary fluconazole prophylaxis is not routinely recommended without positive cryptococcal antigen or symptomatic disease; treat the candidiasis if symptomatic. (Source: ASHM HIV Management in Australasia)

Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole double strength daily covers Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and, at CD4 below 100 with toxoplasma seropositivity, toxoplasmosis. Mycobacterium avium complex prophylaxis with azithromycin 1200 mg weekly is considered at CD4 below 50 (historical threshold; modern guidance recognises many regions now defer if antiretroviral therapy is imminent, but the threshold and agent remain examinable).
