Stopping at 3 months for unprovoked proximal deep vein thrombosis leaves the patient at approximately 10 percent recurrence in year 1; indefinite extended therapy is preferred when bleeding risk is acceptable. (Source: THANZ: Extended Anticoagulation)

Aspirin reduces recurrence by only around 30 percent versus about 80 percent for direct oral anticoagulants; a direct oral anticoagulant is preferred where bleeding risk is acceptable. (Source: THANZ: Extended Anticoagulation)

AMPLIFY EXT and other trials support extended prophylaxis at 2.5 mg twice daily with maintained efficacy and lower bleeding; the reduced dose is standard after 6 months. (Source: THANZ: Extended Anticoagulation)

Direct oral anticoagulants have equivalent or superior efficacy with lower major bleeding compared with warfarin in venous thromboembolism prevention and are preferred first line in AU. (Source: THANZ: Extended Anticoagulation)

explanation.summary: Opportunistic infection prophylaxis in HIV is stratified by CD4 count and pathogen specific risk. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia prophylaxis is indicated at CD4 below 200 cells per microlitre, CD4 percentage below 14, oral thrush, or previous PJP; first line is trimethoprim plus sulfamethoxazole 160 plus 800 mg daily (or 3 times weekly). Alternatives for sulfa allergy include dapsone (screen glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase), atovaquone or pentamidine. Toxoplasmosis prophylaxis is added when CD4 is below 100 and Toxoplasma IgG is positive; trimethoprim plus sulfamethoxazole covers both. Mycobacterium avium complex primary prophylaxis (azithromycin 1200 mg weekly) is no longer routinely recommended when antiretroviral therapy is started promptly. Latent tuberculosis prophylaxis (isoniazid 9 months) is indicated when interferon gamma release assay or tuberculin skin test is positive. Cryptococcal antigen screening at CD4 below 100 identifies patients needing fluconazole pre-emptively.
key_points: PJP prophylaxis at CD4 below 200 (or oral thrush): trimethoprim plus sulfamethoxazole first line.
Toxoplasmosis prophylaxis at CD4 below 100 only if Toxoplasma IgG positive.
MAC primary prophylaxis is no longer routine with prompt antiretroviral therapy; screen cryptococcal antigen at CD4 below 100.
explanation.pearls: Trimethoprim plus sulfamethoxazole 160 plus 800 mg daily is the AU first line PJP prophylaxis at CD4 below 200; add nothing extra when Toxoplasma IgG is negative and antiretroviral therapy is starting.

options.rationale: MAC primary prophylaxis is no longer recommended when antiretroviral therapy is started promptly; toxoplasmosis prophylaxis is only needed if Toxoplasma IgG positive. (Source: ASHM: HIV Guidelines)

AU guidance: PJP prophylaxis at CD4 below 200 cells per microlitre or thrush; MAC prophylaxis is no longer routine with immediate antiretroviral therapy; toxoplasmosis prophylaxis is only for Toxoplasma IgG positive with CD4 below 100. (Source: ASHM: HIV Guidelines)
Trimethoprim plus sulfamethoxazole is first line for PJP prophylaxis (more effective than pentamidine which is second line for sulfa allergy or intolerance). (Source: ASHM: HIV Guidelines)

Primary cryptococcal prophylaxis is not routinely recommended in AU when serum cryptococcal antigen is negative; PJP prophylaxis is the key indication at this CD4 count. (Source: ASHM: HIV Guidelines)

Latent tuberculosis prophylaxis is indicated when tuberculosis infection is documented (interferon gamma release assay or tuberculin skin test positive); it is not universal at CD4 below 200. (Source: ASHM: HIV Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Patients with adrenal insufficiency require peri-operative stress dose glucocorticoid to prevent adrenal crisis. Standard AU practice for moderate surgery (laparoscopic cholecystectomy or comparable) is intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg at induction of anaesthesia followed by 200 mg per 24 hours by continuous infusion or 50 mg every 6 hours until the patient is eating and drinking, then double the oral maintenance dose for 24 to 48 hours before tapering to baseline. Minor procedures under local anaesthetic require only an extra 20 mg hydrocortisone at the time. Major surgery, sepsis, prolonged intensive care admission or eclampsia may need 200 mg intravenous continuous infusion or up to 300 mg over 24 hours. Fludrocortisone is continued in primary adrenal insufficiency. Sick day rules teach patients to double oral hydrocortisone during infection with temperature above 38 degC, and to give intramuscular hydrocortisone 100 mg (via a pre-supplied ampoule) if vomiting or unable to keep oral doses down.
key_points: Moderate surgery: hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenous at induction then 200 mg per 24 hours until oral intake.
Continue fludrocortisone in primary adrenal insufficiency; dexamethasone has no mineralocorticoid activity.
Sick day rules: double oral hydrocortisone for temperature above 38 degC; intramuscular 100 mg if vomiting.
explanation.pearls: For moderate surgery in primary adrenal insufficiency, give hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenous at induction then 200 mg per 24 hours by infusion (or 50 mg every 6 hours) until eating and drinking, then double oral dose for 24 to 48 hours.

options.rationale: Any general anaesthetic surgery in primary adrenal insufficiency requires stress dose hydrocortisone; failure to give it risks intraoperative adrenal crisis. (Source: ESE: Adrenal Insufficiency)
Methylprednisolone lacks mineralocorticoid activity and a single dose is not adequate cover; hydrocortisone bolus plus infusion (or repeated dosing) is standard. (Source: ESE: Adrenal Insufficiency)

AU practice for moderate surgery is intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg at induction and 200 mg per 24 hours by infusion (or 50 mg every 6 hours) until oral intake resumes, then double oral dose for 24 to 48 hours. (Source: ESE: Adrenal Insufficiency)
Dexamethasone has no mineralocorticoid activity; it does not provide adequate replacement in primary adrenal insufficiency where fludrocortisone effect matters. (Source: ESE: Adrenal Insufficiency)

Fludrocortisone should be continued and parenteral hydrocortisone is required as oral absorption cannot be relied on peri-operatively; prednisolone alone is not standard peri-op cover. (Source: ESE: Adrenal Insufficiency)

explanation.summary: Warfarin reversal is guided by the international normalised ratio and by the presence of bleeding, planned surgery and the indication for anticoagulation. For international normalised ratio between 4.5 and 10 without bleeding, withhold warfarin and consider oral vitamin K 1 to 2 mg (0.5 to 1 mg if a mechanical valve to avoid over reversal). For international normalised ratio above 10 without bleeding, withhold warfarin and give oral vitamin K 3 to 5 mg. For major or life threatening bleeding, give intravenous prothrombin complex concentrate 25 to 50 IU per kg (adjusted for weight and international normalised ratio) plus intravenous vitamin K 5 to 10 mg. Fresh frozen plasma is used only if prothrombin complex concentrate is unavailable. Search for and address drug interactions (trimethoprim plus sulfamethoxazole, metronidazole, amiodarone and macrolides potentiate warfarin) and dietary changes (reduced vitamin K intake). Re-check international normalised ratio at 24 hours and restart at an adjusted dose when back in range; involve cardiology or haematology for mechanical valves.
key_points: International normalised ratio 4.5 to 10 without bleeding: withhold warfarin, oral vitamin K 1 to 2 mg (0.5 to 1 mg for mechanical valve).
Major bleeding: prothrombin complex concentrate 25 to 50 IU/kg plus intravenous vitamin K 5 to 10 mg.
Address drug interactions (trimethoprim plus sulfamethoxazole, amiodarone, macrolides potentiate warfarin).
explanation.pearls: For international normalised ratio between 4.5 and 10 without bleeding, withhold warfarin and give oral vitamin K 1 to 2 mg (0.5 to 1 mg for a mechanical valve to avoid over reversal) and re-check the international normalised ratio at 24 hours.

options.rationale: Prothrombin complex concentrate is reserved for major bleeding or urgent surgery; using it in an asymptomatic patient with a mechanical valve risks thrombosis. (Source: THANZ: Warfarin Reversal)

International normalised ratio above 4.5 to 5 without bleeding still warrants dose adjustment; simply repeating in 24 hours without withholding the next dose or considering low dose vitamin K is not standard. (Source: THANZ: Warfarin Reversal)

Intramuscular vitamin K risks haematoma in an anticoagulated patient and 10 mg over reverses; oral or intravenous low dose is preferred and antibiotic drug interaction should be addressed. (Source: THANZ: Warfarin Reversal)

AU practice for international normalised ratio above 4.5 without bleeding in a mechanical valve patient is oral vitamin K 1 to 2 mg with warfarin held, target reversal to therapeutic range, plus manage the drug interaction. (Source: THANZ: Warfarin Reversal)
Fresh frozen plasma alone is inferior to prothrombin complex concentrate for urgent reversal and is not used in a non bleeding patient; oral vitamin K is preferred. (Source: THANZ: Warfarin Reversal)

explanation.summary: Chronic (over 48 hours) severe hyponatraemia (sodium below 125 mmol/L) requires cautious correction to avoid osmotic demyelination syndrome. Correction should be limited to 6 to 8 mmol/L in 24 hours (maximum 10 mmol/L) and no more than 18 mmol/L in 48 hours. For symptomatic severe hyponatraemia (seizure, coma, severe confusion) give a 100 to 150 mL bolus of 3 percent sodium chloride over 10 minutes, repeated up to twice more to a total rise of 4 to 6 mmol/L in the first hour, aiming to stop seizures rather than to normalise sodium. Address the underlying cause (thiazide, syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion, adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism). Frequent monitoring (2 to 4 hourly initially) is essential. If sodium is overcorrecting (rise above the ceiling), re-lower with 5 percent glucose 3 mL per kg per hour or desmopressin 2 to 4 microgram intravenously to prevent osmotic demyelination syndrome. High risk groups (alcohol misuse, malnutrition, hypokalaemia, liver disease, older women on thiazides) require the lowest ceiling and the closest monitoring.
key_points: Chronic hyponatraemia correction ceiling: 6 to 8 mmol/L in 24 hours (maximum 10); 18 mmol/L in 48 hours.
Symptomatic severe hyponatraemia: 3% sodium chloride 100 to 150 mL over 10 minutes for a 4 to 6 mmol/L rise in the first hour.
Overcorrection rescue: 5% glucose 3 mL/kg/h or desmopressin 2 to 4 microgram intravenous to prevent osmotic demyelination syndrome.
explanation.pearls: For chronic thiazide induced hyponatraemia in an older woman cap the sodium rise at 6 to 8 mmol/L in 24 hours and be ready to re-lower with 5 percent glucose or desmopressin if overcorrection; osmotic demyelination syndrome risk peaks at correction above 10 mmol/L per 24 hours.

options.rationale: Uncapped rapid saline in chronic hyponatraemia risks overcorrection and osmotic demyelination syndrome; 500 mL bolus is reserved for severe symptomatic (seizure, coma) presentations and must be capped. (Source: eTG: Hyponatraemia)
12 mmol/L per 24 hours exceeds the safe correction ceiling in chronic hyponatraemia (8 to 10 mmol/L per 24 hours) and risks osmotic demyelination syndrome. (Source: eTG: Hyponatraemia)
Fluid restriction is slow and inadequate for symptomatic severe hyponatraemia at 108 mmol/L; demeclocycline is not first line and risks nephrotoxicity. (Source: eTG: Hyponatraemia)
Tolvaptan is not first line for thiazide induced hyponatraemia and can cause rapid overcorrection; hepatotoxicity limits use. (Source: eTG: Hyponatraemia)

AU chronic severe symptomatic hyponatraemia: 100 to 150 mL 3 percent sodium chloride bolus for symptoms, sodium rise capped 6 to 8 mmol/L per 24 hours (maximum 10) with 5 percent glucose or desmopressin rescue if overcorrection to prevent osmotic demyelination syndrome. (Source: eTG: Hyponatraemia)

explanation.summary: The sepsis hour-1 bundle asks the clinician to measure lactate, take blood cultures before antibiotics, give broad spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, start 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate over 4, and start vasopressor if MAP remains under 65 mmHg. Noradrenaline is first line and may be commenced peripherally through a large forearm cannula until central access is placed. Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day is added for refractory shock requiring rising vasopressor. Repeat lactate at 2 to 4 hours to monitor response. In elderly with limited reserve, avoid mandatory fluid overload beyond 30 mL/kg without dynamic assessment.
key_points: Hour-1 bundle: lactate, cultures before antibiotics, antibiotics within 1 hour, 30 mL/kg crystalloid, vasopressor if MAP under 65
Noradrenaline is first line vasopressor
Peripheral noradrenaline is acceptable via large cannula for a limited time
Hydrocortisone for refractory shock only
Target glucose 6 to 10 mmol/L, not 4 to 6
explanation.pearls: The Surviving Sepsis 2021 update endorses initiating vasopressor within the first hour rather than waiting the full 3 hours of fluid, provided the initial fluid response is inadequate; earlier vasopressor is associated with reduced mortality.

options.rationale: Empirical antifungal is not part of the initial hour-1 bundle in most sepsis and is added only for identified risk factors such as immunosuppression or prolonged broad spectrum antibiotic exposure (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
Steroids are added only for shock refractory to fluid and vasopressor; giving before vasopressor is initiated is out of order (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign).
Fluid resuscitation is 30 mL/kg over the first 3 hours but further boluses need dynamic assessment; escalation should be vasopressor rather than reflex fluid (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign).

Surviving Sepsis and ANZICS guidance advise starting noradrenaline early alongside fluid resuscitation when MAP remains under 65 mmHg after an initial bolus; peripheral use is acceptable until central access (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign; ANZICS Statement on Peripheral Vasopressors).
Tight glucose control (4 to 6 mmol/L) worsens outcomes in critical illness; target is 6 to 10 mmol/L and it is not part of the hour-1 bundle (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign).

explanation.summary: Bacterial meningitis in adults is a medical emergency. Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis account for the majority; Listeria is a concern in patients over 50, pregnant, or immunosuppressed and adds benzylpenicillin (or add amoxicillin) to ceftriaxone. Dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours for 4 days reduces mortality and neurological sequelae in pneumococcal meningitis when given before or within 15 minutes of the first antibiotic dose. Do not delay antibiotics for CT or LP: draw blood cultures then give the first dose. CT before LP is required for reduced consciousness, focal signs, seizures, immunosuppression, or papilloedema.
key_points: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV plus dexamethasone 10 mg IV without delay
Dexamethasone must be given before or with first antibiotic
Add benzylpenicillin (or amoxicillin) for Listeria over 50
CT before LP if reduced consciousness, focal signs, seizures
Do not delay antibiotic for CT or LP
explanation.pearls: In meningococcal disease dexamethasone gives no mortality benefit but is not withheld empirically because the aetiology is unknown at the bedside; the pneumococcal benefit dominates AU practice.

options.rationale: Empirical coverage under Therapeutic Guidelines is ceftriaxone rather than benzylpenicillin monotherapy because pneumococcus is the most common adult pathogen and resistant strains exist (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
Any delay in antibiotic administration in suspected bacterial meningitis worsens outcome; CT and LP can follow the first dose (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

AU Therapeutic Guidelines advise not delaying antibiotics in suspected bacterial meningitis; ceftriaxone 2 g IV plus dexamethasone 10 mg IV are given before or with LP and dexamethasone must be given before or within 15 minutes of antibiotics for maximum benefit (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

Dexamethasone must be given before or with the first antibiotic dose to blunt the inflammatory response; delaying dexamethasone until CSF returns forfeits mortality benefit in pneumococcal meningitis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

Aciclovir is added when encephalitis features (focal signs, seizures, altered mental state without meningism) are present; her picture is meningitis and needs antibiotic plus steroid (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Necrotising soft tissue infection has a mortality that rises sharply for every hour of delay to source control. Clinical hallmarks are pain out of proportion, systemic toxicity, dusky discolouration, haemorrhagic bullae, and rapid extension. LRINEC uses CRP, WCC, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine and glucose with a score at least 6 warranting strong suspicion and at least 8 making it highly likely. Empirical antibiotics are broad polymicrobial (piperacillin tazobactam plus vancomycin plus clindamycin for toxin suppression), and the definitive treatment is urgent surgical exploration and debridement.
key_points: Pain out of proportion is the earliest sign
LRINEC at least 6 suspicious, at least 8 highly likely
Empirical polymicrobial cover including clindamycin
Urgent surgical debridement is definitive treatment
Imaging must not delay operation
explanation.pearls: Clindamycin is added even in beta lactam cover because it suppresses streptococcal exotoxin production in the ribosome-bound state, unaffected by the inoculum effect that reduces beta lactam efficacy in high bacterial load.

sources.label: AU Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection Consensus

options.rationale: Pain out of proportion, haemorrhagic bullae, systemic toxicity, and high LRINEC score (Hb, WCC, Na, creatinine, CRP, glucose scoring at least 8) mandate urgent surgical debridement rather than imaging or antibiotics alone (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; AU Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection Consensus).
source_refs: AU Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection Consensus

options.rationale: Flucloxacillin monotherapy does not cover the polymicrobial spectrum and delays the definitive surgical intervention that is time critical (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

MRI delays surgery in a haemodynamically compromised patient with high clinical suspicion; imaging cannot rule out necrotising infection and clinical judgement drives operation (Source: AU Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection Consensus).
source_refs: AU Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection Consensus

options.rationale: Hyperbaric oxygen is an adjunct after surgical debridement not a substitute; delaying surgery increases mortality (Source: AU Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection Consensus).
source_refs: AU Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection Consensus

options.rationale: IVIG may be adjunctive in streptococcal toxic shock but does not replace source control by surgical debridement (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Iatrogenic adrenal insufficiency is the most common cause of adrenal crisis in Australia and occurs in patients on the equivalent of prednisolone 5 mg or more for more than 4 weeks. Illness stress dose failure (vomiting, gastroenteritis, sepsis, trauma, surgery) precipitates crisis presenting with hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia. Immediate management is hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus then 200 mg over 24 hours (as infusion or 50 mg 6 hourly) plus 0.9 percent sodium chloride resuscitation and glucose correction. Once stable, taper to twice or thrice usual daily oral dose during illness and educate about sick day rules and injectable emergency kits.
key_points: Steroid over 5 mg prednisolone for 4 weeks risks HPA suppression
Crisis presents with hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia
Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus then 200 mg over 24 hours
IV fluid and glucose correction alongside steroid
Educate on sick day rules and injectable emergency hydrocortisone
explanation.pearls: The sick day rule taught by Australian endocrine services is to double the usual oral dose for minor illness and triple for major illness; parenteral hydrocortisone 100 mg IM is used if oral cannot be tolerated.

options.rationale: Vasopressor without steroid does not address the underlying cortisol deficiency and delays the definitive treatment (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

Dexamethasone does not interfere with cortisol assay but delays mineralocorticoid effect; hydrocortisone provides both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid activity and is the AU standard in crisis (Source: Endocrine Society Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline).
Oral therapy cannot be absorbed reliably in a vomiting patient with shock and does not deliver the stress dose required in crisis (Source: Endocrine Society Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline).

Fludrocortisone provides mineralocorticoid effect at 3 to 6 hours and is unnecessary while high dose hydrocortisone (which has intrinsic mineralocorticoid activity) is running (Source: Endocrine Society Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline).

Iatrogenic adrenal insufficiency from chronic steroid can precipitate crisis when stress dosing fails during illness; hydrocortisone 100 mg IV plus fluid resuscitation is the immediate treatment before further investigation (Source: Endocrine Society Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline; Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

explanation.summary: Massive transfusion in Australia is activated for suspected requirement of at least 5 units of red cells in the first 3 hours, haemorrhagic shock with pending or ongoing bleeding, and validated triggers (Assessment of Blood Consumption score, shock index, base deficit). The National Blood Authority pack delivers red cells, FFP and platelets in a 1:1:1 unit ratio, supported by the PROPPR trial showing lower haemorrhagic death at 24 hours. Add tranexamic acid 1 g IV loading then 1 g over 8 hours if within 3 hours of trauma, and correct hypocalcaemia, acidosis and hypothermia.
key_points: 1:1:1 unit ratio (RBC:FFP:platelets) supported by PROPPR
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours of trauma
Cryoprecipitate when fibrinogen under 1.5 g/L
Correct calcium (citrate binds), avoid hypothermia and acidosis
Definitive control is surgical or angiographic
explanation.pearls: Every 4 units of packed red cells contain around 12 mmol of citrate; give 10 mL of 10 percent calcium gluconate IV after every 4 units to prevent hypocalcaemia-induced hypotension and coagulopathy.

sources.label: National Blood Authority Massive Transfusion Guidelines

options.rationale: Whole blood is not routinely stocked in Australian civilian trauma centres; component therapy in 1:1:1 remains the standard (Source: National Blood Authority Massive Transfusion Guidelines).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Massive Transfusion Guidelines

options.rationale: PROPPR showed improved 24 hour mortality from haemorrhage with 1:1:1 rather than 2:1:1 ratios; withholding platelets is not AU practice (Source: PROPPR trial; National Blood Authority Massive Transfusion Guidelines).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Massive Transfusion Guidelines

options.rationale: Cryoprecipitate is added when fibrinogen falls under 1.5 g/L (or under 2.0 in obstetric haemorrhage) and is not part of the initial 1:1:1 pack (Source: National Blood Authority Massive Transfusion Guidelines).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Massive Transfusion Guidelines

options.rationale: Australian trauma pathways align with PROPPR trial evidence and NBA guidance using 1:1:1 unit ratio (RBC:FFP:platelets) in the first pack of massive transfusion (Source: National Blood Authority Massive Transfusion Guidelines; ANZCA Blood Management).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Massive Transfusion Guidelines

options.rationale: PCC is used for warfarin reversal or specific factor deficiency rather than as first line trauma pack; component ratio is the primary approach (Source: National Blood Authority Massive Transfusion Guidelines).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Massive Transfusion Guidelines

explanation.summary: Aortic dissection is classified as type A (involves ascending aorta, surgical emergency) or type B (descending only, medical management first with endovascular repair if complicated). Impulse control lowers shear stress driving propagation: heart rate 60 to 80 with intravenous beta blocker (esmolol, labetalol, metoprolol) before or simultaneously with vasodilator (sodium nitroprusside, glyceryl trinitrate) for systolic under 120 mmHg. Vasodilator monotherapy causes reflex tachycardia and worsens shear. Analgesia is essential. Complicated type B (malperfusion, rupture, refractory pain or hypertension) requires TEVAR (thoracic endovascular aortic repair).
key_points: Type A is surgical emergency, type B is medical first
Heart rate control before vasodilator to avoid reflex tachycardia
Target HR 60 to 80, systolic BP under 120 mmHg
Esmolol is titratable IV beta blocker of choice
Complicated type B needs TEVAR
explanation.pearls: Systolic blood pressure difference of at least 20 mmHg between arms in the setting of tearing chest or back pain has a positive likelihood ratio around 5 for dissection; measure both arms in every suspected case.

options.rationale: Vasodilator monotherapy causes reflex tachycardia and increases aortic shear stress, worsening dissection propagation; beta blockade first is essential (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Aortic Dissection Position Statement).

Type B dissection is managed initially with impulse control: heart rate 60 to 80 first with a short-acting intravenous beta blocker (esmolol titratable), then vasodilator (GTN, sodium nitroprusside) for systolic target under 120 mmHg to reduce shear stress (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Aortic Dissection Position Statement; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).
Analgesia is important adjunct but does not achieve haemodynamic targets alone; pharmacological impulse control is required (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).

Hydralazine causes reflex tachycardia and is contraindicated as first line in dissection; impulse control requires beta blockade before vasodilator (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Aortic Dissection Position Statement).
Type B dissection without branch vessel or organ malperfusion is managed medically first; type A is the surgical emergency (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Aortic Dissection Position Statement).

explanation.summary: Phaeochromocytoma is a catecholamine secreting tumour classically presenting with paroxysms of headache, palpitations, and diaphoresis and elevated fasting fractionated plasma metanephrines. Beta blockade must never precede alpha blockade because unopposed alpha stimulation causes catastrophic vasoconstriction and hypertensive crisis. In crisis, cease any beta blocker and use intravenous phentolamine (short-acting alpha antagonist) or sodium nitroprusside. Preoperative preparation uses oral phenoxybenzamine (non selective, long acting) titrated over 7 to 14 days plus liberal salt and fluid intake to restore intravascular volume; beta blockade is added only after alpha blockade is established to control reflex tachycardia. Laparoscopic adrenalectomy is definitive.
key_points: Alpha before beta blockade in phaeochromocytoma
Fasting fractionated plasma metanephrines confirms diagnosis
IV phentolamine or nitroprusside in acute crisis
Preoperative phenoxybenzamine 7 to 14 days plus salt loading
Definitive treatment is laparoscopic adrenalectomy
explanation.pearls: Suspect phaeochromocytoma in patients with the triad of headache, palpitations and diaphoresis plus hypertension (positive likelihood ratio around 6 when all three present); the biochemical test of choice is fasting fractionated plasma metanephrines.

options.rationale: Unopposed beta blockade in phaeochromocytoma leaves alpha-mediated vasoconstriction to worsen hypertensive crisis; ceasing metoprolol and giving intravenous alpha blockade (phentolamine) reverses the pathophysiology (Source: Endocrine Society Pheochromocytoma Guideline; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).
Increasing unopposed beta blockade worsens alpha mediated vasoconstriction in phaeochromocytoma; alpha blockade must be established first (Source: Endocrine Society Pheochromocytoma Guideline).
GTN reduces preload but does not address the catecholamine driven alpha vasoconstriction; suboptimal in crisis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).

Oral phenoxybenzamine is used for preoperative preparation over 7 to 14 days; in acute crisis intravenous phentolamine (or nitroprusside plus alpha blockade) is required (Source: Endocrine Society Pheochromocytoma Guideline).

Operating without alpha blockade risks intraoperative catecholamine storm with fatal arrhythmia and hypertension; preoperative preparation over at least 7 days is mandatory (Source: Endocrine Society Pheochromocytoma Guideline).

explanation.summary: Hyponatraemia after subarachnoid haemorrhage is common and the distinction between SIADH and cerebral salt wasting is critical because their treatments are opposite. SIADH is euvolaemic (or slightly hypervolaemic), with urine osmolality above 100 mmol/kg, urine sodium above 30 mmol/L, and treated with fluid restriction. CSW is hypovolaemic, has high urine output, high urine sodium, rising urea to creatinine ratio, and treated with volume plus sodium replacement (isotonic or hypertonic saline). In SAH, fluid restriction is dangerous because vasospasm and delayed cerebral ischaemia are precipitated by hypovolaemia between days 4 and 14. Correction rate is 8 to 10 mmol/L in 24 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination.
key_points: SIADH is euvolaemic; CSW is hypovolaemic
CSW after SAH is treated with volume plus sodium
Fluid restriction in SAH-related CSW worsens vasospasm risk
Sodium correction 8 to 10 mmol/L per 24 hours
Nimodipine reduces delayed cerebral ischaemia after SAH
explanation.pearls: Rising fractional excretion of urate (FEurate over 12 percent) and elevated BNP have been proposed to help distinguish CSW from SIADH but volume status remains the primary bedside discriminator in Australian practice.

options.rationale: Fluid restriction is the SIADH answer but is dangerous in cerebral salt wasting after SAH because hypovolaemia predisposes to delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm; the pattern here (hypovolaemia, polyuria, rising urea) is CSW not SIADH (Source: Neurocritical Care Society Guideline; Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

Tolvaptan (vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist) treats SIADH but is contraindicated in hypovolaemic hyponatraemia and worsens CSW; the fluid balance and hypotension here point to CSW (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

Cerebral salt wasting after SAH is treated with volume replacement and sodium; hypertonic saline restores intravascular volume and sodium simultaneously, corrects the hyponatraemia at a safe rate, and preserves cerebral perfusion (Source: Neurocritical Care Society Guideline; ANZICS SAH Consensus).

Demeclocycline treats SIADH by producing nephrogenic diabetes insipidus but is inappropriate for CSW where the pathophysiology is inappropriate natriuresis rather than water retention (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).
Mannitol adds osmotic diuresis and worsens hypovolaemia; fluid restriction reduces cerebral perfusion in vasospasm risk period (Source: Neurocritical Care Society Guideline).

explanation.summary: New-onset atrial fibrillation without haemodynamic compromise is managed with rate control, decision on anticoagulation using CHA2DS2-VA (the Australian score omitting the sex modifier), and consideration of rhythm control based on symptoms and duration. Beta blockers and non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (diltiazem, verapamil) are first-line rate-control agents in patients with preserved LV function. Digoxin is reserved for sedentary older patients or as add-on because it does not control the rate on exertion. Amiodarone is a rhythm-control agent for structural heart disease. Emergency electrical cardioversion is reserved for instability, ischaemia, or heart failure.
key_points: Beta blocker or non-dihydropyridine CCB is first-line rate control
Digoxin is second-line and does not control exertional rate
Amiodarone is a rhythm-control agent, not rate-control
Cardioversion reserved for instability, ischaemia, heart failure
CHA2DS2-VA drives anticoagulation decision
explanation.pearls: The Australian CHA2DS2-VA score removes the female sex modifier used in the international CHA2DS2-VASc because sex-based risk elevation in AF appears to be a marker rather than an independent driver; a score of 2 or more on this AU-modified score is the threshold for anticoagulation regardless of biological sex.

options.rationale: Digoxin is second-line to beta blockers and non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers in AF rate control because it is ineffective at rate control on exertion and only reasonable in sedentary older patients or as add-on therapy (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline).

In symptomatic AF without haemodynamic compromise and with preserved LV function, a beta blocker such as metoprolol is first-line rate control; oral loading is appropriate for a haemodynamically stable patient (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).

Amiodarone is a rhythm-control not a rate-control agent and is reserved for structural heart disease when other rhythm-control options are unsuitable; it is not first-line for uncomplicated new-onset AF (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline).

Emergency cardioversion is reserved for haemodynamic instability, active ischaemia, or heart failure; this patient is stable so rate control and anticoagulation decision precede any rhythm strategy (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline).

IV verapamil is a reasonable alternative rate-control choice in AF but oral therapy is preferred in a haemodynamically stable ambulant patient and IV verapamil carries risk of hypotension and bradycardia particularly if the patient later needs a beta blocker (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline).

explanation.summary: Antibiotic decisions in COPD exacerbation use the Anthonisen criteria of increased dyspnoea, increased sputum volume, and sputum purulence. Patients with all three (type 1) or with sputum purulence plus one other (type 2) benefit from antibiotics; type 3 patients with only one criterion do not clearly benefit. First-line oral therapy in AU eTG for a non-severe infective exacerbation is amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 5 days, or doxycycline in penicillin allergy. Systemic corticosteroids (prednisolone 30 to 50 mg orally daily for 5 days) shorten exacerbation duration and reduce relapse. IV antibiotics are reserved for severe exacerbation or pneumonia.
key_points: Anthonisen criteria: dyspnoea, sputum volume, sputum purulence
All three or two-with-purulence: benefit from antibiotics
Amoxicillin 500 mg TDS 5 days is first-line oral in AU
Prednisolone 30 to 50 mg daily for 5 days shortens exacerbation
IV antibiotics reserved for severe exacerbation or pneumonia
explanation.pearls: Sputum purulence is the single strongest predictor of bacterial infection in a COPD exacerbation and is a better trigger for antibiotics than CRP or white cell count; a clear-sputum exacerbation with a raised CRP is more likely viral or eosinophilic than bacterial and typically responds to steroid alone.

options.rationale: IV third-generation cephalosporin is reserved for severe exacerbation with hospital-level care or pneumonia, and this patient has an oral-treatable non-severe exacerbation with no consolidation on chest radiograph (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

Doxycycline is an appropriate alternative to amoxicillin in penicillin allergy but 14 days is longer than the 5 day eTG duration and this patient has no penicillin allergy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

All three Anthonisen criteria (increased dyspnoea, increased sputum volume, sputum purulence) are met, which selects patients who benefit from antibiotics in a COPD exacerbation; amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 5 days is first-line in eTG for non-severe infective exacerbation (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; TSANZ/Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X).

Short-course azithromycin has activity against atypicals but is not first-line for infective COPD exacerbation in AU eTG; macrolide resistance in Streptococcus pneumoniae is a concern (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

All three Anthonisen criteria present define the subgroup of COPD exacerbation that derives clear antibiotic benefit; withholding antibiotics forgoes an evidence-based recovery gain (Source: TSANZ COPD-X).

explanation.summary: Adult DKA management runs on three parallel tracks: rapid fluid resuscitation with 0.9 percent sodium chloride to restore intravascular volume, fixed-rate insulin infusion at 0.1 unit/kg/hour to reverse ketogenesis, and potassium replacement once serum potassium falls below 5.5 mmol/L. The first-hour fluid is around 1000 mL of 0.9 percent sodium chloride, then a maintenance rate of 250 to 500 mL per hour with added potassium. Dextrose is introduced once plasma glucose falls below 14 mmol/L. Bicarbonate is reserved for pH under 6.9. Insulin infusion should follow rather than precede fluid resuscitation to avoid precipitating potassium shifts in a volume deplete patient.
key_points: 0.9 percent sodium chloride 1000 mL over first hour
Fixed-rate insulin at 0.1 unit/kg/hour follows the fluid
Potassium added once serum potassium under 5.5 mmol/L
Dextrose added once plasma glucose under 14 mmol/L
Bicarbonate reserved for pH under 6.9
explanation.pearls: The AU shift from divided fluid boluses to a fixed first-hour 1000 mL of 0.9 percent sodium chloride reflects the finding that under-resuscitation early in DKA drives acute kidney injury and prolongs ICU stay more than the previously feared over-resuscitation drives cerebral oedema in adults, though the paediatric caution against rapid volume correction still applies.

options.rationale: Dextrose-containing fluids are reserved for when the plasma glucose falls below 14 mmol/L during the insulin infusion; giving dextrose as first-hour resuscitation is inappropriate at a glucose of 26 mmol/L (Source: RACP/ADS Adult DKA Guideline).

AU adult DKA pathways recommend 0.9 percent sodium chloride as the initial resuscitation fluid at approximately 1000 mL over the first hour to restore intravascular volume and initiate osmotic correction; potassium is added to subsequent bags once serum potassium is under 5.5 mmol/L (Source: RACP/ADS Adult DKA Guideline; Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

Hartmann's solution contains lactate that will be metabolised to bicarbonate and may transiently worsen glycaemic and osmolar shifts; AU pathways specify 0.9 percent sodium chloride first before considering balanced solutions (Source: RACP/ADS Adult DKA Guideline).
Sodium bicarbonate in DKA is reserved for pH under 6.9 and is not recommended for pH 7.12; it worsens intracellular acidosis and cerebral oedema risk (Source: RACP/ADS Adult DKA Guideline).

Fixed-rate insulin infusion (0.1 unit/kg/hour) not bolus is the AU recommendation, and IV fluid must be running before insulin because insulin drives potassium into cells and precipitates hypotension in the volume deplete patient (Source: RACP/ADS Adult DKA Guideline).

explanation.summary: Community-acquired pneumonia severity in Australia is scored with CORB (Confusion, respiratory Rate over 30, systolic Blood pressure under 90, SpO2 under 90). A score of 2 or more identifies severe CAP requiring IV therapy and inpatient care. First-line empirical therapy for severe CAP in AU eTG is benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV six-hourly plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily plus single-dose gentamicin 4 to 5 mg/kg IV, or ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus azithromycin as an alternative. Broader cover with meropenem or vancomycin is reserved for specific risk factors. Blood cultures and urinary Legionella and pneumococcal antigens are collected before antibiotic administration.
key_points: CORB scores confusion, RR over 30, systolic BP under 90, SpO2 under 90
Score 2 or more defines severe CAP
Severe CAP: benzylpenicillin + azithromycin + single-dose gentamicin
Ceftriaxone + azithromycin is the AU alternative
Blood and urinary antigens before first antibiotic dose
explanation.pearls: CORB replaced CURB-65 in AU practice because urea is not needed as an independent severity marker once respiratory rate, blood pressure and confusion have been captured; the omission avoids the delay of waiting for biochemistry before starting IV antibiotics in the septic patient.

options.rationale: Meropenem is reserved for severe CAP with risk factors for multi-drug-resistant gram-negatives (bronchiectasis, structural lung disease, recent hospitalisation with broad-spectrum antibiotics); it is not first-line here and drives resistance pressure (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

Oral therapy is inappropriate for severe CAP; the CORB score is 3 (confusion, RR over 30, systolic BP under 90) and lactate is 3.2, mandating IV therapy in an inpatient setting (Source: TSANZ CAP Guideline).

Ceftriaxone monotherapy misses atypical pathogens (Mycoplasma, Legionella) that account for around 15 percent of severe CAP; macrolide addition is required for severe presentations (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

Severe community-acquired pneumonia (CORB score 3) requires empirical cover for Streptococcus pneumoniae, atypicals and gram-negatives; the AU eTG severe CAP regimen is benzylpenicillin plus azithromycin plus a single-dose gentamicin (or ceftriaxone plus azithromycin as an alternative) (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; TSANZ CAP Guideline).

MRSA and staphylococcal cover is not first-line for CAP unless there is post-influenza necrotising pneumonia or bacteraemia risk factors; this misses the typical Streptococcus pneumoniae and atypical spectrum (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency anaemia in Australia is managed first by identifying and treating the source of loss, then by replacing iron. Oral iron in a single daily or alternate-day dose is first-line for stable outpatients. IV iron is indicated when oral iron has failed or is not tolerated, when rapid replacement is required (surgery, third-trimester pregnancy, functional class 3 heart failure), when ongoing losses exceed oral absorption capacity, or in inflammatory bowel disease with malabsorption. Ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg IV as a single dose or iron polymaltose 1000 mg IV as a single or divided dose are the standard AU parenteral options.
key_points: Investigate the cause of iron deficiency before or in parallel with treatment
IV iron for oral failure, intolerance, or rapid replacement needs
Ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg IV single dose is AU standard
Alternate-day oral dosing improves fractional absorption
Preoperative IV iron reduces postoperative transfusion
explanation.pearls: Hepcidin rises for 24 to 48 hours after an oral iron dose, which is why alternate-day dosing gives fractional absorption almost double that of daily dosing at half the gastrointestinal side effect burden; this is now the RACGP-preferred oral schedule when the clinical timeline allows.

options.rationale: Preoperative iron deficiency is a modifiable risk factor for postoperative complications and higher transfusion rates; deferring intervention forgoes the AU Patient Blood Management preoperative optimisation pathway (Source: NBA Patient Blood Management Guidelines Module 2).

Higher-frequency dosing worsens tolerance without proportional gain because hepcidin blocks absorption for 24 to 48 hours after each dose; alternate-day dosing improves fractional absorption but here the timeline before surgery does not allow it (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology).

Preoperative transfusion for a stable Hb over 80 g/L does not correct iron stores, exposes the patient to transfusion risk, and misses the correctable cause; IV iron is the AU Patient Blood Management first-line option (Source: NBA Patient Blood Management Guidelines Module 2).

IV iron is indicated for iron deficiency anaemia when oral iron has failed or is not tolerated, when rapid replacement is required (such as before surgery in 4 weeks), or in ongoing losses that exceed oral absorption; ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg is a single-visit AU standard dose (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology; PBAC/NBA Iron Product Guidance).

Endoscopy is warranted in an unexplained iron deficient patient but the clear obstetric-menstrual cause with a normal faecal immunochemical test in a low-risk age group does not mandate endoscopy before treating; treatment and evaluation can proceed in parallel (Source: RACGP Iron Deficiency in Adults Guideline).

explanation.summary: Hypertension in type 2 diabetes with albuminuria is managed with an ACE inhibitor (or ARB if intolerant) as first-line therapy because these agents slow albuminuria and progression to end-stage kidney disease independent of blood pressure lowering. Target blood pressure in this population is under 140/90 mmHg in general and under 130/80 mmHg where tolerated (albuminuria present). Combination therapy is usually needed to reach target, adding a calcium channel blocker and/or thiazide next. SGLT2 inhibitors have additional cardiorenal benefit in diabetic kidney disease and are added when eGFR and glycaemic control allow. Beta blockers are reserved for specific indications.
key_points: ACE inhibitor is first-line in albuminuric diabetic hypertension
Target BP under 130/80 mmHg in albuminuria where tolerated
Check creatinine and potassium at 1 to 2 weeks after starting
Add CCB or thiazide next to reach target
SGLT2 inhibitor adds cardiorenal benefit in diabetic kidney disease
explanation.pearls: A rise in creatinine of up to 30 percent from baseline after starting an ACE inhibitor in albuminuric CKD is expected and is not a reason to stop; only a rise beyond 30 percent, a fall in eGFR, or a potassium above 5.5 mmol/L should trigger dose reduction or cessation.

options.rationale: Thiazide diuretics are first-line for older non-diabetic hypertensives but do not have the renoprotective effect of an ACE inhibitor and can worsen glycaemic control at higher doses; they are second-line here (Source: NHFA Hypertension Guideline).

Calcium channel blockers control blood pressure well but do not have the specific renoprotective effect of ACE inhibitors or ARBs in albuminuric diabetic kidney disease; they are second-line when an ACE inhibitor is contraindicated (Source: NHFA Hypertension Guideline).

In hypertensive type 2 diabetes with albuminuria, an ACE inhibitor (or ARB if intolerant) is first-line because it slows albuminuria progression and progression to end-stage kidney disease independent of blood pressure lowering; perindopril 4 mg titrated is the AU eTG regimen (Source: NHFA Hypertension Guideline; KDIGO Diabetes and CKD Guideline).

Beta blockers are reserved for hypertension with a specific indication (ischaemic heart disease, heart failure, AF rate control); they are not first-line for uncomplicated hypertension and do not have the renoprotective specificity of an ACE inhibitor (Source: NHFA Hypertension Guideline).

Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists are fourth-line for resistant hypertension in the NHFA algorithm; they are not initial monotherapy and carry hyperkalaemia risk when combined with the ACE inhibitor typically required in albuminuric diabetes (Source: NHFA Hypertension Guideline).

explanation.summary: Cellulitis is managed by severity: uncomplicated cellulitis without systemic features responds to oral therapy (cefalexin or dicloxacillin 500 mg four times daily). Escalation to IV therapy is indicated for systemic features (fever, tachycardia, rigor, hypotension), failure of oral therapy at 24 to 48 hours, immunocompromise, or extensive involvement, with flucloxacillin 2 g IV six-hourly the first-line agent. MRSA cover (vancomycin) is added when specific risk factors are present. Necrotising infection requires urgent surgical debridement and broad-spectrum antibiotics, with treatment of chronic tinea pedis to reduce cellulitis recurrence. Blood cultures should be collected when systemic features are present before antibiotic administration.
key_points: Systemic features or oral failure trigger IV escalation
Flucloxacillin 2 g IV six-hourly is first-line
MRSA cover added only for specific risk factors
Necrotising features mandate surgical review
Treat tinea pedis to reduce recurrence
explanation.pearls: Pain out of proportion to visible signs, crepitus, bullae, or rapidly advancing margin over hours are the necrotising fasciitis red flags that override the antibiotic-only pathway and mandate immediate surgical review; the absence of these signs in a systemically unwell patient with typical erythema selects an antibiotic escalation trial before considering theatre.

sources.label: Hospital in the Home Society Australia

options.rationale: Oral clindamycin monotherapy is not first-line for cellulitis with systemic features; C. difficile risk is high and oral therapy at home is unsafe in a septic patient failing initial oral cover (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

Adding anaerobic cover is not indicated for uncomplicated cellulitis and continuing oral therapy that has failed at 24 hours delays effective treatment in a systemically unwell patient (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

Cellulitis with systemic features (fever, tachycardia, rigor) and failure of first-line oral therapy meets AU eTG criteria for IV escalation; flucloxacillin 2 g IV six-hourly covers Streptococcus pyogenes and methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus with a switch to oral once systemically improved (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Hospital in the Home Society Australia).
source_refs: Hospital in the Home Society Australia

options.rationale: Necrotising fasciitis features (rapidly spreading pain out of proportion, crepitus, bullae, systemic toxicity requiring vasopressors) are not present; there is no indication for immediate debridement over an antibiotic escalation trial (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

Empirical MRSA and broad-spectrum gram-negative cover is not indicated for community-acquired cellulitis without MRSA risk factors (recent hospitalisation, aged care residence, prior MRSA colonisation, injection drug use) (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: High-risk TIA (ABCD2 4 or more) or minor ischaemic stroke (NIHSS under 4) without indication for anticoagulation is managed with dual antiplatelet therapy for the first 21 days followed by single antiplatelet long-term. Aspirin is loaded 300 mg then continued at 100 mg daily and clopidogrel is added at 75 mg daily (with a 300 mg loading dose in some pathways) for the 21 day window. This regimen reduces recurrent stroke over the first 90 days without a significant increase in major bleeding. Anticoagulation is reserved for cardioembolic sources (AF, mechanical valve, LV thrombus). Extended rhythm monitoring for occult paroxysmal AF is recommended in cryptogenic events.
key_points: High-risk TIA: ABCD2 score 4 or more
Dual antiplatelet for 21 days then single antiplatelet long-term
Aspirin load 300 mg then 100 mg; add clopidogrel 75 mg
Anticoagulation reserved for cardioembolic source
Extended rhythm monitoring for occult AF
explanation.pearls: The 21 day dual antiplatelet window is derived from CHANCE and POINT which showed the recurrent stroke reduction is driven by events in the first 21 days and the bleeding excess accumulates beyond it, which is why the AU pathway stops one agent at day 21 rather than day 90 as originally trialled.

options.rationale: Empirical anticoagulation for possible occult AF is not indicated; extended rhythm monitoring is the AU standard while single antiplatelet or dual antiplatelet cover runs based on the current sinus rhythm findings (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines).

Single antiplatelet monotherapy in high-risk TIA misses the early window (first 21 days) where dual antiplatelet therapy reduces recurrence; a loading dose is standard for the first day (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines).

Anticoagulation is reserved for a cardioembolic source (AF, mechanical valve, LV thrombus); this patient is in sinus rhythm with no cardiac source, so antiplatelet not anticoagulation is indicated (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines).

High-risk TIA (ABCD2 4 or more) or minor ischaemic stroke without indication for anticoagulation is managed with 21 days of dual antiplatelet therapy started within 24 hours of symptom onset, then long-term single antiplatelet; this reduces recurrent stroke risk based on CHANCE and POINT trial evidence adopted by the Stroke Foundation (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

Aspirin plus dipyridamole is a reasonable long-term single-agent alternative combination but is not the AU first-line for the first 21 days after high-risk TIA; that role is filled by aspirin plus clopidogrel (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Statin-associated muscle symptoms are common (10 to 15 percent of patients on high-intensity statin) but immune-mediated necrotising myopathy is rare (around 2 to 3 per 100,000). CK measurement discriminates: a normal CK with preserved power steers toward a benign statin-associated pattern with a high pretest probability of rechallenge tolerance, while a CK over 1000 with weakness triggers workup for immune-mediated necrotising myopathy including anti-HMGCR antibody. Management of the benign pattern is a 2 to 4 week statin pause, symptom reassessment, then rechallenge at a lower dose or a different statin. Coenzyme Q10 is not effective. Ezetimibe or PCSK9 inhibitor add-on is reserved for confirmed statin intolerance after multiple rechallenge attempts.
key_points: Normal CK with preserved power favours benign statin-associated muscle symptoms
2 to 4 week supervised pause then rechallenge at lower dose
Up to 70 percent tolerate rechallenge
Coenzyme Q10 is not effective
Anti-HMGCR immune-mediated necrotising myopathy is a rare mimic
explanation.pearls: The nocebo component of statin-associated muscle symptoms is substantial: in the SAMSON and StatinWISE double-blind crossover trials, over 90 percent of the symptom burden reported on active statin was reproduced by placebo, which is why a supervised pause and blinded rechallenge remains the diagnostic strategy of choice.

options.rationale: Immune-mediated necrotising myopathy classically presents with proximal weakness, CK over 1000, and a positive anti-HMGCR antibody; a CK of 138 with preserved power does not meet the pretest probability threshold for biopsy (Source: RCPA Autoantibody Guideline).

Coenzyme Q10 has been repeatedly negative in randomised trials for statin-associated muscle symptoms and is not recommended by AU or international lipid guidelines; it does not address the diagnostic uncertainty (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Lipid Management Guideline).

Secondary prevention statin therapy carries a large mortality benefit and abandonment before a rechallenge trial forgoes that benefit; the diagnostic uncertainty here does not justify permanent cessation (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Lipid Management Guideline).

Ezetimibe monotherapy delivers around 20 percent LDL reduction versus 50 percent from high-intensity statin; switching before establishing a causal link risks losing statin benefit that most patients would tolerate on rechallenge (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Lipid Management Guideline).

Statin-associated muscle symptoms with normal CK are managed by a supervised statin pause of 2 to 4 weeks to establish causal linkage and then a rechallenge with a lower dose or a different statin (usually rosuvastatin at low dose given its potency), because up to 70 percent of patients with self-reported statin muscle symptoms tolerate rechallenge; secondary-prevention statin therapy must not be abandoned without a rechallenge trial (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Lipid Management Guideline; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).

explanation.summary: Antiphospholipid syndrome is a clinical and laboratory diagnosis: at least one clinical criterion (arterial, venous, or small-vessel thrombosis, or defined pregnancy morbidity) plus persistent laboratory positivity (lupus anticoagulant, anti-cardiolipin IgG or IgM, or anti-beta 2 glycoprotein I IgG or IgM) at least 12 weeks apart. Triple-positive APS (all three antibodies positive) has the highest thrombotic risk. Warfarin with a target INR of 2.5 (range 2.0 to 3.0) is the anticoagulant of choice; the TRAPS trial and subsequent evidence show DOACs are inferior in triple-positive APS with higher arterial event rates. Duration of anticoagulation is indefinite for a defined APS diagnosis after a thrombotic event.
key_points: Triple-positive APS: lupus anticoagulant + anti-cardiolipin + anti-beta 2 GPI
DOACs are inferior to warfarin in triple-positive APS
Target INR 2.5 (range 2.0 to 3.0) on warfarin
Indefinite anticoagulation after a thrombotic event
Confirmatory antibody testing at 12 weeks
explanation.pearls: The confirmatory laboratory diagnosis of APS requires persistent antibody positivity 12 weeks apart because a single transiently positive result may be reactive (recent infection, medications, or acute thrombosis itself); triple positivity carries roughly a 10-fold recurrence risk over single positivity and is what has driven the warfarin-only recommendation in recent guidance.

sources.label: ISTH SSC Statement on APS and DOACs

options.rationale: Antiphospholipid syndrome mandates indefinite anticoagulation given recurrence risk; ceasing after 3 months contradicts the unprovoked-plus-APS profile that carries a very high recurrence rate (Source: HSANZ Antiphospholipid Syndrome Guideline).

DOACs are inferior to warfarin in triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome; ongoing DOAC exposes the patient to a higher recurrent thrombosis risk, particularly arterial events (Source: ISTH SSC Statement on APS and DOACs).
source_refs: ISTH SSC Statement on APS and DOACs

options.rationale: Adding aspirin to a DOAC in APS increases bleeding without matching warfarin efficacy; combination therapy is not a substitute for switching to a vitamin K antagonist (Source: HSANZ Antiphospholipid Syndrome Guideline).

Switching between DOACs does not address the class-level failure of factor Xa inhibitors in triple-positive APS demonstrated in TRAPS; the patient still needs a vitamin K antagonist (Source: ISTH SSC Statement on APS and DOACs).
source_refs: ISTH SSC Statement on APS and DOACs

options.rationale: Triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome (lupus anticoagulant plus anti-cardiolipin plus anti-beta 2 glycoprotein I) has a higher rate of thrombosis on DOAC than on warfarin in the TRAPS and other trials; the AU HSANZ and ISTH consensus recommends switching from DOAC to warfarin with a target INR of 2.5 (Source: HSANZ Antiphospholipid Syndrome Guideline; ISTH SSC Statement on APS and DOACs).
source_refs: ISTH SSC Statement on APS and DOACs

explanation.summary: Severe hyperkalaemia (potassium 6.5 mmol/L or above, or any potassium with ECG changes) requires immediate sequenced management. Step one is myocardial membrane stabilisation with IV calcium gluconate 10 percent 10 mL over 2 to 3 minutes (or IV calcium chloride 10 percent 5 mL through a central line), acting within 1 to 3 minutes to prevent arrhythmia. Step two is intracellular potassium shift with IV actrapid insulin 10 unit in 50 mL 50 percent glucose over 15 minutes, and nebulised salbutamol 10 to 20 mg as an adjunct. Step three is definitive removal (dialysis, potassium binder, or reversal of the precipitating drug or condition). Withdrawal of the ACE inhibitor and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist is essential.
key_points: Sequence: stabilise, shift, then remove
IV calcium is the first step when ECG changes are present
Insulin-dextrose gives shift over 15 to 30 minutes
Salbutamol nebulised is an adjunct shifting agent
Dialysis is the definitive removal for renal failure
explanation.pearls: The QRS widening of hyperkalaemia represents the loss of the rapid depolarisation phase and heralds imminent sine-wave morphology and asystole within minutes; IV calcium is the only intervention that acts on that timescale, and it can be safely repeated at 5 to 10 minute intervals until ECG normalisation while insulin and definitive removal are being organised.

options.rationale: Salbutamol is an adjunct shifting agent (0.5 to 1.0 mmol/L reduction) that acts over 30 minutes; it is not sufficient monotherapy for a potassium of 7.4 with QRS widening (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

Insulin-dextrose is essential but is a shifting step that acts over 15 to 30 minutes; myocardial stabilisation with IV calcium must come first when the QRS is widening (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

Severe hyperkalaemia with QRS widening and PR prolongation requires immediate myocardial membrane stabilisation with IV calcium, which works within 1 to 3 minutes; insulin-dextrose and salbutamol drive intracellular shift and definitive removal comes from dialysis, but calcium is the first step (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology; KHA-CARI Hyperkalaemia Guideline).

Dialysis is the definitive potassium removal but cannot be delivered fast enough to prevent asystole from a widening QRS; medical bridging with calcium and insulin-dextrose is mandatory during vascular access and dialysis initiation (Source: KHA-CARI Hyperkalaemia Guideline).

Potassium binders act over hours to remove potassium and have no acute role in severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes; immediate cardiac protection with IV calcium is first (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

explanation.summary: The diagnostic algorithm for hyponatraemia proceeds through three questions: is the plasma osmolality low (true hypotonic hyponatraemia), what is the urine osmolality, and what is the volume status. Hypotonic hyponatraemia with urine osmolality over 100 mOsm/kg indicates inappropriate ADH activity. Adding a euvolaemic volume status and a urine sodium over 30 mmol/L, in the absence of thyroid or adrenal insufficiency, defines SIADH. Common causes include central nervous system pathology, pulmonary disease (pneumonia), malignancy (especially small cell lung cancer), and drugs (SSRIs, carbamazepine, chemotherapy agents). Management begins with fluid restriction under 1 litre per day for asymptomatic patients; hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia.
key_points: SIADH: euvolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia with urine osmolality over 100
Urine sodium over 30 mmol/L supports SIADH over hypovolaemia
Fluid restriction under 1 litre is first-line for asymptomatic SIADH
Hypertonic saline for severe symptoms only
Correct at maximum 8 to 10 mmol/L per 24 hours to avoid demyelination
explanation.pearls: The KHA-CARI correction cap is 8 to 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours (6 mmol/L in chronic hyponatraemia with high demyelination risk), and if you overshoot the AU rescue is 5 percent dextrose plus desmopressin to re-lower the sodium and then correct at a controlled rate over the next 24 hours.

options.rationale: Demeclocycline is second-line for chronic SIADH refractory to fluid restriction and carries nephrotoxicity risk; first-line management of asymptomatic SIADH is fluid restriction (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

Giving isotonic saline in SIADH can paradoxically worsen hyponatraemia because free water is retained while sodium is excreted; isotonic saline is only appropriate in hypovolaemic hyponatraemia, which is not present here (Source: KHA-CARI Hyponatraemia Guideline).

Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizure, altered consciousness) or profound acute drops; the patient here is asymptomatic and hypertonic saline risks osmotic demyelination if the sodium is corrected too rapidly (Source: KHA-CARI Hyponatraemia Guideline).

The euvolaemic patient with hypotonic hyponatraemia, urine osmolality over 100 mOsm/kg (in this case 462), and urine sodium over 30 mmol/L, with normal thyroid and adrenal axes, meets criteria for SIADH; fluid restriction to under 1 litre daily is first-line for asymptomatic SIADH (Source: KHA-CARI Hyponatraemia Guideline; Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

Tolvaptan is reserved for SIADH refractory to fluid restriction, has PBS restrictions in Australia, and carries risks of overly rapid correction and hepatotoxicity requiring inpatient initiation; it is not first-line for asymptomatic SIADH (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

explanation.summary: Acute severe ulcerative colitis is defined by Truelove and Witts criteria (at least 6 bloody stools per day plus one of pulse over 90, temperature over 37.8, haemoglobin under 105 g/L, ESR over 30, or CRP over 30) and is managed with admission for IV corticosteroid (hydrocortisone 100 mg six-hourly). Response is assessed at day 3 to 5 using the Oxford Travis criteria: over 8 bloody stools per day, or 3 to 8 bloody stools per day with CRP over 45 mg/L, identifies steroid-refractory disease requiring rescue therapy. Rescue options are infliximab 5 mg/kg IV or ciclosporin 2 mg/kg/day IV. Reassessment at 72 hours after rescue selects patients for colectomy if there is no response. Immediate surgery is reserved for perforation, haemorrhage, or toxic megacolon.
key_points: Truelove and Witts: acute severe UC diagnosis
Oxford Travis criteria at day 3 to 5: steroid-refractory
Rescue with infliximab 5 mg/kg IV or ciclosporin
Reassess response at 72 hours after rescue
Colectomy for perforation, haemorrhage, toxic megacolon or rescue failure
explanation.pearls: Travis criteria at day 3 predict a colectomy risk of around 85 percent without rescue therapy and around 30 percent with infliximab or ciclosporin rescue, which is why day 3 assessment is the pivot point in the AU pathway and delays beyond it are strongly associated with worse outcomes.

options.rationale: Thiopurines have onset over 8 to 12 weeks and are useful for maintenance not rescue; they have no role in acute severe steroid-refractory disease as monotherapy (Source: GESA Ulcerative Colitis Guideline).

Continuing IV steroids beyond the day 3 to 5 assessment window when Travis criteria are met delays effective rescue therapy and increases the risk of complications including colonic dilatation and perforation (Source: GESA Ulcerative Colitis Guideline).

Immediate colectomy is reserved for perforation, uncontrolled haemorrhage, toxic megacolon (over 5.5 cm with systemic toxicity), or failure of a documented rescue therapy trial; rescue medical therapy is offered first (Source: GESA Ulcerative Colitis Guideline).

The Oxford Travis criteria (over 8 stools per day, or 3 to 8 stools per day plus CRP over 45 mg/L at day 3 of IV steroid) identify steroid-refractory acute severe ulcerative colitis; rescue therapy with infliximab or ciclosporin is indicated before colectomy is considered, with reassessment at 72 hours (Source: GESA Ulcerative Colitis Guideline; Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).

Step-down to oral steroid is appropriate when IV therapy has produced clinical response, not when the patient meets Travis criteria for steroid-refractory disease; escalating not stepping down is required here (Source: GESA Ulcerative Colitis Guideline).

explanation.summary: Fluid resuscitation in acute pancreatitis has shifted from aggressive (10 mL/kg bolus and 3 mL/kg/hour for 48 hours) to moderate goal-directed strategy based on the WATERFALL trial and subsequent AU HPB Society guidance. A balanced crystalloid (Hartmann's or Plasma-Lyte) at 200 to 250 mL per hour titrated to urine output over 0.5 mL/kg/hour, haematocrit trend, and improvement in urea and lactate is now standard. The change reflects consistent findings of fluid overload harm (acute respiratory distress syndrome, abdominal compartment syndrome, and multiorgan failure) without a mortality benefit from aggressive resuscitation. Analgesia (usually IV opioid), early oral or nasojejunal nutrition, and treatment of the underlying cause (early ERCP for cholangitis, laparoscopic cholecystectomy on the same admission for gallstone pancreatitis) round out the pathway.
key_points: Moderate goal-directed replaces aggressive resuscitation in AU practice
Hartmann's or Plasma-Lyte at 200 to 250 mL/hour is standard
Titrate to urine output over 0.5 mL/kg/hour and haematocrit trend
Aggressive resuscitation causes ARDS and abdominal compartment syndrome
Early cholecystectomy on same admission for gallstone pancreatitis
explanation.pearls: The WATERFALL trial stopped early for harm in the aggressive resuscitation arm, driven by fluid overload without a pancreatitis benefit, which is why the AU HPB Society guidance now caps first-24-hour fluid volume at around 5 litres for most adults rather than the previous 6 to 8 litre targets.

sources.label: AU HPB Society Acute Pancreatitis Guideline

options.rationale: The 2022 WATERFALL trial and subsequent AU HPB Society guidance moved from aggressive to moderate goal-directed fluid resuscitation in acute pancreatitis; a Hartmann's or Plasma-Lyte rate of 200 to 250 mL per hour titrated to urine output 0.5 mL/kg/hour and haematocrit reduces fluid overload without worsening pancreatitis outcomes (Source: AU HPB Society Acute Pancreatitis Guideline; WATERFALL trial; Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).
source_refs: AU HPB Society Acute Pancreatitis Guideline

options.rationale: Aggressive fluid resuscitation was standard until 2022 but WATERFALL and subsequent trials showed higher fluid overload and worse outcomes without pancreatitis benefit; the AU guidance shifted to moderate goal-directed fluid rates (Source: AU HPB Society Acute Pancreatitis Guideline).
source_refs: AU HPB Society Acute Pancreatitis Guideline

options.rationale: Balanced crystalloids (Hartmann's, Plasma-Lyte) are preferred over 0.9 percent sodium chloride in acute pancreatitis because saline resuscitation worsens hyperchloraemic acidosis without any pancreatitis-specific benefit (Source: AU HPB Society Acute Pancreatitis Guideline).
source_refs: AU HPB Society Acute Pancreatitis Guideline

options.rationale: Restrictive fluid strategy in a patient with a urine output of 30 mL over 4 hours and elevated haematocrit and urea perpetuates hypovolaemia and drives acute kidney injury; goal-directed rather than restrictive is the current standard (Source: AU HPB Society Acute Pancreatitis Guideline).
source_refs: AU HPB Society Acute Pancreatitis Guideline

options.rationale: Colloid resuscitation in acute pancreatitis has no evidence of benefit over balanced crystalloid, is significantly more expensive, and CVP-guided resuscitation is not recommended in current AU practice for acute pancreatitis (Source: AU HPB Society Acute Pancreatitis Guideline).
source_refs: AU HPB Society Acute Pancreatitis Guideline

explanation.summary: Perioperative anticoagulation planning stratifies patients by thromboembolic risk (annualised) and bleeding risk of the procedure. Mechanical mitral valves fall into the high-risk category with annualised thromboembolic risk over 10 percent, and warfarin interruption for surgery mandates therapeutic-dose low molecular weight heparin bridging (enoxaparin 1 mg/kg subcutaneously twice daily). Warfarin is stopped 5 days pre-op, LMWH is started when INR falls under 2, the last therapeutic-dose LMWH is 24 hours before surgery (12 hours for prophylactic dose), and warfarin is resumed the evening of surgery with LMWH continued until INR is therapeutic. Low-risk atrial fibrillation with CHA2DS2-VA of 3 or below and no prior stroke does not require bridging.
key_points: Mechanical mitral valve is high thromboembolic risk (over 10% annualised)
Therapeutic-dose LMWH bridging required around warfarin interruption
Last therapeutic LMWH 24 hours before surgery
DOACs are contraindicated in mechanical valves
Low-risk AF with CHA2DS2-VA 3 or below does not require bridging
explanation.pearls: The BRIDGE trial found that low-risk AF (CHA2DS2-VASc 3 or below) does not benefit from bridging and suffers more bleeding, but the same trial excluded mechanical valves and rheumatic mitral disease; those two groups remain the residual indication for therapeutic bridging in current AU perioperative guidance.

sources.label: ANZ Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis Perioperative Anticoagulation Guideline

options.rationale: DOACs are contraindicated in mechanical valves after the RE-ALIGN trial showed increased thrombosis and bleeding on dabigatran versus warfarin; apixaban has no TGA indication for mechanical valves (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).
source_refs: ANZ Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis Perioperative Anticoagulation Guideline

options.rationale: An intra-operative INR of 2.0 is unsafe for laparotomy and hemicolectomy; continuing warfarin through surgery is only appropriate for minor procedures with predictable haemostasis (Source: ANZ Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis Perioperative Anticoagulation Guideline).
source_refs: ANZ Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis Perioperative Anticoagulation Guideline

options.rationale: No bridging in a mechanical mitral valve leaves a high-risk patient unprotected during the 10 to 14 day period of subtherapeutic INR around surgery; the AU standard is therapeutic-dose LMWH bridging (Source: ANZ Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis Perioperative Anticoagulation Guideline).
source_refs: ANZ Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis Perioperative Anticoagulation Guideline

options.rationale: A mechanical mitral valve is a high thromboembolic risk category (annualised risk over 10 percent) and mandates therapeutic-dose bridging with low molecular weight heparin around perioperative warfarin interruption; the ANZ Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis and ACC 2017 update place this patient in the group where bridging benefit outweighs bleeding harm (Source: ANZ Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis Perioperative Anticoagulation Guideline; ACC 2017 Perioperative Anticoagulation Update).
source_refs: ANZ Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis Perioperative Anticoagulation Guideline

options.rationale: Prophylactic-dose LMWH does not provide thromboembolic protection for a high-risk mechanical mitral valve; therapeutic-dose enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily is required in this indication (Source: ANZ Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis Perioperative Anticoagulation Guideline).
source_refs: ANZ Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis Perioperative Anticoagulation Guideline

explanation.summary: STEMI with expected PCI delay over 120 minutes from first medical contact is treated with fibrinolysis at the regional site (tenecteplase weight based) followed by transfer to a PCI centre for review. Rescue PCI applies when there is failure of reperfusion at 90 minutes with persistent ST elevation or ongoing pain. Primary PCI is preferred only when it can be achieved within the 120 minute window from first medical contact.
key_points: PCI within 120 minutes preferred; otherwise fibrinolysis.
Rescue PCI after failed fibrinolysis (persistent ST elevation, ongoing pain).
Do not defer reperfusion for troponin results.
explanation.pearls: STEMI at a regional site more than 120 minutes from primary PCI is fibrinolysis now with transfer for rescue PCI, not helicopter transfer without reperfusion.

options.rationale: ST elevation meeting STEMI criteria mandates immediate reperfusion; awaiting troponin delays therapy without changing the diagnosis (Source: CSANZ Australian ACS Guidelines).

Waiting to reach primary PCI when the total time is likely to exceed 120 minutes from first medical contact adds ischaemic time; fibrinolysis at the regional site is preferred (Source: CSANZ Australian ACS Guidelines).

CSANZ recommends fibrinolysis when primary PCI cannot be delivered within 120 minutes of first medical contact; expected door in to balloon time here exceeds 120 minutes, so tenecteplase now with transfer for rescue PCI is preferred (Source: CSANZ Australian ACS Guidelines).
Analgesia and nitrate infusion are supportive but must not defer reperfusion in STEMI (Source: CSANZ Australian ACS Guidelines).
Delayed angiography is appropriate for stable NSTEMI at intermediate risk, not for STEMI where time-critical reperfusion is mandatory (Source: CSANZ Australian ACS Guidelines).

explanation.summary: This is adult DKA without frank shock. ADS treats with 1 L 0.9% saline over the first hour, then insulin infusion at 0.1 unit/kg/hour, with potassium added once serum K falls below 5.5 mmol/L. Bicarbonate is only considered when pH is below 6.9.
key_points: First hour: 0.9% saline 1 L in adult DKA.
Insulin infusion 0.1 unit/kg/hour after first bag.
Add potassium when serum K falls below 5.5 mmol/L; bicarbonate only if pH under 6.9.
explanation.pearls: The ADS adult DKA opening move is 1 L 0.9% saline over 1 hour, then insulin infusion at 0.1 unit/kg/hour, with potassium added when serum K drops below 5.5 mmol/L.

sources.label: ADS Guidelines for the Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults

options.rationale: Bicarbonate is only considered for severe acidaemia with pH under 6.9 in adults; it is not indicated at pH 7.10 (Source: ADS Guidelines for the Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults).
source_refs: ADS Guidelines for the Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults

options.rationale: A 2 L rapid bolus over 15 minutes is not standard in adult DKA without shock; dextrose is added when glucose falls to 12 to 14 mmol/L (Source: ADS Guidelines for the Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults).
source_refs: ADS Guidelines for the Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults

options.rationale: Insulin without volume resuscitation shifts potassium intracellularly, worsens hypoperfusion, and increases arrhythmia risk (Source: ADS Guidelines for the Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults).
source_refs: ADS Guidelines for the Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults

options.rationale: The ADS DKA pathway gives 1 L 0.9% saline over the first hour and starts a fixed rate insulin infusion at 0.1 unit/kg/hour; add potassium once serum potassium falls below 5.5 mmol/L (Source: ADS Guidelines for the Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults).
source_refs: ADS Guidelines for the Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults

options.rationale: Subcutaneous rapid insulin has unpredictable absorption in shock or dehydration; intravenous infusion is preferred alongside fluid resuscitation (Source: ADS Guidelines for the Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults).
source_refs: ADS Guidelines for the Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults
