explanation.summary: Apixaban reduces to 2.5 mg BD only when two of three criteria are met: age 80 or above, weight 60 kg or less, or serum creatinine 133 micromol/L or above. She meets only one criterion so the standard 5 mg BD dose continues. Anticoagulation is warranted with CHA2DS2-VA 5.
key_points: Apixaban dose reduction requires 2 of 3 criteria.
eGFR 34 mL/min is not itself an apixaban contraindication in Australia.
CHA2DS2-VA 5 favours continued anticoagulation.
explanation.pearls: Apixaban reduces to 2.5 mg BD only when at least 2 of 3 apply: age 80 or above, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 micromol/L or above.

options.rationale: CHA2DS2-VA 5 confers a substantial stroke risk that outweighs bleeding risk in most patients and warrants continued anticoagulation (Source: CSANZ Australian AF Guidelines).

A single criterion is insufficient for dose reduction; two of three (age 80 or above, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 micromol/L or above) are required (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook Apixaban).

Apixaban is not contraindicated at eGFR 34 mL/min; it remains preferred over warfarin in most patients with CrCl above 25 mL/min in Australian practice (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook Apixaban).
Dabigatran is more renally cleared than apixaban and is not preferred at eGFR 34 mL/min without a specific indication (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook Dabigatran).

Apixaban dose reduction to 2.5 mg BD requires two of age 80 years or above, weight 60 kg or less, or serum creatinine 133 micromol/L or above; she meets only the creatinine criterion so the standard 5 mg BD dose continues (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook Apixaban).

explanation.summary: SMART-COP identifies severe community-acquired pneumonia. This man meets several criteria (systolic BP under 90, albumin under 35, RR at or above 30, tachycardia at or above 125, pO2 60 to 70 on air), so he needs high acuity or ICU care with intravenous ceftriaxone plus azithromycin and titrated oxygen. Mild to moderate regimens and outpatient care are inappropriate.
key_points: SMART-COP identifies patients needing intensive support.
Severe CAP: intravenous ceftriaxone plus azithromycin.
Do not use hospital acquired regimens or defer for viral results.
explanation.pearls: Severe community-acquired pneumonia by SMART-COP is admitted to high acuity or ICU for IV ceftriaxone plus azithromycin; mild to moderate oral regimens do not cover this severity.

sources.label: Charles et al. SMART-COP validation Clin Infect Dis 2008

options.rationale: SMART-COP components met include systolic BP under 90, multilobar not applicable but albumin under 35, respiratory rate 30 or above, tachycardia 125 or above, and pO2 60 to 70 mmHg on room air; the total predicts need for intensive respiratory or vasopressor support; TG antibiotics are ceftriaxone plus azithromycin (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Charles et al. SMART-COP validation Clin Infect Dis 2008).
Discharge is not appropriate for SMART-COP high risk with hypoxia and hypotension; hospitalisation is mandatory (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
This regimen is TG mild to moderate community-acquired pneumonia and does not cover severe pneumonia; a high acuity bed is required (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

This presentation is community-acquired pneumonia rather than hospital acquired; broadening to antipseudomonal cover is not indicated without specific risk factors (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
Antibiotic therapy for severe pneumonia is not deferred pending viral panels; consolidation, hypoxia, and toxicity mandate empirical antibiotics now (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: This is a high risk TIA in a previously untreated patient with no haemorrhage on imaging. Australian guidance uses short course DAPT (aspirin plus clopidogrel) for 21 days followed by single antiplatelet, alongside high intensity statin therapy and BP optimisation. Alteplase is only for persisting deficit. Endarterectomy is for 70 to 99% symptomatic stenosis.
key_points: High risk TIA: aspirin plus clopidogrel for 21 days then single antiplatelet.
Carotid endarterectomy is for 70 to 99% symptomatic stenosis within 2 weeks.
Alteplase requires persisting deficit.
explanation.pearls: After a high risk TIA (ABCD2 4 or above) with no haemorrhage, load aspirin 300 mg and clopidogrel 300 mg then continue both for 21 days before stepping down to single antiplatelet.

options.rationale: Aspirin alone in the first 21 days after high risk TIA is inferior to short course DAPT for recurrent stroke prevention as shown by CHANCE and POINT (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines).

The Stroke Foundation Australia guideline and CHANCE/POINT trials recommend short course dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) with aspirin plus clopidogrel for 21 days after a high risk TIA (ABCD2 4 or above) or minor stroke without haemorrhage, followed by single antiplatelet (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines).

Anticoagulation is only indicated when atrial fibrillation or another cardioembolic source is documented; ECG is in sinus rhythm and workup has not yet identified one (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines).
Carotid endarterectomy is recommended for symptomatic stenosis 70 to 99% ideally within 2 weeks; 50% is not a mandatory surgical stenosis (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines).
Alteplase is for acute ischaemic stroke with a persisting deficit; a fully resolved TIA does not meet the treatment criteria (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines).

explanation.summary: New temporal headache with jaw claudication and grossly elevated ESR and CRP in a woman over 50 is GCA until proven otherwise. Start prednisolone 40 to 60 mg daily immediately and arrange temporal artery biopsy within 14 days; do not delay steroids. Pulse methylprednisolone is reserved for visual involvement or ischaemic complications.
key_points: Start prednisolone 40 to 60 mg daily now.
Temporal artery biopsy within 14 days; positivity persists on treatment.
Reserve pulse methylprednisolone for visual or ischaemic involvement.
explanation.pearls: In suspected GCA start prednisolone 40 to 60 mg daily immediately and biopsy within 14 days; visual complications escalate to pulse methylprednisolone.

sources.label: BSR Guideline for the diagnosis and treatment of giant cell arteritis 2020

options.rationale: Pulse methylprednisolone is reserved for GCA with visual involvement or ischaemic complications, not for uncomplicated presentations (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association GCA guidance).
Delaying steroids risks irreversible visual loss and biopsy remains diagnostic despite up to 2 weeks of treatment (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association GCA guidance).

Australian and BSR guidance start prednisolone 40 to 60 mg daily immediately for suspected GCA and biopsy within 1 to 2 weeks; steroids should not be delayed pending biopsy because temporal biopsy findings persist for weeks (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association GCA guidance; BSR GCA guideline 2020).
Tocilizumab is a steroid sparing adjunct in relapsing GCA, not a monotherapy induction agent (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association GCA guidance).
NSAIDs are not adequate treatment for GCA and delay effective immunosuppression while irreversible visual loss can occur (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association GCA guidance).

explanation.summary: Cancer associated VTE now typically uses apixaban or rivaroxaban over LMWH. In gastric or other luminal GI cancers apixaban is preferred because of a lower luminal bleeding signal than rivaroxaban. Continue for at least 6 months and while cancer or chemotherapy remains active.
key_points: DOAC over LMWH for most cancer VTE.
Apixaban preferred in luminal GI cancers.
Duration at least 6 months and while active cancer.
explanation.pearls: For DVT in gastric or other luminal GI cancer, apixaban is preferred over rivaroxaban because of a lower major GI bleeding signal in the Caravaggio and SELECT-D data.

sources.label: SELECT-D trial (Young et al. J Clin Oncol 2018)

options.rationale: Aspirin is not adequate acute anticoagulation for a proximal DVT in cancer; it is reserved for extended prophylaxis in specific low risk contexts (Source: TSANZ Australian VTE Guidelines).
Rivaroxaban is associated with a higher major GI bleeding signal in gastrointestinal malignancy than apixaban and is not preferred in gastric cancer (Source: TSANZ Australian VTE Guidelines).
Warfarin is inferior to LMWH and DOACs in active cancer because of drug interactions with chemotherapy and unstable INR from vomiting or nutritional swings (Source: TSANZ Australian VTE Guidelines).

Australian and international cancer VTE guidance now supports DOACs (apixaban or rivaroxaban) over LMWH for most patients without upper GI or genitourinary tumours; gastric cancer requires case by case review given bleeding risk, but apixaban is preferred over rivaroxaban in gastric or GI cancers because of a lower luminal bleeding signal (Source: TSANZ Australian VTE Guidelines; Caravaggio and SELECT-D trials).

IVC filters are reserved for absolute contraindication to anticoagulation; she has no active bleeding and her platelets are 168, so anticoagulation is preferred (Source: TSANZ Australian VTE Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Chronic prednisolone therapy suppresses the hypothalamic pituitary adrenal axis and an intercurrent illness with vomiting can precipitate an adrenal crisis. Treatment is intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus then 200 mg per 24 hours, 0.9% saline resuscitation, and glucose replacement. Dexamethasone lacks mineralocorticoid effect and should not replace hydrocortisone in crisis.
key_points: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus then 200 mg per 24 hours.
Fluid resuscitate with 0.9% saline; correct hypoglycaemia with 10% dextrose.
Do not use dexamethasone as substitute; do not defer for synacthen test.
explanation.pearls: In adrenal crisis give IV hydrocortisone 100 mg then 200 mg per 24 hours by infusion; dexamethasone lacks mineralocorticoid activity and is not the substitute of choice.

options.rationale: Corticosteroid replacement is definitive in adrenal crisis and must not be delayed while titrating vasopressors; inotropes remain refractory without steroid (Source: ESA Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline).
Oral therapy is unreliable in vomiting shocked patients; parenteral hydrocortisone is required for adrenal crisis (Source: ESA Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline).
Dexamethasone lacks mineralocorticoid activity needed in adrenal crisis; deferring hydrocortisone for a synacthen test delays life saving treatment (Source: ESA Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline).
Fludrocortisone is not available in a parenteral form suitable for crisis and does not replace hydrocortisone in acute adrenal insufficiency (Source: ESA Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline).

This is an adrenal crisis in a chronically suppressed patient; the Endocrine Society of Australia recommends hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus then 200 mg per 24 hours by infusion with fluid resuscitation and glucose correction (Source: ESA Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline; Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

explanation.summary: The first branch point in dysphagia is whether difficulty is for solids alone, which suggests a mechanical narrowing, or for solids and liquids equally, which suggests a motility disorder. Achalasia is the archetype of the latter and is caused by loss of inhibitory ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus, producing failure of lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation and absent peristalsis. It typically presents in the fourth to sixth decades with slowly progressive dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food, nocturnal cough, weight loss and years of ineffective reflux treatment. Endoscopy is performed first, principally to exclude a tumour at the cardia that can mimic the manometric picture, and barium swallow may show the tapered distal narrowing, but high resolution manometry is the diagnostic standard and identifies the subtype that guides treatment. Options include pneumatic dilatation, laparoscopic myotomy with fundoplication, peroral endoscopic myotomy, and botulinum toxin injection for those unfit for definitive treatment.
key_points: Equal difficulty with liquids and solids from the start indicates a motility disorder
Endoscopy comes first to exclude a tumour at the cardia mimicking achalasia
High resolution manometry is the diagnostic standard and defines the subtype
Years of ineffective proton pump inhibitor therapy is a characteristic history
Treatment options are dilatation, myotomy, peroral endoscopic myotomy or botulinum toxin
explanation.pearls: Suspect a malignancy at the cardia rather than primary achalasia when the history is shorter than six months, weight loss is disproportionate, or the patient is over sixty, because tumour infiltration of the myenteric plexus reproduces the manometric findings exactly and cross sectional imaging or endoscopic ultrasound is then required before any dilatation is attempted.

options.rationale: Dysphagia to liquids and solids equally from the outset, with regurgitation of undigested food and failure of acid suppression, indicates a motility disorder rather than a structural one, and endoscopy has already excluded mechanical obstruction. Manometry is the diagnostic standard and also subtypes the disorder, which determines whether pneumatic dilatation, myotomy or a peroral endoscopic approach is chosen. (Source: GESA: Oesophageal disorders)

A normal endoscopy with negative biopsies has already answered the structural and eosinophilic questions, and repeating it is unlikely to reveal a motility abnormality that endoscopy cannot assess. It is worth repeating only if the first study was technically limited or symptoms change. (Source: GESA: Oesophageal disorders)

Ambulatory pH testing evaluates reflux disease and is useful when symptoms persist despite acid suppression and the diagnosis of reflux is in doubt. Regurgitation of undigested food rather than acid, with equal difficulty for liquids, points away from reflux as the mechanism. (Source: GESA: Oesophageal disorders)

A tumour at the cardia can imitate this picture and is the classic pseudo presentation, which is exactly why endoscopy comes first and has been normal here. Cross sectional imaging is added when the history is short, the weight loss is rapid, or manometry findings are combined with an older patient. (Source: GESA: Oesophageal disorders)

Videofluoroscopy assesses oropharyngeal swallowing and is used when there is coughing at the start of a swallow, nasal regurgitation or a neurological cause. This woman localises the problem to the chest and initiates swallows normally. (Source: GESA: Oesophageal disorders)

explanation.summary: Eosinophilic oesophagitis is a chronic immune mediated disease that has become the leading cause of food impaction in young adults, typically men with a background of asthma, allergic rhinitis or eczema. Patients often normalise years of adaptive behaviour such as prolonged chewing, cutting food finely, drinking with every mouthful and avoiding meat and bread, so the history must be sought directly. Endoscopy shows concentric rings, linear furrows, white exudate, oedema and sometimes a narrow calibre oesophagus, but appearances can be normal, so the diagnosis rests on histology with at least six biopsies from two oesophageal levels and a threshold of fifteen eosinophils per high power field. Treatment options are a proton pump inhibitor trial, swallowed topical corticosteroid formulated to coat the mucosa, and dietary elimination, each assessed by repeat biopsy rather than by symptoms alone. Dilatation addresses established fibrostenotic narrowing but does not treat the inflammation.
key_points: Recurrent food impaction in a young atopic adult should prompt this diagnosis
At least six biopsies from two levels are required because the infiltrate is patchy
Fifteen eosinophils per high power field is the histological threshold
Adaptive eating behaviours conceal years of symptoms unless asked about directly
Response is assessed histologically because symptoms improve ahead of inflammation
explanation.pearls: Ask directly how long a meal takes and whether the patient avoids steak, bread and rice, because these adaptive behaviours are the most sensitive historical clue and patients almost never volunteer them, having assumed for years that everyone eats that way.

options.rationale: Manometry is the correct test for dysphagia to solids and liquids equally with a normal endoscopy, and abnormal motility can coexist here. It does not establish the diagnosis when the endoscopic appearance already points to a mucosal inflammatory disease that biopsy can confirm. (Source: GESA: Oesophageal disorders)

Rings, furrows and exudate in a young atopic man with recurrent impaction is the endoscopic signature of eosinophilic oesophagitis, but the diagnosis is histological and requires at least six biopsies from two levels because the infiltrate is patchy. Confirming it changes management to topical corticosteroid, dietary elimination or a proton pump inhibitor trial with a defined histological endpoint. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)

Specific immunoglobulin E and skin prick testing correlate poorly with the foods that actually drive this disease, which is not classically immunoglobulin E mediated. Elimination guided by panel testing produces unnecessarily restricted diets without reliable histological remission. (Source: ASCIA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)

Dilatation relieves fibrostenotic narrowing and has a role in established strictures, but the endoscopist reported no stricture and dilatation does not treat the underlying inflammation. Dilating before controlling inflammation also carries a higher risk of mucosal tearing. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)

Asthma and this oesophageal condition share an atopic background but inhaled therapy delivered to the airway does not treat oesophageal inflammation. The formulations used for the oesophagus are deliberately designed to be swallowed and to coat the mucosa. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)

explanation.summary: Idiopathic facial nerve palsy is diagnosed clinically and the single most important examination step is to test the forehead, since sparing of frontalis indicates an upper motor neuron lesion requiring urgent stroke assessment while involvement of the forehead localises to the nerve itself. Associated features that support a peripheral lesion include postauricular pain, hyperacusis from stapedius involvement, and altered taste on the anterior tongue. A corticosteroid started within seventy two hours of onset improves the rate of complete recovery, and the evidence for adding an antiviral is weaker but it is often given alongside in severe or complete palsy. Eye care is essential and must be prescribed explicitly, since incomplete closure with a reduced blink reflex causes exposure keratopathy. Ramsay Hunt syndrome must be excluded by inspecting the external ear canal, pinna and palate for vesicles, because it requires antiviral therapy and carries a worse prognosis.
key_points: Forehead involvement separates a lower motor neuron lesion from a stroke
Corticosteroid within seventy two hours improves the rate of complete recovery
Antiviral monotherapy is inferior and is never used in place of the steroid
Prescribe lubricant and overnight eye protection to prevent exposure keratopathy
Inspect the ear canal and palate for vesicles indicating Ramsay Hunt syndrome
explanation.pearls: Review any patient whose facial weakness fails to show some recovery by three months, because the diagnosis of idiopathic palsy assumes improvement begins within weeks, and a slowly progressive or non recovering facial weakness demands imaging of the nerve along its whole course to exclude a parotid malignancy or a schwannoma.

options.rationale: Electrophysiology has a prognostic role in complete palsy but is generally performed after the first week once degeneration would be detectable, and it does not alter the immediate decision to treat. Delaying the corticosteroid to obtain it would waste the treatment window. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Most patients do recover spontaneously, which is why this advice feels safe, but a corticosteroid given within the first three days meaningfully increases the proportion achieving complete recovery. Watching and waiting also leaves an unprotected cornea exposed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Involvement of the forehead localises the lesion to the lower motor neuron, and a corticosteroid started within seventy two hours of onset significantly improves the chance of complete recovery. Eye protection is equally important because incomplete closure with reduced blinking risks exposure keratopathy and corneal ulceration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

A stroke affecting the facial nerve nucleus or its supranuclear supply spares the forehead because of bilateral cortical innervation to the upper face, and it is usually accompanied by limb or speech findings. Complete forehead involvement with no other deficit points to a peripheral lesion. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Antiviral therapy alone is inferior to corticosteroid and is not recommended as monotherapy in this condition. Adding an antiviral to a corticosteroid is considered in severe or complete palsy, but it never replaces the steroid. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Vertigo is best sorted by timing and triggers rather than by the quality of the sensation. Brief episodes lasting seconds to a minute provoked by head position change indicate benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, attacks of twenty minutes to hours with fluctuating hearing loss and tinnitus indicate Meniere disease, and a single prolonged episode lasting days with continuous vertigo indicates vestibular neuritis or, if there are central signs, a posterior circulation stroke. The Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre both confirms posterior canal involvement and identifies the affected side, with nystagmus that has a brief latency, lasts under a minute and fatigues on repetition. The Epley repositioning manoeuvre is the treatment and is effective in most patients within one or two attempts. Vestibular sedatives are reserved for short term symptom control in acute continuous vertigo, since they hinder the central compensation that recovery depends on.
key_points: Timing and trigger separate positional vertigo from Meniere disease and neuritis
Dix-Hallpike confirms the diagnosis and identifies the affected side
Latency, duration under a minute and fatigability characterise peripheral nystagmus
Epley repositioning is the treatment and works in most patients quickly
Vestibular sedatives impair compensation and are not used for positional vertigo
explanation.pearls: Treat direction changing or gaze evoked nystagmus, nystagmus without latency that does not fatigue, or truncal ataxia so severe the patient cannot sit unsupported as central until proven otherwise, since a cerebellar infarct can present with isolated vertigo and a superficially reassuring examination.

options.rationale: Imaging is directed at features suggesting a central lesion such as gaze evoked or direction changing nystagmus, ataxia out of proportion to the vertigo, other cranial nerve signs, or new headache. None of those are present and imaging without them has a very low yield. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

This regimen targets Meniere disease, which produces attacks lasting twenty minutes to several hours with fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness. Her episodes are far shorter and her hearing is entirely normal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Vestibular rehabilitation is valuable for incomplete central compensation after vestibular neuritis and for residual unsteadiness once repositioning has succeeded. It is slower and less effective than a repositioning manoeuvre for canal debris and should not displace it as first treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Episodes lasting under a minute triggered by head position change, with no symptoms between attacks and a normal neurological and otological examination, is positional vertigo of the posterior semicircular canal, and the Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre reproduces it with a characteristic latency and fatigable upbeating torsional nystagmus. A positive result is treated immediately with the Epley repositioning manoeuvre, which resolves symptoms in the majority after one or two attempts. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Vestibular sedatives are for the continuous vertigo and vomiting of acute vestibular neuritis over a few days, and they impair central compensation when continued. They also do nothing to move the displaced otoconia that generate positional symptoms. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease is common in older adults and its acute attacks most often affect the knee or wrist, frequently triggered by intercurrent illness, surgery or trauma. Chondrocalcinosis on radiograph, seen as linear calcification within fibrocartilage and hyaline cartilage, supports the diagnosis but is a chronic finding present in many asymptomatic older people, so it can never establish the cause of a particular attack. Septic arthritis remains the diagnosis that must not be missed, is clinically indistinguishable at the bedside, and can coexist with crystal arthritis in the same joint, so aspiration for cell count, Gram stain, culture and polarised microscopy precedes treatment. Under polarised light the crystals of calcium pyrophosphate are rhomboid and weakly positively birefringent, in contrast to the strongly negatively birefringent needles of monosodium urate. Once infection is excluded, treatment is with a non-steroidal anti inflammatory, colchicine, or intra-articular or systemic corticosteroid according to comorbidity.
key_points: Chondrocalcinosis is a chronic radiological finding and never proves the cause of an attack
Septic arthritis is indistinguishable clinically and can coexist with crystal disease
Aspirate before antibiotics wherever this does not delay treating a septic patient
Rhomboid positively birefringent crystals indicate calcium pyrophosphate deposition
Attacks are often triggered by intercurrent illness, surgery or trauma
explanation.pearls: Investigate for an underlying metabolic cause when calcium pyrophosphate disease presents before the age of sixty or affects multiple joints, because haemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism, hypomagnesaemia and hypophosphatasia all predispose to it and identifying one changes management well beyond the joint.

options.rationale: Cartilage calcification is a radiological finding that is common in older people and indicates crystal deposition, not that crystals are causing this particular attack. Treating without aspiration risks missing a septic joint, which destroys cartilage within days. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

Empirical antibiotics are correct once the joint has been sampled, but giving them before aspiration reduces the yield of synovial culture and can leave the diagnosis permanently uncertain. Aspiration is quick and should precede the first dose whenever it does not delay treatment of a septic patient. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Urate lowering therapy treats gout and is never started during an acute attack without cover, and her serum urate is within the reference range. The radiographic calcification also points to a different crystal species altogether. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

Magnetic resonance imaging is useful when osteomyelitis is suspected or when the source of infection is unclear after aspiration. It is slower, less available and answers a narrower question than synovial fluid analysis in an acutely swollen joint. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

Any acutely inflamed joint requires aspiration before treatment because septic arthritis and crystal arthritis are clinically indistinguishable and can coexist, and this woman has a concurrent infection and a fever. Polarised microscopy separates the positively birefringent rhomboid crystals of calcium pyrophosphate from the negatively birefringent needles of urate, while culture answers the question that matters most. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

explanation.summary: Carpal tunnel syndrome is the commonest entrapment neuropathy and presents with nocturnal paraesthesiae in the median distribution that patients relieve by shaking or hanging the hand. A characteristic examination finding is preserved sensation over the thenar eminence, because the palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve arises proximal to the flexor retinaculum and is therefore spared, which helps distinguish it from a more proximal median lesion or a C6 radiculopathy. Provocative tests such as Tinel and Phalen have modest sensitivity and specificity and do not exclude the diagnosis when negative. Associated conditions worth screening for include hypothyroidism, diabetes, pregnancy, rheumatoid arthritis and acromegaly. Management for mild to moderate disease begins with a neutral position night splint, with corticosteroid injection as a second option, while surgical decompression is indicated for thenar wasting, persistent sensory loss, severe electrophysiological changes or failed conservative treatment.
key_points: Nocturnal symptoms relieved by shaking the hand is the classic history
Sparing of the thenar eminence reflects the palmar cutaneous branch leaving proximally
Nerve conduction studies grade severity and precede surgery, not conservative treatment
Screen for hypothyroidism, diabetes, pregnancy, rheumatoid arthritis and acromegaly
Thenar wasting or persistent sensory loss moves management to decompression
explanation.pearls: Fit the splint in the neutral position rather than in extension, because the pressure within the carpal tunnel is lowest with the wrist straight and rises with both flexion and extension, so a wrist support designed for sporting use can worsen the very symptoms it is meant to relieve.

options.rationale: Nocturnal paraesthesiae in a median distribution relieved by shaking, with sparing of sensation over the thenar eminence because the palmar cutaneous branch leaves the nerve before the tunnel, is characteristic median nerve compression at the wrist without motor loss. A neutral position night splint is effective first line treatment for mild to moderate disease and avoids both injection and surgery. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Electrophysiology confirms the diagnosis and grades severity and is required before surgery or when the picture is atypical, but it is not needed to start conservative treatment in a classic presentation. Studies are also normal in a proportion of symptomatic patients. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Urgent decompression is driven by thenar wasting, persistent sensory loss or severe changes on nerve conduction studies, and none are present here since power is full and there is no wasting. Surgery remains available if conservative treatment fails. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

A cervical root lesion typically produces neck pain, symptoms provoked by neck movement, and altered reflexes, and its sensory territory extends above the wrist. Painless full neck movement with normal symmetrical reflexes argues against it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Neuromodulator drugs treat neuropathic pain but do not relieve a mechanical compression and carry sedation, dizziness and weight gain. Evidence in this condition is poor compared with splinting or decompression. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper transport that presents between roughly five and forty years of age, with hepatic disease dominating in younger patients and neuropsychiatric features in older ones. The neurological presentation combines tremor, dysarthria, dystonia and clumsiness with personality change and deteriorating academic or work performance, and its combination with unexplained liver enzyme abnormality in a young adult is the pattern to recognise. The commonest diagnostic error is treating a normal or borderline caeruloplasmin as excluding the disease, since it is an acute phase reactant that rises with inflammation, oestrogen and pregnancy and is normal in a meaningful proportion of patients. Diagnosis therefore rests on raised twenty four hour urinary copper excretion together with slit lamp examination for corneal copper deposits, which are present in nearly all patients with neurological involvement, with hepatic copper quantification and genetic testing reserved for unresolved cases. Treatment is lifelong chelation or zinc, and first degree relatives must be screened because presymptomatic treatment prevents disease.
key_points: Liver disease plus a new movement disorder in a young adult should trigger the diagnosis
Caeruloplasmin is an acute phase reactant and a normal value does not exclude the disease
Twenty four hour urinary copper with slit lamp examination is the practical diagnostic pair
Corneal deposits are present in almost all patients with neurological involvement
Screen first degree relatives, since presymptomatic treatment prevents disease
explanation.pearls: Suspect Wilson disease in any young patient with acute liver failure showing haemolysis with a disproportionately low alkaline phosphatase and only modest transaminase elevation, because this pattern identifies fulminant presentations that will not survive without urgent transplant assessment and that are regularly misattributed to a viral or drug induced cause.

options.rationale: Molecular testing is valuable for family screening and for confirming ambiguous cases, but the large number of described mutations means results can take time and may be inconclusive. Biochemical confirmation is quicker in a symptomatic patient who needs treatment now. (Source: GESA: Wilson disease)

Caeruloplasmin is an acute phase reactant and is normal or only marginally low in a substantial minority with this disorder, so a borderline value neither confirms nor excludes it and must never be used alone. Raised twenty four hour urinary copper excretion combined with corneal deposits seen on slit lamp examination, which are present in almost all patients with neurological involvement, establishes the diagnosis without liver biopsy in most cases. (Source: GESA: Wilson disease)

Repeating a test whose limitation is that it cannot exclude the disease adds nothing, and serum copper falls in parallel with caeruloplasmin so it carries the same weakness. The diagnostic value lies in urinary excretion and in the ocular examination. (Source: GESA: Wilson disease)

Brain imaging shows characteristic basal ganglia and midbrain changes and is important for assessing neurological involvement and for baseline comparison. It is supportive rather than diagnostic and does not establish disordered copper handling. (Source: GESA: Wilson disease)

Hepatic copper quantification is the reference standard and is used when non-invasive testing is equivocal, but it carries procedural risk and is not the first step. Urinary copper with slit lamp examination resolves most cases without it. (Source: GESA: Wilson disease)

explanation.summary: Microscopic colitis is a leading cause of chronic watery diarrhoea in older adults, particularly women, and is defined by a macroscopically normal or near normal colonoscopy with characteristic histological changes of either a thickened subepithelial collagen band or a prominent intraepithelial lymphocytosis. Because the endoscopic appearance is normal, the diagnosis is missed entirely unless random biopsies are taken, and sampling must include the right colon since disease can spare the rectosigmoid. Distinguishing features from functional diarrhoea are nocturnal symptoms, weight loss, urgency and incontinence, and a mildly raised faecal calprotectin is common. Recognised associations include coeliac disease, autoimmune thyroid disease, and drugs including proton pump inhibitors, non-steroidal anti inflammatory drugs and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, so a medication review is part of management. First line treatment is budesonide, alongside withdrawal of implicated drugs.
key_points: A normal colonoscopy does not exclude colitis; the diagnosis is histological
Biopsy both right and left colon because disease is patchy and can spare the rectosigmoid
Nocturnal diarrhoea and weight loss argue against a functional disorder
Proton pump inhibitors and non-steroidal anti inflammatory drugs are recognised triggers
Budesonide is first line treatment alongside withdrawal of implicated drugs
explanation.pearls: Review the medication list before escalating treatment, because stopping a proton pump inhibitor or a regular non-steroidal anti inflammatory can resolve the diarrhoea entirely in drug associated cases, and both are so commonly prescribed in this age group that their contribution is routinely overlooked.

options.rationale: Secretory diarrhoea from a hormone secreting tumour is rare and is usually accompanied by very high stool volumes, hypokalaemia and flushing. Pursuing it before completing the standard evaluation inverts the order of probability. (Source: GESA: Chronic diarrhoea)

Serology performed with a normal immunoglobulin A level has good negative predictive value, and starting the diet before duodenal biopsy makes any later assessment for coeliac disease uninterpretable. An empirical dietary change is not a substitute for the histology that is now within reach. (Source: GESA: Coeliac disease)

Chronic non bloody watery diarrhoea with nocturnal symptoms and weight loss in an older woman with a macroscopically normal colonoscopy is the classic setting for microscopic colitis, which is invisible to the endoscopist and diagnosed only on histology. Biopsies must be taken from both the right and left colon because the changes are patchy and can be missed if sampling is limited to the rectosigmoid. (Source: GESA: Chronic diarrhoea)

Antimotility treatment is a reasonable adjunct once the diagnosis is known but here it would suppress symptoms in a patient whose diagnosis is undetermined after a full endoscopy. Nocturnal diarrhoea and weight loss are features that call for a diagnosis rather than symptomatic control. (Source: GESA: Chronic diarrhoea)

Bile acid diarrhoea is a genuine and underdiagnosed cause of chronic watery diarrhoea and this test is the standard way to demonstrate it. It is the right step only once mucosal disease has been excluded histologically, which requires the biopsies that have not yet been taken. (Source: GESA: Chronic diarrhoea)

explanation.summary: Sjogren syndrome is a chronic autoimmune exocrinopathy causing dry eyes and dry mouth, most often in middle aged women, with anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies and characteristic labial gland histology. Its most serious complication is transformation to non Hodgkin lymphoma, usually a mucosa associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma of the parotid, and the risk is many fold higher than in the general population. The recognised predictors are persistent parotid enlargement, palpable purpura, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, cryoglobulinaemia, a monoclonal paraprotein, low complement C4 and lymphopenia, and the falling complement here is among the strongest. A new persistent unilateral glandular mass in a patient with this diagnosis is therefore treated as lymphoma until histology proves otherwise, with biopsy and cross sectional staging arranged together. Recognising this risk at each review, rather than attributing every glandular change to the underlying autoimmune disease, is the practical clinical lesson.
key_points: Lymphoma risk in this condition is many times that of the general population
Persistent unilateral parotid enlargement is the single most important warning sign
Low complement C4, cryoglobulins, paraprotein and purpura are additional predictors
Autoantibody titres do not track disease activity and are not repeated for this purpose
Biopsy with concurrent cross sectional staging is the step that determines treatment
explanation.pearls: Measure complement C4 and cryoglobulins at review rather than repeating anti-Ro titres, because a falling C4 with cryoglobulinaemia identifies the subgroup at highest risk of lymphoma years before a mass appears and justifies closer surveillance of the glands and lymph nodes.

options.rationale: Bacterial parotitis presents acutely with a tender hot gland and pus expressible from the duct, in a patient who is often febrile and dehydrated. Three months of painless firm enlargement without fever does not fit an infective process. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

A duct stone characteristically causes swelling and pain that worsen with eating and then settle, a pattern the history specifically excludes. Constant enlargement unrelated to meals argues against an obstructive cause. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Sjogren syndrome)

Autoantibody titres do not track disease activity in this condition and repeating them will not explain a parotid mass. Cryoglobulins and complement are the serological markers that carry prognostic weight, and the complement result is already abnormal. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Sjogren syndrome)

Persistent unilateral parotid enlargement in this condition, with falling complement, a paraproteinaemia, lymphadenopathy and night sweats, is the described risk profile for transformation to lymphoma, which occurs in these patients at many times the background population rate. Tissue diagnosis with concurrent cross sectional staging is the step that determines treatment, and delay risks progression of a disease that is treatable when identified. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Sjogren syndrome)

Secretagogues and hydroxychloroquine address sicca symptoms and fatigue but have no effect on a structural glandular mass. Intensifying symptomatic treatment while these particular features are present risks a long delay to a serious diagnosis. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Sjogren syndrome)

explanation.summary: Narcolepsy with cataplexy results from loss of hypothalamic orexin producing neurons and presents in adolescence or early adulthood with severe daytime sleepiness, refreshing short naps, hypnagogic hallucinations and sleep paralysis. Cataplexy is the near specific feature and is defined as sudden bilateral loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion, most reliably laughter, with awareness fully preserved throughout, which distinguishes it from atonic seizures and from syncope. Diagnosis requires an adequate overnight polysomnogram, both to exclude another cause of sleepiness and to ensure sufficient sleep before testing, followed the next day by multiple sleep latency testing showing a short mean sleep latency and two or more sleep onset rapid eye movement periods. A common pitfall is stopping at a normal apnoea hypopnoea index and telling the patient the sleep study was normal, when in fact the diagnosis requires the daytime study that follows. Management combines scheduled naps, treatment for sleepiness, agents for cataplexy, and explicit counselling on driving obligations.
key_points: Cataplexy is emotion triggered bilateral atonia with fully preserved awareness
Refreshing naps distinguish narcolepsy from most other causes of sleepiness
The overnight study excludes competing causes; the daytime latency study confirms
Two or more sleep onset rapid eye movement periods support the diagnosis
Preceding actigraphy is needed so insufficient sleep does not confound the result
explanation.pearls: Address driving explicitly at the diagnostic consultation, because Australian commercial and private licence standards require that excessive daytime sleepiness be reported and adequately treated, and documenting that advice protects both the patient and other road users while treatment is being established.

options.rationale: Upper airway resistance syndrome is worth considering in a sleepy patient with a normal apnoea hypopnoea index, but it does not explain cataplexy and this man has a favourable airway with no snoring. The overnight study has already answered the breathing question. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy)

Atonic seizures cause abrupt falls with impaired awareness and are not reliably provoked by emotion. Full preservation of awareness during a laughter triggered episode is the feature that separates cataplexy from a seizure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Secondary narcolepsy from a hypothalamic lesion is rare and is suggested by additional endocrine or neurological deficits, which are absent on his normal examination. Imaging is added selectively rather than as the confirmatory test. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy)

Insufficient sleep syndrome is the commonest cause of daytime sleepiness and actigraphy with a diary is the correct way to demonstrate it, and it is also required before latency testing to ensure the result is interpretable. It cannot account for cataplexy, which is close to specific for narcolepsy. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy)

Sudden bilateral loss of muscle tone triggered by laughter with preserved awareness is cataplexy, which alongside severe sleepiness, sleep onset hallucinations and sleep paralysis indicates narcolepsy, and the overnight study has already excluded significant sleep disordered breathing. Multiple sleep latency testing performed the day after an adequate overnight study confirms the diagnosis by demonstrating short mean sleep latency with rapid eye movement sleep onset periods. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation: Narcolepsy)

explanation.summary: Eradication of Helicobacter pylori matters because it heals ulcers, prevents recurrence and reduces the long term risk of gastric adenocarcinoma and mucosa associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma. Australian first line therapy is a proton pump inhibitor with amoxicillin and clarithromycin, and success has fallen as macrolide resistance has risen. Confirmation of eradication requires a urea breath test or faecal antigen test at least four weeks after finishing antibiotics and with the acid suppressant withheld for two weeks, since both antibiotics and acid suppression produce false negative results. When a clarithromycin containing regimen fails in an adherent patient, resistance is assumed and that agent is not reused, with second line options being bismuth based quadruple therapy or a levofloxacin containing regimen, and a fourteen day duration preferred. Culture with susceptibility testing is reserved for repeated failure.
key_points: Confirm eradication at least four weeks after antibiotics with acid suppression withheld two weeks
Failure of an adherent clarithromycin regimen implies macrolide resistance
Never reuse clarithromycin after a failed course containing it
Second line options are bismuth quadruple therapy or a levofloxacin regimen for fourteen days
Culture directed therapy is reserved for two or more failures
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about any macrolide taken for a chest or sinus infection in previous years before choosing first line therapy, because a single prior exposure substantially raises the probability of clarithromycin resistance and is the most useful piece of history for predicting whether the standard regimen will work.

options.rationale: Failure of a clarithromycin containing regimen taken with full adherence indicates macrolide resistance, and that agent must not be reused because resistance is stable and reduces eradication rates sharply. Australian practice moves to a bismuth based quadruple regimen or to a levofloxacin containing regimen, given for fourteen days rather than seven. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

Extending a regimen containing an antibiotic to which the organism is resistant does not overcome that resistance, and clarithromycin resistance is the commonest reason for first line failure. Reuse also drives further resistance without benefit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

Acid suppression heals ulcers but leaves the organism in place, so ulcers recur and the long term gastric cancer risk associated with persistent infection is unchanged. Eradication remains the objective in a patient with a proven ulcer. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

Culture directed therapy is genuinely useful and is recommended after two or more failed courses or where local resistance is high. Committing to a repeat endoscopy after a single failure, when an effective empirical second line regimen exists, is more invasive than the situation requires. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

The test was performed correctly at eight weeks with the acid suppressant withheld for two weeks, which is exactly the protocol designed to avoid a false result. Repeating it delays treatment of a confirmed persistent infection in a man with a symptomatic ulcer. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

explanation.summary: Uninvestigated dyspepsia in a patient under about fifty five with no alarm features is managed by a test and treat strategy for Helicobacter pylori rather than by endoscopy, which reduces both cost and the number of normal procedures without missing significant disease. Alarm features that override this and mandate endoscopy are dysphagia, odynophagia, persistent vomiting, unintentional weight loss, gastrointestinal bleeding or iron deficiency anaemia, an epigastric mass, and a family history of upper gastrointestinal malignancy. Prevalence of the organism in Australia is around fifteen per cent in the general population but considerably higher in people born in, or whose families come from, East and Southeast Asia, Eastern Europe, the Middle East and South America, and in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities. Diagnosis uses the urea breath test or stool antigen, both of which require acid suppression to be stopped two weeks beforehand and antibiotics or bismuth four weeks beforehand, while serology is not recommended because it cannot separate current from past infection. Eradication uses a seven day course of a proton pump inhibitor with amoxicillin and clarithromycin, and confirmation of cure by breath test at least four weeks after finishing is recommended.
key_points: Test and treat for the organism rather than endoscopy in patients under fifty five without alarm features
Alarm features are dysphagia, vomiting, weight loss, bleeding, anaemia or an epigastric mass
Acid suppression must be stopped two weeks before breath or stool testing
Serology cannot distinguish current from past infection and is not recommended
Confirm eradication with a breath test at least four weeks after treatment
explanation.pearls: Confirmation of cure is not optional in Australian practice because clarithromycin resistance now runs at well over ten per cent in much of the country, so a repeat urea breath test at least four weeks after the course, again off acid suppression for two weeks, is arranged at the time the prescription is written rather than left to chance.

options.rationale: Endoscopy is indicated for dyspepsia with alarm features such as dysphagia, vomiting, weight loss, bleeding or anaemia, or for new dyspepsia over about fifty five, and he has none of these at forty two. Acid suppression also heals and masks lesions, so scoping on treatment lowers the yield further. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

Uninvestigated dyspepsia without alarm features in a patient under fifty five is managed by testing for Helicobacter pylori and eradicating it if present, and his family origin places him in a group with substantially higher prevalence. Acid suppression suppresses bacterial urease activity and produces false negative breath and stool tests, so the drug is withheld for two weeks before testing, as antibiotics and bismuth are for four. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

The test is the right one but performing it on treatment is the classic error, because suppressed urease activity and reduced bacterial load give a false negative in a substantial minority. A negative result obtained this way would wrongly close off the diagnosis. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

Escalating acid suppression may improve symptoms further but leaves an eradicable infection untreated, with its associated risks of peptic ulceration and, over decades, gastric malignancy. Long term acid suppression without a diagnosis is also how patients end up on these drugs indefinitely. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

Antibody testing cannot distinguish current infection from one cleared years ago, because antibodies persist long after eradication, so a positive result in a population with high background prevalence would lead to treating many people who are not infected. It is not recommended for diagnosis in Australia. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

explanation.summary: The commonest reason for an uninterpretable coeliac result in general practice is that the patient has already removed gluten, because both the serology and the duodenal histology normalise on a gluten free diet, often within weeks to months. The diagnosis matters even when symptoms have settled on the diet, because a formal diagnosis brings first degree relative screening, bone density assessment, nutritional monitoring, and access to support and to subsidised food products, and because the lifelong strictness required differs from that of self managed gluten avoidance. Untreated disease in a woman planning pregnancy is associated with iron and folate deficiency, low birth weight and recurrent miscarriage, which sharpens the case for resolving the question now. The standard sequence is serology first, then referral for duodenal biopsy while still consuming gluten, with genetic typing reserved for cases where a challenge is impossible or where a negative result would end the question. Iron deficiency anaemia with a low mean cell volume in a menstruating woman with bowel symptoms is a classic presentation and should never be treated with iron alone without asking why.
key_points: Serology and histology both normalise on a gluten free diet, making tests uninterpretable
An adequate challenge is about four slices of wheat bread daily for six weeks
A formal diagnosis triggers relative screening, bone density and nutritional follow up
Genetic typing has value for excluding the disease, not for confirming it
Untreated disease in pregnancy is linked to low birth weight and miscarriage
explanation.pearls: Warn her before she starts that a challenge after two months off gluten is often far more symptomatic than her original illness, and that the alternative if she cannot complete six weeks is to test the permissive genetic alleles, since a negative result there effectively excludes the disease and ends the need for the diet.

sources.label: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease
Royal Australian College of General Practitioners

options.rationale: The serology cannot be interpreted because the antibodies fall and often disappear within weeks of gluten withdrawal, so this is an uninterpretable test rather than a negative one. Iron deficiency anaemia and a first degree relative with an autoimmune condition also make a functional label premature. (Source: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease)
source_refs: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease

options.rationale: Villous architecture recovers on a gluten free diet in the same way the serology normalises, so biopsy taken after two months of exclusion can be entirely normal in established disease. Biopsy is the right test, but only after gluten has been reintroduced. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

Faecal calprotectin discriminates inflammatory bowel disease from functional symptoms and colonoscopy examines the wrong part of the bowel here, since the disease being considered affects the proximal small intestine. Neither addresses the diagnostic problem created by the diet. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

Both the antibody test and the duodenal histology depend on ongoing gluten exposure, so an adequate challenge, conventionally four slices of wheat bread or equivalent each day for six weeks, must precede retesting. Establishing the diagnosis properly matters more than usual here because of the lifelong diet, the family screening implications and the pregnancy she is planning. (Source: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease)
source_refs: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease

options.rationale: Genetic typing is useful in exactly the opposite direction: around half the Australian population carries one of the permissive alleles so a positive result excludes nothing, while a negative result makes the disease virtually impossible and can spare a challenge. Its value is in ruling out, not ruling in. (Source: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease)
source_refs: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease

explanation.summary: Nephrotic syndrome is defined by proteinuria above 3.5 g per day, hypoalbuminaemia and oedema, usually with hyperlipidaemia, and the urine protein to creatinine ratio in milligrams per millimole approximates the daily protein loss in milligrams per day divided by ten, so a ratio of 620 corresponds to about 6 g. A bland sediment with no red cells or casts points to a purely nephrotic lesion rather than a nephritic one, and in Australian adults the commonest underlying diagnoses are membranous nephropathy, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis and minimal change disease. Adults need a biopsy because these lesions cannot be told apart clinically and their treatments differ, whereas children under ten with typical features are treated empirically with corticosteroid. Complications to anticipate are venous and arterial thrombosis from urinary loss of antithrombin, infection from loss of immunoglobulin, acute kidney injury from intravascular depletion, and accelerated atherosclerosis. Supportive management is common to all causes: salt restriction, loop diuretic, blockade of the renin angiotensin system, statin therapy and vaccination.
key_points: A protein to creatinine ratio of 620 mg/mmol corresponds to roughly 6 g of daily loss
A bland urinary sediment distinguishes a nephrotic from a nephritic lesion
Adults require biopsy because the treatable lesions cannot be separated clinically
Children with typical features are treated empirically with corticosteroid instead
Blockade of the renin angiotensin system reduces proteinuria whatever the histology
explanation.pearls: Suspect renal vein thrombosis if he develops sudden flank pain, visible haematuria or an unexplained rise in creatinine, because urinary loss of antithrombin makes this syndrome genuinely prothrombotic, and the risk is highest in membranous nephropathy with a serum albumin below 20 g/L.

options.rationale: Heavy proteinuria with hypoalbuminaemia, oedema and hyperlipidaemia, in an adult with a bland urinary sediment and negative secondary screen, requires tissue to identify which glomerular lesion is present, because the histology dictates whether immunosuppression is used and which agent. Blockade of the renin angiotensin system is started in parallel because it reduces proteinuria and controls the blood pressure whatever the biopsy shows. (Source: Kidney Health Australia)

Empirical corticosteroid without histology is standard practice in children, in whom minimal change disease accounts for the great majority of cases, but in adults the range of lesions is wide and several of them respond poorly or not at all to steroids. Treating blind risks months of steroid exposure for a lesion that needed something else. (Source: Kidney Health Australia)

Diuresis with salt restriction is a necessary part of symptom control and will be used alongside the correct answer, but as the sole plan it treats the oedema while the glomerular lesion continues unchecked towards chronic kidney disease. (Source: Kidney Health Australia)

Thrombosis is a genuine hazard of this syndrome, and prophylactic anticoagulation is considered once the histology is known, particularly for membranous nephropathy with an albumin below 20 to 25 g/L. It is an adjunct decided after the biopsy rather than the step that replaces it. (Source: Kidney Health Australia)

An occult solid organ malignancy is a recognised secondary cause of membranous nephropathy and is worth pursuing in older patients, but age-appropriate screening rather than whole body imaging is the accepted approach, and it follows rather than precedes the histological diagnosis. (Source: Kidney Health Australia)

explanation.summary: Primary aldosteronism is the commonest specifically treatable cause of hypertension, present in roughly five to ten per cent of all hypertensive patients and closer to twenty per cent of those with resistant hypertension, and it carries excess cardiovascular and renal risk beyond that explained by the blood pressure alone. Only a minority are hypokalaemic, so a normal potassium does not exclude it and screening is indicated in resistant hypertension, hypertension with spontaneous or diuretic induced hypokalaemia, an adrenal incidentaloma, or hypertension with a family history of early stroke. Screening is by the plasma aldosterone to renin ratio drawn mid morning after the patient has been up for at least two hours and seated for five to fifteen minutes. Interpretation depends entirely on preparation: hypokalaemia must be corrected, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists withheld for four to six weeks and potassium wasting diuretics for four weeks, while alpha blockers, slow release verapamil and hydralazine are the safe cover agents. A positive ratio is followed by a confirmatory suppression test and then adrenal vein sampling to separate a unilateral adenoma, which is cured by laparoscopic adrenalectomy, from bilateral hyperplasia, which is treated medically.
key_points: Only a minority of cases are hypokalaemic, so normal potassium does not exclude it
Hypokalaemia suppresses aldosterone and must be corrected before testing
Mineralocorticoid antagonists are withheld four to six weeks and thiazides four weeks
Alpha blockers, slow release verapamil and hydralazine are the safe cover agents
A positive ratio is followed by a confirmatory test and then adrenal vein sampling
explanation.pearls: Remember the direction of each interference rather than a list: drugs that raise renin, including diuretics and blockade of the renin angiotensin system, push the ratio down and cause false negatives, so a positive result on those drugs is still trustworthy, whereas beta blockers lower renin and cause false positives that must be confirmed.

options.rationale: This inverts the rule. Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists are the single class that most reliably invalidates the test by raising renin, and they must be withheld for at least four to six weeks; the calcium channel blocker has only a minor effect and can usually be continued. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

Leaving a blood pressure of 168/102 mmHg untreated for a month to purify a screening test exposes her to stroke and cardiac events for no diagnostic gain, since agents that do not disturb the ratio are available as cover. Complete withdrawal is not required. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

Hypokalaemia directly suppresses aldosterone secretion and can produce a falsely normal ratio, so the potassium is corrected before testing, and potassium wasting diuretics are withheld for four weeks because they raise renin. An alpha blocker, slow release verapamil or hydralazine provides blood pressure cover without disturbing the measurement. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

Her thiazide and her hypokalaemia both push the result towards a false negative, so a normal ratio obtained under these conditions would not exclude the diagnosis and would end the workup prematurely. A positive result under these conditions, by contrast, would still be meaningful. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

Blockade of the renin angiotensin system raises renin and therefore lowers the ratio, so it also biases towards a false negative, but it is generally regarded as acceptable to continue because the direction of the error is conservative. Stopping it while leaving the thiazide and the hypokalaemia in place corrects the smaller problem and leaves the larger ones. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

explanation.summary: Australian practice assesses cardiovascular risk in absolute terms rather than by treating individual risk factors, using the national calculator for adults aged forty five to seventy nine without existing cardiovascular disease, and from thirty for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people. The calculation combines age, sex, smoking status, systolic blood pressure, the ratio of total to protective cholesterol, diabetes status and medication use, and the output is a five year probability of a cardiovascular event. The bands are low below five per cent, intermediate from five to less than ten per cent, and high at ten per cent or above. Low risk is managed with lifestyle advice and reassessment every two years, high risk with blood pressure and lipid lowering treatment alongside lifestyle change, and intermediate risk with a shared decision in which reclassifying factors such as chronic kidney disease, a family history of premature disease, severe mental illness, ethnicity, and in selected cases a coronary artery calcium score, help decide. Some findings bypass the calculator entirely and confer high risk automatically: existing cardiovascular disease, moderate to severe chronic kidney disease, familial hypercholesterolaemia, a low density lipoprotein above 5.0 mmol/L or a systolic pressure of 180 mmHg or more.
key_points: Treat calculated absolute risk, not an isolated abnormal risk factor
Bands are low below five per cent, intermediate five to ten, and high at ten or above
Low risk means lifestyle advice with reassessment every two years
Calcium scoring is for reclassifying intermediate risk, not low risk
Some findings confer high risk automatically and bypass the calculator
explanation.pearls: Know the automatic high risk categories that make the calculator unnecessary: established cardiovascular disease, an estimated filtration rate below 45 mL/min/1.73m2 or persistent albuminuria, familial hypercholesterolaemia, a low density lipoprotein above 5.0 mmol/L, and a systolic pressure of 180 mmHg or a diastolic of 110 mmHg or more, since entering these into the calculator produces a misleadingly reassuring number.

sources.label: Australian guideline for assessing and managing cardiovascular disease risk
Royal Australian College of General Practitioners

options.rationale: Treating the single abnormal number rather than the calculated risk is the error the whole Australian framework exists to prevent, because her high protective fraction, normal blood pressure trajectory, absence of smoking and absence of diabetes place her in the lowest risk band. Lipid lowering becomes appropriate once the calculated risk reaches the treatment threshold. (Source: Australian guideline for assessing and managing cardiovascular disease risk)
source_refs: Australian guideline for assessing and managing cardiovascular disease risk

options.rationale: Combined pharmacotherapy is what the guideline recommends for people at high calculated risk, meaning ten per cent or more over five years, and she is well below that. Her blood pressure also sits below the threshold at which drug treatment is indicated on its own. (Source: Australian guideline for assessing and managing cardiovascular disease risk)
source_refs: Australian guideline for assessing and managing cardiovascular disease risk

options.rationale: Familial hypercholesterolaemia deserves active consideration in anyone with a raised low density lipoprotein, but the diagnosis is supported by a level above about 6.5 mmol/L, tendon xanthomata, or premature coronary disease in a first degree relative, and she has none of those. Referral without those features would flood a scarce service. (Source: Australian guideline for assessing and managing cardiovascular disease risk)
source_refs: Australian guideline for assessing and managing cardiovascular disease risk

options.rationale: A calculated five year risk below five per cent is the low risk band, where the recommendation is lifestyle advice with reassessment rather than drug treatment, because the absolute benefit of medication over that horizon is small and is outweighed by cost, adverse effects and the burden of lifelong therapy. Reassessment every two years catches the rise in risk that comes with age and with any new risk factor. (Source: Australian guideline for assessing and managing cardiovascular disease risk)
source_refs: Australian guideline for assessing and managing cardiovascular disease risk

options.rationale: Calcium scoring has a defined place in reclassifying people whose calculated risk sits in the intermediate band and for whom the decision about medication is genuinely finely balanced. Using it at low risk exposes her to radiation and to the cascade of investigation that follows an incidental finding, without changing the recommendation. (Source: Australian guideline for assessing and managing cardiovascular disease risk)
source_refs: Australian guideline for assessing and managing cardiovascular disease risk

explanation.summary: Undertreatment is the commonest reason adult eczema fails to respond, and the two drivers are choosing a potency below what the site and thickness require and applying far too little for too short a time. Potency is matched to the body region and the chronicity: mild preparations for the face, flexures in infants and short term use, moderate to potent for the limbs and trunk and for lichenified skin, and very potent for palms, soles and resistant plaques. Quantity is taught in fingertip units, one unit being the amount squeezed from the tip of an adult index finger to the first crease, which covers an area about the size of two adult palms. Treatment continues daily until the skin feels smooth rather than stopping when the redness fades, and twice weekly application to the previously affected sites then reduces relapse. Emollient is used liberally alongside, and the conversation about skin thinning is worth having explicitly, because fear of corticosteroids is itself a treatable cause of treatment failure.
key_points: Undertreatment from low potency and small quantities is the usual cause of failure
Match potency to site and thickness, using potent preparations for lichenified limb skin
One fingertip unit covers an area about the size of two adult palms
Continue until the skin is smooth, then use twice weekly maintenance to prevent relapse
Oral corticosteroid produces reliable rebound and is avoided in chronic eczema
explanation.pearls: Ointments outperform creams for lichenified eczema because the greasy base improves hydration and raises potency for the same active drug, so switching from a cream to an ointment of the same corticosteroid is itself a step up the ladder, at the cost of cosmetic acceptability during the working day.

options.rationale: Thickened flexural plaques in an adult represent chronic eczema, and the reason for the failure here is inadequate potency compounded by intermittent application of tiny quantities, not a wrong diagnosis. Moving up the potency ladder to a potent preparation in an ointment base, applied adequately once daily until the skin is smooth, with emollient throughout, is the standard escalation. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists)

Secondary bacterial infection is common in eczema and would justify antibiotics, but it announces itself with weeping, golden crusting or pustules, none of which are present, and the swab grew nothing significant. Oral antibiotics without those signs do not improve eczema outcomes. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

Allergic contact dermatitis is worth investigating in adult eczema that fails adequate treatment, particularly with a suggestive distribution or a new exposure, but neither applies: her distribution is classically flexural and nothing in her contacts has changed. Patch testing becomes reasonable if she fails a proper trial of potent treatment. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists)

Systemic corticosteroid clears eczema quickly and is followed reliably by a rebound flare worse than the original when it stops, which is why it is avoided in chronic eczema except for short rescue courses in severe disease. Escalating the topical potency achieves control without that rebound. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

A fungal infection would show a raised scaly advancing edge with central clearing and would typically be asymmetrical, and her scraping was negative. An antifungal in the flexures will not help, and a combination steroid antifungal preparation blurs the picture further. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

explanation.summary: Chronic hepatitis B moves through phases rather than sitting still, and treatment decisions depend on which phase the patient is in rather than on the surface antigen result alone. In the immune tolerant phase, acquired perinatally and lasting into early adulthood, the e antigen is positive, the viral load is extremely high and the transaminases are normal because there is little immune attack on infected liver cells; antiviral therapy is not indicated, but six monthly monitoring is, because the transition into the immune clearance phase is asymptomatic. Treatment is indicated once there is evidence of liver injury, significant fibrosis or cirrhosis, in pregnancy with a high viral load to prevent transmission, and before immunosuppression or chemotherapy. Hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance with six monthly ultrasound is offered independently of treatment to patients with cirrhosis, to those with a first degree relative with liver cancer, and on the basis of age and background to Asian men from forty and Asian women from fifty. Around a third of Australians living with chronic hepatitis B remain undiagnosed, and contact testing and vaccination of household and sexual contacts is part of every new diagnosis.
key_points: Phase, not surface antigen status alone, determines whether treatment is indicated
Immune tolerant phase has a high viral load with normal transaminases and no fibrosis
Six monthly monitoring detects the silent transition to immune clearance
Treatment is indicated for liver injury, fibrosis, pregnancy with high viral load, or immunosuppression
Household and sexual contacts are tested and vaccinated at diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Flag her file now for antiviral prophylaxis in pregnancy: a maternal viral load above 200000 IU/mL is the threshold at which tenofovir is started in the third trimester, and it reduces mother to child transmission well below what immunoglobulin and vaccination at birth achieve on their own.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Australian consensus recommendations for chronic hepatitis B
Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine

options.rationale: Antiviral treatment is indicated when there is active liver injury, significant fibrosis or cirrhosis, none of which she has, and in this phase the immune system is not attacking infected hepatocytes so suppression yields little while committing her to indefinite therapy. It becomes the right answer the moment her transaminases rise. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Australian consensus recommendations for chronic hepatitis B)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Australian consensus recommendations for chronic hepatitis B

options.rationale: Interferon is a finite course option for selected patients with raised transaminases, lower viral loads and favourable genotype, and a very high viral load with normal enzymes predicts a poor response. Its side effect burden makes it a particularly bad choice in someone who needs no treatment at all. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Australian consensus recommendations for chronic hepatitis B)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Australian consensus recommendations for chronic hepatitis B

options.rationale: Biopsy is now reserved for cases where non-invasive assessment and biochemistry disagree or where another liver disease is suspected, and here elastography, ultrasound and repeated transaminases all agree that there is no significant injury. Biopsy carries a small but real bleeding risk for no added information. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Australian consensus recommendations for chronic hepatitis B)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Australian consensus recommendations for chronic hepatitis B

options.rationale: This phase is not a permanent state: most patients transition to immune clearance with rising transaminases during their twenties or thirties, and the transition is silent until damage accumulates. Discharge also removes the opportunity to test and vaccinate household and sexual contacts. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Australian consensus recommendations for chronic hepatitis B)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Australian consensus recommendations for chronic hepatitis B

options.rationale: Surface and e antigen positive infection with a very high viral load, persistently normal transaminases and no fibrosis describes the immune tolerant phase, in which the appropriate action is structured six monthly surveillance so that the transition to immune clearance is detected when it happens. The monitoring interval is what converts an untreated infection into safe care rather than neglect. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Australian consensus recommendations for chronic hepatitis B)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Australian consensus recommendations for chronic hepatitis B

explanation.summary: Spirometry is read in a fixed order: check the test quality, then the ratio, then the volumes, then the response to bronchodilator. A post bronchodilator ratio below 0.70 defines persistent airflow obstruction and is required to diagnose chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in Australian practice, while severity is graded by the volume as a percentage of predicted, with mild at 60 to 80 per cent, moderate at 40 to 59 and severe below 40. A significant bronchodilator response requires an improvement of at least 12 per cent and at least 200 mL, and both thresholds must be met, which is why the 210 mL matters as much as the percentage.
