Reversibility is not a dichotomy that separates asthma from chronic obstructive disease: many patients with fixed obstruction have a reversible component, and a substantial response with persistent obstruction in a smoker suggests overlapping disease and shifts treatment towards including an inhaled corticosteroid rather than a long-acting bronchodilator alone. A blood eosinophil count helps refine that decision, as higher counts predict benefit from inhaled corticosteroid and lower counts predict pneumonia risk without benefit.
key_points: Read quality, then ratio, then volume, then bronchodilator response, in that order
A post bronchodilator ratio below 0.70 defines persistent airflow obstruction
Severity is graded by the volume as a percentage of predicted, not by the ratio
A significant response needs both 12 per cent and 200 mL, not either alone
Reversibility does not exclude chronic obstructive disease and may indicate overlap
explanation.pearls: Check a blood eosinophil count before choosing her inhaler: a count above 0.3 x10^9/L predicts benefit from adding an inhaled corticosteroid in chronic obstructive disease, while a count below 0.1 x10^9/L predicts little benefit alongside a measurable increase in pneumonia risk, which makes it the cheapest test that changes management here.

sources.label: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X concise guide
Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: The post bronchodilator volume sits at 65 per cent of predicted, well below the normal range, and the ratio of 0.64 is abnormal regardless of the volumes. Reading only the absolute numbers and ignoring the ratio is the commonest error in spirometry interpretation. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X concise guide)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X concise guide

options.rationale: A post bronchodilator ratio below 0.70 establishes persistent airflow obstruction, and the improvement of 210 mL and 14 per cent meets both criteria for a significant bronchodilator response, so both statements are true at once. Significant reversibility does not exclude chronic obstructive disease and, in a heavy smoker with fixed obstruction, raises the possibility of coexisting asthma, which changes the treatment because it makes inhaled corticosteroid appropriate. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X concise guide)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X concise guide

options.rationale: Restriction is suggested by a reduced vital capacity with a preserved or raised ratio, which is the opposite of this pattern, and her ratio is low. Static volumes would be indicated to confirm restriction if the vital capacity were reduced with a normal ratio. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Reversibility and normalisation are different things: her obstruction improved but the ratio remains below 0.70 after the bronchodilator, so the obstruction is persistent rather than reversed. Only complete normalisation of the ratio after bronchodilator argues against the diagnosis. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X concise guide)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X concise guide

options.rationale: The technician has documented three reproducible efforts with acceptable loops, which is the standard for an interpretable test, so there is nothing to repeat. A corticosteroid trial with repeat spirometry is an old approach no longer used to make this diagnosis. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand

explanation.summary: Australian guidance recommends that men aged fifty to sixty nine who decide, after being informed of the benefits and harms, to be tested should have prostate specific antigen every two years, with the offer starting a decade earlier for men with a first degree relative diagnosed young. The action threshold is a total value above 3.0 micrograms/L, and the recommended response to a first raised result is a confirmatory repeat one to three months later rather than immediate referral, because within-person variation, subclinical prostatitis, recent ejaculation, cycling and instrumentation all raise the value transiently. Free to total ratio can add information when the value sits in the intermediate range. If the repeat confirms elevation, referral follows and the contemporary specialist pathway uses multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging to decide whether and where to biopsy, which reduces detection of indolent disease while improving detection of significant cancer. Digital rectal examination adds little as a screening test in general practice but a hard nodule or asymmetry warrants referral regardless of the blood result.
key_points: The Australian action threshold is above 3.0 micrograms/L for men aged fifty to sixty nine
Confirm a first raised result with a repeat at one to three months before referring
Prostatitis, recent ejaculation, cycling and instrumentation raise the value transiently
Magnetic resonance imaging now precedes biopsy in the specialist pathway
A hard nodule on examination warrants referral whatever the blood result
explanation.pearls: If a man is taking finasteride or dutasteride, double the measured value before comparing it with the threshold, because these drugs halve prostate specific antigen within six to twelve months, and a failure to adjust is a recognised cause of delayed diagnosis in men treated for benign enlargement.

sources.label: Prostate Cancer Foundation of Australia and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines
Royal Australian College of General Practitioners

options.rationale: Referring on a single raised value sends a substantial number of men to biopsy whose repeat result will be normal, since the test varies considerably between samples in the same man. Australian guidance also places magnetic resonance imaging before biopsy in the specialist pathway, so this skips two steps. (Source: Prostate Cancer Foundation of Australia and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines)
source_refs: Prostate Cancer Foundation of Australia and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines

options.rationale: A twelve month interval is the surveillance response to a normal result, not to one above the action threshold, and a clinically significant cancer left for a year can progress. Rate of rise over time is also an unreliable basis for referral compared with a confirmed absolute value. (Source: Prostate Cancer Foundation of Australia and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines)
source_refs: Prostate Cancer Foundation of Australia and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines

options.rationale: A result above 3.0 micrograms/L in this age group is an indication for further investigation, but the recommended sequence confirms it with a second sample one to three months later, because biological variation, subclinical prostatitis and recent activity commonly produce a transiently raised value that settles. Confirmation before referral avoids a large number of unnecessary specialist assessments and biopsies. (Source: Prostate Cancer Foundation of Australia and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines)
source_refs: Prostate Cancer Foundation of Australia and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines

options.rationale: Australian guidance uses a single threshold of 3.0 micrograms/L for men aged fifty to sixty nine rather than age adjusted upper limits, so 5.5 is clearly above the action level. Age specific ranges are used in some other countries and applying them here would falsely reassure. (Source: Prostate Cancer Foundation of Australia and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines)
source_refs: Prostate Cancer Foundation of Australia and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines

options.rationale: These drugs treat benign enlargement with obstructive symptoms, which he does not have, and they roughly halve the measured antigen, so starting one now would obscure the very result being investigated. If he were already taking one, the measured value would need doubling before interpretation. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Acute pericarditis is diagnosed when two of four features are present: characteristic positional pleuritic chest pain, a friction rub, widespread ST elevation with PR depression, and a new or worsening pericardial effusion. The tracing is the discriminator that most often decides the case in the emergency department, and the features separating it from occlusive infarction are the diffuse distribution crossing vascular territories, the concave morphology, PR segment depression with reciprocal PR elevation in aVR, and the absence of reciprocal ST depression. Most cases in Australia are viral or idiopathic and follow a respiratory or gastrointestinal illness, while tuberculosis, malignancy, uraemia, autoimmune disease and the post-cardiac injury syndromes account for the remainder. Treatment is a high dose non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug tapered once symptoms and C reactive protein settle, with colchicine for three months, and corticosteroid avoided because it predicts recurrence. Admission is warranted for the high risk features of fever above 38 degrees Celsius, subacute onset, a large effusion or tamponade, failure of anti-inflammatory treatment after a week, a raised troponin indicating myocardial involvement, immunosuppression, trauma or oral anticoagulant use.
key_points: Two of four diagnostic features are required: pain, rub, tracing changes, effusion
Widespread concave elevation with PR depression and no reciprocal depression separates it from infarction
Colchicine for three months halves the recurrence risk and is standard
Corticosteroid relieves symptoms quickly but roughly doubles recurrence
A raised troponin indicates myocardial involvement and warrants admission
explanation.pearls: PR segment elevation in aVR with PR depression everywhere else is close to specific for pericarditis and is the single fastest way to separate it from early repolarisation or occlusion on a crowded tracing, because it reflects atrial injury current rather than ventricular ischaemia.

sources.label: National Heart Foundation of Australia and Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: The ST elevation is widespread across territories supplied by different vessels, is concave rather than convex, has no reciprocal depression and is accompanied by PR depression, none of which fits an occluded artery, and the serial troponins are normal. Activating the catheter laboratory here exposes a young man to an arterial procedure for a condition that is not ischaemic. (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia and Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia and Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Corticosteroid settles the pain quickly and is the intervention most strongly associated with recurrence, roughly doubling the chance of a further episode, so it is reserved for patients who cannot take anti-inflammatory drugs or who have an autoimmune cause. Early symptomatic relief is bought at the cost of a chronic relapsing course. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Positional pleuritic pain with a friction rub, widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression and a raised C reactive protein after a viral illness is acute pericarditis, and the treatment is a high dose anti-inflammatory drug until symptoms and inflammatory markers settle, with colchicine added for three months because it roughly halves the risk of recurrence. Exercise restriction until the markers and the tracing normalise is part of the standard advice. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Pulmonary embolism causes pleuritic pain and must be considered, but he has no risk factors, no tachycardia, no hypoxia and no right heart strain pattern, and anticoagulation in a patient with pericardial inflammation raises the risk of haemorrhagic effusion and tamponade. The positional relief and the friction rub point away from it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

The anti-inflammatory component is correct and this is what was done for decades, but omitting colchicine forgoes the single intervention with randomised evidence of reducing recurrence, and around a quarter to a third of patients treated with an anti-inflammatory alone have a further episode. The difference from the correct answer is the second drug, not the first. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Oxygen induced hypercapnia is one of the few genuinely iatrogenic emergencies in acute medicine, and Australian ambulance and emergency protocols now specify a target saturation of 88 to 92 per cent for patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure. The mechanism is largely a worsening of ventilation and perfusion matching as hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction is released and blood is redirected to poorly ventilated lung, together with the Haldane effect, in which oxygenated haemoglobin carries less carbon dioxide; loss of hypoxic respiratory drive contributes much less than the textbook account suggests, which is why the respiratory rate may be near normal. A randomised Australian prehospital trial found that titrated oxygen roughly halved mortality compared with high flow oxygen in exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Management is controlled oxygen, repeated bronchodilators, systemic corticosteroid, antibiotics where the sputum is purulent, and a repeat gas at twenty to thirty minutes. Non-invasive ventilation is indicated if the pH remains below 7.35 with a carbon dioxide tension above 45 mmHg after that controlled oxygen and medical therapy, and it reduces intubation and mortality.
key_points: Target 88 to 92 per cent saturation in anyone at risk of hypercapnic failure
Ventilation and perfusion mismatch and the Haldane effect drive the rise, not lost drive
A near normal respiratory rate does not exclude oxygen induced hypercapnia
Repeat the gas twenty to thirty minutes after correcting the inspired oxygen
Non-invasive ventilation is indicated if pH stays below 7.35 despite that
explanation.pearls: A bicarbonate of 34 mmol/L tells you this is acute on chronic rather than purely acute retention, because metabolic compensation takes days to develop, and that distinction matters practically: her baseline carbon dioxide is chronically raised, so the treatment target is her usual state rather than a normal gas.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Acute oxygen use
Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X concise guide

options.rationale: Invasive ventilation is reserved for those who fail non-invasive support, cannot protect their airway, are haemodynamically unstable or are in respiratory arrest, and she is rousable with a maintained respiratory rate. Intubating a patient with this degree of airflow obstruction carries a difficult weaning course that is avoided whenever non-invasive measures can work. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X concise guide)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X concise guide

options.rationale: Non-invasive ventilation is the correct treatment for persisting respiratory acidosis and will very likely be needed, but delivering it while the inspired oxygen remains high leaves the driver of the hypercapnia in place, since the machine is entrained with whatever oxygen is supplied. The order of operations matters: titrate the oxygen first, then reassess. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X concise guide)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X concise guide

options.rationale: Removing oxygen entirely from a patient who was at 84 per cent on air twenty five minutes ago risks profound hypoxaemia, which kills faster than hypercapnia. The aim is controlled oxygen to a defined target range, not withdrawal. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Acute oxygen use)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Acute oxygen use

options.rationale: Respiratory stimulants were used before non-invasive ventilation was available and have been superseded because they cause agitation, arrhythmia and seizures while increasing the work of breathing in an already fatiguing patient. There is no current place for this drug in an Australian emergency department. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

A saturation of 99 per cent with a carbon dioxide tension of 78 mmHg after high concentration oxygen is the pattern of oxygen induced hypercapnia, driven mainly by worsened ventilation and perfusion matching and by the Haldane effect rather than by loss of hypoxic drive. Reducing the inspired oxygen to a target of 88 to 92 per cent using a Venturi device, alongside bronchodilators, corticosteroid and antibiotics, corrects the acidosis in many patients, and the repeat gas then decides whether non-invasive ventilation is required. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Acute oxygen use)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Acute oxygen use

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency is present in roughly half of patients with chronic heart failure and is an independent predictor of reduced exercise capacity, poorer quality of life and higher mortality, quite separately from anaemia. The reason ordinary reference ranges mislead is that ferritin behaves as an acute phase protein, so chronic inflammation raises it into the normal range while functional stores are exhausted, and transferrin saturation is therefore the more informative measurement. Heart failure guidelines accordingly use a disease specific definition: ferritin below 100 micrograms/L as absolute deficiency, or ferritin between 100 and 299 micrograms/L with saturation below 20 per cent as functional deficiency. Oral iron does not work in this setting because hepcidin driven by inflammation blocks duodenal absorption, so replacement is intravenous, typically as a single large dose infusion. Guidelines recommend screening for iron deficiency in all patients with new or worsening heart failure and repeating it periodically, and a newly identified deficiency still requires the usual thought about where the iron has gone, including gastrointestinal blood loss and aspirin or anticoagulant use.
key_points: Iron deficiency affects around half of heart failure patients and predicts worse outcomes
Ferritin rises as an acute phase reactant, so the usual lower limit does not apply
The heart failure definition adds ferritin 100 to 299 with saturation below 20 per cent
Oral iron fails because inflammation driven hepcidin blocks absorption
Benefit from intravenous repletion occurs with or without anaemia
explanation.pearls: Check his phosphate four weeks after the infusion: ferric carboxymaltose causes a fibroblast growth factor 23 mediated renal phosphate wasting that produces clinically significant hypophosphataemia in a substantial minority, and repeated infusions without checking have caused osteomalacia and fractures.

sources.label: National Heart Foundation of Australia and Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart failure guidelines
National Blood Authority: Patient blood management guidelines

options.rationale: Oral iron has been tested directly in this population and failed to improve exercise capacity or repletion, because the inflammation of heart failure raises hepcidin and blocks intestinal absorption. The route is what fails here, not the decision to give iron. (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia and Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart failure guidelines)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia and Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart failure guidelines

options.rationale: In heart failure, iron deficiency is defined as ferritin below 100 micrograms/L, or ferritin between 100 and 299 with a transferrin saturation below 20 per cent, and he meets the second limb despite a ferritin inside the laboratory range. Intravenous repletion improves symptoms, quality of life and exercise capacity and reduces heart failure hospitalisation, and the benefit occurs whether or not the patient is anaemic. (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia and Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart failure guidelines)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia and Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart failure guidelines

options.rationale: Transfusion is for symptomatic or severe anaemia, and his haemoglobin of 118 g/L is well above any transfusion threshold, while the volume load carries a real risk of decompensation in a failing ventricle. It also fails to replace the iron stores that are the actual problem. (Source: National Blood Authority: Patient blood management guidelines)
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Patient blood management guidelines

options.rationale: Darbepoetin was tested in systolic heart failure with anaemia and did not improve outcomes while increasing thromboembolic events, so these agents are not used for this indication. They also cannot work without adequate iron available for erythropoiesis. (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia and Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart failure guidelines)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia and Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart failure guidelines

options.rationale: Ferritin is an acute phase reactant and rises with the chronic inflammation of heart failure, so the standard lower limit of 30 micrograms/L does not apply and a value in the low to middle range with a low saturation indicates functional deficiency. Accepting the reference range at face value is the specific error this scenario tests. (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia and Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart failure guidelines)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia and Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart failure guidelines

explanation.summary: Nodular melanoma accounts for around fifteen per cent of Australian melanomas but a disproportionate share of deaths, because it grows vertically from the beginning rather than spreading radially first, and because up to a third are amelanotic and therefore fail every element of the asymmetry, border, colour and diameter rule. The alternative rule for these lesions is elevated, firm and growing for more than a month, and any lesion meeting all three warrants excision regardless of colour or size. Dermatoscopy supports the suspicion when the pigment network is absent and there are polymorphous vessels and milky red areas. The correct diagnostic procedure is complete excisional biopsy with a 2 mm margin extending to subcutaneous fat, because Breslow thickness determines both prognosis and the width of the definitive re-excision, which ranges from 5 mm for in situ disease to 1 cm for tumours up to 1 mm thick and up to 2 cm for thicker lesions. Sentinel lymph node biopsy is discussed for tumours above 0.8 mm thick or with ulceration, primarily for staging and access to adjuvant therapy rather than for a proven survival benefit.
key_points: Up to a third of nodular melanomas are amelanotic and defeat the pigment based rule
Elevated, firm and growing for over a month is the rule that catches them
Complete excisional biopsy with a 2 mm margin to fat preserves depth measurement
Breslow thickness determines prognosis and the width of definitive re-excision
Short interval monitoring is for flat equivocal lesions, never for a growing nodule
explanation.pearls: Any firm pink nodule that has appeared and grown over weeks in an older Australian with heavy sun damage is excised rather than watched, because the median Breslow thickness of nodular melanoma at diagnosis is already above 2 mm and each additional month of observation adds measurable depth to a tumour whose prognosis is set by that number.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Clinical practice guidelines for melanoma
Royal Australian College of General Practitioners

options.rationale: A partial sample can miss the deepest part of the tumour, and because prognosis and the width of the definitive excision both depend on the maximum depth measured in millimetres, an underestimate leads directly to an inadequate margin. Partial biopsy is acceptable only for very large lesions or cosmetically critical sites where complete removal is impractical. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Clinical practice guidelines for melanoma)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Clinical practice guidelines for melanoma

options.rationale: A shave removes the superficial portion and transects the base of a nodular lesion, which destroys the ability to measure depth accurately. It is a reasonable technique for a suspected basal cell carcinoma or a flat pigmented lesion, and a poor one for a raised nodule. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Clinical practice guidelines for melanoma)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Clinical practice guidelines for melanoma

options.rationale: Cryotherapy destroys tissue without providing histology, so a melanoma treated this way is both inadequately removed and rendered impossible to stage. It is appropriate for solar keratoses, of which he has many, but not for a growing nodule. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists)

A firm elevated lesion growing over weeks, with absent pigment network and polymorphous vessels on dermatoscopy, must be treated as a possible nodular melanoma, and complete excisional biopsy with a narrow 2 mm margin taken to the subcutaneous fat is the required technique because it preserves accurate measurement of the tumour depth. The definitive wider margin is then chosen once that depth is known. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Clinical practice guidelines for melanoma)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Clinical practice guidelines for melanoma

options.rationale: Short interval digital monitoring is a legitimate strategy for flat equivocal pigmented lesions, where change over three months distinguishes benign from malignant. It is explicitly not appropriate for a raised, firm, growing nodule, because this subtype grows vertically from the outset and gains depth during the observation period. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Clinical practice guidelines for melanoma)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Clinical practice guidelines for melanoma

explanation.summary: Fibromyalgia is a disorder of central pain processing, not a diagnosis of exclusion, and it is defined by widespread pain for at least three months together with fatigue, unrefreshing sleep and cognitive symptoms, commonly with irritable bowel, headache and mood symptoms alongside. The most useful discriminators from an inflammatory rheumatic disease are stiffness that persists all day rather than easing after the first hour, tenderness on light pressure over muscle rather than joint line tenderness or swelling, and normal inflammatory markers. Polymyalgia rheumatica is the differential that most often leads to harm, because a partial response to corticosteroid is non-specific and, once a patient is on prednisolone, coming off it is difficult and the diagnostic label becomes fixed; true polymyalgia produces girdle pain with marked morning stiffness and raised markers in over ninety per cent. A limited investigation panel covering full blood count, inflammatory markers, creatine kinase, thyroid function and vitamin D is sufficient in the absence of localising features. Treatment is education, graded aerobic exercise, cognitive behavioural therapy and sleep management, with amitriptyline, duloxetine or pregabalin as adjuncts, and opioids and corticosteroids specifically avoided.
key_points: Diagnosed positively on the clinical pattern, not by excluding everything else
All day stiffness and light pressure muscle tenderness argue against inflammatory disease
Normal inflammatory markers make polymyalgia rheumatica very unlikely
Graded exercise, sleep focused therapy and education are first line
Opioids worsen central pain disorders and corticosteroids anchor a wrong diagnosis
explanation.pearls: A diagnostic trial of prednisolone should be declined: response to corticosteroid is not specific to polymyalgia rheumatica, patients with central pain disorders frequently report initial improvement, and the practical consequence is a patient on steroid for years with the adrenal suppression, bone loss and weight gain that go with it.

sources.label: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners

options.rationale: Widespread pain of more than three months with unrefreshing sleep, cognitive difficulty and associated functional bowel symptoms, in the presence of entirely normal inflammatory markers and no synovitis, is a central pain disorder diagnosed positively rather than by exclusion. Graded aerobic exercise and cognitive behavioural therapy directed at sleep and pain related distress have the best evidence, and a confident explanation of the mechanism is the intervention that makes the rest possible. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)

The pattern does not fit polymyalgia rheumatica, which causes proximal shoulder and hip girdle pain with prolonged morning stiffness and a raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate or C reactive protein in the great majority, and her markers are normal while her pain is distal as well as proximal. A partial response to steroid is common in any painful condition and would anchor her to a wrong diagnosis and years of exposure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

Investigating for large vessel vasculitis requires cranial symptoms such as new headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication or visual disturbance, or a raised inflammatory marker, and she has none of these. Imaging a normal artery to answer a question nobody has asked adds cost and a false positive risk. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)

Opioids perform poorly in central pain disorders, and long term use is associated with worsening pain through hyperalgesia, along with dependence and cognitive effects that compound the symptoms she already has. Australian guidance advises specifically against them for this condition. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

Extensive imaging in the absence of objective abnormality reliably produces incidental findings that generate further tests and reinforce the belief that something has been missed, which worsens outcomes in this condition. The diagnosis is made on the clinical pattern with a limited blood panel. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)

explanation.summary: The combination of a diuretic, an inhibitor of the renin angiotensin system and a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug is known as the triple whammy and roughly triples the risk of acute kidney injury, because the diuretic depletes volume, the anti-inflammatory removes the prostaglandin mediated afferent arteriolar dilatation that preserves glomerular perfusion, and the renin blocker removes the angiotensin mediated efferent constriction that preserves filtration pressure. Any acute volume loss on top of that, typically gastroenteritis in an older person, produces exactly this picture. Sick day management plans are issued in Australian practice to patients on these drugs and instruct them to withhold specified medications during any illness with vomiting, diarrhoea, fever or sweats, and to restart when eating and drinking normally for twenty four to forty eight hours. The classes covered are the renin angiotensin blockers, diuretics, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, metformin and sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors. The latter deserve particular attention because they can precipitate ketoacidosis with only modestly raised glucose during illness, so ketones are measured rather than relying on the glucose reading.
key_points: Diuretic plus renin blocker plus anti-inflammatory is the triple whammy of acute kidney injury
Anti-inflammatories remove afferent dilatation and renin blockers remove efferent constriction
Sick day rules also cover metformin and sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors
Restart withheld drugs after twenty four to forty eight hours of normal intake
Statins and most other regular medicines are continued rather than suspended
explanation.pearls: Measure blood ketones rather than glucose in any unwell patient taking a sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor, because ketoacidosis on these drugs typically occurs with a glucose below 14 mmol/L and is missed entirely if the glucose reading is used as the screening test.

sources.label: Kidney Health Australia: Chronic kidney disease management in primary care

options.rationale: The diuretic, the blocker of the renin angiotensin system and the anti-inflammatory are the three drugs that together convert a simple volume loss into acute kidney injury, and all three are withheld. Metformin is withheld because it accumulates and risks lactic acidosis at this level of function, and the sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor because it drives osmotic diuresis and ketogenesis during illness, which is why sick day advice covers five drugs here rather than three. (Source: Kidney Health Australia: Chronic kidney disease management in primary care)
source_refs: Kidney Health Australia: Chronic kidney disease management in primary care

options.rationale: Stopping the three drugs responsible for the haemodynamic injury is the core of the answer and is what most clinicians remember, but continuing metformin at an estimated filtration rate in the twenties risks lactic acidosis, and continuing the glucose lowering agent that acts on the kidney tubule prolongs the fluid losses. (Source: Kidney Health Australia: Chronic kidney disease management in primary care)
source_refs: Kidney Health Australia: Chronic kidney disease management in primary care

options.rationale: Withholding the diabetes medications addresses the metabolic risks and leaves the cause of the injury running, since the combination of a diuretic, a blocker of the renin angiotensin system and a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory is what removes the kidney's ability to defend its filtration pressure during volume depletion. (Source: Kidney Health Australia: Chronic kidney disease management in primary care)
source_refs: Kidney Health Australia: Chronic kidney disease management in primary care

options.rationale: The anti-inflammatory is the most obviously avoidable of the group and the one he chose himself, but removing it alone leaves efferent arteriolar dilatation from the renin blocker and ongoing sodium loss from the thiazide like diuretic in a man who is already volume depleted. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

The statin is neither nephrotoxic nor cleared in a way that matters here, and reflexively stopping everything is how patients end up never restarting drugs with prognostic benefit. Sick day rules name specific classes rather than suspending the whole list. (Source: Kidney Health Australia: Chronic kidney disease management in primary care)
source_refs: Kidney Health Australia: Chronic kidney disease management in primary care

explanation.summary: Hypertensive emergency is severe hypertension accompanied by acute end-organ injury, and the organ involved dictates both the drug and the target. Acute pulmonary oedema, encephalopathy, aortic dissection, eclampsia, acute coronary syndrome and acute kidney injury are the usual syndromes, and without any of them the situation is hypertensive urgency, managed with oral agents over twenty four to forty eight hours and outpatient follow up. In pulmonary oedema the mechanism is afterload mismatch rather than fluid excess, so a titratable nitrate infusion is the primary agent, combined with high flow oxygen and non-invasive ventilation, and diuretic in modest dose only if there is genuine volume overload. The general target is a reduction of no more than twenty to twenty five per cent in the mean arterial pressure in the first hour, then to around 160 over 100 mmHg over the next several hours, because chronic hypertension shifts cerebral autoregulation rightwards and an abrupt normalisation can cause watershed infarction and blindness. The two exceptions that require faster and deeper reduction are aortic dissection, where the systolic target is under 120 mmHg within twenty minutes with beta blockade first, and eclampsia.
key_points: Emergency requires acute end-organ injury; without it the situation is urgency
Pulmonary oedema here is an afterload problem rather than volume overload
A titratable nitrate infusion with oxygen and non-invasive ventilation is first line
Limit the fall to twenty to twenty five per cent of mean pressure in the first hour
Aortic dissection and eclampsia are the exceptions requiring faster reduction
explanation.pearls: Flame haemorrhages without papilloedema place this at grade 3 retinopathy, which tells you the hypertension is severe and accelerated but has not yet produced raised intracranial pressure, and a bedside fundoscopy in a patient who cannot give a history is often the fastest way to establish that the blood pressure is chronic rather than an acute pain response.

sources.label: National Heart Foundation of Australia and Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: These patients are usually not volume overloaded but have redistributed fluid into the lungs under an enormous afterload, so large diuretic doses can worsen intravascular depletion and raise creatinine while doing little for the mechanism. Diuretic is an adjunct, given in modest dose, not the primary treatment. (Source: National Heart Foundation of Australia and Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation of Australia and Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: The pressure target is right but the agent is wrong: intravenous beta blockade in acute pulmonary oedema removes the sympathetic support the failing ventricle is relying on and can precipitate cardiogenic shock. Beta blockade belongs in aortic dissection and after the acute decompensation has resolved. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Severe hypertension with acute pulmonary oedema is driven by afterload, and a titratable nitrate infusion reduces preload at low dose and afterload as it is increased, relieving the oedema within minutes, alongside high flow oxygen and non-invasive ventilation. The reduction is limited to about twenty to twenty five per cent of the mean arterial pressure in the first hour because a chronically hypertensive brain and kidney have shifted their autoregulation and cannot tolerate a rapid fall. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Short-acting sublingual calcium channel blockade produces an uncontrolled and unpredictable fall in pressure and has caused strokes and myocardial infarction, which is why it was abandoned. It combines the wrong route with the wrong target. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Gradual oral reduction over a day is exactly right for severe hypertension without organ damage, which is urgency rather than emergency, but he has acute pulmonary oedema and a rising troponin, so there is organ damage happening now and an oral agent cannot be titrated against it. The distinction between the two situations is the presence of acute end-organ injury. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Infective endocarditis is diagnosed using the modified Duke criteria, in which persistently positive blood cultures with a typical organism and echocardiographic evidence of endocardial involvement are the two major criteria. Because the bacteraemia is continuous rather than intermittent, cultures are positive in the great majority of untreated patients, and the commonest reason for culture negative disease in Australia is antibiotics given before the samples were taken. Three sets from separate sites over an hour are standard in a stable subacute presentation. Empirical therapy is started immediately, without waiting, only when the patient is septic, has a prosthetic valve, or is deteriorating. Transthoracic echocardiography is performed first and transoesophageal imaging follows when it is negative or non diagnostic in a patient with high clinical suspicion.
key_points: Three sets of cultures from separate sites before antibiotics in stable disease
Prior antibiotics are the commonest cause of culture negative endocarditis
Start empirical therapy without waiting if septic or a prosthetic valve is involved
Transoesophageal imaging follows a negative transthoracic study when suspicion is high
A negative echocardiogram does not exclude the diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Ask about intravenous drug use, recent intravascular lines and dental work, and in anyone over 50 with Streptococcus gallolyticus bacteraemia arrange a colonoscopy, because that organism is associated with colonic neoplasia in around half of cases and the endocarditis is what brings the cancer to attention.

sources.label: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Infective endocarditis

options.rationale: A single set is far less sensitive and cannot separate a true pathogen from a contaminant, which matters when the decision is six weeks of intravenous therapy. Immediate empirical treatment is reserved for sepsis, prosthetic valve involvement or haemodynamic instability. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

This empirical combination is used when methicillin resistant organisms or prosthetic material are likely, whereas a stable native valve presentation after dental work is typically viridans streptococcal. Committing to that regimen before the organism is known exposes him to renal and vestibular toxicity he may not need. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

In a haemodynamically stable subacute presentation the priority is a microbiological diagnosis, because a single dose of antibiotic can sterilise the cultures and leave months of therapy directed blindly. Three separate sets substantially raise the yield and help distinguish true bacteraemia from skin contaminants. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Oral therapy does not achieve the sustained bactericidal concentrations needed to sterilise a vegetation, and ambulatory management of suspected endocarditis misses the complications that develop over days. It also contaminates the cultures that have not yet been taken. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Echocardiography is essential but is a parallel investigation rather than a prerequisite, and a negative study does not exclude the diagnosis. Organising it first delays the cultures that must be taken before any antibiotic is given. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Latent tuberculosis infection means viable organisms are contained by an intact immune response, with no symptoms, a normal radiograph and no infectivity. Australia has a low incidence overall, so most latent infection is found in people born overseas in higher incidence countries, and screening is targeted rather than universal. Interferon gamma release assays measure the response to antigens that are absent from the vaccine strain and from most environmental mycobacteria, so a positive result is not explained by previous vaccination. Before starting a tumour necrosis factor inhibitor, active disease must be excluded clinically and radiologically, and latent infection is then treated with isoniazid for six to nine months or rifampicin for four months, with the biologic commenced after at least four weeks. Monthly review for hepatotoxicity and for adherence continues throughout.
key_points: Interferon gamma release assays are not confounded by bacille Calmette Guerin vaccination
Exclude active disease clinically and radiologically before treating as latent
Isoniazid for six to nine months or rifampicin for four months are the options
Start the biologic after at least four weeks of latent infection treatment
Reactivation on these agents is often extrapulmonary or disseminated
explanation.pearls: Check for interacting medications before choosing rifampicin, because it induces cytochrome P450 enzymes strongly enough to render the combined oral contraceptive pill, many direct oral anticoagulants and several antiretrovirals ineffective, and isoniazid is often preferred for that reason despite the longer course.

sources.label: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee: Management of latent tuberculosis infection

options.rationale: Four drug therapy treats active disease, which she does not have given a normal radiograph and no symptoms. Using it for latent infection exposes her to unnecessary hepatotoxicity, ocular toxicity and months of additional treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Repeating the assay to obtain a preferred answer is not a validated strategy, and an indeterminate or discordant repeat leaves the situation less clear rather than more. A positive result in someone from a high incidence country is most likely to be true. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee: Management of latent tuberculosis infection)
source_refs: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee: Management of latent tuberculosis infection

options.rationale: Tumour necrosis factor inhibitors markedly increase the risk of reactivation, so latent infection is treated before the biologic starts, with isoniazid for six to nine months or rifampicin for four months. Four weeks of treatment before starting the biologic is the accepted compromise between reactivation risk and delaying disease control. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Reactivation on these agents is often disseminated or extrapulmonary and can be fatal, so waiting for symptoms forfeits the entire purpose of screening. The screening test was done precisely to prevent this sequence. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Interferon gamma release assays use antigens absent from the vaccine strain, so unlike the tuberculin skin test they are not confounded by prior vaccination. Dismissing the result on that basis is a common and consequential error. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee: Management of latent tuberculosis infection)
source_refs: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee: Management of latent tuberculosis infection

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is the acute failure of cortisol and aldosterone availability to meet demand, and in a patient already on replacement it is usually precipitated by intercurrent illness, particularly gastroenteritis, where the oral dose cannot be absorbed. The clinical picture is hypotension out of proportion to fluid loss, with hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia and a mild metabolic acidosis. Treatment is parenteral hydrocortisone 100 mg given immediately, followed by either repeated doses or a continuous infusion, along with sodium chloride 0.9 percent and glucose. At high doses hydrocortisone provides sufficient mineralocorticoid effect that fludrocortisone is not needed acutely. The sick day rules that prevent this are doubling or tripling the oral dose during febrile illness, and using an intramuscular hydrocortisone ampoule at home when vomiting begins.
key_points: Give parenteral hydrocortisone before any confirmatory investigation
Hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia is the classic biochemistry
Sodium chloride 0.9 percent with glucose restores volume and corrects hypoglycaemia
Dexamethasone is reserved for when the diagnosis is not yet established
Fludrocortisone is unnecessary while high dose hydrocortisone is running
explanation.pearls: Every patient on long term replacement should leave with an intramuscular hydrocortisone ampoule, a written sick day plan and a medical alert bracelet, because the interval between first vomit and circulatory collapse can be a matter of hours and the ampoule given at home is what converts a crisis into a hospital visit.

options.rationale: He has an adrenal crisis, shown by postural hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia in someone who cannot absorb oral steroid. Parenteral hydrocortisone is given before any confirmatory testing, together with fluid and glucose, because delay is what kills in this condition. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Oral steroid cannot be relied upon in a patient who has vomited every dose, and the two hour wait is spent in circulatory failure. Antiemetics are useful adjuncts once parenteral steroid and fluid are running. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Dexamethasone is the agent chosen only when the diagnosis is not yet established and cortisol testing must remain interpretable, because it has negligible mineralocorticoid activity. In known primary adrenal insufficiency hydrocortisone provides both the glucocorticoid and the mineralocorticoid effect needed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Dynamic testing is for establishing the diagnosis in someone not known to have the condition, and he was diagnosed eight years ago. Withholding steroid to preserve a test result in a patient in crisis inverts the priorities. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

A potassium of 5.3 mmol/L does not warrant membrane stabilisation or shifting therapy, and it corrects as the volume deficit and mineralocorticoid deficiency are treated. Treating the electrolyte first delays the treatment that fixes the cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Osteoporosis is defined densitometrically by a T score of minus 2.5 or lower, but it is also defined clinically by a fracture occurring from a fall from standing height or less, and the clinical definition takes precedence where the two disagree. Vertebral fractures are the most common osteoporotic fracture and most occur without a fall at all, often coming to attention incidentally on imaging done for another reason. Their importance is prognostic: a prevalent vertebral fracture multiplies the risk of a further vertebral fracture roughly fivefold and of hip fracture roughly twofold, and the risk is concentrated in the first year. Treatment in Australia is therefore indicated after any minimal trauma fracture in a person over 50 regardless of density, and the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme criteria reflect this. First line agents are oral bisphosphonates, with intravenous zoledronic acid or subcutaneous denosumab where adherence or tolerance is a problem.
key_points: Minimal trauma fracture over age 50 defines osteoporosis irrespective of T score
Vertebral fractures often occur without a fall and are frequently found incidentally
Risk of the next fracture is highest in the twelve months after the first
Calcium, vitamin D and exercise are adjuncts, not substitutes for antiresorptive therapy
Vertebroplasty did not outperform sham in randomised comparisons
explanation.pearls: Measure height at every review and investigate a loss of 3 cm or more, because most vertebral fractures never present with acute pain and a height drop is often the only sign that the patient has already declared herself to be in the highest risk group.

sources.label: RACGP and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management and fracture prevention

options.rationale: Her screening bloods including protein electrophoresis are normal and the radiograph shows no lytic lesion, so secondary causes have been reasonably addressed. Imaging is reserved for atypical features such as neurological signs, fracture above the fourth thoracic vertebra or constitutional symptoms. (Source: RACGP and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management and fracture prevention)
source_refs: RACGP and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management and fracture prevention

options.rationale: Calcium, vitamin D and exercise are adjuncts that do not reduce vertebral fracture risk to any meaningful degree on their own. The year after a vertebral fracture carries the highest risk of the next one, which is exactly when she would be untreated. (Source: RACGP and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management and fracture prevention)
source_refs: RACGP and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management and fracture prevention

options.rationale: Around half of women with a minimal trauma vertebral fracture have a T score above that threshold, so this rule would deny treatment to the group at highest short term risk. Density and fracture are separate and complementary indications. (Source: RACGP and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management and fracture prevention)
source_refs: RACGP and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management and fracture prevention

options.rationale: Randomised trials with sham controls found no meaningful benefit of vertebroplasty over placebo for pain from these fractures, and it does nothing for the systemic disease. The fracture itself usually settles over six to eight weeks with analgesia. (Source: RACGP and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management and fracture prevention)
source_refs: RACGP and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management and fracture prevention

options.rationale: A vertebral fracture from a trivial mechanism establishes osteoporosis clinically and predicts further fractures regardless of the density result, so treatment starts immediately. The scan is still worth doing as a baseline for monitoring, not as a gate to treatment. (Source: RACGP and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management and fracture prevention)
source_refs: RACGP and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management and fracture prevention

explanation.summary: Management of major bleeding on an anticoagulant runs on three parallel tracks: resuscitation with blood products, mechanical or endoscopic control of the source, and reversal of the drug. The reversal agent depends entirely on which drug is involved: warfarin is reversed with vitamin K plus prothrombin complex concentrate. Dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor, has a specific antidote in idarucizumab and is also substantially dialysable because it has low protein binding. The factor Xa inhibitors apixaban and rivaroxaban are highly protein bound, so dialysis is ineffective, and the specific agent andexanet alfa is not routinely available in Australia, leaving prothrombin complex concentrate as the recommended option for life threatening bleeding. Activated charcoal has a role if ingestion was within the preceding two hours, and tranexamic acid may be added for bleeding at a suitable site.
key_points: Prothrombin complex concentrate is used for major bleeding on factor Xa inhibitors
Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran only and does nothing for apixaban
Dabigatran is dialysable because protein binding is low; apixaban is not
Vitamin K and plasma do not reverse direct oral anticoagulants
Reversal never substitutes for source control and transfusion
explanation.pearls: Ask for the time of the last dose, because these drugs have half lives of around twelve hours and a patient who took their last dose more than two half lives ago may need no reversal at all, while one who took it within two hours may benefit from activated charcoal as well as concentrate.

sources.label: National Blood Authority: Patient blood management guidelines

options.rationale: Apixaban is around 87 percent protein bound, so dialysis removes very little, unlike dabigatran which is only 35 percent bound and is dialysable. Arranging dialysis in a shocked patient also consumes time that endoscopy needs. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Plasma does not overcome direct factor Xa inhibition and delivers a large volume that worsens dilution and precipitates fluid overload in an older patient. It is not a reversal agent for these drugs. (Source: National Blood Authority: Patient blood management guidelines)
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Patient blood management guidelines

options.rationale: Vitamin K restores the hepatic synthesis of factors blocked by warfarin and has no effect whatever on a direct factor Xa inhibitor. Giving it wastes the window in which effective reversal is possible. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

For life threatening bleeding on a factor Xa inhibitor, prothrombin complex concentrate is the agent available in Australian hospitals and is recommended alongside source control and transfusion. It restores thrombin generation even though it does not remove the drug from the circulation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Idarucizumab is a monoclonal antibody fragment that binds dabigatran specifically and has no activity against apixaban. Selecting a reversal agent requires knowing which anticoagulant the patient is actually taking. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Acute aortic dissection is classified by whether the ascending aorta is involved: type A involves it and is a surgical emergency, while type B spares it and is usually managed medically unless there is malperfusion or rupture. Mortality in untreated type A disease rises by roughly 1 to 2 percent per hour in the first 48 hours, so the priorities are immediate surgical referral and haemodynamic control while that is arranged. The pharmacological principle is anti impulse therapy: reduce both the blood pressure and the rate of rise of pressure, since the shear force propagating the flap depends on both. Beta blockade to a heart rate below 60 beats per minute comes first, and a vasodilator is added to reach a systolic pressure of 100 to 120 mmHg only after the rate is controlled. Analgesia with opioid also lowers sympathetic drive and is part of the treatment rather than a comfort measure.
key_points: Type A involves the ascending aorta and needs immediate surgery
Control heart rate below 60 beats per minute before adding a vasodilator
Target systolic pressure 100 to 120 mmHg once rate control is achieved
Vasodilator first causes reflex tachycardia and extends the dissection
Anticoagulation is hazardous and reflects the common misdiagnosis
explanation.pearls: Beware the dissection that occludes a coronary ostium, most often the right, producing an inferior pattern on the electrocardiogram in a patient with tearing pain, because thrombolysis or antiplatelet loading given for that apparent infarct is rapidly fatal and the interarm pressure difference is often the only clue.

sources.label: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Aortic disease

options.rationale: A vasodilator given before rate control produces reflex tachycardia and a steeper rate of pressure rise, which is the specific force that extends the dissection. The order of these two drugs is the whole point of the question. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Nitrate monotherapy causes the same reflex tachycardia problem and treating to a symptom endpoint leaves the haemodynamic targets unmet. Analgesia is important but is an adjunct to rate and pressure control. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Propagation of the tear depends on the rate of rise of aortic pressure as well as the pressure itself, so rate control comes first and the vasodilator follows once the heart rate is controlled. Esmolol is preferred because its very short half life allows rapid titration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Anticoagulation and antiplatelet therapy are actively dangerous here and reflect the commonest misdiagnosis, since the pain and the interarm difference can be mistaken for an acute coronary syndrome. The imaging has already excluded that pathway. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Hydralazine is a direct arteriolar dilator with an unpredictable response and marked reflex tachycardia, and bolus dosing produces exactly the pressure swings that must be avoided. Continuous infusions with short half lives are used instead. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Pleural fluid is separated into transudate and exudate because the two point to different disease groups: transudates arise from altered hydrostatic or oncotic pressure in heart failure, cirrhosis or nephrotic syndrome, while exudates reflect pleural inflammation, infection, malignancy or infarction. Light's criteria classify fluid as exudative if the pleural to serum protein ratio exceeds 0.5, the pleural to serum lactate dehydrogenase ratio exceeds 0.6, or the pleural lactate dehydrogenase exceeds two thirds of the upper limit of the serum reference range. The criteria are highly sensitive for exudates but misclassify roughly a quarter of transudates, most often in patients who have been diuresed, because removing water concentrates the solutes left behind. When the clinical picture is clearly heart failure, a serum to pleural albumin gradient above 12 g/L reclassifies the fluid as a transudate and prevents a fruitless search for pleural disease.
key_points: Light's criteria are sensitive for exudates but overcall transudates after diuresis
A serum to pleural albumin gradient above 12 g/L indicates a transudate
Drainage decisions in infection rest on pH, glucose, pus and microbiology
Malignant effusions are usually unilateral and often blood stained
Interpret the fluid alongside the clinical syndrome, not in isolation
explanation.pearls: Send pleural fluid for pH in a blood gas syringe on ice and analyse it in a blood gas machine rather than sending it in a plain tube to the general laboratory, because delay and air exposure shift the value and pH is the single measurement that decides whether a parapneumonic effusion needs a drain.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease

options.rationale: The protein ratio of 0.52 does exceed the threshold, but applying the criteria without accounting for four days of aggressive diuresis produces a false positive. Acting on that label leads to unnecessary investigation of an effusion that is resolving. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

Drainage is indicated by pleural pH below 7.2, low glucose, frank pus or positive microbiology, none of which is present, and he is afebrile with no pleuritic pain. Draining on the basis of protein alone exposes him to an avoidable procedure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

A validated correction already resolves this apparent conflict without an invasive procedure, so proceeding to biopsy would be treating the discrepancy rather than the patient. Biopsy is reserved for a genuine undiagnosed exudate after less invasive testing. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

Diuresis concentrates protein and lactate dehydrogenase in the pleural space and shifts a genuine transudate across the exudative thresholds in about a quarter of treated patients. The albumin gradient, here 14 g/L, is the correction applied in exactly this situation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

Malignant effusions are usually unilateral, often blood stained and frequently reaccumulate rapidly, and a straw coloured bilateral effusion in decompensated heart failure fits a different mechanism. Cytology is still sent, but it is not the leading hypothesis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

explanation.summary: Vitamin B12 is a cofactor for methylmalonyl coenzyme A mutase and methionine synthase, so deficiency causes accumulation of methylmalonic acid and homocysteine before the haematological picture changes. Neurological disease can therefore precede anaemia entirely, and around a quarter of patients with subacute combined degeneration have a normal blood count and a normal mean corpuscular volume. The serum assay measures total rather than biologically available vitamin and is unreliable between roughly 150 and 250 picomol/L, which is where metabolite testing earns its place. Metformin reduces ileal absorption and long term acid suppression impairs release of dietary vitamin from protein, and both are common Australian contributors. Treatment of neurological disease is with parenteral hydroxocobalamin, loading on alternate days and then maintaining three monthly, and the prognosis depends heavily on how long symptoms have been present before replacement starts.
key_points: Neurological disease can precede any change in the blood count
Methylmalonic acid confirms deficiency when the serum level is low normal
Extensor plantars and a positive Romberg test point away from diabetic neuropathy
Parenteral replacement is used when there is neurological involvement
Metformin and long term acid suppression are common contributing causes
explanation.pearls: Check the vitamin level before giving folate to anyone with macrocytosis, because folate corrects the anaemia while cobalamin deficiency continues to demyelinate the cord, and the patient who looks better haematologically is the one who arrives later with an irreversible gait disorder.

options.rationale: The raised methylmalonic acid establishes functional deficiency at the tissue level despite a serum value inside the reference interval, and neurological involvement mandates parenteral loading rather than oral replacement. Maintenance continues indefinitely while the causes, here metformin and acid suppression, remain. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Serum vitamin B12 measures total rather than active vitamin and performs poorly in the low normal range, which is why methylmalonic acid was measured. Repeating an insensitive test while the cord is progressively demyelinating is the classic avoidable error. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Diabetic neuropathy does not produce extensor plantar responses or a positive Romberg test, because it spares the corticospinal tracts and dorsal columns. Those two findings are the disconfirming features that redirect the diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Folate given when the real deficiency is cobalamin corrects the blood picture while the neurological damage continues and can accelerate it. Folate is replaced only after cobalamin status has been addressed. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

High dose oral replacement works for uncomplicated deficiency through passive absorption, but neurological disease is treated parenterally because the deficit becomes irreversible if correction is slow or incomplete. Three months of uncertainty is too long when the cord is involved. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Inhaled corticosteroid in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is not for everyone: it reduces exacerbations in some patients and raises the risk of pneumonia in all of them, so selection matters. The blood eosinophil count has emerged as the practical biomarker, with little benefit below 0.1 x10^9/L, uncertain benefit between 0.1 and 0.3, and a clear reduction in exacerbations at 0.3 x10^9/L and above. Australian practice escalates from a single long-acting bronchodilator, to dual bronchodilation, to triple therapy in patients who continue to exacerbate, and adds the corticosteroid on the basis of exacerbation frequency and eosinophil count rather than symptom burden alone. Before escalating, adherence, inhaler technique, smoking status, vaccination, pulmonary rehabilitation and alternative diagnoses such as bronchiectasis and heart failure should all be reviewed, since each is a commoner reason for apparent treatment failure than the inhaler itself.
key_points: Blood eosinophils of 0.3 x10^9/L or above predict benefit from inhaled corticosteroid
Below 0.1 x10^9/L the pneumonia risk outweighs the benefit
Escalate to triple therapy rather than swapping one agent for another
Check adherence, technique and alternative diagnoses before escalating
Prophylactic macrolide is a later option requiring hearing and cardiac screening
explanation.pearls: Recheck the eosinophil count when the patient is well and off systemic corticosteroid, because a sample taken during an exacerbation or within weeks of a prednisolone course is suppressed and will wrongly place a steroid responsive patient in the group predicted not to benefit.

options.rationale: Withdrawing the muscarinic antagonist removes the bronchodilator with the strongest evidence for preventing exacerbations, so this trades one benefit for another rather than adding to it. Triple therapy outperforms either dual combination in this group. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X plan)

Switching within the same class rarely changes exacerbation frequency when adherence and technique are already good, and it delays escalation in a woman having an exacerbation every three months. Device switches matter more than molecule switches in this class. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X plan)

Prophylactic macrolide is a reasonable option for frequent exacerbators but sits after inhaled escalation, particularly when the eosinophil count predicts corticosteroid response. It also requires baseline hearing assessment and electrocardiography for the corrected QT interval. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X plan)

Long term systemic corticosteroid has no place in stable disease and causes osteoporosis, diabetes, myopathy and skin fragility for no reduction in exacerbations. Repeated courses are an argument for inhaled escalation, not for continuous oral steroid. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X plan)

A blood eosinophil count of 0.3 x10^9/L or above predicts a worthwhile reduction in exacerbations from inhaled corticosteroid in someone still exacerbating on dual bronchodilation. Her frequent exacerbations and hospital admission make that benefit likely to outweigh the pneumonia risk. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia: COPD-X plan)

explanation.summary: Necrotising soft tissue infection is distinguished from cellulitis not by the redness but by the combination of severe pain out of proportion to appearance, rapid progression despite antibiotics, systemic toxicity, tense oedema extending beyond the erythema, skin anaesthesia from destruction of cutaneous nerves, and later bullae or dusky skin. Diabetes, immunosuppression, injecting drug use and recent surgery or trauma are the common predisposing factors. Laboratory scores such as the widely used soft tissue risk score combine C reactive protein, white cell count, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine and glucose, but they were designed to prompt suspicion and lack the negative predictive value needed to rule the diagnosis out. The only reliable diagnostic test is surgical exploration, which is also the treatment, and survival depends primarily on the interval from presentation to first debridement. Broad spectrum antibiotics with anti toxin cover and intensive care support are essential adjuncts.
key_points: Pain out of proportion and skin anaesthesia are the key discriminating findings
Progression despite appropriate antibiotics argues strongly against simple cellulitis
Risk scores raise suspicion but cannot exclude the diagnosis
Surgical exploration is both the diagnostic test and the treatment
Mortality rises with every hour of delay to first debridement
explanation.pearls: Mark the edge of the erythema with a pen and record the time, because an advance of several centimetres in a few hours on appropriate antibiotics is one of the most useful bedside discriminators available and gives a defensible reason to call the surgical registrar back before any imaging returns.

sources.label: Australasian Society for Infectious Diseases: Skin and soft tissue infection

options.rationale: Pain out of proportion, rapid advance despite appropriate antibiotics, skin anaesthesia and systemic toxicity describe necrotising infection, and the diagnosis is surgical rather than radiological or biochemical. Every hour to debridement measurably increases mortality. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Imaging can support the diagnosis but a normal scan does not exclude it, gas is present in a minority, and the transfer and scanning time costs an hour in a condition measured in hours. Imaging is for when the diagnosis is genuinely uncertain and the patient is stable. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Broadening antibiotics is necessary but cannot sterilise tissue whose blood supply has been thrombosed by the infection, which is why medical management alone has a mortality approaching 100 percent. Four hours of reassessment is four hours of ongoing necrosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

That score was derived to raise suspicion, not to exclude the diagnosis, and around one in ten proven cases score in the low risk band on presentation. Pain far out of proportion to the skin findings calls for surgical exploration now, whatever the score. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

A limited bedside procedure cannot assess the extent of fascial involvement or achieve the wide debridement required, and it delays the theatre visit while offering the illusion of action. Tissue sampling happens in theatre alongside definitive surgery. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Myasthenic crisis is respiratory failure from weakness of the diaphragm, intercostal and bulbar muscles, most often precipitated by infection, surgery, pregnancy or a drug such as an aminoglycoside, a fluoroquinolone, magnesium or a beta blocker. The critical teaching point is that oxygen saturation and arterial blood gases remain normal until decompensation is imminent, because ventilation is maintained by increasing effort until that effort can no longer be sustained. Monitoring is therefore by serial bedside mechanics: forced vital capacity, negative inspiratory force, and the single breath count as a rough surrogate. A vital capacity below roughly 15 to 20 mL/kg or below 1 litre in an adult, a rapidly falling trend, or significant bulbar weakness all indicate intubation. Definitive treatment is plasma exchange or intravenous immunoglobulin, with corticosteroid adjustment, and the precipitant treated in parallel.
key_points: Oximetry and blood gases stay normal until immediately before collapse
Monitor with serial forced vital capacity and single breath count
Vital capacity below about 15 to 20 mL/kg indicates intubation
Bulbar weakness makes non-invasive ventilation unreliable
Plasma exchange or immunoglobulin is the definitive treatment in crisis
explanation.pearls: Review the medication chart at every crisis admission, because aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, magnesium, beta blockers and intravenous iodinated contrast all worsen neuromuscular transmission, and a crisis precipitated by a drug given on the ward is both common and entirely preventable.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists: Myasthenia gravis

options.rationale: Non-invasive support can help selected patients without bulbar involvement, but weak bulbar muscles and an ineffective cough make aspiration likely and mask ventilation unreliable. Her nasal speech and head drop place her in the group in whom it fails. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

A forced vital capacity falling below about 15 mL/kg with bulbar weakness predicts respiratory arrest, and the gas and oximetry stay normal until immediately before that happens because the failure is mechanical rather than gas exchange. Elective intubation with immunomodulation is far safer than emergency intubation after collapse. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

This test is obsolete in Australian practice, carries a risk of bradyarrhythmia, and does not alter the immediate need for airway protection in a patient with this vital capacity. The airway decision is made on mechanics, not on aetiology. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Hypercapnia in neuromuscular respiratory failure is a terminal finding, appearing when the patient can no longer compensate at all. Waiting for it means intubating a patient who has already arrested or aspirated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Escalating an anticholinesterase in crisis increases secretions and risks a cholinergic picture that is difficult to distinguish from the crisis itself, and many units withhold it during ventilation for that reason. It does not address the mechanism in time. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Herpes simplex encephalitis is the commonest sporadic viral encephalitis and typically presents with fever, headache, personality or behavioural change, confusion and seizures over a few days. The virus has a predilection for the medial temporal lobes, insula and orbitofrontal cortex, giving a recognisable magnetic resonance pattern and often lateralised periodic discharges on electroencephalography. Cerebrospinal fluid shows a lymphocytic pleocytosis with mildly raised protein and normal glucose, and diagnosis rests on polymerase chain reaction, which is highly specific but can be falsely negative when fluid is sampled within the first seventy two hours of symptoms or after several days of antiviral therapy. Because mortality without treatment is around 70 percent and aciclovir is comparatively safe, the rule is to continue treatment and repeat the sample rather than to stop on a single early negative result. Autoimmune causes, particularly antibodies against the N methyl D aspartate receptor, are tested in parallel.
key_points: Medial temporal and insular involvement is the characteristic imaging pattern
Early cerebrospinal fluid sampling produces around 10 percent false negatives
Continue aciclovir and repeat the sample rather than stopping treatment
Untreated mortality is around 70 percent and survivors are often disabled
Send autoimmune encephalitis antibodies in parallel, not instead
explanation.pearls: Maintain generous hydration while aciclovir is running and check renal function daily, because crystal nephropathy is common at treatment doses and dose reduction for a rising creatinine is a frequent route to undertreatment in a condition where the full fourteen to twenty one day course matters.

options.rationale: Ganciclovir targets cytomegalovirus, which causes encephalitis almost exclusively in profound immunosuppression and does not produce this temporal lobe pattern. Adding it exposes him to marrow suppression without addressing the likely pathogen. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Biopsy was the historical standard but has been superseded by polymerase chain reaction and imaging, and it carries real neurosurgical risk for a result that would not change treatment. It is reserved for undiagnosed deterioration despite full treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Polymerase chain reaction sampled within the first seventy two hours of symptoms has a false negative rate of around 10 percent, and the imaging and electroencephalogram findings here are close to characteristic. Treatment continues while a repeat sample is obtained, since stopping on a single early negative has produced avoidable deaths. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Autoimmune encephalitis is an important differential and antibody testing should be sent, but it usually evolves over weeks with psychiatric features and movement disorder rather than over days with fever. Immunosuppressing an untreated herpes infection is dangerous. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)
