The test is highly specific but its sensitivity falls when cerebrospinal fluid is sampled very early, so a negative result in this clinical and radiological context does not exclude the diagnosis. Untreated herpes encephalitis carries a mortality around 70 percent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms is a delayed hypersensitivity reaction with a characteristically long latency of two to eight weeks, which is why the culprit is often overlooked in favour of a more recently started medication. The classic features are an extensive morbilliform eruption, facial oedema, fever, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia or atypical lymphocytosis, and involvement of at least one internal organ, most often the liver. Allopurinol, aromatic anticonvulsants, sulfonamides, vancomycin and minocycline are the usual culprits in Australian practice. Treatment is immediate and permanent withdrawal of the drug, with systemic corticosteroid tapered slowly over six to twelve weeks when there is significant organ involvement. Two features distinguish it from other drug eruptions in follow up: symptoms can flare weeks after withdrawal as herpesviruses reactivate, and autoimmune sequelae such as thyroiditis and type 1 diabetes may appear months later, so monitoring continues well beyond recovery.
key_points: Latency of two to eight weeks distinguishes it from other drug eruptions
Eosinophilia or atypical lymphocytosis with organ involvement defines it
Allopurinol and aromatic anticonvulsants are the commonest culprits
Withdraw the drug permanently and treat organ involvement with corticosteroid
Monitor for late thyroiditis and other autoimmune sequelae for months
explanation.pearls: Consider testing for the HLA-B*58:01 allele before starting allopurinol in people of Han Chinese, Thai or Korean background, since carriage raises the risk of severe cutaneous reactions many fold, and always start at 50 to 100 mg daily with slow titration rather than at a dose chosen to reach target urate quickly.

sources.label: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions

options.rationale: Continuing the culprit drug in any form perpetuates the reaction, and this drug has a long lived active metabolite so even a reduced dose maintains exposure. Complete withdrawal is the single most important intervention. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

That spectrum is defined by mucosal erosions and epidermal detachment with a positive Nikolsky sign, and he has neither. The eosinophilia, facial oedema and six week latency point away from it towards a different severe reaction pattern. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions

options.rationale: Withdrawal alone is appropriate for a simple morbilliform drug eruption, but transaminases at nine times the upper limit with renal impairment place this in a different category. Undertreating visceral involvement is associated with progression and with a mortality around 10 percent. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions

options.rationale: Eosinophilia, atypical lymphocytes, facial oedema, hepatitis and fever six weeks after starting the drug describe a drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms, where visceral involvement justifies systemic corticosteroid. Prolonged monitoring is needed because relapse and late thyroiditis are characteristic. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions

options.rationale: Immunoglobulin has no established role in this reaction pattern and is expensive and volume loaded. It is considered in epidermal necrolysis and in refractory cases, not as first line for corticosteroid responsive visceral involvement. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions

explanation.summary: Sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors lower plasma glucose by causing glycosuria, which reduces insulin secretion and raises glucagon, shifting metabolism towards ketogenesis. Under the stress of surgery, fasting, dehydration or acute illness this can produce a full ketoacidosis while the plasma glucose remains below 14 mmol/L, so the diagnosis is missed if glucose is used as the screening variable. The clues are a high anion gap metabolic acidosis with a normal lactate, Kussmaul respiration, nausea and abdominal pain in a patient taking one of these drugs, and the confirmation is a raised blood ketone level. Treatment is an insulin infusion with concurrent intravenous glucose, since insulin is needed to suppress ketogenesis but the blood sugar cannot tolerate insulin alone, along with saline and potassium replacement. The Australian Diabetes Society advises withholding these drugs for at least two days before elective surgery, and the drug is not restarted until the patient is eating normally and the acidosis has fully resolved.
key_points: Ketoacidosis can occur with a glucose below 14 mmol/L on these drugs
A high anion gap with a normal lactate should prompt ketone measurement
Treat with insulin plus intravenous glucose, not insulin alone
Withhold the drug at least two days before elective surgery
Do not restart the drug until eating normally and fully recovered
explanation.pearls: Measure blood beta hydroxybutyrate rather than urine ketones, because the urine dipstick detects acetoacetate and reads falsely low early in ketoacidosis when beta hydroxybutyrate predominates, and can paradoxically appear to worsen during successful treatment as the ratio shifts back.

sources.label: Australian Diabetes Society: Periprocedural diabetic ketoacidosis with SGLT2 inhibitor use

options.rationale: Metformin associated acidosis is a lactic acidosis and her lactate is 1.4 mmol/L with normal renal function, so the mechanism does not fit. Bicarbonate would mask the gap without addressing ongoing ketogenesis. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Deep sighing respiration with a pH of 7.21 is respiratory compensation for a metabolic acidosis, not a pain response, and four hours of observation allows the acidosis to deepen. Attributing her symptoms to the surgery delays treatment of the ketoacidosis. (Source: Australian Diabetes Society: Periprocedural diabetic ketoacidosis with SGLT2 inhibitor use)
source_refs: Australian Diabetes Society: Periprocedural diabetic ketoacidosis with SGLT2 inhibitor use

options.rationale: A high anion gap acidosis with a normal lactate and a glucose below the usual threshold in a patient on a sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor is euglycaemic ketoacidosis until disproven. Insulin is required to switch off ketogenesis, and concurrent glucose is given because the blood sugar is already near normal. (Source: Australian Diabetes Society: Periprocedural diabetic ketoacidosis with SGLT2 inhibitor use)
source_refs: Australian Diabetes Society: Periprocedural diabetic ketoacidosis with SGLT2 inhibitor use

options.rationale: She is afebrile with clean wounds, a normal lactate and a soft abdomen, none of which supports an infective source. Anchoring on sepsis delays the insulin that is the actual treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Continuing the cotransporter inhibitor sustains glycosuria and the ketogenic state that caused the problem, and oral agents cannot reverse an established ketoacidosis. The drug must be withheld until well after recovery. (Source: Australian Diabetes Society: Periprocedural diabetic ketoacidosis with SGLT2 inhibitor use)
source_refs: Australian Diabetes Society: Periprocedural diabetic ketoacidosis with SGLT2 inhibitor use

explanation.summary: A thunderclap headache reaching peak intensity within a minute always requires exclusion of subarachnoid haemorrhage, and computed tomography within six hours followed by lumbar puncture for xanthochromia is the Australian pathway. When that pathway is negative and the headaches recur over days to weeks, reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome becomes the leading diagnosis. It is characteristically triggered by exertion, coughing, sexual activity or bathing, and the recognised precipitants are the postpartum state, serotonergic drugs, sympathomimetics including pseudoephedrine and cocaine, and immunoglobulin infusions. Angiographic imaging shows segmental beading of the intracranial arteries that resolves within three months, although it can be normal in the first week. Management is withdrawal of precipitants, nimodipine for symptom control, blood pressure control and strict avoidance of triptans and ergots, since the complications are convexity subarachnoid haemorrhage, ischaemic stroke and posterior reversible encephalopathy.
key_points: Exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage first with imaging and cerebrospinal fluid
Repeated thunderclap headaches over days point to vasoconstriction syndrome
Postpartum state and sympathomimetic drugs are the classic precipitants
Angiography may be normal in the first week and should be repeated if negative
Triptans and ergots are contraindicated because they worsen vasoconstriction
explanation.pearls: Ask what the patient was doing at the exact moment each headache began, because a syndrome in which every episode starts with coughing, straining, showering or orgasm is almost never migraine, and that single historical pattern separates this diagnosis from the far commoner postpartum headaches long before any imaging is arranged.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Association of Neurologists: Headache

options.rationale: Venous sinus thrombosis is an important postpartum diagnosis but typically produces a progressive headache over days with seizures, papilloedema or focal deficits rather than repeated discrete thunderclap events. Venography should be included in the imaging, but anticoagulation before a diagnosis is not justified. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Recurrent thunderclap headaches over days, triggered by cough and bathing, in the postpartum period and with a vasoconstrictor on board describe reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome. Angiographic imaging demonstrates segmental narrowing, and management is removal of precipitants with calcium channel blockade. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Low cerebrospinal fluid pressure headache is postural, worsening within minutes of standing and relieved by lying flat, and hers is not. A blood patch for a non postural headache treats the wrong mechanism. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Triptans are vasoconstrictors and can precipitate stroke in this syndrome, so they are contraindicated even though the headache pattern may superficially suggest migraine. Catheter angiography is also rarely needed when non-invasive imaging is available. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Idiopathic intracranial hypertension causes a constant daily headache with visual obscurations and papilloedema, and her fundi and fields are normal. Repeating the tap adds risk without addressing the episodic explosive pattern. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Cancer raises the risk of venous thromboembolism several fold through tumour procoagulants, immobility, central venous access and chemotherapy, and the thrombosis is often found incidentally on staging imaging. Incidental events are treated as though they were symptomatic because their recurrence risk is comparable. Low molecular weight heparin was the standard for years on the basis of lower recurrence than warfarin, and direct oral anticoagulants have since been shown to be at least as effective, which makes them attractive for the avoidance of daily injections. The important exception is the patient with an intact luminal gastrointestinal or genitourinary tumour, in whom rivaroxaban and edoxaban produced a clear excess of major bleeding, so heparin or apixaban is preferred. Anticoagulation continues for at least six months and for as long as the cancer is active or treatment continues. Platelet count, renal function and the evolving bleeding risk are reviewed at every cycle.
key_points: Incidental pulmonary embolism in cancer is treated like a symptomatic event
Rivaroxaban and edoxaban increase bleeding with intact luminal tumours
Low molecular weight heparin is preferred in that specific subgroup
Warfarin performs poorly in cancer because control is erratic
Continue at least six months and while the cancer remains active
explanation.pearls: Reassess the choice after the tumour is resected or has responded, because the reason for choosing injections disappears with the friable lesion and many patients can then switch to an oral agent, which materially improves adherence over the years that anticoagulation may need to continue.

options.rationale: Vitamin K antagonists perform poorly in cancer because appetite, vomiting, antibiotics and chemotherapy make control erratic, and the randomised evidence favours heparin over warfarin for recurrence. It is reserved for when neither preferred option is possible. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Filters are for patients in whom anticoagulation is absolutely contraindicated, and his bleeding is minor and from a tumour that treatment will shrink. They do not treat the existing clot and increase the rate of subsequent deep vein thrombosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Rivaroxaban and edoxaban raise major gastrointestinal bleeding in patients with an intact luminal tumour, and this man is already bleeding from a friable rectal lesion. Low molecular weight heparin avoids that specific excess and remains the preferred option in this subgroup, continuing while the cancer is active. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

The randomised comparisons that established direct oral anticoagulants in cancer associated thrombosis showed their benefit was offset by major gastrointestinal bleeding concentrated in patients with luminal gastrointestinal tumours. He is the patient those trials warn about. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Incidentally detected pulmonary embolism in cancer carries a recurrence and mortality risk comparable with symptomatic events, so it is treated the same way. Withholding treatment on the basis of how the clot was found is not supported. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Lambert Eaton myasthenic syndrome is caused by antibodies against presynaptic voltage gated calcium channels, which reduce the quantity of acetylcholine released at the neuromuscular junction and also impair autonomic cholinergic transmission. The clinical triad is proximal limb weakness worst in the legs, autonomic features such as dry mouth, constipation and impotence, and depressed or absent reflexes. The distinguishing sign is facilitation: both power and reflexes improve briefly after sustained or repeated contraction, the opposite of the fatigability seen in myasthenia gravis, and on nerve conduction studies this appears as a marked increment after brief exercise or high frequency stimulation. Around half of cases are paraneoplastic, almost always with small cell lung cancer, and the neurological syndrome commonly precedes the tumour by months to years, so a normal chest radiograph must be followed by computed tomography and by periodic re screening. Treatment addresses the tumour and uses amifampridine, with immunosuppression or immunoglobulin where needed.
key_points: Presynaptic calcium channel antibodies reduce acetylcholine release
Proximal weakness, autonomic features and absent reflexes form the triad
Post exercise facilitation distinguishes it from myasthenia gravis
Half of cases are paraneoplastic, almost always small cell lung cancer
A normal chest radiograph does not exclude a central tumour
explanation.pearls: Repeat the tumour search at intervals for two years even when the first computed tomography is clear, since the neurological syndrome can precede a detectable small cell lung cancer by that long, and positron emission tomography is the next step when conventional imaging remains negative in a heavy smoker.

options.rationale: An inflammatory myopathy would be expected to raise the creatine kinase and would not produce absent reflexes that reappear after exercise or autonomic symptoms. Biopsy would be invasive and uninformative here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Osteomalacic myopathy is a reasonable cause of proximal weakness but does not abolish reflexes, cause autonomic symptoms or show facilitation, and a normal alkaline phosphatase would be unusual. It does not account for the neurophysiological signature. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Anticholinesterase treatment helps postsynaptic disease and is much less effective here, and the negative antibody with post exercise facilitation already points away from that diagnosis. Three months of trial delays the cancer search. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Post exercise facilitation of reflexes with autonomic features and proximal weakness describes a presynaptic neuromuscular junction disorder, which in a heavy smoker is associated with small cell lung cancer in around half of cases. A normal radiograph does not exclude a central tumour, so cross sectional imaging is required alongside the antibody. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

A radiculopathy produces sensory change in a root distribution and does not explain the dry mouth, constipation or the strengthening with repeated effort. The distribution here is symmetrical and not radicular. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Falls in older people are multifactorial, and the assessment covers gait and balance, vision, footwear, cognition, continence, home hazards, orthostatic blood pressure, and medications. Among these, medication review is the element most often neglected and among the most effective, because the drug classes implicated are prescribed for symptoms that seem minor. Anticholinergic agents such as oxybutynin and amitriptyline impair attention, cause dry mouth and blurred vision and add directly to cognitive load, while benzodiazepines impair postural reflexes and reaction time with a risk that persists no matter how long the person has taken them. Withdrawal must be planned and gradual, particularly for benzodiazepines after years of use, with an alternative offered for the symptom that prompted the original prescription. The strongest evidence for falls reduction combines this deprescribing with a progressive strength and balance program delivered for several months.
key_points: Anticholinergics and benzodiazepines are the highest yield targets on the list
Long standing use does not confer tolerance to the falls risk
Taper benzodiazepines gradually rather than stopping abruptly
Combine deprescribing with a progressive strength and balance program
Bone protection reduces fracture severity but not the frequency of falls
explanation.pearls: Offer a specific alternative for the symptom that earned each drug its place, such as bladder training and a topical oestrogen for urge incontinence or sleep restriction therapy for insomnia, because deprescribing that leaves the original complaint unaddressed is the commonest reason a stopped medication reappears on the list within six months.

sources.label: RACGP: Falls prevention in older people

options.rationale: These three drugs carry the highest falls attributable risk on her list through anticholinergic burden, sedation and postural instability, and withdrawal combined with exercise has the strongest evidence for preventing further falls. Tapering rather than stopping abruptly is essential after twenty years of benzodiazepine use. (Source: RACGP: Falls prevention in older people)
source_refs: RACGP: Falls prevention in older people

options.rationale: Bone protection after a minimal trauma fracture is clearly indicated and should happen, but it reduces the consequence of the next fall rather than its likelihood. The question is which intervention reduces falls. (Source: RACGP: Falls prevention in older people)
source_refs: RACGP: Falls prevention in older people

options.rationale: Her attention and recall deficits are most plausibly caused by the anticholinergic and sedative load rather than by a degenerative dementia, and treating them with a cholinesterase inhibitor while continuing oxybutynin sets one drug against another. Cognition should be reassessed after withdrawal. (Source: RACGP: Falls prevention in older people)
source_refs: RACGP: Falls prevention in older people

options.rationale: A fall of 24 mmHg systolic without symptoms does not meet the definition of orthostatic hypotension, and adding a mineralocorticoid brings oedema, hypokalaemia and supine hypertension for no established benefit. Her postural change is not what is driving her falls. (Source: RACGP: Falls prevention in older people)
source_refs: RACGP: Falls prevention in older people

options.rationale: All benzodiazepines increase falls and a shorter half life does not remove that risk, while the substitution signals that the drug class is acceptable to continue. Home hazard assessment is useful but has modest effect as a standalone measure. (Source: RACGP: Falls prevention in older people)
source_refs: RACGP: Falls prevention in older people

explanation.summary: Australia has among the highest melanoma incidence rates in the world, and the prognosis depends overwhelmingly on how deeply the tumour has invaded at the time of excision. Breslow thickness, measured in millimetres from the granular layer to the deepest tumour cell, drives the definitive excision margin, the decision about sentinel lymph node biopsy and the staging conversation, which is why the initial biopsy must deliver an intact full thickness specimen. Ulceration and mitotic rate add further prognostic information from the same specimen. Once the thickness is reported, definitive wide local excision follows with margins graded to thickness, ranging from 5 mm for melanoma in situ up to 2 cm for thicker tumours.
key_points: Excision biopsy with a 2 mm margin and full depth is the standard diagnostic procedure
Breslow thickness determines definitive margins, sentinel node biopsy and staging
Partial and shave biopsies risk under-staging by missing the deepest tumour
Definitive margins range from 5 mm for in situ disease to 2 cm for thick melanoma
Sequential dermoscopic imaging is only for equivocal flat lesions without melanoma features
explanation.pearls: Sentinel lymph node biopsy is discussed for melanoma of Breslow thickness above 1 mm, and for thinner lesions with ulceration, because it provides staging information that determines eligibility for adjuvant immunotherapy rather than because it improves melanoma specific survival on its own.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Melanoma Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Short term sequential imaging is a legitimate tool for flat equivocal lesions without dermoscopic features of melanoma, allowing change to be detected over months. A lesion already showing an atypical network with irregular streaks and a documented history of growth has met the threshold for excision. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Melanoma Clinical Practice Guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Melanoma Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: A shave transects the lesion at an arbitrary depth and destroys the deep margin with diathermy, making thickness unmeasurable. Both remove tissue, but only full thickness excision preserves the depth the pathologist must report. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Melanoma Clinical Practice Guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Melanoma Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Sampling part of a lesion risks missing the deepest focus and therefore under-reporting Breslow thickness, which misdirects every subsequent management decision. Partial biopsy is acceptable only for very large lesions or sites such as the face where complete excision is not initially feasible. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Melanoma Clinical Practice Guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Melanoma Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Excisional biopsy including the full depth of the lesion allows the pathologist to measure Breslow thickness accurately, which is the single most important determinant of staging, definitive margins and whether sentinel node biopsy is offered. A narrow 2 mm margin is used because definitive wider excision follows once the thickness is known. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Melanoma Clinical Practice Guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Melanoma Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.rationale: Definitive margins are determined by Breslow thickness, which is not yet known, so excising widely now may be both excessive for a thin lesion and inadequate for a thick one. Performing a wide excision first can also disrupt lymphatic drainage and compromise later sentinel node mapping. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Melanoma Clinical Practice Guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Melanoma Clinical Practice Guidelines

explanation.summary: Inflammatory back pain is defined by a cluster of features that together separate it from the far more common mechanical causes: onset before 45 years, insidious onset, duration beyond three months, morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes, improvement with exercise but not with rest, and night pain that wakes the patient in the second half of the night. Recognising it matters because the average delay to diagnosis of axial spondyloarthritis has historically been measured in years, during which irreversible structural change accumulates. The disease is now understood as a spectrum, with non-radiographic disease at one end and ankylosing spondylitis with established radiographic sacroiliitis at the other, and magnetic resonance imaging is what makes the earlier end visible. Extra-articular features including acute anterior uveitis, psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease frequently accompany it and are often the clue that reframes a long history of back pain.
key_points: Inflammatory back pain improves with exercise, worsens with rest and wakes the patient at night
Plain radiographic sacroiliitis takes years to appear and its absence does not exclude disease
Magnetic resonance imaging with fat suppression shows active subchondral bone marrow oedema
Human leucocyte antigen B27 supports but never establishes the diagnosis
Acute anterior uveitis, psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease are associated features
explanation.pearls: Acute anterior uveitis affects up to 40% of people with axial spondyloarthritis and is typically unilateral, painful and recurrent, so a young adult presenting to an optometrist with a red painful photophobic eye and a history of chronic back pain should be asked directly about night pain and morning stiffness.

options.rationale: Dedicated views add little to a standard anteroposterior pelvic film, and waiting two years for structural change to appear delays treatment through the window in which it best preserves function. Radiographic progression is the natural history the treatment aims to prevent. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial Spondyloarthritis)

This marker is useful as one element within a classification framework and raises the probability substantially in the right clinical context, but around 8% of the Australian population carries it and most carriers never develop disease. It cannot confirm the diagnosis alone and a negative result does not exclude it. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial Spondyloarthritis)

Computed tomography shows established structural damage better than plain films but is insensitive to the active inflammation that precedes it, and it delivers a substantial pelvic radiation dose to a young man. It detects the same late changes the radiograph is waiting for. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial Spondyloarthritis)

Radiographic sacroiliitis takes years to develop, so a normal plain film in a young man with inflammatory back pain does not exclude the diagnosis and instead defines the non-radiographic form of the disease. Fat suppressed sequences demonstrate bone marrow oedema in the subchondral bone, which is the imaging criterion used for diagnosis. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial Spondyloarthritis)

Lumbar spine imaging investigates mechanical and discogenic pain, which characteristically worsens with activity and improves with rest, the opposite of his pattern. It also images the wrong joints, since the disease begins at the sacroiliac joints. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial Spondyloarthritis)

explanation.summary: Prolactinomas are the commonest functioning pituitary tumour and present differently by sex: women usually present early with amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea from a microadenoma, while men typically present late with hypogonadism and mass effect from a macroadenoma, because the endocrine symptoms are insidious and easily attributed to other causes. Before attributing a raised prolactin to a tumour it is essential to exclude the far commoner alternatives, which are pregnancy, hypothyroidism, renal failure, chest wall stimulation, stress and above all drugs such as antipsychotics, metoclopramide and some antidepressants. The magnitude of elevation is informative, since a level in the thousands with a macroadenoma indicates a prolactin secreting tumour, whereas a modest rise with a large sellar mass suggests stalk compression from a non-functioning tumour interrupting dopamine delivery. That distinction changes management completely, because stalk effect requires surgery while a prolactinoma responds to a dopamine agonist.
key_points: Prolactinomas are the only pituitary macroadenoma treated medically before surgically
Cabergoline is preferred to bromocriptine for efficacy and tolerability
Exclude pregnancy, hypothyroidism, renal failure and drug causes before diagnosing a tumour
Modest hyperprolactinaemia with a large mass suggests stalk compression rather than a prolactinoma
Surgery is reserved for resistance, intolerance, apoplexy or progressive visual loss
explanation.pearls: A very large prolactinoma can produce a falsely normal prolactin through the hook effect, in which massive antigen excess saturates both antibodies in the immunoassay, so a big sellar mass with an unexpectedly modest prolactin should be retested on a 1 in 100 dilution before it is called non-functioning.

options.rationale: Prolactin secreting tumours are the one pituitary macroadenoma treated medically first, because dopamine agonists shrink them dramatically and normalise prolactin in the great majority, often improving visual fields within days to weeks. Cabergoline is preferred over bromocriptine for greater efficacy and better tolerability. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Hyperprolactinaemia)

His hypogonadism is secondary to prolactin suppressing gonadotrophin releasing hormone pulsatility, so lowering prolactin restores the axis without exogenous hormone. Replacing testosterone alone leaves the tumour compressing his chiasm. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Hyperprolactinaemia)

Chiasmal compression would mandate urgent surgery for almost any other pituitary tumour, but here the mass usually shrinks faster with a tablet than it could be safely resected. Surgery is reserved for dopamine agonist resistance or intolerance, apoplexy, or progressive visual loss despite medical therapy. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Hyperprolactinaemia)

Radiotherapy works slowly over years, carries a high long term rate of hypopituitarism and cannot relieve chiasmal compression in a useful timeframe. It is a third line option for tumours resistant to both medical and surgical treatment. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Hyperprolactinaemia)

Watchful waiting is an option only for a small asymptomatic microadenoma with normal visual fields in a man not seeking fertility. Observing established chiasmal compression risks permanent visual loss. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Hyperprolactinaemia)

explanation.summary: Chronic plaque psoriasis is an immune mediated disease of accelerated keratinocyte turnover producing sharply demarcated erythematous plaques with adherent silvery scale on extensor surfaces, scalp, nails and the natal cleft. Treatment intensity is matched to the extent of disease and its impact, with topical therapy for limited disease, phototherapy for more widespread involvement, and systemic conventional or biologic agents for severe or arthropathic disease. Topical corticosteroid potency is selected by site rather than by preference, since thin skin on the face, flexures and genitalia is vulnerable to atrophy while thick plaques on elbows and knees need potent preparations to penetrate. Psoriasis also carries systemic associations that a skin-only consultation misses, including psoriatic arthritis in up to a third of patients, and increased cardiovascular and metabolic risk that warrants screening.
key_points: A potent corticosteroid with calcipotriol is first line for localised plaque disease
Topical corticosteroid potency is chosen by body site, not by disease severity alone
Systemic therapy is for extensive disease, major functional impact or psoriatic arthritis
Screen for psoriatic arthritis, which affects up to a third of people with psoriasis
Cardiovascular and metabolic risk is increased and should be assessed
explanation.pearls: Abrupt withdrawal of systemic corticosteroid in psoriasis can precipitate generalised pustular or erythrodermic disease, which is why oral prednisolone is avoided in psoriasis even when a patient with severe plaques requests something to clear it quickly.

options.rationale: Phototherapy is effective for widespread disease that topical treatment cannot cover, and it requires repeated hospital attendance. For four localised plaques the treatment burden far exceeds what topical therapy would ask of her. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

Mild preparations are appropriate for the face, flexures and genitalia where skin is thin, but they are insufficient for thick scaly plaques on extensor surfaces and have already failed. Repeating an inadequate potency simply extends the time she remains untreated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

Systemic therapy is considered for extensive disease, usually above 10% body surface area, for significant functional or psychological impact, or for psoriatic arthritis, none of which is present. Committing her to weekly monitoring for four small plaques is disproportionate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

Coal tar is effective and still used, particularly for scalp disease and in specialist settings, but it stains skin and clothing and smells strongly, so adherence is poor. It sits behind the corticosteroid and vitamin D analogue combination in the Australian sequence. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

Combining a potent corticosteroid with a vitamin D analogue is first line for localised chronic plaque disease and outperforms either component alone, because the steroid addresses inflammation while calcipotriol normalises keratinocyte proliferation. Extensor surfaces tolerate potent preparations well, unlike the face and flexures. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

explanation.summary: Fibromyalgia is a disorder of central pain processing rather than of peripheral tissue damage, characterised by widespread pain lasting beyond three months together with fatigue, unrefreshing sleep and cognitive difficulty that patients often describe as brain fog. It is a positive clinical diagnosis made on the symptom pattern, not a diagnosis of exclusion, though a limited screen for inflammatory, metabolic and endocrine mimics is appropriate. Overinvestigation is actively harmful because incidental findings invite structural explanations and procedures that do not help. Management is built on education, graded exercise, sleep and psychological approaches, with medication playing a secondary role through agents that act centrally such as amitriptyline, duloxetine and pregabalin, while opioids and non-steroidal agents are ineffective.
key_points: Fibromyalgia reflects central sensitisation rather than peripheral inflammation
It is a positive clinical diagnosis, not one of exclusion after exhaustive testing
Graded aerobic exercise has the strongest evidence of any intervention
Opioids and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are ineffective and cause harm
Centrally acting agents such as amitriptyline and duloxetine are adjuncts, not first line
explanation.pearls: Low dose amitriptyline at 10 to 25 mg taken two hours before bed is the most commonly used pharmacological adjunct in Australian practice, chosen for its effect on sleep continuity rather than its antidepressant action, and the dose used is far below the antidepressant range.

options.rationale: Graded aerobic exercise has the strongest and most consistent evidence of any intervention for this condition, improving pain, function and fatigue, and it is paired with explanation of the diagnosis because understanding central pain amplification reduces fear and improves engagement. Non-pharmacological management is first line in every major guideline. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

Opioids are ineffective for this condition and cause harm through tolerance, opioid induced hyperalgesia, dependence and cognitive impairment that compounds her existing concentration difficulty. They are specifically recommended against. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

Serological testing without clinical features of connective tissue disease generates false positives, since a low titre antinuclear antibody is present in a substantial minority of healthy people. That result then drives further investigation and diagnostic uncertainty rather than resolving it. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Fibromyalgia)

These agents work on peripheral inflammation, which is absent here, and trials show no meaningful benefit in this condition. Long term use adds gastrointestinal, renal and cardiovascular risk without addressing central sensitisation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

Imaging in widespread pain without neurological signs or red flags commonly shows age related degenerative change that is unrelated to the symptoms. Attributing the pain to incidental findings leads to unnecessary procedures and reinforces a structural explanation that is not correct. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Fibromyalgia)

explanation.summary: Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis are a single disease continuum of drug induced keratinocyte apoptosis, separated by the extent of epidermal detachment: below 10% of body surface area is Stevens-Johnson syndrome, above 30% is toxic epidermal necrolysis, and between the two is the overlap category. Anticonvulsants, allopurinol, sulfonamides, nevirapine and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs cause most cases, with onset typically 4 days to 4 weeks after the drug is started. Prodromal fever, sore throat and painful eyes precede the rash and are commonly mistaken for a viral illness, and mucosal involvement at two or more sites is close to universal. The SCORTEN score, calculated in the first 24 hours from age, heart rate, malignancy, body surface area detached, urea, bicarbonate and glucose, predicts mortality, which remains substantial in the more extensive form.
key_points: Stopping the culprit drug early is the intervention most associated with survival
Detachment below 10% is Stevens-Johnson syndrome and above 30% is toxic epidermal necrolysis
Management mirrors major burns care and belongs in a burns or intensive care unit
Early ophthalmology review prevents permanent ocular scarring and vision loss
Prophylactic antibiotics and routine systemic corticosteroids are not recommended
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine carries a particularly high risk of severe cutaneous reaction when titrated too quickly or combined with valproate, which inhibits its metabolism, so the Australian dose escalation schedule is halved when a patient is already taking valproate.

sources.label: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

options.rationale: Prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended because they select resistant organisms without reducing sepsis, and cultures with clinical surveillance guide treatment instead. Admitting to a general medical ward also denies her the nursing and wound care expertise the condition demands. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

options.rationale: Early withdrawal of the culprit drug is the single intervention most consistently associated with reduced mortality, and management otherwise mirrors major burns care with fluid balance, temperature control, wound care, analgesia and infection surveillance. Mucosal and ocular involvement also requires early ophthalmology review to prevent permanent scarring and vision loss. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

options.rationale: Dose reduction has no role because the reaction is immunologically mediated rather than dose dependent, and detachment progresses over days regardless. Observing for a day allows a potentially fatal reaction to extend. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

options.rationale: Systemic immunomodulation remains contested in this condition with no agent clearly established, and steroids may increase infection risk. Continuing the drug that is causing the reaction is the more serious half of this error. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

options.rationale: Biopsy is valuable to confirm full thickness epidermal necrosis and exclude autoimmune blistering disease, and it should be taken, but it takes time and the clinical picture already demands action. Waiting on histology before stopping the drug wastes the intervention that most affects survival. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

explanation.summary: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms is distinguished from other severe cutaneous adverse reactions by three features: a long latency of two to eight weeks after drug initiation, prominent facial oedema, and internal organ involvement accompanied by eosinophilia and atypical lymphocytes. The liver is affected most often, followed by the kidney, lung, heart and thyroid, and it is organ failure rather than the skin that causes death. Aromatic anticonvulsants, allopurinol, sulfasalazine, vancomycin, minocycline and dapsone account for most cases, and reactivation of human herpesvirus 6 and other herpesviruses is characteristically involved in the pathogenesis and helps explain the prolonged and relapsing course. Late autoimmune sequelae including thyroiditis and type 1 diabetes can emerge months after apparent recovery, so follow-up extends well beyond discharge.
key_points: Latency of two to eight weeks distinguishes this from other drug eruptions
Facial oedema, eosinophilia and atypical lymphocytes are characteristic
The liver is the most commonly involved internal organ, followed by the kidney
Systemic corticosteroid with a slow taper over weeks to months prevents relapse
Late autoimmune sequelae such as thyroiditis warrant follow-up for months
explanation.pearls: Allopurinol hypersensitivity is strongly associated with the HLA-B*58:01 allele, which is why Australian practice starts allopurinol at 50 to 100 mg daily with slow upward titration against urate rather than beginning at a full dose, and why the risk is higher in patients with renal impairment.

sources.label: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

options.rationale: Burns unit transfer is the pathway for epidermal detachment with mucosal erosion, and his skin is intact with no shearing and no mucosal involvement. The organ dysfunction here is internal rather than a barrier failure. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

options.rationale: Topical treatment alone is appropriate for a simple morbilliform drug eruption without systemic features. The transaminitis, acute kidney injury and eosinophilia place this in a different category requiring systemic treatment. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

options.rationale: Facial oedema, eosinophilia, atypical lymphocytes, lymphadenopathy and both hepatic and renal involvement six weeks after allopurinol describe drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms, in which organ involvement justifies systemic corticosteroid. The taper must be slow over weeks to months because rapid withdrawal frequently causes relapse. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

options.rationale: The reaction is immunologically mediated and will progress on any dose, so reduction offers no protection while the kidney and liver injury worsens. Fluids support the kidney but do not address the cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

A drug taken unchanged for three years is very unlikely to be responsible, whereas the latency of two to eight weeks fits the agent started six weeks ago precisely. Allopurinol is among the commonest causes of this syndrome worldwide. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions

explanation.summary: Acromegaly results from growth hormone excess, almost always from a pituitary somatotroph adenoma, and because the changes accrue over years the diagnosis is typically delayed by around a decade. Comparing current appearance with old photographs is one of the most useful clinical manoeuvres available. The clinical burden extends well beyond appearance, since growth hormone and insulin-like growth factor 1 excess drive hypertension, cardiomyopathy, obstructive sleep apnoea, insulin resistance, arthropathy, carpal tunnel syndrome and an increased incidence of colonic polyps, and untreated disease shortens life expectancy mainly through cardiovascular disease. Diagnosis follows a fixed sequence of screening with insulin-like growth factor 1, confirming with growth hormone suppression during an oral glucose tolerance test, then localising with magnetic resonance imaging. Transsphenoidal surgery is first line treatment, with somatostatin analogues, the growth hormone receptor antagonist pegvisomant, and radiotherapy for residual disease.
key_points: Insulin-like growth factor 1 is the screening test because it integrates pulsatile secretion
A random growth hormone level cannot confirm or exclude the diagnosis
Confirmation is failure of growth hormone suppression during an oral glucose tolerance test
Imaging follows biochemical confirmation because pituitary incidentalomas are common
Transsphenoidal surgery is first line, with medical therapy for residual disease
explanation.pearls: People with acromegaly have an increased risk of colorectal neoplasia, so Australian practice offers colonoscopy at diagnosis with ongoing surveillance intervals guided by the findings and by whether insulin-like growth factor 1 remains elevated after treatment.

options.rationale: This investigates cortisol excess, which also causes hypertension, glucose intolerance and skin changes, but produces central obesity, proximal myopathy, striae and easy bruising rather than acral enlargement and prognathism. The skeletal changes here point to a different hormone. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Acromegaly)

Pulsatile secretion means a healthy person can have an undetectable level between pulses and a high level during one, so a random measurement neither confirms nor excludes the diagnosis. This is the most common error in investigating suspected growth hormone excess. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Acromegaly)

Growth hormone is secreted in pulses and has a short half life, so a single random level is uninterpretable, whereas insulin-like growth factor 1 is produced by the liver in proportion to integrated growth hormone exposure and is stable through the day. A raised age-adjusted level is the accepted screening test. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Acromegaly)

Imaging localises the adenoma once biochemical excess is established, but pituitary incidentalomas are found in around 10% of scans in the general population. Imaging first risks attributing her symptoms to an unrelated incidental lesion. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Acromegaly)

Failure of growth hormone to suppress after a glucose load is the confirmatory test and remains the reference standard, but it is performed after a raised insulin-like growth factor 1 has flagged the diagnosis. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Acromegaly)

explanation.summary: Axial spondyloarthritis behaves immunologically unlike rheumatoid arthritis, and the practical consequence is that the conventional synthetic disease modifying drugs which anchor rheumatoid treatment do essentially nothing for axial disease. The treatment ladder is therefore short: exercise and physiotherapy throughout, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs first line with at least two agents trialled for around four weeks each, then biologic therapy for persistently active disease. Tumour necrosis factor inhibitors and interleukin 17 inhibitors are both effective, and the choice between them is shaped by comorbidity, since inflammatory bowel disease and recurrent uveitis favour a monoclonal tumour necrosis factor inhibitor while interleukin 17 inhibition can worsen bowel disease. In Australia access is governed by Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme criteria requiring documented disease activity scores and failed non-steroidal trials, and all patients need latent tuberculosis and hepatitis screening before starting.
key_points: Methotrexate and sulfasalazine are ineffective for axial disease but may help peripheral arthritis
Systemic corticosteroids are ineffective in axial spondyloarthritis
Escalate to biologic therapy after two adequate non-steroidal trials with ongoing activity
Screen for latent tuberculosis and viral hepatitis before any biologic agent
Exercise and physiotherapy continue lifelong alongside drug treatment
explanation.pearls: Interleukin 17 inhibitors such as secukinumab can precipitate or worsen inflammatory bowel disease, so a patient with axial spondyloarthritis and coexisting Crohn disease should receive a monoclonal tumour necrosis factor inhibitor rather than an interleukin 17 agent or etanercept.

options.rationale: Conventional synthetic disease modifying drugs are ineffective for axial disease, a difference from rheumatoid arthritis that surprises many clinicians and reflects distinct underlying immunology. Methotrexate retains a role only for peripheral arthritis in this condition, which he does not have. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial Spondyloarthritis)

Systemic corticosteroids are notably ineffective in axial disease, unlike in most other inflammatory arthritides, and long term use adds osteoporosis risk to a skeleton already vulnerable. Local corticosteroid injection into a sacroiliac joint is a different and sometimes useful intervention. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial Spondyloarthritis)

Sulfasalazine has modest evidence for peripheral joint involvement in spondyloarthritis but none for axial disease. Both are disease modifying, but only biologic therapy acts on axial disease. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial Spondyloarthritis)

Exercise and physiotherapy are the foundation of management and must continue alongside any drug, but they are not sufficient for persistently active disease with a C-reactive protein of 32 mg/L. Six months of ongoing inflammation permits further structural progression. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial Spondyloarthritis)

Biologic therapy is the recommended escalation for active axial disease that has failed at least two non-steroidal agents, and tumour necrosis factor inhibitors substantially improve symptoms, function and inflammatory markers. Latent tuberculosis and viral hepatitis screening has already been completed, which is the prerequisite for starting. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Axial Spondyloarthritis)

explanation.summary: Anticoagulant associated intracerebral haemorrhage carries a substantially higher risk of haematoma expansion and death than spontaneous bleeding, and expansion occurs predominantly within the first few hours, which is what makes reversal a time-critical intervention rather than a considered one. The decisive point in this case is that routine coagulation assays cannot be used to decide whether a direct oral anticoagulant is active: the prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time are insensitive to apixaban in particular, and only a calibrated anti-factor Xa assay quantifies drug effect, which is rarely available overnight in a regional hospital. Reversal strategy follows the drug class, with idarucizumab for dabigatran, andexanet alfa for factor Xa inhibitors where stocked, and prothrombin complex concentrate as the Australian fallback. Alongside reversal, blood pressure lowering, neurosurgical consultation and seizure and airway management run concurrently rather than sequentially.
key_points: Prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time cannot exclude apixaban effect
Prothrombin complex concentrate is the fallback when andexanet alfa is unavailable
Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran only and has no effect on factor Xa inhibitors
Renal impairment prolongs direct oral anticoagulant elimination and raises drug levels
Haematoma expansion occurs early, so reversal precedes confirmatory drug assays
explanation.pearls: Dabigatran is around 35% protein bound and therefore dialysable, while apixaban and rivaroxaban exceed 85% protein binding and are not, which is why haemodialysis appears in the reversal pathway for one direct oral anticoagulant class and not the other.

sources.label: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Anticoagulant Reversal
Stroke Foundation: Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.rationale: The prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time are insensitive to apixaban and can be normal at therapeutic drug concentrations, so they cannot be used to exclude anticoagulation. Reassuring routine tests invite dangerous inaction. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Anticoagulant Reversal)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Anticoagulant Reversal

options.rationale: Idarucizumab is a monoclonal antibody fragment specific to dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor, and has no activity against factor Xa inhibitors. The target enzyme differs: one class inhibits thrombin and the other inhibits factor Xa. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Anticoagulant Reversal)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Anticoagulant Reversal

options.rationale: Vitamin K and plasma reverse warfarin by replacing vitamin K dependent factors, but apixaban directly inhibits factor Xa, so supplying more factor X in plasma at low concentration is ineffective. Plasma also carries volume overload risk in a frail 58 kg woman. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Anticoagulant Reversal)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Anticoagulant Reversal

options.rationale: Charcoal only helps within a few hours of ingestion, which cannot be established here, and apixaban is highly protein bound so dialysis removes very little. Dialysis is a genuine option for dabigatran, which is minimally protein bound, but not for this drug. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Anticoagulant Reversal)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Anticoagulant Reversal

options.rationale: With specific reversal unavailable, prothrombin complex concentrate is the recommended Australian alternative for life threatening bleeding on a factor Xa inhibitor and should be given immediately rather than awaiting drug level assays. Normal screening coagulation tests do not exclude a clinically significant apixaban effect, and her renal impairment prolongs elimination, so an unknown dose time must be assumed to mean she is anticoagulated. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Anticoagulant Reversal)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand: Anticoagulant Reversal

explanation.summary: Hypercalcaemia with a parathyroid hormone that is not suppressed narrows the differential to parathyroid hormone dependent causes, and the important distinction within that group is between primary hyperparathyroidism and familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia. The latter is an autosomal dominant condition caused by an inactivating variant in the calcium sensing receptor gene, which resets the set point at which the parathyroid gland and the renal tubule perceive calcium as adequate, producing lifelong mild hypercalcaemia with avid renal calcium reabsorption and no end-organ damage. The features that should raise suspicion are a young patient, an absence of renal stones and bone disease, a stable calcium over years, an affected first degree relative and a negative localisation scan. The calcium creatinine clearance ratio is the discriminating test, with values below 0.01 favouring the familial disorder and above 0.02 favouring primary hyperparathyroidism, and genetic testing confirming the diagnosis in the indeterminate zone.
key_points: Unsuppressed parathyroid hormone with hypercalcaemia indicates a parathyroid hormone dependent cause
Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia is autosomal dominant and caused by calcium sensing receptor variants
A calcium creatinine clearance ratio below 0.01 supports the familial condition
The familial condition causes no end-organ damage and requires no surgery
A family history of asymptomatic hypercalcaemia and a negative localisation scan are key clues
explanation.pearls: Thiazide diuretics and lithium both reduce urinary calcium excretion and can push the calcium creatinine clearance ratio into the familial range, so either drug must be stopped for several weeks before the ratio is measured or the result will be uninterpretable.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Hyperparathyroidism

options.rationale: Granulomatous disease raises calcium through unregulated conversion of vitamin D to its active form, which suppresses parathyroid hormone. It also would not explain the identical biochemistry in his mother and sister. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Hyperparathyroidism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Hyperparathyroidism

options.rationale: Repeat localisation imaging assumes the diagnosis is primary hyperparathyroidism and merely asks where the gland is. A negative sestamibi in this context is a clue to reconsider the diagnosis rather than an indication to image harder. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Hyperparathyroidism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Hyperparathyroidism

options.rationale: A mildly raised calcium with an inappropriately unsuppressed parathyroid hormone occurs in both primary hyperparathyroidism and familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia, and the two are separated by urinary calcium handling, with a ratio below 0.01 indicating the familial condition. Distinguishing them is essential because parathyroidectomy does not cure the familial disorder and exposes the patient to an unnecessary operation. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Hyperparathyroidism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Hyperparathyroidism

options.rationale: Bone markers and serial densitometry help decide whether asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism has met operative criteria, so they belong after the diagnosis is settled. His density is already normal, which does not discriminate between the two candidate diagnoses. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Hyperparathyroidism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Hyperparathyroidism

options.rationale: This pursues malignancy associated hypercalcaemia, in which parathyroid hormone is suppressed rather than unsuppressed, and which presents with a short history and higher calcium levels. His two year stable course with a normal parathyroid hormone points elsewhere. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Hyperparathyroidism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Hyperparathyroidism

explanation.summary: Tumour necrosis factor inhibitors are among the most effective drugs in rheumatology, and their safety profile is dominated by infection risk, which is what most monitoring is built around. Central and peripheral demyelination is a less common but clinically decisive adverse effect, and it is counterintuitive because tumour necrosis factor blockade was originally trialled as a treatment for multiple sclerosis and made the disease worse. The practical consequences are twofold: a personal or family history of demyelinating disease is a contraindication to starting this class, and a new demyelinating event during treatment means permanent cessation and class avoidance rather than a switch within the class. Recognising the syndrome depends on localising the lesions clinically, and here optic neuritis with a thoracic sensory level demonstrates disease at two separate sites in the central nervous system. Alternative biologic classes with different mechanisms remain available for her arthritis once the neurological situation is characterised.
key_points: Demyelination is a class adverse effect of tumour necrosis factor inhibitors, not agent specific
A personal or family history of demyelinating disease contraindicates starting this class
A new demyelinating event means permanent cessation and avoidance of the whole class
Optic neuritis presents with pain on eye movement and a relative afferent pupillary defect
Alternative biologic classes with different mechanisms can be used for the arthritis
explanation.pearls: A relative afferent pupillary defect with normal fundi is the classic sign of retrobulbar optic neuritis and is elicited by the swinging torch test, in which the affected pupil paradoxically dilates as the light swings onto it because its afferent signal is weaker than the consensual one.

sources.label: Australian Rheumatology Association: Biologic Therapy Safety

options.rationale: Rheumatoid vasculitis occurs in poorly controlled longstanding seropositive disease with high inflammatory markers, nodules and mononeuritis multiplex, whereas her arthritis is in remission with a C-reactive protein of 3 mg/L. Escalating immunosuppression for a misdiagnosed cause would expose her to substantial toxicity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

Optic neuritis with a sensory level and upper motor neuron signs describes central demyelination, a recognised class adverse effect of tumour necrosis factor inhibitors that can unmask or precipitate a demyelinating illness. The drug is stopped permanently and the class avoided in future, while imaging of brain and spinal cord characterises the lesions. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Biologic Therapy Safety)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Biologic Therapy Safety

options.rationale: Corticosteroid will shorten the acute attack and is part of the treatment, but continuing the drug that precipitated it leaves the cause in place and risks further demyelinating events. The class is contraindicated once this has occurred. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Biologic Therapy Safety)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Biologic Therapy Safety

options.rationale: Demyelination is a class effect rather than a property of one molecule, so switching within the class reproduces the risk. Avoiding the whole class, rather than substituting another agent, matters far more here than for infection related switching. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Biologic Therapy Safety)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Biologic Therapy Safety

options.rationale: Biologic therapy does raise the risk of tuberculosis and other opportunistic infection, so infection deserves consideration, but she is afebrile with a normal C-reactive protein, a negative pre-treatment screening test and a three week progressive course. The clinical syndrome localises to two separate white matter sites rather than to a mass or meningitic process. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Biologic Therapy Safety)
source_refs: Australian Rheumatology Association: Biologic Therapy Safety

explanation.summary: Microcytic anaemia has three common causes, iron deficiency, thalassaemia trait and anaemia of chronic disease, and distinguishing them prevents both unnecessary endoscopy and inappropriate long-term iron therapy. Several indices help: thalassaemia trait produces a mean corpuscular volume that is disproportionately low for the degree of anaemia, a red cell count that is normal or raised rather than reduced, and a normal red cell distribution width, whereas iron deficiency raises the distribution width and lowers the red cell count. The Mentzer index, mean corpuscular volume divided by red cell count, below 13 favours thalassaemia trait and above 13 favours iron deficiency, though it is a guide rather than a rule. Confirmation is by haemoglobin electrophoresis with chromatography, where a raised haemoglobin A2 establishes beta thalassaemia trait; alpha thalassaemia trait gives normal electrophoresis and needs genetic testing. Identification matters most for reproductive counselling, since two carriers risk a child with transfusion dependent disease, and iron deficiency should be corrected first because it can falsely lower haemoglobin A2.
key_points: A very low mean corpuscular volume with a raised red cell count and normal distribution width suggests thalassaemia trait
A normal ferritin and no response to 6 months of adherent oral iron argues strongly against iron deficiency
Haemoglobin electrophoresis with chromatography confirms beta thalassaemia trait through a raised haemoglobin A2
Alpha thalassaemia trait has normal electrophoresis and requires genetic testing to confirm
Diagnosis matters mainly for partner testing and reproductive counselling
explanation.pearls: Correct any coexisting iron deficiency before requesting electrophoresis, because iron deficiency lowers haemoglobin A2 and can mask beta thalassaemia trait on the very test used to diagnose it.

sources.label: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Thalassaemia clinical practice resources
Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency clinical update

options.rationale: A very low mean corpuscular volume with a raised red cell count, a normal red cell distribution width and a normal ferritin that has not responded to 6 months of iron is the pattern of a thalassaemia trait rather than iron deficiency, and Mediterranean ancestry with an untreated anaemic parent supports it. Electrophoresis with chromatography quantifies haemoglobin A2 and F, which confirms beta thalassaemia trait and allows partner testing before she conceives. (Source: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Thalassaemia clinical practice resources)
source_refs: Haematology Society of Australia and New Zealand: Thalassaemia clinical practice resources

options.rationale: Parenteral iron is the right answer for genuine iron deficiency with intolerance or malabsorption of oral iron, but her ferritin and transferrin saturation are both normal, so further iron risks overload without benefit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology)

Endoscopic investigation is driven by proven iron deficiency, particularly in men and postmenopausal women, and her iron stores are demonstrably adequate, so the procedures would be investigating a deficiency she does not have. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Iron deficiency clinical update

options.rationale: Alternate day dosing genuinely improves absorption by avoiding the hepcidin rise that follows a dose, but changing the salt or the schedule cannot help when iron stores are already replete. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology)

Reducing menstrual loss is appropriate where heavy bleeding is causing deficiency, but three pads a day for 4 days is not heavy, and her iron studies confirm that loss is not the problem. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Haematology)

explanation.summary: Carcinoid syndrome arises when a neuroendocrine tumour releases serotonin and other vasoactive mediators into the systemic circulation, which for a midgut primary generally requires liver metastases, since the liver would otherwise clear the mediators from portal blood. The clinical picture combines dry flushing, secretory diarrhoea that persists with fasting, and in a minority bronchospasm, alongside hepatomegaly from metastatic disease. Carcinoid heart disease affects the right side of the heart because the mediators are inactivated in the pulmonary circulation, producing tricuspid regurgitation and pulmonary stenosis from fibrous endocardial plaques, and it is a major determinant of prognosis. Screening is by 24 hour urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid with dietary restriction, followed by cross-sectional imaging and functional imaging with a gallium-68 labelled somatostatin analogue. Somatostatin analogues control symptoms and slow tumour growth, and every patient needs a plan for carcinoid crisis, which can be precipitated by anaesthesia, surgery or tumour manipulation.
key_points: Dry flushing without sweating plus secretory diarrhoea and weight loss should raise carcinoid syndrome
Systemic symptoms from a midgut primary generally imply liver metastases, since the liver otherwise clears mediators
Carcinoid heart disease affects the right heart because mediators are inactivated in the lungs
Urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid requires dietary restriction of serotonin-rich foods to be interpretable
Chromogranin A is falsely elevated by proton pump inhibitors, which must be withheld before testing
explanation.pearls: Cover any anaesthetic, biopsy or interventional procedure in a patient with carcinoid syndrome with an octreotide infusion, because tumour manipulation can precipitate a carcinoid crisis with profound vasodilatory shock that does not respond to catecholamines.

sources.label: Australasian Neuroendocrine Tumour Society: Guidelines for neuroendocrine tumours

options.rationale: Mast cell activation and mastocytosis produce flushing, but they characteristically cause itch, urticaria and hypotension, and the tricuspid regurgitation and hepatomegaly here point to a different process. (Source: Australasian Neuroendocrine Tumour Society: Guidelines for neuroendocrine tumours)
source_refs: Australasian Neuroendocrine Tumour Society: Guidelines for neuroendocrine tumours

options.rationale: Chromogranin A is a useful neuroendocrine tumour marker, but proton pump inhibitors raise it substantially through hypergastrinaemia, so a level taken without withholding the drug for about 2 weeks is uninterpretable. The limitation here is drug interference, not the marker's biology. (Source: Australasian Neuroendocrine Tumour Society: Guidelines for neuroendocrine tumours)
source_refs: Australasian Neuroendocrine Tumour Society: Guidelines for neuroendocrine tumours

options.rationale: Catecholamine excess causes episodic headache, palpitations, sweating and hypertension, and flushing in phaeochromocytoma is uncommon, with pallor being more typical during a paroxysm. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Vasomotor flushing of menopause is accompanied by sweating and night waking and does not cause diarrhoea, weight loss, hepatomegaly or a right sided murmur, all of which demand another explanation. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Vasomotor symptoms)

Dry flushing without sweating, secretory diarrhoea, weight loss, hepatomegaly and a tricuspid regurgitant murmur together describe carcinoid syndrome with liver metastases and carcinoid heart disease, and urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid is the established screening test for serotonin overproduction. Dietary restriction of serotonin-rich foods such as bananas, avocado, walnuts and pineapple is essential or the result will be falsely raised. (Source: Australasian Neuroendocrine Tumour Society: Guidelines for neuroendocrine tumours)
source_refs: Australasian Neuroendocrine Tumour Society: Guidelines for neuroendocrine tumours

explanation.summary: Cardiac amyloidosis was long regarded as rare but is now recognised as an underdiagnosed cause of heart failure with preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction in older adults, particularly the wild-type transthyretin form. The diagnostic clue that should prompt suspicion is a mismatch between marked increase in wall thickness on echocardiography and low or normal QRS voltages on the electrocardiogram, which is the opposite of what hypertensive or hypertrophic disease produces. Extracardiac clues accumulate over years before the cardiac presentation: bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar spinal stenosis and biceps tendon rupture all reflect amyloid deposition and commonly precede heart failure by 5 to 10 years. Intolerance of angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors and beta blockers, autonomic features and a persistently elevated troponin without an acute pattern are further pointers. The diagnostic algorithm is sequential and its order matters, since bone scintigraphy uptake cannot be interpreted as transthyretin disease until a monoclonal protein has been excluded, and disease-modifying therapy such as tafamidis is now available for transthyretin cardiomyopathy.
key_points: Increased wall thickness with low electrocardiographic voltages is the mismatch that suggests infiltration
Apical sparing on longitudinal strain is a characteristic echocardiographic pattern
Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome and lumbar spinal stenosis often precede the cardiac presentation by years
Exclude a plasma cell disorder with free light chains and electrophoresis before interpreting bone scintigraphy
Standard heart failure drugs are often poorly tolerated because the stiff ventricle is preload and rate dependent
explanation.pearls: Digoxin and calcium channel blockers bind avidly to amyloid fibrils and can cause toxicity at ordinary serum concentrations, so both are generally avoided once cardiac amyloidosis is suspected.

sources.label: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on cardiac amyloidosis

options.rationale: A troponin that is persistently elevated without any rise or fall reflects chronic myocardial injury rather than an acute coronary syndrome, and angiography carries contrast nephropathy risk in a man with impaired renal function and no ischaemic history. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on cardiac amyloidosis)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on cardiac amyloidosis

options.rationale: Standard heart failure therapy is characteristically poorly tolerated in infiltrative disease, because a stiff restricted ventricle depends on rate and preload, and reflexively re-challenging with a beta blocker repeats the hypotension that already occurred. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on cardiac amyloidosis)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on cardiac amyloidosis

options.rationale: Increased wall thickness with paradoxically low electrocardiographic voltages, apical sparing on strain, a history of bilateral carpal tunnel release and intolerance of standard heart failure drugs together describe cardiac amyloidosis. The diagnostic pathway begins by excluding a plasma cell disorder with free light chains and electrophoresis, since a positive result mandates a different workup, and only then does a grade 2 or 3 bone scintigraphy uptake establish transthyretin amyloidosis without biopsy. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on cardiac amyloidosis)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on cardiac amyloidosis

options.rationale: Endomyocardial biopsy remains the reference standard but is reserved for cases where non-invasive testing is equivocal or a plasma cell disorder is present, since the combination of negative light chains and strong bone scintigraphy uptake is sufficient for diagnosis. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on cardiac amyloidosis)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on cardiac amyloidosis

options.rationale: Functional ischaemia testing addresses a diagnosis the history does not support and would be poorly tolerated in a man with symptomatic postural hypotension and decompensated heart failure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Acute intermittent porphyria results from partial deficiency of porphobilinogen deaminase in the haem synthesis pathway, and attacks are precipitated when demand for haem synthesis rises, classically through oestrogens, cytochrome P450 inducing drugs, fasting, alcohol, infection and stress.
